questions.question: Meridian is designing its first internal phishing simulation. HR proposes docking bonuses for employees who click; the security team disagrees. To genuinely reduce the bank's phishing susceptibility over time, what should the program's standard response to a failed simulation be?

options.A: Immediate, brief remedial training delivered to the person who clicked.
options.B: Recording the click in aggregate program metrics that steer next quarter's training content.
options.C: A formal written warning placed in the employee's personnel file.
options.D: A follow-up simulated phish sent within thirty days to verify the lesson held.

questions.explanation: A simulation is a teaching instrument, and its highest-value moment is the seconds after the click, when the lesson is concrete and personal: short, immediate remedial training (A) converts the failure into learning while preserving the behavior the program needs most: people voluntarily reporting real clicks fast. B is genuinely good practice (aggregate click metrics should steer the curriculum) but it operates at program level and a quarter later, giving the person who clicked nothing at the teachable moment; B is the right answer when the question asks how to measure and evolve the program itself. C formalizes fear, exactly as HR proposed: once a failed simulation carries personnel-file consequences, self-reporting a genuine mistake becomes self-incrimination, and detection loses its best early-warning source. An unreported real compromise is how TechSafe's stolen credential stayed useful for two weeks; escalating consequences belong only with repeated, willful policy violations. D is also real practice, since re-testing verifies that learning stuck, but it measures before it remediates: without training first, the retest simply re-samples the same gap, so it is the right follow-up a month after remedial training, not the standard response to the click. Measure simulations by reporting rates as much as click rates. A program that drives mistakes underground is training the workforce to hide incidents.

questions.question: Meridian's consultants report that SOC analysts had stopped escalating vendor anomalies partly because leadership had, for years, treated security spending as pure cost and questioned each escalation's business justification. Which explanation BEST captures why the fix must start at the executive level?

options.A: Staff read real priorities from what leadership funds and reinforces, so culture flows downward.
options.B: Formal revisions to the bank's risk appetite for vendor incidents require board-level approval.
options.C: Executive sponsorship is required to fund the SOC tooling and staffing that make escalations sustainable.
options.D: Escalation procedures are policy documents, and policy approval authority rests at the executive level.

questions.explanation: The analysts' silence was learned: years of leadership signaling that escalations were an expensive nuisance taught the SOC that raising vendor anomalies was career friction, and staff read real priorities from what the top funds, praises, and tolerates. Culture flows downward (A), which is why 'tone at the top' is a governance concept rather than an HR slogan. B is true as far as it goes (risk appetite is set and revised at board level) but the analysts were not applying a documented appetite; they were reading informal signals, so revising the paper threshold changes nothing until the signals change; B wins where an explicit appetite statement genuinely set the escalation bar too high. C is also true, since durable SOC funding does ride on executive sponsorship, but resources address capacity, and the consultants' finding describes incentive: analysts who had the means to escalate and had learned not to; C wins when the barrier is workload or tooling rather than culture. D leans on the real policy hierarchy, and policies do carry executive approval, but escalation procedures are operational documents the SOC's own leadership can change tomorrow, and a perfect procedure under discouraging leadership still produces no escalations. Sustained security behavior follows leadership's demonstrated priorities: fix the incentives at the top, or every downstream process fix decays back to the old culture.

questions.question: Meridian is rebuilding its training program and must allocate content across very different audiences: tellers who face card skimmers at branch ATMs, SOC analysts who face triage decisions, and vendor technicians who face credential phishing. Which training design principle BEST fits this situation?

options.A: Gamification, using competition and rewards to drive higher completion rates.
options.B: Role-based training, tailoring content to the risks each job actually encounters.
options.C: Microlearning, splitting one shared curriculum into short modules on a recurring schedule.
options.D: Computer-based training, delivering a single standardized course to every employee.

questions.explanation: The stem describes three audiences with three disjoint threat surfaces, so the design problem is targeting: a teller needs to spot a skimmer overlay, an analyst needs triage judgment, a technician needs phishing resistance, and role-based training (B) is the principle that maps content to each job's actual risks. The breach itself showed what mismatched training costs: TechSafe staff untrained on targeted phishing, SOC staff untrained on vendor-activity verification. A addresses motivation, not relevance; a gamified course on the wrong risks is an engaging waste, though gamification layers well on top of role-based content. C addresses format and retention; short recurring modules are a fine delivery vehicle, but 'one shared curriculum' keeps the core defect of everyone studying material mostly aimed at someone else. D optimizes delivery cost and consistency while explicitly standardizing content, the exact opposite of what three disjoint risk profiles require. Decide what each role must learn before deciding how to deliver it. Engagement and format choices cannot rescue mistargeted content.

questions.question: Two years into Meridian's rebuilt awareness program, annual quiz pass rates run at 98 percent, yet a red team's pretext phone calls still talk staff into disclosing internal details. The steering committee is debating what the program's true measure of success should be. Which outcome should the committee adopt?

options.A: A year-over-year reduction in confirmed security incidents attributed to human error across the bank.
options.B: Higher average scores on the security knowledge assessment administered each year.
options.C: Durable change in daily behavior, such as verifying and reporting suspicious requests.
options.D: A falling click rate measured across the quarterly internal phishing simulation campaigns.

questions.explanation: The stem is the argument: knowledge metrics are maxed out while a phone pretext still works, so the program is succeeding at everything except its purpose. Awareness programs exist to change what people do under pressure (pausing, verifying, reporting), and durable behavioral change (C) is the only measure that would have caught the gap the red team found. A is a genuinely attractive outcome measure, since fewer human-error incidents is what the board ultimately wants, but it is lagging and confounded: attack volume, detection changes, and luck all move it, so it cannot tell the committee what the program itself achieved this year; A is the right evidence for long-horizon program value, not for steering. B measures recall in a quiz context; the 98 percent pass rate co-existing with successful pretexting is the textbook divergence between knowing and doing. D is behavioral and worth tracking, but it watches one channel and one failure mode: click rates on email simulations say nothing about the phone pretexts that actually succeeded, and a falling click rate can reflect recognizable lures as easily as real vigilance; D is the right leading indicator for email susceptibility specifically. Grade awareness programs on behavior under realistic conditions and across channels. Completion counts, quiz scores, and single-channel click rates are proxies, and all can look perfect while the program fails.

questions.question: Meridian's assessment calendar lists a quarterly exercise in which testers send deceptive emails to staff and measure who divulges credentials, alongside separate network scans and exploit-based tests. An auditor asks how the email exercise should be categorized in the assessment inventory. What is the correct classification?

options.A: A vulnerability assessment, since it enumerates weaknesses without exploiting them.
options.B: A penetration test, since testers actively attempt to gain unauthorized access.
options.C: A risk control self-assessment, since business units evaluate their own exposure.
options.D: A social engineering assessment, since it measures human susceptibility to manipulation.

questions.explanation: Classify an assessment by what it measures: this exercise probes whether people can be manipulated into surrendering credentials, which is the definition of a social engineering assessment (D), the same category as the pretext that opened the TechSafe breach, which is why Meridian tests it separately and quarterly. A fails on the target and the method: vulnerability assessments enumerate technical flaws via scanning and configuration review, and this exercise exploits rather than enumerates. B is the close call, and the tiebreaker is scope: penetration tests attempt unauthorized access through technical attack paths, and a full-scope pentest may include phishing as one technique, but a standalone email campaign measuring click and disclosure rates is categorized by its human target, not by the fact that testers are adversarial. C removes the testers entirely: a risk control self-assessment is a business unit judging its own controls in a workshop, with no simulated attack involved. Name assessments by target and method, people versus systems and enumeration versus exploitation, and the inventory classifies itself.

questions.question: Meridian's CISO wants security represented inside business units like vendor management, where risk decisions, such as trusting TechSafe's claimed controls, were being made without security input. A security champion program is proposed. What is the mechanism by which champions would have helped?

options.A: Champions form an elite response team that takes over incidents from the SOC.
options.B: Champions reward colleagues who report the highest number of security incidents.
options.C: Champions serve as the single approved contact point for all press inquiries.
options.D: Champions embed security perspective in each unit's decisions and raise concerns early.

questions.explanation: A champion program works by placement: trained advocates sitting inside each business unit, carrying security thinking into decisions the CISO's office never sees (D). A champion inside vendor management is the person who asks 'have we actually verified TechSafe's MFA?' at contract time, the question that, unasked, cost $2.5 million. The value is early influence at the point of decision, plus a trusted path for concerns to travel upward before they become incidents. A confuses champions with a CSIRT; champions are embedded generalists doing prevention and advocacy, not a response unit, and pulling incident handling away from the SOC would fragment response. B warps the idea into a perverse incentive: rewarding incident volume invites over-reporting and gaming, where champions should be improving decisions so fewer incidents occur. C describes crisis communications, a role the incident response plan assigns to corporate communications precisely so it stays controlled.

questions.question: During the investigation, a certified ISC2 member on TechSafe's staff admitted routinely sharing his VPN password with colleagues to speed up maintenance work. An ethics complaint is filed, and the review board must decide which canon the conduct MOST directly violated. Which canon should it cite?

options.A: Protect society, the common good, necessary public trust and confidence, and the infrastructure.
options.B: Act honorably, honestly, justly, responsibly, and legally.
options.C: Provide diligent and competent service to principals.
options.D: Advance and protect the profession.

questions.explanation: Ask to whom the breached duty was owed: the technician's employer and its client, his principals, were entitled to professional-grade service, and routinely sharing credentials that guard a bank's infrastructure is a basic competence failure in the service he was engaged to provide (C). The conduct was not deceit or self-dealing; it was substandard professional practice, and that is the canon addressed to it. A is the defensible runner-up, since the sloppiness ultimately endangered the public, but the tiebreaker is 'MOST directly': societal harm arrived downstream through the breach, while the duty the sharing itself violated was owed to his principals; A leads when conduct threatens the public directly, such as concealing an active danger. B targets dishonesty and illegality; he hid nothing and broke no law, he cut a corner. D concerns the profession's collective standing, cited for conduct like falsifying credentials that discredits the certification itself. When several canons brush against the same conduct, cite the one whose protected party the act most directly wronged.

stimuli.title: Meridian: the Ridgeline acquisition
stimuli.text: Meridian Financial Services, a regional bank of 2,400 staff, is buying Ridgeline Savings, a 40-branch thrift with its own core banking platform and a customer analytics contract with a processor in Bangalore. The deal signs in six weeks. Ridgeline has never had a CISO, and its board minutes record one penetration test, in 2021. Meridian's board has told the CISO that security must not delay the closing. The examiner will review the combined entity nine months after close. Ridgeline's analytics contract renews automatically thirty days after any change of control.

profile.organization: Meridian Financial Services · acquiring Ridgeline Savings, 40 branches
profile.regime: GLBA · state breach notification · examination nine months after close
profile.environment: Two core banking platforms · Ridgeline analytics processor in Bangalore
profile.state: Six weeks to signing, no security due diligence performed

stimuli.title: Meridian: the document set
stimuli.text: Meridian's new CISO inherits a document set that grew by accident. There is a thirty-page information security policy last approved in 2019, four standards that contradict it on password length, a wiki of procedures written by whoever last did the task, and a recommended practices page nobody can say is binding. The board approved the policy; nobody can say who approved the standards. Meanwhile two branch regions are merging and 300 staff are changing roles, and the awareness program still teaches a threat catalog written before the bank used any cloud service at all.

profile.regime: GLBA · PCI DSS · state banking examination
profile.environment: Policy approved 2019 · four conflicting standards · procedures on a wiki
profile.state: 300 staff changing roles during a branch-region merger

stimuli.title: A maintenance vendor with standing access
stimuli.text: Meridian Financial Services outsources maintenance of its 1,200 ATMs to a firm that holds a standing VPN account into the fleet. Attackers phished one of that firm's technicians, used the stolen username and password, and were not challenged for a second factor. Meridian's own security policy was strict, its contract with the firm carried security requirements, and nobody ever checked whether the firm met them. At the board review a director asks why the bank's risk program should cover an outside company at all. The CISO has to answer that, and then say what changes.

profile.organization: Meridian Financial Services · regional bank, 2,400 staff
profile.regime: PCI DSS · GLBA · state breach notification
profile.environment: 1,200 ATMs · maintenance outsourced · vendor VPN into the fleet
profile.state: Intrusion confirmed, source traced to the vendor

stimuli.title: Rebuilding how vendors are assessed
stimuli.text: Cordell Trust is rebuilding the way it assesses suppliers. Forty firms hold some form of network access, several with standing remote sessions into payment systems, and the contracts all carry a right-to-audit clause that nobody has ever invoked. One supplier will hold permanent remote access to a cash machine fleet. Another has agreed in contract to run annual security awareness training for its staff, and the vendor manager wants to know how the bank can be confident that actually happens. The risk committee also wants a defensible cadence for reviewing what each supplier can reach.

profile.environment: Forty suppliers with network access · right-to-audit clauses never used

stimuli.title: An alert that sat for a fortnight
stimuli.text: Harborline Bank's security operations center receives about four thousand alerts a day, fewer than one percent of which turn out to be actionable, and morale is poor. One alert read only 'Unusual Remote Desktop Activity' on a payment server at three in the morning. A Tier 1 analyst could not tell whether it was scheduled supplier maintenance, logged it as exactly that, and the intrusion behind it ran for fourteen days. The CISO wants the underlying problem fixed rather than masked, and the detection engineering team wants alerts that survive triage.

profile.environment: 4,000 alerts a day · under 1% actionable · supplier VPN into payment systems
profile.state: Intrusion ran fourteen days before anyone looked

stimuli.title: Cutting the dwell time
stimuli.text: Pinemark Bank's response team has confirmed that malware is live across its ATM fleet and that the attackers can still reach it through the management server. The intrusion arrived on a supplier's VPN account and ran unnoticed for two weeks, partly because the bank assumed the supplier was watching that connection while the supplier assumed the bank was. The bank is evaluating an orchestration platform and wants to know what automation would have changed. It is also adding continuous monitoring over supplier sessions so a repeat would surface quickly.

profile.environment: Supplier VPN · SOAR platform under evaluation · malware live on the fleet
profile.state: Attackers still reaching the fleet through the management server

stimuli.title: What the review found afterwards
stimuli.text: Meridian Financial Services is running its lessons-learned review. Before the breach the incident response plan had never been rehearsed against a supplier-compromise scenario. Monitoring of the supplier's connection fell between two organizations, each assuming the other was doing it. The bank said nothing publicly until police connected overnight cash-outs to its machines, by which point 50,000 customers' card details were in criminal hands. The security operations lead wants a capability that would catch a valid account behaving unlike itself, since no signature would ever have fired on a legitimate login.

profile.regime: GLBA · state breach notification · PCI DSS
profile.environment: Response plan never rehearsed against a supplier compromise

stimuli.title: A business impact analysis that missed the fleet
stimuli.text: Ashfield Building Society rated a single cash machine as a medium-impact asset, and let the machine network as a whole inherit that rating. Every one of those machines is administered through one management server. After a compromise that reached the entire fleet at once, an analyst is arguing the rating was wrong and the impact analysis is being redone. Policy required a risk assessment 'at least annually', and the review is also establishing what should have triggered one between cycles. The risk register entry for the incident has to record the threat, the weakness and the relationship between them.

profile.organization: Ashfield Building Society · 400 branches and machines
profile.environment: One management server administers every machine · annual risk assessment cycle
profile.state: Impact analysis being redone after a fleet-wide compromise

stimuli.title: Putting numbers in front of the board
stimuli.text: Calder Insurance lost two and a half million dollars to a single incident, and threat intelligence suggests a similar attack could succeed roughly once every five years. The board wants the loss expressed in the quantitative model it already uses, and it wants to know what the recovery position looks like. The company holds a cyber insurance policy and has filed a claim; the insurer's investigators have learned that the operations team dismissed fourteen days of alerts and that a control the company's own policy required was never enforced. Executives had treated recent clean audit reports as proof of security.

profile.organization: Calder Insurance · claims and payments operations
profile.environment: Cyber insurance policy in force · quantitative risk model
profile.state: Board report being prepared after a $2.5m loss

stimuli.title: One server, twelve hundred machines
stimuli.text: Every one of Meridian Financial Services' 1,200 cash machines is administered through a single management server, and the forensic team is mapping each stage of the attack that reached it against a defense chosen for that stage. Investigators also established that the supplier's technicians all shared one set of VPN credentials, so the bank cannot establish which technician was phished or tie any session to a person. The malware did two things once installed: it dispensed cash on command, and it silently recorded card details from live transactions.

profile.environment: 1,200 machines administered through one server · shared supplier credentials
profile.state: Forensic mapping of the attack complete

stimuli.title: What the regulator and the card brands want
stimuli.text: Northgate Bank's acquirer has confirmed that a breach involved a PCI DSS Requirement 8 violation: no second authentication factor on remote access into the cardholder data environment. The remediation plan has to cite the authority under which that factor was already required before the breach. The bank's assessor has separately recommended network segmentation before next year's assessment, and the incoming CISO is writing the charter for a rebuilt security governance program and must state what the program is fundamentally for. Staff had stopped raising concerns because leadership treated security spending as pure cost.

profile.organization: Northgate Bank · card acquiring and issuing
profile.regime: PCI DSS · FFIEC · card brand rules
profile.environment: Cardholder data environment not segmented · assessment due next year
profile.state: Acquirer has confirmed a Requirement 8 violation

stimuli.title: The negligence claim
stimuli.text: Customers harmed by card fraud have filed a negligence claim against Meridian Financial Services, and defense counsel is briefing executives before discovery. The plaintiffs argue the bank failed the standard of due care. Counsel must be clear on what that standard actually demands and on what the plaintiffs will have to establish. In parallel the bank's lawyers are rebuilding the supplier relationship and must decide where enforceable security obligations belong: mandatory second-factor authentication, monitoring duties, penalties. An ethics question also sits open, about whether the bank should have disclosed promptly or waited for the investigation and the quarter to close.

profile.organization: Meridian Financial Services · legal and vendor management
profile.environment: Master service agreement under renegotiation · discovery pending
profile.state: Customers harmed by card fraud have filed suit

stimuli.title: Rebuilding the governance around it
stimuli.text: Rowan Federal Credit Union is rebuilding its security governance after a supplier's controls were trusted rather than verified. Risk decisions of that kind were being taken inside business units with no security input, and a security champion program has been proposed to change that. The board is also asking why meeting the regulator's requirements should be treated as a starting position rather than a finishing one. Separately, a certified member of a supplier's staff has admitted routinely sharing a password with colleagues to speed up work, and an ethics complaint has been filed. Training is being redesigned for very different audiences.

profile.environment: Security has no representation in business unit decisions

stimuli.title: Measuring whether the training works
stimuli.text: Two years into a rebuilt awareness program, Lowell Savings Bank sees annual quiz pass rates of 98 percent, yet a red team's pretext phone calls still talk staff into disclosing internal details. The steering committee is debating what the program's true measure of success should be. The bank is also designing its first internal phishing simulation, and human resources has proposed docking the bonuses of anyone who clicks. An auditor reviewing the assessment calendar wants the quarterly deceptive-email exercise correctly categorized alongside the network scans and exploit-based tests, and the supplier ecosystem gets one awareness investment this year.

profile.environment: Annual quiz pass rate 98% · quarterly phishing simulation · red team on retainer
profile.state: Two years into a rebuilt awareness program

questionsV2.question: The board has said security must not delay the closing. Which contribution to the acquisition process is the BEST use of the CISO's remaining six weeks?

options.A: Withhold approval of the transaction until Ridgeline's controls match Meridian's.
options.B: Defer the security review until after close, when Meridian controls the systems.
options.C: Complete a full control assessment of Ridgeline before the six weeks expire.
options.D: Quantify Ridgeline's security risk so the board can price it into the deal.

questionsV2.explanation: An acquisition is a risk transfer with a price attached, and the only lever available before signing is the price. A number the board can put next to the purchase price is worth more than an objection it will overrule. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SA-4 Acquisition Process requires security and privacy requirements to be included in the contract for the thing being acquired, and PM-30 Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy sets the organization-wide approach behind it. NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 (upd 1) Section 3.1 treats acquisition as the moment when a supplier's posture becomes the acquirer's exposure. A is not the decision-maker's, because the board owns the transaction and the CISO informs it. B is wrong phase: after close the risk is owned, the price is fixed and the leverage is gone. C is wrong scope, since six weeks buys material findings rather than a complete assessment, and demanding the impossible is how security gets left out of the next deal. Price the risk instead of blocking the deal.
questionsV2.recallLine: The board will not let security delay a closing. What is the best use of six weeks?

optionsShort.C: Full control assessment in six weeks

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: Who decides whether a transaction proceeds when the risk is judged unacceptable?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What work genuinely does belong to the integration period rather than to due diligence?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What would the CISO scope if the deal timetable were nine months instead of six weeks?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-4 Acquisition Process; PM-30 Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy
NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 (upd 1) | Section 3.1 C-SCRM in Acquisition

questionsV2.question: Ridgeline's analytics contract renews automatically thirty days after any change of control. Which action MOST reduces the risk Meridian inherits with it?

options.A: Add the processor to Meridian's vendor register with an annual review.
options.B: Use the change-of-control window to renegotiate security terms before renewal.
options.C: Require the processor to complete Meridian's standard security questionnaire.
options.D: Obtain the processor's most recent third-party audit report from Ridgeline.

questionsV2.explanation: A supplier contract is easiest to change at the one moment it is open, and this one is open for thirty days and then shut for a term nobody at Meridian negotiated. Everything else on the list can be done in month four; only B expires. NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 (upd 1) Section 3.1 places supply-chain requirements in the acquisition and contracting activity for exactly this reason, and NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SR-3 Supply Chain Controls and Processes, SR-5 Acquisition Strategies, Tools, and Methods and SA-9 External System Services are where the requirements land. Note that the copy of SP 800-161 Rev 1 in circulation carries a NIST notice superseding it with the Rev 1 errata update, which renumbers nothing. A is wrong phase, a steady-state process applied to a moment that closes. C is a correct action but not the first one, evidence gathering while the leverage expires. D is the right control for a different problem, describing the processor's controls without changing Meridian's position. Move while the door is open.
questionsV2.recallLine: An inherited vendor contract auto-renews in thirty days. What most reduces the inherited risk?

optionsShort.A: Add to vendor register, annual review
optionsShort.B: Renegotiate terms in the open window

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: How should this processor be governed once its contract terms are settled?

C.label: correct but not first
C.wouldAnswer: How does Meridian assess a supplier whose contract is not about to renew?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: What evidence should Meridian collect to judge whether the processor's controls are adequate?

sources: NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 (upd 1) | Section 3.1 C-SCRM in Acquisition
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SR-3 Supply Chain Controls and Processes; SR-5 Acquisition Strategies, Tools, and Methods; SA-9 External System Services

questionsV2.question: The analytics dataset includes EU residents who bank at two Ridgeline branches, and the processor is in Bangalore. Which requirement applies MOST directly to that flow?

options.A: The data must be encrypted in transit and at rest throughout the processing chain.
options.B: The processor must be named in Meridian's incident response plan as a notification party.
options.C: The transfer needs an adequacy decision, appropriate safeguards, or a stated derogation.
options.D: The dataset must be reduced to the minimum fields the analytics contract requires.

questionsV2.explanation: Personal data leaving the European Economic Area needs a lawful basis for the transfer itself, separate from any basis for processing it. Chapter V of the General Data Protection Regulation, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, states the general principle at Article 44, adequacy decisions for a destination country at Article 45, appropriate safeguards including standard contractual clauses and binding corporate rules at Article 46, and the narrow derogations at Article 49. Onward transfers must not undermine the protection. On the control side, NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-12 Information Location and SA-9(5) External System Services | Processing, Storage, and Service Location are how an organization knows and restricts where its data physically sits. A is the right control for a different problem: encryption protects the data and does not make the transfer lawful. B is wrong scope, an incident-handling arrangement rather than a transfer basis. D is a correct action but not the first one, since minimisation is a genuine obligation that reduces exposure without supplying a basis. Lawfulness first, then protection.
questionsV2.recallLine: An offshore processor handles EU residents' data. Which requirement applies most directly to the transfer?

optionsShort.A: Encrypt in transit and at rest
optionsShort.B: Name the processor in the IR plan

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What protects the dataset against interception or theft along the processing chain?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: What must be arranged so a processor's breach reaches Meridian's responders quickly?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: What principle limits how much personal data a processor should receive at all?

sources: EU GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) | Chapter V, Articles 44, 45, 46 and 49
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-12 Information Location; SA-9(5) Processing, Storage, and Service Location

questionsV2.question: At the examination nine months after close, the examiner asks how Meridian satisfied itself about Ridgeline. Which pair of facts BEST evidences due diligence and due care?

options.A: The pre-close risk assessment, and the assessments run on Ridgeline's systems since close.
options.B: The signed purchase agreement, and the security clauses Meridian wrote into it.
options.C: Ridgeline's 2021 penetration test, and Meridian's remediation plan for its findings.
options.D: Meridian's own examination record, and the policy set now applied to both entities.

questionsV2.explanation: The pair is a sequence, not a synonym. Due diligence is the investigation made before a commitment; due care is the continuing exercise of oversight after it, and an examiner asking about both wants evidence from each side of the closing date. Only A supplies both. NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 (upd 1) Section 3.1 describes the pre-contract investigation, and NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SR-6 Supplier Assessments and Reviews carries the ongoing half. Worth saying plainly: no NIST document defines the due care and due diligence pair, which is a legal liability concept rather than a controls concept, so an answer that leans on a control number alone has missed the question. B is wrong scope, evidencing what was agreed rather than what was investigated or overseen. C is wrong phase, a four-year-old test that predates the transaction and records Ridgeline's activity, not Meridian's. D is the right control for a different problem, describing Meridian's own posture. Show the before and the after.
questionsV2.recallLine: An examiner asks how the acquirer satisfied itself about the acquired bank. Which pair evidences it?

optionsShort.B: Purchase agreement and its security clauses
optionsShort.C: Ridgeline's 2021 test and a remediation plan
optionsShort.D: Meridian's own record and unified policy

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: What shows that Meridian secured contractual protection in the transaction?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: What did Ridgeline itself do about assurance before it was acquired?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: What demonstrates that the combined entity now operates under one governance regime?

sources: NIST SP 800-161 Rev 1 (upd 1) | Section 3.1 C-SCRM in Acquisition
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SR-6 Supplier Assessments and Reviews
No NIST source defines due care / due diligence; recorded as a legal-liability concept

questionsV2.question: Two standards specify different minimum password lengths and both cite the same policy. Which action BEST resolves the conflict at its source?

options.A: Assign one owner to approve every standard, and reissue the two under that authority.
options.B: Adopt the stricter of the two lengths and update the weaker standard to match it.
options.C: Move the requirement into the policy so that the board's approval settles it.
options.D: Publish a guideline recommending the stricter length until the standards are rewritten.

questionsV2.explanation: Two standards contradict each other because two people were allowed to issue standards, and no choice between the two numbers changes that. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 makes the point structurally: every control family opens with a Policy and Procedures control, AC-1, AT-1, AU-1 and so on through SR-1, each requiring a documented policy, dissemination to defined roles, a designated official to manage its development and review, and review and update on a defined frequency and after defined events. NIST CSF 2.0 states the same in GV.PO-01 and GV.PO-02. Note that the policy, standard, procedure and guideline hierarchy itself, and the mandatory versus discretionary distinction, is CISSP-canon rather than NIST text. B is symptom not cause, resolving this contradiction and leaving the process that made it. C is wrong scope, pushing a parameter into a document meant to outlive parameters. D is the right control for a different problem, because a guideline is discretionary and cannot settle a mandatory requirement. Fix the authority, not the number.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two standards contradict each other on a parameter. What resolves the conflict at its source?

optionsShort.C: Move the number into the policy

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: What should the reissued standard say once a single owner has been appointed?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What belongs in a policy rather than in a standard beneath it?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which instrument is right for advice that teams may reasonably decline to follow?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | the '-1' Policy and Procedures control in every family (AC-1 through SR-1)
NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | GV.PO-01, GV.PO-02
NIST SP 800-18 Rev 1 | Section 3, plan development and structure

questionsV2.question: A director asks why the security plan classifies controls one way and the risk report another. Which explanation is MOST accurate?

options.A: The plan uses the catalog's families because they are mandatory; the report's categories are optional.
options.B: The two are the same taxonomy under different names, so either may be used interchangeably.
options.C: The plan groups controls by family, while the report groups them by the function they serve.
options.D: The report's categories replaced the families when the bank adopted the newer framework.

questionsV2.explanation: These are two axes over the same controls, not two competing lists, and a director who understands that stops asking which one is right. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 Chapter 2 organizes controls into twenty families and characterizes each by implementation responsibility, organization or system, and by whether it is a base control or an enhancement. It never classifies a control as preventive, detective or corrective. That functional taxonomy, together with deterrent, directive and compensating, is CISSP-canon and appears in no NIST publication. The one near-member is the compensating control, which lives in NIST SP 800-53B Chapter 2 as tailoring guidance rather than as a class of control. A is symptom not cause, asserting a status difference where both are descriptions of the same set. B is wrong scope, collapsing two organizing axes into one. D is wrong phase, implying a supersession that never happened. Know which axis a question is asking about.
questionsV2.recallLine: Why does one document group controls by family and another by preventive or detective function?

optionsShort.C: One groups by family, one by function

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: Which control set is a US federal system actually obliged to implement?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: When can two classification schemes be treated as interchangeable for reporting?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What did change between Revision 4 and Revision 5 of the control catalog?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | Chapter 2, control structure, families and implementation responsibility
NIST SP 800-53B | Chapter 2, compensating controls in tailoring guidance
The preventive/detective/corrective taxonomy has no NIST source and is attributed to CISSP-canon material

questionsV2.question: Three hundred staff are changing roles as two branch regions merge. Which control MOST directly addresses the risk that creates?

options.A: Requiring every transferring employee to re-sign the acceptable use agreement.
options.B: Reviewing and revising each transferring employee's access to match the new role.
options.C: Disabling each transferring employee's account for the day the move takes effect.
options.D: Requiring managers to certify their team's access at the end of each quarter.

questionsV2.explanation: A transfer adds rights and almost never subtracts them, so 300 transfers produce 300 people holding two jobs' worth of access and one job's worth of need. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PS-5 Personnel Transfer is the control written for this: review and confirm the ongoing operational need for current logical and physical access authorizations when individuals are reassigned or transferred, initiate the resulting transfer or reassignment actions within a defined period, and modify access authorization as needed. PS-4 Personnel Termination handles the leavers and AC-2 Account Management the accounts themselves. A is the right control for a different problem, reaffirming the rules of behavior while the entitlements ride along untouched. C is symptom not cause, an interruption rather than a revision, and the account comes back exactly as it was. D is detective when preventive is asked, finding accumulated access one quarter after it accumulated. Revise at the moment of the move.
questionsV2.recallLine: Three hundred staff change roles in a merger. Which control most directly addresses the risk?

optionsShort.B: Review and revise access to the new role
optionsShort.C: Disable the account for the move day

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: How does the bank refresh each employee's acknowledgement of the rules of behavior?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does the bank prevent access being used during an unsupervised handover window?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: How does the bank catch entitlements that accumulated despite the transfer process?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PS-5 Personnel Transfer; PS-4 Personnel Termination; AC-2 Account Management

questionsV2.question: The awareness program still teaches a threat catalog written before the bank used any cloud service. Which change BEST fixes the underlying problem?

options.A: Add a cloud module to this year's curriculum and reissue the threat catalog.
options.B: Replace the annual course with quarterly phishing simulations for all staff.
options.C: Have each business unit write the module that covers its own systems and threats.
options.D: Schedule a content review on a set cadence and after defined trigger events.

questionsV2.explanation: The content is stale because nothing in the program has a date on which it expires, and adding one module leaves the same gap ready to reopen next year. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AT-2 Literacy Training and Awareness requires literacy training and awareness content to be updated on an organization-defined frequency and following organization-defined events, which is precisely the cadence-plus-trigger arrangement the option describes, and AT-3 Role-Based Training carries the same obligation for role-specific material. Note the Revision 5 title: AT-2 was called Security Awareness Training in Revision 4, so older material names it differently. NIST CSF 2.0 places the same idea under PR.AT. A is symptom not cause, patching this year's gap by the same means that produced it. B is the right control for a different problem, measuring susceptibility rather than refreshing content. C is not the decision-maker's, distributing authorship without establishing when anything gets reviewed. Give the content an expiry date.
questionsV2.recallLine: Awareness content predates the technology it should cover. What fixes the underlying problem?

optionsShort.A: Add a cloud module this year
optionsShort.C: Each unit writes its own module
optionsShort.D: Review on a cadence and on triggers

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: What should this year's curriculum include once a review cadence exists?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How does the bank measure whether awareness training is changing behavior?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: How can role-specific content stay accurate for systems the central team does not run?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AT-2 Literacy Training and Awareness (renamed from Rev 4 Security Awareness Training); AT-3 Role-Based Training
NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | PR.AT Awareness and Training

questionsV2.question: Meridian's wire-transfer system records the name of the officer who approved each payment. During a control walkthrough the auditor discovers that an administrator can edit those records afterwards, and that nothing in the system marks a record as having been changed. Which security objective does the gap MOST directly undermine?

options.A: Confidentiality, because the record can be read by staff who did not approve it.
options.B: Integrity, because the record can be altered and the alteration cannot be shown.
options.C: Availability, because the record cannot be relied on when the examiner needs it.
options.D: Authenticity, because the record no longer proves who was at the console.

questionsV2.explanation: The loss the stem describes is silent modification, and modification is integrity in either framing a candidate might be carrying. This is a place where the two framings differ and the difference is worth knowing. FIPS 199, Section 3, quoting 44 U.S.C. 3542, defines exactly three security objectives, and its integrity definition reads as guarding against improper information modification or destruction, and includes ensuring information non-repudiation and authenticity. The five pillars that add authenticity and non-repudiation as peers of confidentiality, integrity and availability are ISC2's framing, not FIPS 199's, so never cite FIPS 199 as the source of a five-pillar claim. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 supplies the control-level split where it is needed: SI-7 for information integrity, AU-9 Protection of Audit Information, and AU-10 Non-repudiation. A is wrong scope, describing reading where the stem describes editing. C is symptom not cause, naming the examiner's difficulty rather than the mechanism. D is the right control for a different problem, and under FIPS 199 it is inside integrity anyway. Read the loss, then name the objective.
questionsV2.recallLine: An approval record can be silently edited by an administrator. Which objective is undermined?

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Which objective is lost when payment approvals can be read by staff with no business need?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: Which objective is lost when the record cannot be produced at all during an examination?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: Which objective is at stake when an attacker signs a message as somebody else?

sources: FIPS 199 | Section 3, Security Objectives (three objectives; integrity includes non-repudiation and authenticity)
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SI-7 Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity; AU-9 Protection of Audit Information; AU-10 Non-repudiation

questionsV2.question: A Meridian customer disputes a $180,000 transfer, saying she never authorized it. The bank's records show a successful sign-in from a machine she has used before, and an approval recorded at 11:04. The dispute is heading for court, and Meridian is redesigning the approval step so a future dispute can be settled. Which control contributes MOST directly to that goal?

options.A: Recording the session with full packet capture retained for one year.
options.B: Requiring a one-time code sent to the customer's registered phone.
options.C: Restricting large transfers to sessions from previously seen devices.
options.D: Signing the instruction with a private key that the customer alone holds.

questionsV2.explanation: Non-repudiation needs evidence that only one party could have produced, and that rules out anything the bank could have produced too. A signature made with a key the customer alone holds leaves Meridian outside the set of possible authors, which is what makes the evidence survive a dispute. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-10 Non-repudiation is the control: protect against an individual falsely denying having performed an action, and provide the means to determine whether the individual took it. SC-23 Session Authenticity covers the related but distinct property of the session itself. FIPS 199 folds non-repudiation and authenticity into its integrity objective, so AU-10 and SC-23 are where the two are addressed separately. A is wrong scope, capturing what crossed the wire rather than who originated it. B is the right control for a different problem, since a code Meridian generated and Meridian verified is evidence Meridian could have manufactured. C is symptom not cause, lowering the chance of an unfamiliar actor without producing evidence. Ask who else could have made this.
questionsV2.recallLine: Which control best keeps a customer from credibly denying that they authorized a transfer?

optionsShort.A: Full packet capture kept a year
optionsShort.B: One-time code to the registered phone
optionsShort.D: Sign with a key only the customer holds

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: How does the bank reconstruct exactly what was transmitted during a disputed session?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How does the bank raise confidence that the person signing in is the account holder?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does the bank reduce the chance of a transfer being made from an unfamiliar machine?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-10 Non-repudiation; SC-23 Session Authenticity
FIPS 199 | Section 3 (non-repudiation and authenticity sit inside the integrity objective)

questionsV2.question: Meridian's fraud team wants to embed a vendor's scoring library in an internal tool that will run inside the bank and never be distributed to customers. The library's license requires derivative works to be published under the same terms, and the team has already written three weeks of code against it. Which action should the CISO require BEFORE the build proceeds?

options.A: A legal review of whether the tool becomes a derivative work under that license.
options.B: A software composition scan listing every third-party component the tool will include.
options.C: A vendor attestation that the library contains no known security vulnerabilities.
options.D: An entry in the software inventory recording the library and its license terms.

questionsV2.explanation: The question the license raises is whether shipping this tool obliges Meridian to publish its own fraud-scoring logic, and that is a legal determination about a specific set of facts, not a security judgement. Getting it wrong is expensive in a way that a vulnerability is not. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-10 Software Usage Restrictions is the control that requires software and associated documentation to be used in accordance with contract agreements and copyright law, and that license quantities be tracked and controlled. Be honest about the limits of that citation: copyright, patent, trademark and trade-secret law are the governing sources for intellectual property generally, none of them is a NIST publication, and CM-10 covers only the software-license compliance sliver. B is a correct action but not the first one, an inventory of components that does not answer the question the license poses. C is the right control for a different problem, a vulnerability question wearing license clothing. D is wrong phase, recording a decision that has not been made. Ask a lawyer a legal question.
questionsV2.recallLine: A library's license requires derivative works to be published. What should be required before building?

B.label: correct but not first
B.wouldAnswer: How does the team discover which third-party components and licenses it has taken on?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: What assurance is wanted about the security of a third-party component being adopted?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What record should exist once the library has been approved for use?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-10 Software Usage Restrictions
Intellectual property statute is the governing source and is not a NIST publication; CM-10 covers only software-license compliance

questionsV2.question: Meridian is opening a development office abroad and plans to give its engineers there access to the source of its hardware security module integration, which implements the bank's key wrapping. The office opens in nine weeks, the engineers are already hired, and the program manager has asked the CISO to confirm that nothing stops the repository being opened to them. Which requirement should be checked FIRST?

options.A: That the source is stored in a repository located outside the European Union.
options.B: That the engineers sign confidentiality agreements enforceable in the destination country.
options.C: That the encryption technology is authorized for export to that destination.
options.D: That the bank's data classification policy permits source code to leave the country.

questionsV2.explanation: Cryptographic software and the technology behind it are export-controlled goods, and a regulation is not something an internal policy or a contract can satisfy. The Export Administration Regulations, 15 CFR Parts 730 to 774, control the export of encryption software and technology through the Commerce Control List, principally Category 5 Part 2, Information Security; defense articles including some cryptographic and satellite technology sit instead under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations, 22 CFR Parts 120 to 130. One trap worth carrying into the exam: releasing controlled technology to a foreign person is treated as an export even when the release happens inside the United States, so hiring rather than offshoring does not avoid the question. Neither regulation is a NIST publication, and the specific answer depends on the Commerce Control List entry and any license exception for the item, which has to be checked rather than assumed. A is wrong scope, a data-residency question. B is the right control for a different problem, since confidentiality is not authorization. D is not the decision-maker's, because internal classification cannot authorize what a regulation controls. Regulation outranks policy.
questionsV2.recallLine: Engineers abroad will get source implementing key wrapping. Which requirement is checked first?

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: Where must personal data of EU residents be stored or transferred under Chapter V of the GDPR?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How does the bank protect trade secrets shared with staff in another jurisdiction?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: What internal rule governs which classification of material may be shared with an overseas office?

sources: Export Administration Regulations | 15 CFR Parts 730 to 774, Commerce Control List Category 5 Part 2 (Information Security)
ITAR | 22 CFR Parts 120 to 130, US Munitions List
Neither is a NIST publication; the standards map records this outline item as unmapped

questionsV2.question: Meridian suspects a branch manager of falsifying loan documents. Internal audit has pulled six files and the pattern is consistent, but the general counsel has not yet decided whether this ends in dismissal, in a civil claim to recover the losses, or in a referral to prosecutors. The security team has been asked to collect the manager's mailbox and workstation. Which approach to evidence is MOST appropriate now?

options.A: Handle it as an administrative matter and re-collect to a higher standard if it escalates.
options.B: Collect and document to the standard the strictest possible outcome would demand.
options.C: Refer it to law enforcement now so that the collection standard becomes theirs to set.
options.D: Collect what the disciplinary policy requires and no more until counsel advises.

questionsV2.explanation: Evidence cannot be re-collected to a higher standard later, because the thing that would have to be redone is the handling, and the handling has already happened. When the destination is unknown, the only safe assumption is the most demanding one. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3, Section 2.3, makes this a preparation obligation: decide in advance what will be collected, by whom and to what standard, because those decisions cannot be made credibly after the fact. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9 Protection of Audit Information, AU-11 Audit Record Retention and IR-4(12) Incident Handling | Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis are the supporting controls. Be aware of the sourcing limit: no held standard enumerates the administrative, criminal, civil and regulatory investigation types by their burdens of proof, which is a matter of legal procedure, and NIST SP 800-86 is the guide that covers forensic technique. A is wrong phase. C is not the decision-maker's, and it forecloses the administrative route. D is wrong scope, sizing collection to the least demanding outcome. Collect for the worst case you might end up in.
questionsV2.recallLine: The investigation may end in dismissal or prosecution. What standard should evidence be collected to?

optionsShort.C: Refer to police and let them set it
optionsShort.D: Only what the disciplinary policy needs

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: How should evidence be handled when the matter is definitively internal and will stay internal?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: Who decides whether a suspected crime is reported to law enforcement, and when?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What is the minimum an employer must document to support a disciplinary decision?

sources: NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 | Section 2.3 Incident Response Policies, Processes, and Procedures
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9; AU-11 Audit Record Retention; IR-4(12) Malicious Code and Forensic Analysis
No held standard enumerates investigation types by burden of proof; SP 800-86 is the forensic-technique source

questionsV2.question: Meridian is filling three vacancies this month: a branch teller, a database administrator who will hold production access to the core banking platform, and a contract cleaner who will have unescorted after-hours access to the head office floors. HR has asked the CISO what background checking each of the three requires. Which approach to screening is MOST defensible?

options.A: Screen all three identically so the process cannot be challenged as inconsistent.
options.B: Screen the two employees to the bank's standard and exempt the contractor's employer.
options.C: Screen according to seniority, with the most senior of the three screened most thoroughly.
options.D: Assign each position a risk designation first, then screen against that designation.

questionsV2.explanation: Screening depth should follow what the position can reach, and that is a property of the job rather than of its title or its pay grade. The sequence is explicit in NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PS-2 Position Risk Designation: assign a risk designation to all organizational positions, establish screening criteria for individuals filling those positions, and review and update the designations on a defined frequency. PS-3 Personnel Screening then screens individuals prior to authorizing access and rescreens according to defined conditions, and PS-7 External Personnel Security extends the requirement to third-party personnel; note that PS-7 was titled Third-Party Personnel Security in Revision 4. A is wrong scope, one depth for a whole population regardless of reach. B is not the decision-maker's, delegating a decision to a supplier without setting the requirement, and the cleaner has the building at 3 a.m. C is symptom not cause, since seniority is a proxy for access and here it points away from the risk. Designate the position, then screen the person.
questionsV2.recallLine: Three roles with very different access are being hired. Which screening approach is most defensible?

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: What screening applies to a population of positions that genuinely share one risk designation?

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: How should a contractor's own screening obligations be established and evidenced?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: When does seniority happen to be a reasonable proxy for the access a role carries?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PS-2 Position Risk Designation; PS-3 Personnel Screening
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PS-7 External Personnel Security (renamed from Rev 4 Third-Party Personnel Security)

questionsV2.question: Meridian's risk register lists phishing as a risk, scored with a likelihood of 4 and an impact of 5 by the operations manager who entered it. Preparing the quarterly report for the risk committee, an analyst argues that the entry cannot be assessed as written and should be sent back. What is the MOST accurate objection?

options.A: It names a threat without naming the vulnerability it would exploit or the asset harmed.
options.B: It names a control failure rather than a risk, so the entry belongs in the findings log.
options.C: It uses a qualitative likelihood where the register's own method requires a quantitative one.
options.D: It has no named owner, so nobody can be asked to reduce the likelihood it records.

questionsV2.explanation: Phishing is an event somebody might attempt, not a risk Meridian holds. A risk statement has to say what the attempt would exploit and what harm follows, because until it does, neither likelihood nor impact has anything to attach to and neither number is defensible. NIST SP 800-30 Rev 1, Chapter 3, models risk as a threat source initiating a threat event that exploits a vulnerability, producing an adverse impact, and its Appendix D and Appendix E supply the threat source and threat event taxonomies a register is populated from. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 RA-3 Risk Assessment is the control obligation behind it. B is wrong scope, recategorizing the entry rather than completing it. C is symptom not cause, a formatting objection that leaves an unassessable statement unassessable in a different notation. D is a correct action but not the first one, since ownership is genuinely required and does not make the entry assessable. Write the sentence with all its parts in it.
questionsV2.recallLine: A risk register entry reads only 'phishing' with a likelihood and impact. What is wrong with it?

optionsShort.B: It is a control failure, not a risk

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: Where should an entry go that records a control that was found not to be operating?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: What objection applies when a well-formed risk is scored in the wrong notation?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: What is missing when a well-formed risk sits in the register with nobody accountable for it?

sources: NIST SP 800-30 Rev 1 | Chapter 3; Appendix D Threat Sources; Appendix E Threat Events
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | RA-3 Risk Assessment

questionsV2.question: Meridian's internal audit team has assessed the vendor access policy that was rewritten after the TechSafe breach, and its report says only that the policy is in place and has been distributed. The CISO returns the report, saying that is a statement about a document rather than an assessment result. What is MOST clearly missing?

options.A: The date the policy was approved and the official who approved it.
options.B: The number of vendors that the policy currently applies to.
options.C: Evidence that the policy operated as intended over the period examined.
options.D: A comparison of the policy against the equivalent control in the framework.

questionsV2.explanation: A control assessment answers three questions and existence is only the first of them. NIST SP 800-53A Rev 5 structures its assessment procedures around determining whether controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended and producing the desired outcome with respect to meeting the security and privacy requirements, and it applies the examine, interview and test methods to reach that determination. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-2 Control Assessments is the obligation to run them and to produce the assessment report. A policy that exists and is ignored fails the second and third questions, which is the situation Meridian was in with TechSafe's contract. A is wrong scope, provenance of the document rather than its operation. B is the right control for a different problem, the scope of applicability. D is wrong phase, a design comparison that precedes the question of whether the thing works. Existence is not effectiveness.
questionsV2.recallLine: An assessor reports that a policy is in place. What is missing from that as an assessment result?

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: What should the document register hold about each approved policy?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What does the CISO need to know to judge how much of the vendor estate a policy reaches?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What check confirms that the bank's policy set covers each control the framework requires?

sources: NIST SP 800-53A Rev 5 | assessment procedures and the examine, interview and test methods
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-2 Control Assessments

questionsV2.question: Meridian assesses its controls once a year, in March, and the last assessment reported no significant findings. Since then the bank has migrated two applications to a cloud provider and has changed its vendor access model twice. At the December board meeting a director asks why an annual control assessment is not enough. Which answer BEST states the case for continuous monitoring?

options.A: It reduces the cost of assessment by spreading the same work across the year.
options.B: It keeps the authorization decision informed by the system's current state.
options.C: It satisfies the examiner's expectation of testing more often than annually.
options.D: It detects attacks sooner, because the monitoring is running all the time.

questionsV2.explanation: The point of monitoring controls continuously is that the decision to run the system rests on information that is still true. An annual assessment authorizes a system as it was in March and says nothing about the seven changes made since. NIST SP 800-137 defines information security continuous monitoring as maintaining ongoing awareness of information security, vulnerabilities and threats to support organizational risk management decisions, and NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 makes the consequence explicit in its MONITOR step, where ongoing authorization replaces a point-in-time decision. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-7 Continuous Monitoring is the control. A is symptom not cause, a cost argument that would hold even if the information were worthless. C is not the decision-maker's, making the examiner the reason rather than the risk. D is the right control for a different problem, and it is the seductive answer: security control monitoring and intrusion detection are different activities, and SI-4 System Monitoring is where the second one lives. Monitor so the decision stays current.
questionsV2.recallLine: Why is an annual control assessment not sufficient? State the case for continuous monitoring.

optionsShort.A: Spreads assessment cost across the year

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: What is a secondary benefit of moving from one annual push to a steady assessment cadence?

C.label: not the decision-maker's
C.wouldAnswer: What does the bank tell an examiner who asks how often controls are tested?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: What does SI-4 System Monitoring provide that a control assessment does not?

sources: NIST SP 800-137 | information security continuous monitoring definition and process
NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 | Chapter 3, MONITOR step and ongoing authorization
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-7 Continuous Monitoring; SI-4 System Monitoring

questionsV2.question: An outside adviser reports Meridian at Tier 2 and recommends reaching Tier 4 within two years, at a cost the adviser has already estimated. The CISO has been asked to endorse the recommendation before it goes to the board in January, and nobody has yet written down what the bank needs. Which response BEST reflects how the framework is meant to be used?

options.A: Adopt Tier 4 as the target and budget the program against the gap it implies.
options.B: Ask the consultant to reassess each business unit so the bank holds a Tier for each.
options.C: Benchmark the reported Tier against peer banks before accepting it as a target.
options.D: Set a target profile from the bank's own risk appetite, then read the Tier against it.

questionsV2.explanation: The framework's own improvement mechanism is the gap between a Current Profile and a Target Profile, and the Target Profile is derived from what the organization needs rather than from the top of a scale. NIST CSF 2.0, published as NIST CSWP 29, defines four Tiers, Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable and Adaptive, describing the rigor of an organization's cybersecurity risk governance and risk management practices, and it is explicit that the Tiers are not maturity levels even though they are routinely used as if they were. A Tier read against a target the bank chose is diagnostic; a Tier treated as a score is a budget request. A is a correct action but not the first one, because a target is needed and taking the highest available as the target skips the step that decides what the bank requires. B is the right control for a different problem, resolution rather than direction. C is symptom not cause, since a peer's posture does not establish this bank's risk appetite. Decide what you need, then measure the distance.
questionsV2.recallLine: A consultant reports a Tier and recommends a higher one. How should the framework actually be used?

optionsShort.A: Adopt the top Tier as the target
optionsShort.D: Set a target profile, read the Tier against it

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: What does the program do once a target has been chosen and the gap is understood?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How does a large organization get useful resolution when its units differ widely in practice?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does a board judge whether its posture is unusual for an institution of its size?

sources: NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | the four Tiers and the Organizational Profile mechanism
NIST states the Tiers are not maturity levels; CMM and CMMI are not NIST publications

questionsV2.question: Meridian is examined against banking supervisory expectations, processes card data under the card brand rules, and reports to a European parent whose group audit committee asks for ISO alignment. The CISO has one control assessment team and a calendar that already carries three audits. Which approach to frameworks is MOST workable?

options.A: Pick one framework as the system of record and map the others onto it.
options.B: Run each framework separately so that every audience receives its own artefacts.
options.C: Adopt whichever framework has the most controls, so the others are covered by it.
options.D: Let each business unit choose the framework that its own regulator names.

questionsV2.explanation: Three audiences do not require three programs; they require one set of controls and three views of it, because a control assessed once can be reported many times but a control assessed three ways is assessed badly three times. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 PM-9 Risk Management Strategy requires a single organization-wide strategy, and NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 Chapter 3 gives the RMF steps that a mapped control set resolves into, with NIST SP 800-53B supplying the baselines. NIST CSF 2.0's Organizational Profile is itself designed as the mapping surface. Two of the frameworks named here, ISO/IEC 27005 and COBIT, are paywalled, so a reader should expect to buy them rather than follow a link. B is the right control for a different problem, satisfying audiences at the cost of one coherent risk picture. C is symptom not cause, because control count is not coverage and each framework's set is selected against its own scope. D is wrong scope, fragmenting a strategy the organization is meant to hold once. One system of record, many reports.
questionsV2.recallLine: Three audiences demand three frameworks. What is the most workable way to organize the program?

optionsShort.A: One system of record, map the rest
optionsShort.C: Adopt the one with most controls
optionsShort.D: Each unit picks its regulator's framework

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: How does the bank produce artefacts in the exact format each audience expects?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: When is a larger control set genuinely the right starting point for a program?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: How should a unit with a unique regulatory obligation extend the common control set?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PM-9 Risk Management Strategy
NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 | Chapter 3, the RMF steps; NIST SP 800-53B baselines
NIST CSF 2.0 (NIST CSWP 29) | Organizational Profile as a mapping mechanism
Neither ISO/IEC 27005 nor COBIT is held here; both are paywalled

questionsV2.question: Meridian's team is modeling threats to a new mobile deposit feature before any code is written. The session opens with each engineer listing attacks they have read about in the last year, and after forty minutes the list is long, nobody has opened the design, and the architect is losing patience. Which starting point would make the model MOST useful?

options.A: The vulnerabilities the last penetration test found in the existing mobile application.
options.B: The feature's data flows and the trust boundaries that each flow crosses.
options.C: The controls the bank already runs, so that gaps show up against them.
options.D: The threat intelligence feed's current list of campaigns against retail banks.

questionsV2.explanation: A threat model is a model of the system, and a list of remembered attacks is a model of the team. Starting from data flows and trust boundaries forces the exercise to enumerate the places where something crosses from one level of trust to another, which is where attacks land whether or not anyone has read about them. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SA-8 Security and Privacy Engineering Principles names threat modeling in its discussion as the means of identifying use cases, threat agents, attack vectors and patterns, and SA-11(2) Developer Testing and Evaluation | Threat Modeling and Vulnerability Analyses requires it at defined breadth and depth. NIST SP 800-218 PW.1.1 puts risk modeling at design time, before code exists, so the design itself can still change. Note that STRIDE, PASTA and DREAD are named throughout CISSP study material and appear in no NIST publication. A is wrong phase, starting from findings against a system that already exists. C is symptom not cause, modeling the defense rather than the thing defended. D is wrong scope, and a model built from current campaigns expires with them. Model the system, then populate it with threats.
questionsV2.recallLine: A team starts threat modeling from remembered attacks. What starting point makes the model useful?

optionsShort.A: Findings from the last penetration test

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: What should drive remediation planning for the mobile application already in production?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does the bank establish which of its existing controls the new feature can inherit?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What keeps a completed threat model current as adversary behavior changes?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-8 Security and Privacy Engineering Principles; SA-11(2) Threat Modeling and Vulnerability Analyses
NIST SP 800-218 | PW.1.1 risk modeling at design time
STRIDE, PASTA and DREAD appear in no NIST publication and are attributed to CISSP-canon material

questionsV2.question: Which response gives the BEST justification for covering an outside firm in the bank's own risk program?

options.A: Regulators assign legal liability for a breach to whichever party first introduced the exploited weakness.
options.B: Vendor contracts are usually negotiated by procurement without any security review step.
options.C: A connected vendor holds trusted access that lets attackers step past Meridian's perimeter defenses.
options.D: Vendors commonly require administrative privileges, which conflicts with separation of duties.

questionsV2.explanation: Risk follows access, not ownership: because TechSafe held a trusted path into Meridian's network, any compromise of TechSafe was automatically a compromise of Meridian's perimeter. That is why vendors belong inside the bank's own risk program (C), and it is precisely how this breach unfolded. A is wrong on the law and on accountability: the data owner generally remains answerable to regulators and customers regardless of where the attacker entered, so liability cannot be outsourced with the maintenance contract. B describes a real process weakness, but it argues for fixing procurement, not for the principle of enterprise-wide vendor risk coverage; it is a supporting observation, not the justification. D overgeneralizes: many vendors operate with narrowly scoped rights, and separation of duties governs how tasks are split and approved, not vendor connectivity itself; it would be the right answer to a question about structuring vendor roles. Your risk boundary is drawn by who can touch your systems, not by who employs them.

questionsV2.question: An auditor notes the bank assumed the firm ran equivalent controls and never exercised its right to audit. This points MOST directly to a gap in which discipline?

options.A: Business continuity planning for service outages affecting the bank's critical external service providers.
options.B: Supply chain risk management covering the security posture of connected third parties.
options.C: Privacy impact assessment for the systems that process customer card data.
options.D: Internal classification and valuation of the assets in the ATM estate.

questionsV2.explanation: Assuming a vendor's controls instead of verifying them is the defining failure of supply chain risk management (B): the discipline exists precisely so that risk introduced through third parties is identified, assessed, and monitored rather than presumed away. A concerns keeping operations running when a provider becomes unavailable; TechSafe never went down, so continuity planning would not have surfaced a security posture gap. It is the right discipline for a different failure mode. C evaluates how processing affects individuals' privacy; it might have flagged data-handling issues but says nothing about a vendor's authentication hygiene, a legitimate assessment aimed at the wrong subject. D addresses knowing what assets are worth; Meridian's classification of the ATMs was indeed flawed, but that is a separate finding: D answers the question of why the ATM network was under-protected relative to its value, not why vendor assumptions went unverified.
