questions.explanation: Concealing data inside an innocuous carrier file so that the very existence of the message is hidden is steganography, and because pixel-level payloads rarely survive lossy recompression or resizing, transforming every outbound image is the countermeasure that breaks the channel without blocking legitimate mail (D). A misreads the evidence: encryption scrambles content but announces itself. An encrypted blob looks like noise, whereas these files still displayed as valid holiday photos; entropy quarantine is the right response when exfiltration uses encrypted archives. B names the wrong covert medium, since timing channels signal through when packets are sent, not through file contents, so interval normalization would leave the pixels untouched. C inverts the technology: watermarking embeds marks to assert ownership or trace copies, openly or invisibly, and stripping metadata removes EXIF fields rather than payloads woven into image data. Steganography defeats inspection by hiding existence, so effective countermeasures alter the carrier (recompress, resize, transcode) instead of searching the content.

questions.question: An assessment discovers ATM malware signaling captured card numbers to a nearby receiver by modulating the fascia status LED, a component never intended to carry data. Which term BEST describes this exfiltration route?

options.A: A covert channel, deliberately communicating in violation of the security policy.
options.B: A side channel, leaking secrets through unintended physical emissions of the hardware.
options.C: An out-of-band channel, an alternate interface authorized for management traffic.
options.D: A backdoor, an undocumented function granting remote administrative access.

questions.explanation: Two cooperating parties, the implanted malware sending and the nearby receiver listening, are moving information over a path the security policy never authorized for communication, which is the definition of a covert channel, here a storage-style channel built on an LED (A). B is the near-miss that decides this question: a side channel has no cooperating sender, because the attacker passively observes leakage the device produces naturally, as with power-analysis attacks on the EPP; the moment malware deliberately modulates the emission, the channel is covert, not side. C fails on authorization: out-of-band channels such as a dedicated management network are sanctioned alternate paths, and this one is illicit by design. D describes the access method an attacker might have used to plant the malware, not the exfiltration route itself; a backdoor would be the right answer if the finding were a hidden maintenance interface accepting remote commands. Classify leakage by intent: an unwitting device leaks via a side channel, while a willing sender abusing an unintended path creates a covert one.

questions.question: A cryptanalyst evaluating a vendor's proprietary cipher flips a single bit of the plaintext and observes that only the corresponding byte of ciphertext changes, with the rest identical. Which property is missing, and why does its absence matter MOST?

options.A: Collision resistance; two distinct inputs could be found that produce the same output.
options.B: The avalanche effect; localized changes let analysts map ciphertext structure back to plaintext.
options.C: Forward secrecy; a stolen long-term key would expose previously recorded traffic.
options.D: Key-generation entropy; predictable keys would narrow an attacker's search space.

questions.explanation: A strong cipher must exhibit the avalanche effect, a one-bit input change flipping roughly half the output bits, because it is the visible evidence of diffusion; when a change stays localized, ciphertext regions correspond to plaintext regions, and an analyst can recover structure, spot repeated fields, and mount statistical attacks without the key (B). A imports a hash-function requirement: collision resistance matters where distinct inputs must never share an output, as in signatures over digests, and its absence there enables forgery, a different primitive's failure. C concerns key-management architecture rather than cipher internals; it is the property to demand of a protocol whose recorded traffic must survive later key theft, and no block cipher provides it by itself. D is a real and fatal weakness when present, but the test performed here held the key fixed and varied plaintext, so it measured the cipher's mixing, not the randomness of key generation. Diffusion failures show up exactly this way in testing; treat a missing avalanche as proof the cipher leaks structure, and reject it.

questions.question: Field reports show SlimLine service panels being opened with picks and bump keys in under a minute. Replacement locks must resist those attacks and also give the bank an audit trail identifying who opened each panel and when. Which choice BEST meets both requirements?

options.A: High-security pin-tumbler locks with restricted keyways and patent-protected key blanks.
options.B: Warded locks re-keyed uniquely per ATM so that one key opens only a single unit.
options.C: Electronic locks with per-technician credentials and centrally logged opening events.
options.D: Paired wafer locks installed so the panel opens only with two keys turned together.

questions.explanation: Only an electronic lock satisfies both halves of the requirement at once: removing the mechanical keyway defeats picking and bumping outright, and per-person credentials produce the attributable log the bank asked for (C). A is the strong runner-up on the first half, since restricted keyways and quality pin-tumbler designs genuinely resist covert entry, but a mechanical key leaves no record of who used it, so the audit requirement fails; it is the right answer where budget or environment rules out electronics. B improves key management while worsening the attack resistance: warded locks are among the easiest designs to defeat with simple tools, so per-unit keying just means picking each one individually. D adds dual control, which is valuable for cash-loading procedures, yet wafer mechanisms are also readily picked and two anonymous keys still write no audit trail. Read compound requirements as an AND. A control that excels at one clause and silently drops the other is not a partial success but a wrong answer.

questions.question: City planners ask the bank where to site new walk-up ATMs so as to discourage both skimmer installation and robbery, applying crime prevention through environmental design rather than paying for guards. Which recommendation BEST reflects CPTED principles?

options.A: Screen each ATM behind fencing and dense planting so customers enter their PINs shielded from onlookers.
options.B: Move the ATMs into interior corridors reachable only through staffed building entrances.
options.C: Rotate ATM placements every month so criminals cannot learn local traffic patterns.
options.D: Site the ATMs in open, well-lit locations with clear sightlines and steady natural foot traffic.

questions.explanation: CPTED's core levers are natural surveillance, natural access control, and territorial reinforcement: shaping the environment so ordinary people's presence and sightlines make crime feel observable and risky, which is precisely what open, well-lit, well-trafficked siting delivers for both the robber and the skimmer installer who needs unobserved minutes at the fascia (D). A applies a security instinct backwards. Concealment protects PIN privacy at the shoulder-surfing scale, but screening the whole machine creates the hidden workspace attackers want, defeating natural surveillance. B does reduce crime but through staffing and access control by personnel, which the stem explicitly set aside; it is the right answer where a guarded lobby already exists. C confuses environmental design with unpredictability tactics. Moving targets inconvenience customers, break accessibility planning, and offer no surveillance benefit once the new location is found. CPTED asks what the place itself makes easy: design for eyes on the asset, not for hiding it or garrisoning it.

questions.question: A consultancy audits both Nexus Bank and its direct competitor. Management wants access enforcement in which a consultant who opens one bank's engagement files becomes dynamically barred from the competitor's files, based on that access history. Which security model BEST fits this requirement?

options.A: Brewer-Nash, enforcing dynamic conflict-of-interest classes over datasets.
options.B: Bell-LaPadula, enforcing hierarchical confidentiality labels and clearances.
options.C: Clark-Wilson, enforcing well-formed transactions with separation of duties.
options.D: Biba, preventing lower-integrity information from contaminating higher levels.

questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature in the stem is that permissions change as a consequence of the subject's own past reads: access to one competitor's data walls off the other's. That history-dependent, conflict-of-interest behavior is exactly what Brewer-Nash, the Chinese Wall model, was built to formalize (A). B is static by comparison: Bell-LaPadula grants access from fixed clearances and labels, and a Secret-cleared consultant would keep whatever the lattice allows regardless of what they read yesterday; it is the right model for classified hierarchies. C protects how data is modified (certified procedures, duty separation, reconciliations) and has no notion of one dataset excluding another; it fits the question 'how do we keep ledger updates trustworthy?'. D governs the direction of information flow for integrity and likewise never consults access history. When a scenario says permissions depend on what the subject already accessed, the words 'conflict of interest' and 'dynamic' should trigger Brewer-Nash before any of the classic static models.

questions.question: Two of the bank's host gateways must agree on a fresh symmetric session key across an untrusted carrier network. No secret has been pre-shared between them, and the key itself must never travel over the wire. Which mechanism is the MOST direct fit?

options.A: AES in Galois/Counter Mode, negotiated through an initial handshake message.
options.B: Diffie-Hellman key agreement, preferably using ephemeral parameters per session.
options.C: A one-time pad distributed to both gateways during their initial commissioning.
options.D: Kerberos tickets issued to both gateways by the carrier's authentication server.

questions.explanation: The stem lists Diffie-Hellman's defining conditions: no pre-shared secret, an untrusted channel, and a requirement that the key be derived rather than transmitted. Each side combines its private value with the other's public value, and both arrive at the same secret without it ever crossing the wire (B). A names a cipher mode, not an agreement protocol: GCM is what you use the session key for once it exists, and 'negotiated through a handshake' quietly assumes the key-establishment step this question is asking about. C contradicts the stem twice. Commissioning-time distribution is pre-sharing, and pad material equal in length to all future traffic must itself travel securely; a one-time pad answers a question about information-theoretic secrecy with a trusted courier. D outsources trust to the carrier's server, which requires every party to pre-share keys with that KDC, trust the stem never grants, over infrastructure defined as untrusted. 'Agree on a key without sending it, with no prior secret' is the signature of Diffie-Hellman; it establishes keys, while ciphers and modes consume them.

questions.question: During a fraud investigation, an administrator claims a disputed transfer order did not originate from her. The bank demonstrates to the regulator that the order's signature could only have been produced by the private key on her personal smart card. Which security service makes that demonstration possible?

options.A: Confidentiality, because the order traveled through an encrypted channel end to end.
options.B: Integrity, because any alteration of the order after signing would break the signature.
options.C: Authentication, because the session verified her identity when she first logged in.
options.D: Non-repudiation, because the signature is provable to a third party after the fact.

questions.explanation: What the bank needed was evidence that stands up in front of someone else, a regulator, against the signer's own denial, and that is the specific service called non-repudiation: a digital signature binds the order to the sole holder of the private key, so origin cannot be plausibly disclaimed later (D). B is true but answers a narrower claim: the signature does prove the order was not altered, yet the administrator is denying authorship, not alleging tampering; integrity would be the winning service if the dispute were about modification in transit. C also genuinely occurred, but session authentication is evidence between the two communicating parties at that moment. It convinces the server, not a third party reviewing events afterwards, and shared-credential logins can be disputed. A is orthogonal: encryption hides the order from outsiders and proves nothing about who created it. Authentication convinces the counterparty now; non-repudiation convinces a third party later. The private-key signature is what upgrades the first into the second.

questions.question: In the monitoring retrospective, an engineer argues the bank's network intrusion detection should have caught the shim, which operated purely at the physical layer of the internal USB connection. What is the MOST accurate response to this argument?

options.A: Physical-layer tampering inside the chassis is invisible to network monitoring; detection requires hardware integrity controls at the device.
options.B: The network IDS would have observed the shim if its sensor had been placed inline between the ATM and the bank host.
options.C: Enabling deep-packet inspection on the existing sensors would have revealed the injected dispense commands.
options.D: Correlating the carrier's NetFlow records against transaction logs would have exposed the additional device.

questions.explanation: Monitoring can only see traffic that reaches its sensor, and the shim's entire activity (PIN capture and command injection) happened on an internal peripheral bus that never touches the network stack, so no network tool at any placement had visibility. The detectable evidence lives in hardware integrity checks, peripheral authentication failures, or tamper alarms at the device itself (A). B changes the sensor's location but not its blind spot: inline placement sees ATM-to-host traffic, and the fraudulent dispenses were injected downstream of everything that path carries. C deepens inspection of the same wrong stream: DPI parses payloads crossing the network, and the injected commands crossed only a USB cable. D could plausibly flag secondary effects such as cash-balance discrepancies during reconciliation, making it a reasonable fraud-analytics answer, but it detects the theft's accounting shadow, not the device. Before crediting a monitoring control, trace where the malicious traffic actually flows; a sensor on the wrong bus detects nothing, no matter how deeply it inspects.

questions.question: A disgruntled developer at the ATM software vendor embeds a routine that will corrupt the dispenser driver on the first business day after his contract ends. Which classification fits this threat, and which practice is MOST likely to catch it before release?

options.A: A worm, best caught by network anomaly detection as it propagates between systems.
options.B: Ransomware, best caught by monitoring for mass file encryption on the build servers.
options.C: A logic bomb, best caught by peer code review and change control over the build pipeline.
options.D: A rootkit, best caught by comparing shipped boot images and drivers against known-good vendor reference hashes.

questions.explanation: Malicious code that lies dormant until a condition is met, here a date tied to the author's departure, is a logic bomb, and because it does nothing observable until it fires, runtime defenses rarely see it. The realistic catch point is human and procedural: review of source changes and enforced change control expose an unexplained time-conditioned branch before it ships (C). A misclassifies on mechanism, since a worm self-replicates across systems and this routine spreads only by being compiled into the product; network anomaly tools would be the right net for propagation behavior. B pattern-matches the wrong payload. Destruction on a trigger date is sabotage, not extortion, and no mass-encryption signal exists to monitor. D fails on location: rootkits conceal an intruder's presence within a running system, and image-hash comparison verifies shipped binaries against the build, but this code is in the build, so the hashes would match perfectly. Insider code threats defeat integrity checking that trusts the source; the control that works is scrutiny of changes before they become the trusted baseline.

questions.question: Fuzz testing shows the ATM core's USB driver crashes whenever a peripheral sends a malformed descriptor longer than 64 bytes, and the crash overwrites adjacent memory. Which remediation MOST directly addresses the root cause of this finding?

options.A: Deploy endpoint anti-malware on the core, tuned to recognize known USB exploit payloads.
options.B: Validate the length and structure of every descriptor in the driver before processing it.
options.C: Enable data execution prevention so injected code placed in data pages is unable to run.
options.D: Fit locking covers over the core's accessible USB ports to keep rogue devices off the bus.

questions.explanation: The defect is that the driver trusts input from the wire: it copies an attacker-controlled length into a fixed buffer, and everything downstream (crash, overwrite, exploitability) flows from that missing check, so bounds and structure validation at the trust boundary is the root-cause fix (B). C is the strongest wrong answer because it genuinely raises the exploitation bar, but it is a compensating mitigation: the overflow still corrupts memory, the driver still crashes, and techniques like return-oriented programming routinely work around non-executable pages; DEP is the right answer when you cannot change vulnerable code. A is detective and signature-bound. It might flag known payloads, yet the fuzzer just demonstrated the flaw falls to arbitrary malformed input no signature anticipates. D shrinks the attack surface but leaves the trusted path wide open: the EPP and dispenser cables remain on the bus, and the shim incident proved attackers reach exactly those. Fix injection-class findings where untrusted data enters. Validation at the boundary removes the flaw, while DEP, anti-malware, and port locks only argue with its consequences.

questions.question: An engineer proposes that every request from any process to reach the dispenser API must pass through a single small enforcement component that is tamper-proof, impossible to bypass, and small enough to be fully verified. Which classical concept is being applied?

options.A: A security perimeter, drawing the boundary that separates the TCB from the rest of the system.
options.B: An audit subsystem, recording every access decision for later independent review.
options.C: A trusted recovery process, returning the platform to a secure state after any failure.
options.D: A reference monitor, mediating every access by subjects to objects under a defined policy.

questions.explanation: The three demanded properties (tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify) are the textbook requirements of the reference monitor concept, the abstract mediator that checks every subject-to-object access against policy, implemented concretely as a security kernel (D). A describes where trust ends rather than what enforces it: a perimeter delimits the TCB but performs no mediation of individual requests; it is the right term when the question asks what separates trusted from untrusted components. B is a consumer of the mediator's work. Logging decisions supports accountability and forensics, but a recorder that can be bypassed satisfies none of the three properties, and recording is not enforcing. C belongs to a different phase of the security lifecycle entirely, governing how a system fails and restarts without exposing protected state; it would be the right answer for a question about crash behavior in high-assurance designs. When a design demands complete mediation by something verifiable and untamperable, the concept being invoked is the reference monitor. Everything else in the TCB supports it.

questions.question: An auditor finds the fleet-management console stores administrator passwords as unsalted SHA-256 hashes, and notices two administrators who chose the same password have identical stored values. Which risk does this create, and which fix is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Hash collisions; migrate the console from SHA-256 to SHA-3 to restore output uniqueness.
options.B: Key reuse; issue each administrator a distinct symmetric key for encrypting credentials.
options.C: Precomputed-table cracking; add a unique random salt per password and use a slow, iterated hash.
options.D: Pass-the-hash replay; encrypt the stored hash values at rest under the console's TLS private key.

questions.explanation: Unsalted fast hashes fail in exactly the way the auditor observed: identical passwords collapse to identical digests, so one rainbow table or one cracked value breaks every account sharing it. The remedy is a per-user random salt to make every digest unique plus a deliberately slow function such as PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 to price out bulk guessing (C). A misdiagnoses with the scariest-sounding word: a collision is two different inputs hashing alike, whereas these are identical inputs behaving deterministically, and SHA-3 would produce the same problem unsalted; migrating hash families answers a question about a broken algorithm. B applies key-management vocabulary to a storage problem. Password verification needs no per-admin encryption keys, and wrapping hashes in symmetric keys just relocates the secret. D borrows a Windows lateral-movement attack that concerns authenticating with a stolen hash, and encrypting the database under a key stored on the same host protects little once that host falls. For stored passwords the two mandatory words are salted and slow: uniqueness defeats precomputation, cost defeats scale.

questions.question: Card thieves have captured a batch of encrypted PIN blocks and are attempting offline recovery by systematically trying every possible cryptographic key against the ciphertext. Which factor MOST determines how long this attack needs before it succeeds?

options.A: The effective key space of the encryption algorithm protecting the blocks.
options.B: The account lockout threshold configured at the card issuer's host.
options.C: The entropy of the four-digit PIN values the customers selected.
options.D: The collision resistance of the hash function used by the terminals.

questions.explanation: Exhaustive key search runs at the attacker's own pace against captured ciphertext, so its expected duration is governed by how many keys must be tried: the effective key space, which is why 56-bit DES falls in hours while 128-bit AES remains beyond feasible computation (A). B is the classic online/offline confusion: lockout thresholds throttle guesses submitted to a live host, and an attacker holding the ciphertext never talks to the issuer; lockout is the right answer when the scenario is PIN guessing at the terminal. C misidentifies the search target. The thieves are trying keys, not PINs, and once the key is found every PIN in the batch falls at once; PIN entropy would dominate if the attack were guessing PINs through the protocol. D names a property of a primitive the scheme does not use for this purpose, since PIN blocks are reversibly encrypted for translation between hosts; nothing in the scheme hashes them. For any brute-force question, first fix what is being enumerated and where. Offline key search answers only to key space, and no online control touches it.

questions.question: A new battery-powered micro-ATM platform needs asymmetric cryptography for remote key loading, but the processor budget is tight, power draw matters, and certificates must stay small for the slow link. Which algorithm family is MOST appropriate?

options.A: RSA with 4096-bit moduli, buying the security margin of the larger key.
options.B: Triple-DES with frequent rotation, avoiding asymmetric operations altogether.
options.C: Diffie-Hellman over a 1024-bit prime group, minimizing the computation per exchange.
options.D: Elliptic-curve cryptography, matching RSA-grade security at far smaller key sizes.

questions.explanation: Elliptic-curve algorithms deliver equivalent strength to RSA at a fraction of the key length (a 256-bit curve corresponds to roughly a 3072-bit RSA modulus), which translates directly into cheaper computation, lower power draw, and compact certificates, the three constraints the stem names (D). A satisfies security while maximizing every cost the platform must avoid: 4096-bit private-key operations are among the most expensive in common use, and the certificates are correspondingly bulky. B ignores a stated requirement rather than weighing it. The design needs asymmetric key loading precisely because symmetric schemes presuppose the shared secret being established, and rotation does not remove that bootstrap problem; it would be a fair answer for bulk encryption after keys exist. C economizes into known weakness: 1024-bit finite-field groups are within reach of well-resourced precomputation attacks and have been deprecated by standards bodies, so the savings are bought with the security margin itself. Constrained devices are ECC's home ground. Shrink the key and keep the strength; never shrink the strength to keep an old algorithm.

questions.question: Exploit developers demonstrate that a crafted message from a rogue peripheral can place shellcode into the ATM driver's data buffer and then redirect the processor into executing that buffer. Which platform protection MOST directly defeats this specific technique?

options.A: Address space layout randomization, hiding the buffer's location from the exploit.
options.B: Data execution prevention, marking data pages in memory as non-executable.
options.C: Full-disk encryption, protecting the driver binary from tampering at rest.
options.D: Stack canaries, detecting corruption of saved return addresses before they are used.

questions.explanation: The technique's essential step is executing instructions out of a memory region that holds data, and non-executable page protection refuses precisely that: when control transfers into the buffer, the processor faults instead of running the shellcode, regardless of how the redirect was achieved (B). A is a genuine obstacle but a probabilistic one aimed at a different step. Randomization makes the buffer hard to find, yet an attacker with an information leak or a spray strategy recovers the address, and once found the page still executes; ASLR is the right answer when the question targets reliable addressing. C protects the wrong copy at the wrong time: the binary on disk was never modified, and the corruption happens in live memory, where disk encryption has no reach. D watches one specific structure. If the redirect overwrites a function pointer or uses a heap buffer, no canary is disturbed; canaries win when the described technique is smashing a stack return address. Map the mitigation to the exploit step it interrupts: DEP kills execute-from-data itself, while ASLR and canaries only harass the steps that lead there.

questions.question: Nexus Bank subscribes to a vendor-hosted fleet-management application: the vendor operates the servers, operating systems, and application code, while bank staff simply log in to manage the ATMs. Under the cloud shared-responsibility model, which security duty remains MOST squarely with the bank?

options.A: Testing and applying patches to the application platform and middleware serving the management console.
options.B: Hardening the host operating systems running in the vendor's data centers.
options.C: Governing its user accounts, their entitlements, and the data it places in the service.
options.D: Maintaining the hypervisor layer that isolates tenants from one another.

questions.explanation: The arrangement described, consuming a finished application over the network with no visibility into its stack, is SaaS, the model in which the customer's retained duties compress to the two things no provider can own: who may access the tenant, with what privileges, and the classification and handling of the data entrusted to it (C). A sits on the provider's side of the SaaS line, since the customer cannot even see the middleware; platform patching becomes a customer duty only down at IaaS, where the customer builds atop rented infrastructure. B fails the same test one layer lower. OS hardening belongs to the customer in IaaS, but here the vendor runs the operating systems. D is provider territory in every service model; no cloud tenant administers the hypervisor, which is exactly why tenant-isolation assurance is sought through the provider's audits and certifications instead. As the service model climbs from IaaS to SaaS the provider absorbs layer after layer, but identity governance and data accountability never transfer; those stay with the customer in every model.

questions.question: To keep serving customers through carrier outages, the redesigned fleet performs stand-in transaction authorization locally at each ATM and reconciles with the host once connectivity returns. Which security consequence of this edge-computing design should the risk assessment weigh MOST heavily?

options.A: Authorization logic and sensitive data become distributed across many physically exposed endpoints.
options.B: Delayed reconciliation can postpone the detection of duplicate or over-limit withdrawals.
options.C: The management platform must now scale to synchronize state with thousands of units.
options.D: Customers may experience slower transaction responses while the carrier link is down.

questions.explanation: Moving authorization to the edge relocates the crown jewels: decision logic, approval authority, and cached account data now live on thousands of machines standing unattended in public space, the least defensible tier the bank owns, so the compromise of any one unit yields capabilities that previously existed only in the data center (A). B is the strongest competitor and a real, quantifiable exposure, but it is bounded by design, since stand-in limits and reconciliation windows cap the fraud, whereas A is the structural change that creates B and several other exposures besides; B would win if the question asked which fraud scenario stand-in processing enables. C is a genuine engineering cost with no direct security dimension; scalability planning belongs in the architecture review. D is backwards in fact, because local authorization is what keeps responses fast during outages, and customer latency is a service metric, not a risk-register entry. When a design pushes function toward the edge, the first question for the risk register is what new value now sits on the most exposed devices.

questions.question: A bank data warehouse must let lower-clearance staff query a table that also holds rows about covert fraud investigations. The design must conceal even the existence of those rows: a blocked insert at a key must never reveal that a hidden row occupies it. Which database technique MOST directly addresses this inference problem?

options.A: Views that restrict each role to an approved subset of columns and rows.
options.B: Row-level encryption with keys held only by the investigation team.
options.C: Referential integrity constraints enforced across the investigation tables.
options.D: Polyinstantiation, letting rows at different classification levels share one key.

questions.explanation: The scenario is the classic multilevel-database inference attack: a low-cleared user inserts at a key, the insert is rejected because a classified row already sits there, and the rejection itself leaks that something secret exists. Polyinstantiation defeats it by permitting two rows, one at each level, to coexist at the same key, so the low-level insert simply succeeds and reveals nothing (D). A hides content but not existence, which is the failure the stem forbids: a filtered view still cannot let the insert proceed at an occupied key without either lying or leaking. B has the same boundary. Ciphertext in a visible row conceals values while confirming the row is there, and a key conflict still surfaces. C works against the design goal: integrity constraints exist to expose conflicts loudly, which is precisely the signal that must be suppressed. When the secret is that data exists rather than what it says, filtering and encryption are the wrong tools; existence-hiding in multilevel databases is what polyinstantiation is for.

questions.question: Designers of the fleet console need formal rules for how administrator subjects and device objects are securely created and deleted, and how access rights are granted, transferred, and revoked between them. Which security model MOST directly provides this?

options.A: Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman, analyzing whether a given right can ever leak to an unauthorized subject.
options.B: Bell-LaPadula, constraining how information may flow between clearance levels.
options.C: Graham-Denning, defining the primitive operations for managing subjects, objects, and rights.
options.D: Sutherland, addressing inference by constraining permissible information flows.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle the designers describe (create and delete subjects and objects; grant, transfer, and revoke rights) is exactly the set of eight protection rules Graham-Denning formalizes over the access-control matrix; it is the model about administering protection state, independent of any one policy (C). A is its close descendant and the tempting near-miss: Harrison-Ruzzo-Ullman takes a Graham-Denning-style system and asks a different question, whether a right can ever escape to where it should not be, a safety-analysis result famous for its undecidability proof; HRU wins when the stem asks whether rights leakage can be proven impossible. B supplies a specific confidentiality policy and simply has no vocabulary for creating subjects or transferring rights. D is aimed at the inference problem of preventing low-level observations from revealing high-level facts, and likewise never addresses rights administration. Sort the matrix models by their question: Graham-Denning says how to manipulate rights safely, HRU asks whether the rules can leak them, and the flow models say nothing about administration at all.

questions.question: Two independently evaluated PIN-pad products are shortlisted: one certified at EAL4, the other at EAL2. The CISO asks what the higher number actually buys before approving the premium. Which statement is the MOST accurate guidance?

options.A: EAL4 certifies that fewer exploitable vulnerabilities will remain in the product during live operation.
options.B: EAL4 reflects deeper design review and testing rigor on a scale running to EAL7.
options.C: EAL4 doubles the cryptographic strength requirements that were applied at EAL2.
options.D: EAL4 products are approved for classified environments, while EAL2 products are commercial only.

questions.explanation: Evaluation Assurance Levels grade the depth of the evaluation, not the strength of the product: EAL2 is structurally tested, EAL4 is methodically designed, tested, and reviewed, and the scale tops out at EAL7's formally verified design, so the premium buys higher confidence that the product meets its stated security target (B). A voices the misconception the CISO must be warned about. Assurance rigor reduces the likelihood of undiscovered flaws but certifies a process, and EAL4-certified products have shipped with exploitable bugs; no EAL is a vulnerability warranty. C invents a linkage that does not exist: cryptographic strength comes from the algorithms and any FIPS validation, and a product can reach a high EAL with modest cryptography if that is what its security target claims. D imports the retired TCSEC habit of mapping levels to authorized environments; accreditation decisions rest with each scheme and authorizing official, not with the EAL number. Read an EAL as 'how hard did evaluators look', never as 'how strong is it', then check what the security target actually claimed.

questions.question: Phishing simulations show kiosk users readily typing their Windows credentials into a full-screen fake login page. The hardening team wants every user to have a guaranteed way of summoning the genuine login screen that no application-level malware is able to imitate or suppress. Which mechanism BEST provides this?

options.A: A secure attention key that invokes a trusted path directly to the operating system.
options.B: A password manager configured to auto-fill only on the legitimate login screen.
options.C: A login banner warning users against disclosing credentials to unofficial prompts.
options.D: An inactivity timeout that locks the kiosk session after a period of idle use.

questions.explanation: The hardening team needs a route to the real OS that user-mode software can neither fake nor intercept, and that is the secure attention key, the Ctrl+Alt+Del pattern: the keystroke is reserved by the kernel, so pressing it tears down whatever is on screen and yields the authentic secure desktop, a trusted path no fake login page survives (A). B offers real protection in browsers, where fill logic can bind to a verified origin, but a full-screen native fake is pixels, not a URL; the manager has nothing reliable to bind to on a kiosk, and users can still type manually. C is administrative only: a banner instructs the very users the simulation just proved will comply with a convincing fake, and the fake can display its own banner. D limits how long a hijacked or abandoned session stays open, worthwhile hygiene that does nothing to distinguish real login screens from counterfeit ones. Spoofed-login threats are beaten by trusted path, not by training or timers. Give users one reserved gesture that always reaches the kernel.

questions.question: A defense contractor's document system must confine information flow so material moves only upward or laterally within compartments, with each user's access bounded by the highest and lowest classification labels they may touch. Which access control approach is the MOST natural fit?

options.A: Role-based access control, mapping users to permissions through defined job functions.
options.B: Discretionary access control, letting document owners share their files as they judge best.
options.C: Lattice-based access control, assigning each subject upper and lower bounds over labels.
options.D: Rule-based access control, evaluating each request against an ordered list of conditions.

questions.explanation: Bounded flow between ordered labels and compartments is the lattice structure itself: every subject and object sits at a point in a partially ordered set, each pair of labels has a least upper and greatest lower bound, and models like Bell-LaPadula and Biba are enforced over exactly this scaffolding. The stem's 'highest and lowest labels' is the lattice's defining feature (C). A organizes permissions around job function, which suits enterprises well but carries no notion of dominance or flow direction; a role grants what it grants, with no mathematics forcing information upward only. B is the opposite philosophy, since owner discretion is precisely what mandatory flow control exists to remove; an owner could share downward at will. D is generic machinery: firewall-style condition lists can approximate many policies but provide no inherent ordering, so the flow guarantees would live in hand-maintained rules rather than in the model. When a scenario talks about label dominance, compartments, and bounded information flow, the underlying answer is a lattice; the named models are policies riding on it.

questions.question: The cash-loading room keeps suffering tailgating incidents: an authorized courier badges in, and an unauthorized person slips through behind them before the door closes. Which physical control MOST directly defeats this specific behavior?

options.A: A camera covering the doorway, with footage retained for ninety days of review.
options.B: An upgraded reader requiring a PIN in addition to the badge at the door.
options.C: A guard posted to review the door's access log at the end of each shift.
options.D: A mantrap of two interlocked doors that admits only one person at a time.

questions.explanation: Tailgating exploits the interval when an open door admits more bodies than credentials, so the direct counter is a control that physically meters passage: a mantrap's interlocked doors create a holding space in which one person is authenticated before the far door releases, making the piggyback physically impossible rather than merely against the rules (D). A records the violation without resisting it. Footage supports investigation and deters the casual, but the intruder is inside either way; cameras are the right answer for attribution after the fact. B strengthens the authentication of the person who badges anyway, and the tailgater was never authenticating at all; the same open door still admits them. Two-factor at the door answers a stolen-badge scenario. C is doubly detective: the log never saw the tailgater, and end-of-shift review adds hours of delay to a record of an event it cannot contain. Match the control to the exploited mechanism. Tailgating is a throughput problem at the doorway, and only single-person interlocks close it.

questions.question: Regulators reviewing the bank's new fingerprint-enabled ATMs demand that a breach of the biometric database must not hand attackers images of customers' fingerprints. Which property of a well-designed biometric system should the design team cite in response?

options.A: Raw scans are retained, but encrypted under keys lodged with an independent escrow agent.
options.B: Only mathematical templates are stored, from which the original fingerprint image cannot be rebuilt.
options.C: Fingerprint images are hashed with SHA-256 at enrollment and compared by digest thereafter.
options.D: Scans are held solely at the central host rather than on the individual ATM units.

questions.explanation: Well-designed biometric systems never keep the picture: enrollment extracts a template, a mathematical summary of minutiae features, and matching compares fresh templates against it, so a stolen database yields feature vectors rather than reproducible fingerprint images, which is exactly the assurance the regulator asked for (B). A keeps the dangerous artifact and bets everything on key custody. Escrowed keys can be compelled, leaked, or stolen, and the moment they are, full images spill; escrow answers a lawful-recovery requirement, not a data-minimization one. C misapplies a password technique to fuzzy data: two scans of the same finger never match bit-for-bit, so cryptographic digests of images can never be compared successfully; the scheme simply does not function. D changes where the images sit, not whether they exist, and centralization may even raise the stakes by pooling every customer's biometric in one breachable place. Biometric privacy comes from storing derived, non-reversible templates; controls that merely encrypt or relocate raw images leave the irrevocable secret intact.

questions.question: A vendor pitches a proprietary cipher whose strength, it argues, comes from keeping the algorithm itself secret; a competitor offers standard AES with disciplined key management. On which principle should the security architect ground the recommendation between them?

options.A: Defense in depth: deploy both ciphers in layers so each covers the other's weaknesses.
options.B: Security through obscurity: an unpublished algorithm denies attackers the starting point that any practical cryptanalysis requires.
options.C: Kerckhoffs's principle: assume the algorithm is known and let security rest on the key alone.
options.D: Crypto-agility: select whichever cipher will be easiest to swap out in later years.

questions.explanation: Cryptography's foundational design rule is that a system must remain secure even when everything about it except the key is public. That is Kerckhoffs's principle, and it decides this vendor choice cleanly: AES has survived decades of open, worldwide analysis, while the proprietary cipher's secrecy is both its only defense and a guarantee it was never seriously reviewed (C). B is the pitch itself restated, and the reason it fails is practical: algorithms leak through reverse engineering, departing staff, and binary analysis, restoring the 'denied' starting point in full, and unlike a key, a leaked algorithm cannot be rotated. A misuses a sound principle as a tiebreaker dodge. Layering a weak cipher adds complexity and a false sense of margin, and depth was never meant to launder unvetted components into a design. D is a genuine engineering virtue that presupposes the question already answered: agility governs how easily you replace an algorithm, not which algorithm deserves trust today, and it would in fact argue for the standard, widely supported option. Trust ciphers that survive publication, not ciphers that depend on it never happening; secrecy belongs in keys, because keys can be changed.

stimuli.title: Nexus: the platform split
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank is replacing the fleet-management platform that administers its SlimLine terminals. Today it is one Windows server in the bank's own data center. The target design splits it four ways: a browser console for branch staff, an application tier of Linux containers on a shared cluster, event-driven functions at a cloud provider that reconcile cash balances overnight, and the legacy dispenser-control service, which nobody will rewrite and which will run as a guest on the bank's hypervisor. The migration board has ten weeks and no budget for a second cluster. Security must sign off on each tier separately, and the board meets once a month.

profile.organization: Nexus Bank · SlimLine subway ATM fleet
profile.environment: Browser console · shared container cluster · cloud functions · one hypervisor
profile.state: Ten weeks to migrate, four tiers to sign off separately

stimuli.title: Nexus: the SlimLine II program
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank has funded a replacement for its SlimLine subway terminal, the SlimLine II, after an interposer device fitted inside the original captured PINs at dozens of sites. The program board meets monthly and has just approved the architecture. Three decisions are still open: how the security requirements become a concrete control set, how the new dispenser interface will be joined to the existing transaction switch, and how 900 SlimLine units leave service. The bank's examiner has asked for evidence at each gate. Finance wants the retired units sold to a secondary-market refurbisher, which pays considerably more than a recycler does and collects from the branch loading dock.

profile.organization: Nexus Bank · SlimLine II replacement program
profile.environment: 900 SlimLine units in service · new dispenser interface · existing transaction switch
profile.state: Architecture approved, control set not yet chosen

stimuli.title: A device between the pad and the core
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank has recovered small interposer devices from dozens of its SlimLine subway terminals. Each sat on the internal USB bus between the encrypting PIN pad and the Windows core, reading keystrokes and injecting its own traffic. The cash dispenser accepted dispense commands from that unauthenticated device without question. The pad shipped with a compatibility mode enabled that sent the first keystrokes of each PIN in clear text unless an installer opted out. The bank assumes its communication keys will eventually be stolen and wants recorded past sessions to stay unreadable when that happens.

profile.environment: Encrypting pad on an internal USB bus to a Windows core · units in unattended public space
profile.state: Interposer devices recovered from dozens of machines

stimuli.title: What integrity measurement does not reach
stimuli.text: Nexus Bank's board wants to know why the controls it already paid for missed an interposer fitted inside its terminals. Every unit has a trusted platform module and measured boot. The network intrusion detection system watches all terminal traffic. Panel locks were the only barrier between passers-by and the internal bus, and the units stand in public subway space around the clock. Forensic examiners have since recovered a later device that never touched the data lines at all: it inferred PINs from tiny fluctuations in the pad's power draw as each digit was processed.

profile.environment: Trusted platform modules across the fleet · panel locks · network intrusion detection
profile.state: Board asking why existing controls missed it

stimuli.title: Designing the terminal that replaces it
stimuli.text: Calderwood Payments is designing the terminal that will replace its current self-service estate. The proposal treats the large general-purpose core as untrusted and runs all PIN handling inside a small sealed module. Engineers want a fleet in which even a fully compromised core would have no independent ability to dispense cash. They also want architectural assurance that when a customer types a PIN, the keystrokes reach the trusted hardware over a route software on the core cannot intercept or imitate, and that the link between the two carries nothing readable if another device is ever installed on it.

profile.environment: Thin-client design proposed · all PIN handling in a sealed module · untrusted general-purpose core
profile.state: Architecture under review, ten weeks to sign-off

stimuli.title: Buying cryptography that will still be acceptable
stimuli.text: Calderwood Payments is replacing the PIN-block encryption across its estate as part of a payment-industry compliance program, and wants a choice that will remain acceptable as the standards evolve. Procurement is drafting the requirements for replacement pads and wants independent, third-party assurance that the modules physically resist intrusion and erase their keys when the enclosure is breached. It will only buy software whose security functionality has been independently evaluated against a published protection profile. One vendor's pads ship with their protective configuration switched off unless the installer turns it on.

profile.environment: Triple-DES being phased out · replacement pads on tender · protection profile required

stimuli.title: Getting keys into thousands of machines
stimuli.text: Vessel Bank must load initial symmetric keys into thousands of new terminals across untrusted carrier networks, and each terminal has to verify that key-loading messages genuinely come from the bank's host. Once loaded, those keys protect PIN blocks in transit. Thieves have already captured a batch of encrypted PIN blocks and are attempting offline recovery by trying every possible key. A settlement dispute is separately running with a card processor over a batch file each side says the other sent. Thieves also pried a pad out of one machine and carried it off.

profile.environment: Thousands of new terminals · untrusted carrier networks · offline attacks on captured blocks

stimuli.title: Who really sent the instruction
stimuli.text: During a fraud investigation at Vessel Bank an administrator claims a disputed transfer order did not originate from her. The bank can show the order's signature could only have been produced by the private key on her personal smart card, and must explain to the regulator what that demonstrates. Two of the bank's host gateways separately need to agree a fresh session key across an untrusted carrier network with no pre-shared secret, and the key itself must never cross the wire. A data warehouse must let lower-clearance staff query a table that also holds covert investigation records.

profile.organization: Vessel Bank · fraud investigation and data services
profile.environment: Smart cards issued to administrators · warehouse serving cleared and uncleared staff

stimuli.title: Stored passwords and the arithmetic against them
stimuli.text: An auditor at Linden Systems finds the fleet-management console stores administrator passwords as unsalted SHA-256 hashes, and notices two administrators who chose the same password have identical stored values. A cryptanalyst evaluating a vendor's proprietary cipher separately reports that flipping a single bit of plaintext changes only the corresponding byte of ciphertext. A code review of the console's log-encryption routine finds every record encrypted in CBC mode under the same fixed initialization vector, so identical entries produce identical ciphertext. Exploit developers have shown shellcode placed in a driver's data buffer and then executed.

profile.environment: Console passwords stored as unsalted digests · proprietary cipher under evaluation

stimuli.title: Conflicts of interest in a shared consultancy
stimuli.text: Harrow Advisory audits two banks that compete directly with each other, and management wants access enforcement in which a consultant who opens one bank's engagement files becomes dynamically barred from the other's, based on that access history. The same platform must offer kiosk users a guaranteed way to summon the genuine login screen that no application-level malware can imitate or suppress, after phishing simulations showed staff typing credentials into full-screen fakes. A new battery-powered device program needs asymmetric cryptography on a tight processor budget, with certificates small enough for a slow link.

profile.organization: Harrow Advisory · consultancy to competing banks
profile.environment: Engagement files for competing clients on one platform · constrained device program

stimuli.title: Managing rights, tenancy and identity
stimuli.text: Harrow Advisory's platform team is settling three designs at once. The console needs formal rules for how administrator subjects and device objects are created and deleted, and how access rights are granted, transferred and revoked between them. The firm subscribes to a vendor-hosted fleet application in which the vendor operates the servers, operating systems and application code while the firm's staff simply log in. A redesigned field unit will authorize transactions locally during connectivity outages and reconcile later. Regulators reviewing planned fingerprint enrollment want assurance about what a database breach would expose.

profile.regime: Client confidentiality agreements · cloud provider terms
profile.environment: Vendor-hosted fleet application · stand-in authorization at the edge · fingerprint enrollment planned
profile.state: Design decisions open across three areas

stimuli.title: Everything through one gate
stimuli.text: An engineer at Linden Systems proposes that every request from any process to reach the dispenser interface pass through a single small enforcement component that is tamper-proof, impossible to bypass, and small enough to be fully verified. On the same platform an engineer must encrypt high-volume transaction logs on hardware with a constrained processor, where symmetric keys can be provisioned to each unit securely in advance. A disgruntled developer at the software supplier has embedded a routine that will corrupt a driver on the first business day after his contract ends, and a data-loss investigation is running.

profile.environment: Single enforcement component proposed for the dispenser API · departing contractor with commit access
profile.state: Design and personnel risks under review

stimuli.title: Signals leaving by unintended routes
stimuli.text: An assessment of Stonebridge Rail's station payment machines has found malware signaling captured card numbers to a nearby receiver by modulating the fascia status LED, a component never intended to carry data. City planners are separately asking the operator where to site new walk-up machines so as to discourage both skimmer installation and robbery, without paying for guards. Fuzz testing has shown that a machine's USB driver crashes whenever a peripheral sends a malformed descriptor longer than 64 bytes, overwriting adjacent memory. A vendor is pitching a cipher whose strength rests on keeping the algorithm secret.

profile.environment: Machines in unattended concourses · fascia status LEDs · siting decisions with city planners

stimuli.title: One key for the whole estate
stimuli.text: Attackers opened the service panels of dozens of Stonebridge Rail's machines using a single stolen vendor key that fitted the entire estate. The operator wants to make sure one lost key can never again expose everything. Its assurance team is separately shortlisting two independently evaluated payment-pad products, one certified at a higher assurance level than the other, and the finance director wants to know what the higher number actually buys before approving the premium. A consultant is also modeling the payment platform formally, with account balances as constrained data and raw customer input arriving unconstrained.

profile.environment: One service-panel key fits every unit · two evaluated products shortlisted

questionsV2.question: The browser console hides the cash-limit field from any user whose role is not permitted to change it. Which finding about that console design is MOST serious?

options.A: Authorization is enforced in console code the user controls, not on the server.
options.B: The console is served over TLS 1.2 rather than TLS 1.3, which weakens the transport.
options.C: The console hides the field with client script instead of a server-rendered template.
options.D: The console does not write cash-limit changes to the bank's central audit repository.

questionsV2.explanation: Anything a browser enforces is advice. The user owns the machine, the script and the request, so a hidden field can be restored from a developer console or the request replayed with the field set, and Nexus has no server-side objection ready. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-3 Access Enforcement puts the obligation on the system to enforce approved authorizations, and OWASP Top 10:2025 lists enforcement that happens only on the client under A01 Broken Access Control. B is a real transport finding and the right control for a different problem: TLS protects the request from a third party on the wire and does nothing about the party sending it. C is symptom not cause, because a server-rendered page hides the field more tidily and the server still accepts whatever arrives. D is detective when preventive is asked; the log would name whoever raised a limit, after the cash left. Decide where enforcement runs before deciding how the interface looks.
questionsV2.recallLine: A browser console hides a privileged field by role. What is the most serious design finding?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: Which transport setting should be raised when the concern is a third party reading the session?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How should a field be hidden once the server already enforces the rule?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: What is missing if the question is how the bank would later prove who changed a limit?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement
OWASP Top 10:2025 | A01 Broken Access Control

questionsV2.question: The migration will lift the existing server image into the new environment unchanged, including services nobody has used in three years. Which action BEST reduces the attack surface it carries across?

options.A: Run an authenticated vulnerability scan against the image and remediate the findings it reports.
options.B: Place the server behind a firewall that inspects traffic to each of its listening ports.
options.C: Rebuild the image from a documented baseline limited to the services the platform needs.
options.D: Deploy host-based intrusion detection so an unused service raises an alert when it is touched.

questionsV2.explanation: A three-year-old service nobody uses is not a vulnerability to be patched, it is a capability that should not be there. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7 Least Functionality requires the system to be configured to provide only mission-essential capabilities, with defined functions, ports, protocols and services prohibited or restricted, and CM-2 Baseline Configuration is where that configuration is recorded and held. A is a correct action but not the first one: a scan tells Nexus what is listening and removes none of it, and it will report on services that should have been deleted rather than fixed. B is the right control for a different problem, because boundary filtering governs who reaches a port, not whether the port should exist at all, and the shared cluster puts plenty of traffic inside the boundary. D is detective when preventive is asked and accepts the service as permanent. Remove capability first, then defend what is left.
questionsV2.recallLine: A legacy server image moves unchanged into a new environment. What best reduces the surface it carries?

optionsShort.A: Scan the image and remediate findings
optionsShort.B: Firewall in front of listening ports
optionsShort.C: Rebuild from a minimal documented baseline
optionsShort.D: Host intrusion detection on unused services

A.label: correct but not first
A.wouldAnswer: How would the team discover which unused services the image is actually running?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What protects a service that must keep running but should be reachable only from named networks?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: What gives warning if a service that cannot be removed is used unexpectedly?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7 Least Functionality
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-2 Baseline Configuration

questionsV2.question: The application tier will pull its base images from a public registry at build time. Which control MOST directly addresses the risk that introduces?

options.A: Network policy restricting which pods in the cluster may open connections to each other.
options.B: Verification of a digital signature on every image before the cluster is allowed to run it.
options.C: Scanning each built image for known-vulnerable packages before it is promoted to production.
options.D: A read-only root filesystem in each container so a compromised process cannot write to disk.

questionsV2.explanation: Pulling from a public registry means the cluster runs whatever answers to a name and a tag, and both are attacker-controllable in a way a version number is not. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-14 Signed Components requires the organization to prevent installation of defined components without verification that the component was signed with a certificate the organization recognizes and approves, and SR-4 Provenance and SR-11 Component Authenticity carry the supply-chain half of the same obligation. NIST's dedicated container publication is SP 800-190; the control obligation above stands on its own. A is the right control for a different problem, lateral movement once a pod is compromised. C is symptom not cause: it finds known-bad packages inside an image whose origin is still unverified, so a purpose-built malicious image with current packages passes. D is wrong phase, limiting what a running container can do after an unverified image has already been admitted. Decide what is allowed to run before deciding how it may behave.
questionsV2.recallLine: Base images come from a public registry at build time. Which control most directly addresses that risk?

optionsShort.C: Scan built images for known CVEs

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What limits how far an attacker moves once one pod is compromised?

C.label: symptom not cause
C.wouldAnswer: How does the team find images carrying package versions with published vulnerabilities?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What reduces the damage a compromised container process can do at runtime?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-14 Signed Components
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SR-4 Provenance; SR-11 Component Authenticity
NIST SP 800-190 (Application Container Security Guide), named as the dedicated source

questionsV2.question: The architects note that the provider patches the function runtime and isolates tenants. Given that division, which control should the bank's own review focus on MOST?

options.A: Hardening the guest operating system image the reconciliation functions run inside.
options.B: Agreeing an availability service level for the overnight reconciliation window.
options.C: Scheduling a quarterly vulnerability scan of the provider's platform endpoints.
options.D: Scoping each function's execution role to the permissions it actually needs.

questionsV2.explanation: When the provider owns the host, the runtime and the tenant boundary, what is left for Nexus to get wrong is the identity the function runs as and what that identity may reach. A function with a broad role is a standing credential that executes on a schedule with nobody watching. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 Least Privilege requires access authorizations to be no more than necessary for assigned tasks, and SA-9 External System Services requires the organization to define and document the roles and responsibilities of external providers rather than assume them, which is what makes the division above a contractual fact instead of a hope. A is not the decision-maker's: there is no guest image here that Nexus owns. B is the right control for a different problem, an availability commitment rather than a security surface. C is wrong scope, testing someone else's platform where the bank has neither authorization nor residual risk. Ask what the provider has not taken away.
questionsV2.recallLine: A provider patches the runtime and isolates tenants. Where should the bank's own review concentrate?

A.label: not the decision-maker's
A.wouldAnswer: What would the bank harden if it had chosen to run these jobs on its own virtual machines?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What should the contract say if the concern is the reconciliation finishing before branches open?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What testing does the bank owe on the systems it operates and is authorized to test?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 Least Privilege
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SA-9 External System Services

questionsV2.question: The dispenser-control service will run as a hypervisor guest and the team plans to keep a snapshot of every release. Which practice MOST reduces the risk that arrangement creates?

options.A: Encrypting the guest's virtual disk so its contents are unreadable if the file is copied.
options.B: Restricting access to the hypervisor management console to a named administrator group.
options.C: Enrolling every guest and retained snapshot in the same inventory and patching program as physical hosts.
options.D: Taking a fresh snapshot before every change so the service can be rolled back quickly.

questionsV2.explanation: A guest is created by an API call and a snapshot by a menu item, so virtual estates grow faster than the processes that are supposed to govern them, and a snapshot is a complete machine holding whatever data it held on the day it was taken. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-8 System Component Inventory requires an inventory that accurately reflects the system and is updated as components are installed or removed, CM-2 Baseline Configuration governs what each of those components should look like, and SA-22 Unsupported System Components is what a forgotten legacy guest eventually becomes. Note that the catalog contains no hypervisor-specific control; the obligation rides on the general ones. A is the right control for a different problem, protecting a disk file at rest. B is wrong scope, governing who administers the platform rather than the population of guests that accumulates on it. D is wrong phase and makes the problem larger, because it is a rollback measure that manufactures more of the artefacts the stem is worried about. Count the machines before hardening them.
questionsV2.recallLine: A legacy service runs as a hypervisor guest and every release is snapshotted. What most reduces the risk?

optionsShort.C: Inventory and patch guests and snapshots

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What protects a virtual disk copied off the datastore by someone with storage access?

B.label: wrong scope
B.wouldAnswer: What limits who can create, clone or destroy guests on the platform?

D.label: wrong phase
D.wouldAnswer: What lets the team undo a bad change to the dispenser-control service quickly?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-8 System Component Inventory
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-2 Baseline Configuration; SA-22 Unsupported System Components

questionsV2.question: The program board asks how the SlimLine II's control set should be arrived at. Which sequence BEST describes a defensible selection?

options.A: Adopt the control set the previous SlimLine program used, then add controls for the new interface.
options.B: Categorize the system by impact, take the matching baseline, then tailor it with documented justification.
options.C: Take the highest baseline available and remove the controls the examiner agrees are not applicable.
options.D: Ask the examiner which controls it expects to see and build the set from that answer.

questionsV2.explanation: Selection is a chain, and each link supplies the reason for the next. FIPS 199 Section 3 categorizes the system by the impact a loss of confidentiality, integrity or availability would have. FIPS 200 Section 3 turns that category into an obligation to apply the corresponding minimum controls. NIST SP 800-53B Chapters 2 and 3 supply the Low, Moderate and High baselines and the tailoring guidance, and SP 800-53 Rev 5 made both steps auditable in their own right with PL-10 Baseline Selection and PL-11 Baseline Tailoring. SP 800-37 Rev 2 Section 3.3 walks the same ground as RMF tasks S-1 through S-6. A is wrong scope: the old set was selected against the old terminal's categorization, and the new one has a different interface and a different impact. C is wrong phase, using tailoring in place of selection so that nothing states what the system needs. D is not the decision-maker's; the system owner categorizes and selects, and the examiner assesses what was done. Categorize first, and the argument writes itself.
questionsV2.recallLine: How should a new terminal's control set be arrived at so the choice can be defended?

optionsShort.A: Reuse the previous program's control set
optionsShort.B: Categorize, take baseline, tailor with justification
optionsShort.C: Start highest and subtract by agreement
optionsShort.D: Build from what the examiner names

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: What is a reasonable starting draft when two systems share a categorization and an environment?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: What does an organization do after a baseline has been selected and some controls do not fit?

D.label: not the decision-maker's
D.wouldAnswer: Who determines whether the selected controls were implemented and are working?

sources: FIPS 199 | Section 3, Security Objectives and categorization
FIPS 200 | Section 3, Minimum Security Requirements
NIST SP 800-53B | Chapters 2 and 3, baselines and tailoring
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | PL-10 Baseline Selection; PL-11 Baseline Tailoring
NIST SP 800-37 Rev 2 | Section 3.3 SELECT, tasks S-1 to S-6

questionsV2.question: The new dispenser interface and the existing transaction switch were built by different teams against the same written specification. Which activity is MOST likely to expose a defect neither team's own testing found?

options.A: A static analysis run over each team's source code against the bank's coding standard.
options.B: A penetration test of the assembled terminal conducted after it has entered production.
options.C: A design review comparing each team's architecture document with the approved specification.
options.D: Integration testing of the assembled interfaces against cases where the two readings disagree.

questionsV2.explanation: Two teams reading one specification produce two specifications, and the gap between them is invisible to any test that examines one side alone. NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.8 Integration is the lifecycle process that synthesizes system elements into a realized system, and it is precisely where interface and composition weaknesses surface, because it is the first activity that exercises the seam rather than the parts. SP 800-53 Rev 5 CA-3 Information Exchange governs the resulting connection; note that Rev 5 renamed it from the Rev 4 title System Interconnections, so material still using the older name is dated. A is wrong scope, testing each element on the terms each team already passed. B is wrong phase, arriving after the terminal is live and after the cheapest moment to fix a seam has gone. C is the right control for a different problem, comparing documents with a document while the defect lives in behavior. Test the joint, not the pieces.
questionsV2.recallLine: Two teams built either side of one interface from one specification. What best exposes a seam defect?

A.label: wrong scope
A.wouldAnswer: What finds coding-standard violations and common weaknesses inside one team's own source?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What validates the assembled terminal against an adversary once it is fielded?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: What confirms that each team's intended architecture matches what was approved?

sources: NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.8 Integration
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CA-3 Information Exchange (renamed from Rev 4 System Interconnections)

questionsV2.question: Fifty SlimLine II units are ready and the board wants them in service this quarter. Which condition should the security lead insist on BEFORE the first unit is cut over?

options.A: A documented back-out procedure and the retained configuration the units would be restored to.
options.B: A signed statement from the vendor that the units meet the approved specification.
options.C: A penetration test report covering the units in their final production configuration.
options.D: An updated asset inventory listing each unit's serial number and installation site.

questionsV2.explanation: Cutover is the moment a design becomes an operating system, and the only property that makes it survivable is reversibility. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-2(3) Baseline Configuration | Retention of Previous Configurations exists for exactly this, requiring a defined number of previous baseline versions to be retained to support rollback, and its discussion counts hardware, software, firmware, configuration files and records among them. NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.10 Transition frames the wider obligation: preserve the system's verified security characteristics through an orderly, planned move into the operational environment. B is not the decision-maker's; a vendor statement is evidence the bank weighs, not the bank's own gate. C is wrong phase, because verification belongs earlier in the lifecycle and a report is not a way back. D is the right control for a different problem, since an inventory is needed to operate the fleet and does nothing to make the first fifty reversible. Never move something you cannot move back.
questionsV2.recallLine: Fifty new terminals are ready to cut over. What condition should the security lead insist on first?

B.label: not the decision-maker's
B.wouldAnswer: What does the bank ask a supplier to provide as evidence in the acceptance pack?

C.label: wrong phase
C.wouldAnswer: What belongs at the verification gate, before units are declared ready?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: What does operations need in order to maintain and account for the fielded fleet?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-2(3) Retention of Previous Configurations
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.10 Transition
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control

questionsV2.question: Finance wants the 900 retired SlimLine units sold to a refurbisher. Which step MOST directly addresses the disposal risk the security lead must sign off?

options.A: A contract clause making the refurbisher liable for any data recovered from the units.
options.B: Removing each unit from the asset inventory once the refurbisher confirms collection.
options.C: Sanitizing every storage component to a level matched to the data it held, with verification recorded.
options.D: Physically destroying the encrypting PIN pad in each unit before the units leave the site.

questionsV2.explanation: A retired terminal is a filing cabinet on wheels: card data, logs, keys, configuration and whatever a technician once copied to it locally. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 MP-6 Media Sanitization requires media to be sanitized before disposal, release out of organizational control or release for reuse, using defined techniques and procedures, and SR-12 Component Disposal, new in Rev 5, extends that to the component itself. SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 Appendix H.14 Disposal is the lifecycle process, which includes removing information and deactivating accesses and dependencies. NIST SP 800-88 is the guide that decides between clear, purge and destroy; cite it without pinning a revision, because Revision 1 was withdrawn on 26 September 2025 and superseded by Revision 2. A is the right control for a different problem, moving liability rather than removing data. B is wrong phase, a records step that follows sanitization and would otherwise erase the bank's own account of what left. D is wrong scope, treating one component while the customer data sits on the terminal's storage. Sanitize to the data, not to the device.
questionsV2.recallLine: Retired terminals are being sold to a refurbisher. What most directly addresses the disposal risk?

optionsShort.B: Retire units from the asset inventory
optionsShort.C: Sanitize storage to the data's level, verified

A.label: right control, wrong problem
A.wouldAnswer: What should the contract say about the refurbisher's obligations once sanitized units leave the bank?

B.label: wrong phase
B.wouldAnswer: What records step closes out an asset after it has been sanitized and collected?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: What is required for the one component that holds cryptographic keys under the card brand rules?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | MP-6 Media Sanitization; SR-12 Component Disposal; SI-12(3) Information Disposal
NIST SP 800-160 Vol 1 Rev 1 | Appendix H.14 Disposal
NIST SP 800-88 (revision not pinned: Rev 1 withdrawn 2025-09-26, superseded by Rev 2)
