options.C: Its signaling messages carry no integrity protection, so their contents can be forged or altered by an interceptor.
options.D: Its short session keys are reused across successive calls and data sessions on the same device, easing later cryptanalysis.

questionsV2.explanation: Impersonation succeeds when one party has no way to test the other's identity: 2G's authentication is one-way, so a modem on 2G will accept any sufficiently strong transmitter claiming to be the network. The rogue tower did not have to break anything to be believed, which is why the same trick failed against 4G's mutual authentication. That direct causal link makes B the answer to 'MOST directly enabled'. (A) is a genuine 2G weakness, but it explains the later decryption of captured traffic, not the acceptance of the fake tower; it would be the right answer to how the attackers read the intercepted stream. (C) describes a real gap that supports related bidding-down tricks, yet the impersonation here needed no forged signaling, only an unauthenticated identity claim. (D) points at key hygiene, which affects cryptanalysis, not attachment decisions. Verifying the network's identity matters as much as the network verifying yours; one-way authentication is an open invitation to rogue infrastructure.

questionsV2.question: Which statement BEST explains why controls higher in the stack had no visibility of the downgrade?

options.A: The radio negotiation happens at the data link and network layers of the cellular stack, below anything the center's application-layer controls can observe.
options.B: The downgrade messages were encrypted with the 2G A5/1 stream cipher, which the center's inspection devices could not decrypt quickly enough to raise an alarm.
options.C: The rogue base station silently discarded the ATMs' logging traffic before it could ever reach the processing center's collectors.
options.D: The modems' TLS sessions renegotiated automatically as the bearer changed, and the monitoring stack treated the renegotiation as a routine handshake rather than an alarm.

questionsV2.explanation: Visibility follows the layer at which a control operates: the forced fallback was negotiated between modem and tower in the lower layers of the cellular stack, and nothing about it is ever presented to equipment inspecting application traffic at the far end. A explains the blindness structurally and would hold for any similar radio-layer attack. (B) misplaces the mechanism: A5/1 encrypts user traffic after the downgrade, and radio signaling between modem and tower never transits the center's inspection path at all; it would be a fair answer if the question were why over-the-air captures were unreadable to bystanders. (C) invents an action the attacker did not need; a relay that quietly forwards traffic is precisely why MITM interception is hard to spot. (D) fails on the facts of the case: the fleet had no TLS configured, which is what made the cleartext capture possible. An attack at layer N is invisible to controls that only see layer N+1's payloads, so monitoring must exist at the layer where the trust decision is made.

questionsV2.question: Which property BEST justifies protecting the payload end to end rather than relying on the carrier?

options.A: The protection travels with the data end to end, so compromise of any intermediate network still yields only ciphertext.
options.B: It operates at a lower layer than the carrier's controls, so it protects the radio negotiation as well as the payload.
options.C: It removes the need to pay for the private APN, releasing recurring carrier costs to fund other controls.
options.D: It authenticates the cellular towers to the modems, closing the downgrade path the attackers used before.

questionsV2.explanation: What failed in the original design was transitive trust: security ended wherever the carrier's link ended, and the data itself crossed the compromise point naked. End-to-end TLS binds confidentiality and integrity to the data rather than to any segment of the path, which is exactly the property that survives a hostile or downgraded underlay, hence A. (B) inverts the stack: TLS rides above the transport, so radio negotiation happens beneath it and is untouched; it would be the right description of a control built into the cellular layer itself. (C) may even be true financially, but cost release is not a security justification, and defense in depth argues for keeping the APN's segregation anyway. (D) attributes a cellular-layer property to an application-layer protocol; TLS authenticates the processing center's endpoint, not towers. Tower authentication is what 4G mutual authentication provides. Place mandatory protection at a layer whose endpoints you own; everything below it is then merely transport.

questionsV2.question: Which change would MOST directly restore call quality on the shared links?

options.A: Increasing the TCP window size on the replication servers so the nightly transfers complete sooner each evening.
options.B: Re-encoding the branch calls with a noticeably higher-bitrate audio codec to improve their perceived sound fidelity.
options.C: Enabling compression on the WAN links to reduce the total volume of traffic they must carry.
options.D: Applying quality-of-service policies so voice packets are queued and forwarded ahead of bulk transfer traffic.

questionsV2.explanation: The symptom pair is diagnostic: bulk TCP transfers ride out congestion by retransmitting and reordering, so they 'complete without error', while real-time voice cannot wait for retransmission; every delayed or jittered packet is a gap the listener hears. The fix is therefore not more capacity arithmetic but scheduling: QoS classifies voice into a priority queue so it crosses the congested link with bounded delay and jitter while the replication absorbs the slack it tolerates so well; that is D. (A) does the opposite of helping: a larger window lets the transfers fill the path more aggressively, deepening the queues that voice is stuck behind; window tuning answers a throughput problem. (B) raises fidelity per packet while making the stream heavier and just as delayed: garbling here is loss and jitter, not codec quality. (C) buys some headroom at the cost of processing delay, and an already-compressed replication stream yields little, and nothing about compression protects voice at the moment of contention. Real-time traffic fails on latency and jitter, elastic traffic on throughput; when they share a link, priority queueing reconciles them.

questionsV2.question: What is the MOST accurate account of what the attackers learned from the subscriber identity captures alone?

options.A: The cardholder PIN blocks queued up for onward transmission by each of the affected festival ATMs.
options.B: The contents of calls and data sessions that passed through the rogue base station while it operated.
options.C: The unique subscriber identity of each nearby SIM, letting individual devices be identified and tracked.
options.D: The street-level home addresses registered by the carrier against each captured subscriber account in its own records.

questionsV2.explanation: An IMSI is the identifier a SIM presents to the network, and an IMSI catcher harvests exactly that: which subscriber identities are present, when, and where. That alone supports identification and movement tracking of everyone near the rogue tower, a privacy harm independent of any decryption, which is what counsel needs stated, so C. (A) confuses the identifier layer with the payload: PIN blocks are application data, obtainable only after the traffic itself was captured and read. It describes the later data-capture stage of this incident, not the IMSI harvest. (B) likewise requires interception and decryption of session content; capturing identities does not open the sessions. (D) reaches into the carrier's subscriber database, which the radio interface never transmits; an attacker would need a separate compromise of carrier records to get it. Identifiers leak presence and movement; metadata is a privacy breach in its own right, even when every payload stays sealed.

questionsV2.question: Which assessment of the engineer's IPsec claim is MOST accurate?

options.A: The tunnel would have stopped the rogue base station from forcing the modems down to 2G in the first place.
options.B: The interception would still have occurred, but the captured traffic would have been unreadable ciphertext instead of cardholder data.
options.C: IPsec's added overhead would have made transactions over a 2G link time out, so the ATMs would simply have gone offline.
options.D: The tunnel would have alerted the SOC as soon as the peer's identity could no longer be cryptographically verified.

questionsV2.explanation: Encryption at a layer the bank controls changes what the attacker obtains, not whether the attacker can sit on the path: the rogue tower would still relay traffic, but every intercepted packet would be ESP ciphertext, so the loss event (cardholder data exposure) is averted even though the attack itself proceeds. That distinction is why B is the accurate assessment and why 'prevented entirely' overstates. (A) puts IPsec at the wrong layer: the downgrade is negotiated in the radio stack beneath the tunnel, which IPsec neither sees nor influences; refusing 2G fallback is a modem configuration, not a VPN feature. (C) is a performance guess, not a security property: IPsec's overhead is modest and 2G, while slow, carries small transaction messages. (D) misunderstands a relay MITM. The attacker forwards the IKE exchange untouched between the true endpoints, so peer authentication succeeds and no alarm exists to raise.

questionsV2.question: Two support laptops on one switch exchange transfers that never appear in the site router's flow logs, while their sessions to the center always do. Which statement BEST explains the difference?

options.A: The laptops negotiate a direct transport-layer session with each other that bypasses the lower network layers entirely.
options.B: The switch routes the local traffic itself using private internal IP addresses that the site's flow-logging router is configured to silently ignore.
options.C: An access list on the router discards the laptops' local traffic before the flow exporter can record it, while permitting their processing-center sessions.
options.D: Frames between hosts on one segment are switched by MAC address and reach the router only when traffic leaves the network.

questionsV2.explanation: The router simply never sees the local traffic: within a segment, delivery is a data link function (the switch forwards frames by learned MAC address), and the network-layer device participates only when a packet's destination lies in another network. Sessions to the processing center cross that boundary and are logged; laptop-to-laptop transfers do not, which D states, and it is the structural explanation requiring no additional assumptions. (A) is impossible as described: transport sessions are carried inside network and data link layers, not around them; layers encapsulate, they cannot be skipped. (B) misassigns roles: a Layer 2 switch forwards frames and consults no routing logic, and 'ignoring' private addresses is not standard router behavior on an internal network. (C) is conceivable in some other network, but it presumes an ACL nobody mentioned, and dropped traffic would still typically be countable; the layered explanation accounts for the evidence without inventing configuration. Knowing which device touches traffic at which layer tells you where visibility exists, and where a monitoring blind spot is architectural, not a fault.

questionsV2.question: A customer portal must be reachable from the internet and query an internal database. Where should the web server be placed?

options.A: On the internal LAN beside the database server, keeping their connection short and simple.
options.B: In a screened subnet (DMZ), with only its specific database port permitted through the inner firewall.
options.C: With an external hosting provider, keeping the exposed service outside the bank's perimeter entirely.
options.D: On the firewall's outside interface, relying on the server's own hardening as its protection.

questionsV2.explanation: Anything internet-reachable must be assumed compromisable, so the design question is what that compromise is adjacent to. A screened subnet puts the portal in a buffer zone with filtering on both sides: the internet reaches only the portal, and the portal reaches the internal network only on the one database port it needs. An attacker who wins the web tier inherits a nearly empty room, which is the containment the architect asked for; hence B. (A) is the worst adjacency: from a compromised portal on the internal LAN, the database, directory and everything else are one hop away with no screen between, so the design contributes nothing once the first host falls. (C) sounds like risk transfer but breaks on the requirement: the portal still needs its database query path into the bank, so the exposure returns as a tunnel from infrastructure the bank neither controls nor monitors. It suits static content with no internal dependencies. (D) leaves a single host's hardening as the entire defense, with no filtered zone around it; hardening is necessary and is not architecture. Place exposed services so that their compromise is the end of a corridor, not the middle of the building; segmentation is designed for the day the host falls.

questionsV2.question: One handheld received an unsolicited anonymous Bluetooth message; another had its contact list retrieved. Which assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: The second event is the more serious: unauthorized retrieval of data (bluesnarfing) breaches confidentiality, while unsolicited messages (bluejacking) are a nuisance.
options.B: The first event is the more serious, because successful message delivery proves the attacker has already completed a pairing relationship with the handheld.
options.C: The two events deserve equal priority, since each one demonstrates the same unauthorized radio-layer reach to devices carried by festival staff.
options.D: Neither event warrants a response, because Bluetooth's short operating range means the attacker will already have moved on and left the venue.

questionsV2.explanation: Triage ranks by impact: pushing an unwanted message at a device (bluejacking) alters nothing and takes nothing (an annoyance and a warning sign), while pulling data off a device (bluesnarfing) is a completed confidentiality breach of whatever was reachable, here a contact list and possibly more; A states the ranking and the reason. (B) rests on a false technical premise: bluejacking abuses the object-push mechanism precisely because it works on discoverable devices without pairing, so delivery proves proximity, not trust; had the stem shown an attacker-initiated pairing, escalation would be right. (C) flattens the distinction triage exists to draw: shared attack surface does not equal shared impact, and treating spam and data theft alike misallocates the SOC's attention. (D) turns a targeting constraint into a dismissal. Short range means the attacker was on-site and close, which at a multi-day festival argues for response (sweeps and a staff notice), not for shrugging. Prioritize by what the attacker achieved against CIA, not by which technology carried the attack. Same radio, very different losses.

questionsV2.question: Which evaluation of the private access point name is MOST accurate?

options.A: It separates the fleet's traffic from other subscribers, but by itself encrypts nothing end to end.
options.B: It encrypts each modem's traffic all the way through to the processing center using keys the carrier manages.
options.C: It makes the cellular towers authenticate themselves to the modems, closing the rogue-base-station attachment path at the radio layer.
options.D: It places a carrier-managed stateful firewall between the fleet and the internet, making any further transit protection redundant.

questionsV2.explanation: A private APN is a segregation construct: the carrier gives the fleet its own access point and routing context, keeping its traffic logically apart from other subscribers and often off the public internet. That is valuable containment, but the data still crosses radio and carrier infrastructure protected only by whatever the link layer offers, which the incident proved breakable; 'separate' was mistaken for 'encrypted', and A names the distinction. (B) asserts a service the APN does not provide: there is no APN-level end-to-end cryptography; believing this is precisely the design error being audited. (C) confuses the APN, which lives in the carrier's core, with radio-layer authentication, which is a property of the cellular generation. The APN was present throughout the downgrade attack and stopped nothing. (D) overstates a side effect: private APNs commonly restrict inbound reachability, but access restriction at the edge does nothing for confidentiality of data in transit, so 'redundant' does not follow. Segmentation controls who shares your path; only encryption controls who can read it, and every 'private network' claim should be tested against that pair.

questionsV2.question: Which change would MOST reduce the impact of an attack of this kind on the fleet?

options.A: Configure the fleet's modems to refuse any 2G/GSM fallback so a forced downgrade cannot occur.
options.B: Terminate an IPsec tunnel from each ATM to the processing center, encrypting the payload.
options.C: Require mutual authentication at the cellular radio layer so the ATM verifies the tower it joins.
options.D: Deploy a wireless IDS on site to detect the rogue base station and alert the SOC.

questionsV2.explanation: The root failure is implicit trust in a layer CityBank does not own. Moving confidentiality and integrity up to a layer they do control means any compromise of the carrier link, this downgrade or any later one, yields ciphertext instead of track data; the discriminator is impact of an attack 'of this kind', and B is the only option whose protection does not depend on predicting the attacker's method. (A) is real, recommended hardening; the case study lists 'Disconnect on 2G' as a missing configuration. But it closes only this one downgrade path while leaving the payload cleartext against any other link-layer compromise; it answers 'which change would have prevented the downgrade step?'. (C) is the correct diagnosis of what 2G lacks, but CityBank cannot impose mutual authentication on a carrier's radio network; it is a property of the network generation, not a control the bank can deploy. (D) is detective where the question asks preventive: by the time the SOC is alerted, the track data is captured; it answers 'how would CityBank detect a rogue base station?'. When a lower layer is untrusted, protect at a layer you control; detection and attack-specific hardening are complements, not substitutes.

questionsV2.question: Transaction messages must arrive intact and in order; status telemetry can lose a sample but must be fresh. Which transport-layer design is MOST appropriate?

options.A: UDP for both flows, because its lower overhead maximises battery life and bandwidth on cellular links.
options.B: TCP for the transaction messages and UDP for the telemetry, matching each flow's delivery requirements.
options.C: TCP for both flows, because a connection-oriented protocol is required before traffic can be encrypted.
options.D: UDP for the transactions and TCP for the telemetry, keeping time-critical payments off the slower protocol.

questionsV2.explanation: Transport selection is requirements matching. Transactions need what TCP's connection, sequencing, acknowledgment and retransmission machinery provides: guaranteed, ordered delivery. Telemetry inverts the trade: a retransmitted stale sample is worth less than the next fresh one, so connectionless UDP's fire-and-forget model fits, and B assigns each flow accordingly. (A) optimises the wrong variable. The efficiency gain is real, but applying it to transactions means a dropped withdrawal message simply vanishes, an unacceptable integrity-of-delivery failure for financial traffic; UDP-everywhere is the right answer only when every flow tolerates loss. (C) rests on a false premise: encryption does not require a connection-oriented transport — DTLS and IPsec protect datagram traffic routinely. (D) reverses the analysis, treating TCP's reliability as mere slowness; payments are exactly the traffic that must not be 'fast but maybe lost'.

questionsV2.question: Which evaluation of the dark fiber argument is MOST accurate?

options.A: It holds: traffic on a point-to-point fiber that the bank alone lights cannot realistically be observed anywhere in transit.
options.B: It holds, provided the fiber's full physical route is inspected on a regular schedule for evidence of splices or taps.
options.C: It fails: dark fiber carries other tenants' wavelengths on the same strand, so their equipment can observe the bank's frames.
options.D: It fails: fiber can be tapped with minimal signal loss along uncontrolled ground, so traffic in transit still requires encryption.

questionsV2.explanation: Leasing dark fiber buys exclusivity of the strand, not custody of the path: the glass runs through ducts, vaults and rights-of-way the bank neither owns nor watches, and optical taps (a bend coupler leaking a fraction of the light) extract traffic with losses small enough to hide in normal attenuation. Exclusive use therefore does not equal confidentiality, and encryption of data in transit remains required; D states why the argument fails. (A) mistakes a commercial arrangement for a physical guarantee: 'we light it' says who transmits, not who can listen along kilometres of accessible cable. (B) converts a preventive requirement into detective comfort: route inspections are periodic and taps are built to be unobtrusive, so the exposure window between visits is exactly what an attacker uses; inspection supplements encryption, it cannot substitute. (C) reaches the right verdict through the wrong facts. Sharing one strand via multiple wavelengths describes a lit/wavelength service; dark fiber is precisely the product where the strand is yours alone, so the stated reason is refutable and would sink the finding. Control of the endpoints is not control of the ground between them. Data crossing territory you cannot secure gets encrypted, whatever the contract says about the medium.

questionsV2.question: Which set of measures is MOST appropriate for the handheld fleet?

options.A: Disable Bluetooth across the whole handheld fleet by written policy until the current festival season has completely ended.
options.B: Rely on Bluetooth's frequency-hopping physical layer, whose channel changes defeat attempts to intercept the pairing and data traffic.
options.C: Instruct staff to keep handhelds within arm's reach and to decline any pairing prompt they were not expecting.
options.D: Make the handhelds non-discoverable, require authenticated pairing, and remove the Bluetooth profiles the sleds do not use.

questionsV2.explanation: The constraint rules out amputation, so the risk has to be engineered down while the radio stays up: non-discoverable mode removes the fleet from casual scanning, authenticated pairing stops unknown devices from establishing the relationship bluesnarfing rides on, and deleting unused profiles removes the very services (object exchange, file transfer) that data-theft attacks call. D layers three cuts into the actual attack path and keeps the sleds working. (A) meets the security goal by failing the business one: the stem says the payment sleds depend on Bluetooth, so a blanket disable trades an incident for an outage; it is the right answer only where no business function needs the radio. (B) mistakes a coexistence mechanism for a security control: frequency hopping fights interference, and every Bluetooth chipset follows the hop sequence as a matter of protocol. (C) is worth issuing and worthless alone: purely procedural, dependent on busy staff noticing prompts, and no barrier to attacks on discoverable services that never prompt. When a risky capability must stay enabled, shrink it: visibility, authentication, and surface (unused services) are the three dials that turn.

questionsV2.question: Which classification BEST fits what the interposed device did during that event?

options.A: A denial-of-service attack, because the ATMs were forced away from the legitimate 4G network they should have used.
options.B: A replay attack, because the transactions captured by the rogue station could be resubmitted at a later time.
options.C: An on-path (man-in-the-middle) attack, because the adversary sat between the endpoints and observed live traffic in transit.
options.D: An injection attack, because the rogue station inserted itself into the carrier's trusted infrastructure.

questionsV2.explanation: Classification should follow the mechanism that caused the loss: an adversary interposed between two communicating parties, relaying their traffic while reading it, is the definition of an on-path/MITM attack, and the stem's details (full relay, silent recording, uninterrupted service) match it exactly, so C. (A) fixes on the forced network change but draws the wrong conclusion: availability was preserved throughout (deliberately, to keep victims transacting), so denial of service misstates the impact; it would fit if the rogue tower had attached the ATMs and then black-holed them. (B) names a real follow-on risk of holding captured transactions, but nothing was resubmitted during the event — replay is what the regulator would be told if duplicate withdrawals had been executed. (D) stretches 'injection', which denotes inserting crafted data into an application or protocol stream, not positioning a device in a path. A MITM's hallmark is service that keeps working while confidentiality quietly fails.

questionsV2.question: Which control MOST directly addresses the compromised certificate authority risk?

options.A: Purchasing extended-validation certificates for the processing center's public hostname from one of the largest and best-known public certificate authorities.
options.B: Increasing the public key length on the processing center's certificate to strengthen its cryptography against attack.
options.C: Checking each certificate's revocation status through OCSP before the session is established, so known mis-issued certificates are rejected.
options.D: Embedding the expected certificate or public key in the ATM software so any other certificate is rejected.

questionsV2.explanation: The threat is mis-issuance: some other trusted CA signing a certificate the bank never requested. Pinning removes that CA ecosystem from the trust decision entirely: the ATM accepts only the specific certificate or key it was built to expect, so even a technically valid rogue certificate fails, which is as direct as a countermeasure gets; hence D, and a closed fleet of bank-owned clients is the ideal place for it. (A) changes the vetting tier of the bank's own certificate but constrains no other CA; a compromised authority can still issue for the hostname. EV answers a question about phishing look-alike sites, not mis-issuance. (B) hardens against cryptanalysis of a key nobody is attacking; the rogue certificate carries its own perfectly good key. (C) helps only after the bad certificate is discovered and revoked, and an on-path attacker can often suppress the check; it is the right hygiene for retiring known-bad certificates. When the CA ecosystem itself is the threat, pin the identity you expect instead of trusting the ecosystem to police itself.

questionsV2.question: A flood of large responses arrives from thousands of legitimate servers the authority never queried. Which property of UDP MOST directly makes that possible?

options.A: It performs no handshake, so a request carrying a forged source address is answered as though the victim had sent it.
options.B: It provides no delivery guarantee, so attack packets lost in transit are simply gone rather than retransmitted.
options.C: It has lower per-packet header overhead than TCP, so each response consumes less of the attacker's own bandwidth.
options.D: It supports broadcast and multicast delivery, letting a single request reach many amplifying servers at once.

questionsV2.explanation: Reflection depends on servers answering someone who never asked, and that requires the victim's address to be forgeable: because UDP exchanges datagrams with no connection establishment, a server has no handshake in which the claimed source must prove it can respond, so it obligingly sends its large reply to the spoofed address. That is the enabling property named in A. TCP's three-way handshake is precisely what defeats this, since a spoofed SYN never completes. (B) is a true UDP property but irrelevant to the mechanism; unreliable delivery describes what happens to lost packets, not why reflectors answer forged ones. (C) is also true and does improve the attacker's amplification economics, but it is a secondary efficiency, of no use without spoofability. (D) misdescribes the technique: reflectors are queried unicast, one request per server; multicast is how the attacker might reach local segments, and answers a different question about one-to-many delivery. Connectionless protocols accept unverified source addresses, and every reflection/amplification attack is built on that single fact.

questionsV2.question: Which change MOST directly shrinks how far broadcasts propagate while keeping the existing switch hardware?

options.A: Enable port security, so each switch port accepts frames from only one learned hardware address.
options.B: Enable spanning tree on the switches, removing the redundant paths that broadcasts can loop across.
options.C: Define VLANs on the switches, dividing the flat network into several smaller broadcast domains.
options.D: Replace the busiest access switches with faster models that can process broadcasts with less delay.

questionsV2.explanation: Broadcast reach is defined by the broadcast domain, and a flat network is one giant domain: every ARP request touches all 500 hosts. VLANs partition the same physical switches into multiple logical domains, so each broadcast now floods only its own segment. Propagation shrinks by design, on existing hardware, exactly as asked; C is the mechanism that maps to the requirement. (A) polices who may send on a port; it neither reduces the number of hosts a legitimate broadcast reaches nor addresses volume at all; port security answers an unauthorized-device question. (B) is the closest miss: spanning tree prevents pathological broadcast storms by blocking forwarding loops, but the stem describes legitimate broadcast load in a loop-free network, and STP leaves the single 500-host domain fully intact. It is the right answer when the capture shows the same frames circulating endlessly. (D) treats propagation as a performance problem: faster switches forward the same broadcasts to the same 500 hosts, merely sooner, and every host still spends cycles processing them. To limit how far broadcasts travel, cut the domain into pieces; VLANs resize broadcast domains without new hardware or new cabling.

questionsV2.question: Which assessment of the parked laptop and a proportionate first response is BEST?

options.A: An active intrusion is underway; disable the branch wireless network until law enforcement arrives on site.
options.B: Probable wireless reconnaissance (war driving); review how far the branch SSIDs propagate and confirm the strength of the authentication they require.
options.C: Harmless behavior; passively observing radio signals from a parking lot yields nothing of value to an attacker.
options.D: An evil twin attack is already in progress; direct branch staff to move every handheld onto its cellular fallback connectivity at once.

questionsV2.explanation: The evidence supports collection, not contact: hours of dwell with a high-gain antenna and zero association attempts is the profile of war driving: passively mapping SSIDs, security modes and signal reach. The proportionate response treats it as a warning about exposure: measure how far the branch networks bleed past the walls, trim transmit power where warranted, and verify that what is reachable from a parking lot demands strong authentication; B matches classification to evidence and response to classification. (A) declares an intrusion the logs refute and answers it by inflicting an availability loss on the branch — self-imposed denial of service as a precaution against observation. (C) waves away the collection phase: SSIDs, hardware vendors, security modes and coverage maps are targeting data, and reconnaissance is how attacks are scoped; 'passive' does not mean 'valueless'. (D) names an attack whose evidence (duplicate SSIDs, client disruptions, certificate warnings) is entirely absent, and triggers an operational upheaval on none of it. Reconnaissance observed is your prompt to shrink what an observer can learn and harden what an observer can reach.

questionsV2.question: Which upgrade MOST directly addresses both the slowdowns and the sniffing, and why?

options.A: Replace the hub with a switch, giving each port its own collision domain and forwarding unicast frames only to the destination port.
options.B: Replace the hub with a small router, so that every PC is placed into a separate IP subnet of its own.
options.C: Cascade a second hub off the first and split the PCs between the two devices, halving the shared load.
options.D: Upgrade to a faster hub, so the shared medium offers more headroom to every attached station.

questionsV2.explanation: Both complaints have one cause: a hub is a shared medium that repeats every bit out of every port, so contention throttles throughput and every NIC in promiscuous mode hears everything. A switch fixes both with one change: per-port collision domains end the contention, and MAC-learned forwarding delivers unicast frames only where they belong, so a sniffer on another port sees broadcasts and its own traffic, no more; A resolves the cause itself. (B) would also isolate traffic, but at the wrong layer and cost: per-PC subnets add addressing and gateway complexity a five-PC workshop does not need. It is the right shape of answer when policy boundaries between segments are required, not connectivity. (C) misunderstands cascading; hubs joined to hubs still form one collision domain and one listening zone, so both problems survive intact. (D) buys speed for a medium that stays shared: contention scales down but persists, and the confidentiality exposure is untouched at any speed. Shared-medium problems, collisions and universal sniffing alike, are solved by switching to per-port forwarding, not by making the shared medium faster or more numerous.

questionsV2.question: After a failed gateway was replaced with a spare using the same address, some machines could reach it only after minutes. Which mechanism BEST explains the delay?

options.A: The kiosks' DNS caches kept resolving the gateway's hostname to the address of the old device.
options.B: The kiosks' ARP caches still mapped the gateway's IP address to the old MAC address until those entries expired.
options.C: Spanning tree kept the replacement's switch port in a blocking state until the topology reconverged.
options.D: The kiosks' DHCP leases still named the failed device as default gateway until each lease renewed.

questionsV2.explanation: The capture is the tell: frames addressed to a hardware address that no longer exists on the wire mean the IP-to-MAC mapping is stale, and that mapping is ARP's. Each kiosk cached the old resolution and kept using it until the entry timed out or was refreshed, exactly producing a minutes-long outage that heals by itself, so B. (A) works at the wrong translation: DNS maps names to IP addresses, and the gateway's IP never changed, so no DNS record was invalidated; DNS staleness answers a scenario where a service moved to a new IP. (C) is a real convergence delay when new switch links come up, but it would block the replacement's traffic wholesale, not cause kiosks to address the wrong MAC; the capture contradicts it. (D) fails the same way as A: the lease hands out a gateway IP, and that IP is unchanged, so renewal alters nothing. Layer-2 reachability lives in ARP caches: when a device is swapped behind a retained IP, stale ARP entries (until cleared or gratuitously updated) are the first suspect.

questionsV2.question: Which limitation of the partner's distance-vector protocol is MOST relevant to rejecting it?

options.A: Spanning Tree Protocol, which detects the loop and blocks one segment of it until a working path fails.
options.B: Storm control, which caps the incoming rate of broadcast and multicast traffic accepted on each individual switch port.
options.C: Link aggregation, which bundles parallel cables between two switches into one logical link.
options.D: Port security, which limits which hardware addresses may be learned on the new uplink port.

questionsV2.explanation: Ethernet frames carry no hop count, so a physical loop recirculates broadcasts forever, amplifying them each lap; that is the storm in the captures. The requirement is to keep the redundant path yet forward over a loop-free topology, and that is spanning tree's whole function: elect a topology, place the loop-forming port in a blocking state, and unblock it automatically when the primary path dies; A delivers redundancy and stability together, which is what the technician actually wanted. (B) is a damage limiter, not a topology manager: rate caps would blunt the storm's peak while the loop keeps regenerating traffic, and legitimate broadcasts get throttled along with the noise. It is right as a second line of defense, wrong as the mechanism. (C) fails on topology: aggregation bundles parallel links between the same two devices; this ring runs through a third switch, which is exactly the case bundling cannot express and spanning tree exists for. (D) filters which MACs may speak on a port; nothing about it detects or breaks forwarding loops. Layer 2 redundancy is safe only under a loop-management protocol; without spanning tree (or a modern equivalent), every backup cable is a scheduled outage.

questionsV2.question: Which observed packet sequence confirms an inbound connection was fully established?

options.A: A SYN from the client, a RST from the server, then a fresh SYN from the client.
options.B: A SYN from the client followed by a SYN-ACK from the server, with nothing further exchanged.
options.C: A SYN from the client, a SYN-ACK from the server, then an ACK from the client.
options.D: An ACK from the client answered by a FIN from the server shortly afterwards.

questionsV2.explanation: Establishment is the three-way handshake completing: the client proposes (SYN), the server agrees and proposes back (SYN-ACK), and the client's final ACK confirms both directions are synchronized. Only after that third packet does either side hold an established connection, so C is the sequence the rule should match. (A) shows the opposite outcome: a RST is the server refusing or aborting the attempt, and the client simply trying again; it is what the analyst would match to detect rejected connections, such as scans of closed ports. (B) is a half-open connection: the server has committed state and is waiting for an ACK that never comes; matching this pattern at volume is how the analyst would detect a SYN flood, not a success. (D) belongs to the wrong phase entirely: FIN initiates orderly teardown of a session, so it presupposes an existing connection; it cannot confirm one being built. SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK is the signature of establishment, and its missing final ACK is the signature of the attack that abuses it.

questionsV2.question: Which risk statement about the readers' short operating range is MOST accurate?

options.A: The range is a hard physical ceiling, so capturing a transaction requires physically tampering with the reader itself.
options.B: The NFC standard already encrypts each session on its own, so the operating range question is largely irrelevant to the workshop's risk analysis.
options.C: Short range raises attacker difficulty, but relay and skimming equipment can still extend or capture transactions, so transaction-layer cryptographic protection remains necessary.
options.D: Interception is a practical concern only in crowded environments, so readers installed in well-supervised branch locations need no additional protective controls beyond supervision.

questionsV2.explanation: Range is an attacker-cost parameter, not a security boundary: purpose-built antennas read NFC from further than the nominal few centimetres, skimming hardware can sit at the reader, and relay attacks defeat proximity entirely by piping the exchange between a victim's card and a distant terminal in real time. So the workshop should treat short range as difficulty, and place the real protection in the payment protocol's cryptography (dynamic per-transaction cryptograms), which is what C says. (A) converts a nominal figure into a physics guarantee; eavesdropping and relay both work without touching the reader, so 'tampering required' understates the surface. (B) misattributes the protection: baseline NFC communication is not encrypted; the confidentiality and anti-replay strength lives in the payment application above it, not in the radio standard. (D) turns risk into a seating chart: a festival ATM is the crowded case, and supervision does not perceive radio-layer relay or a skimmer inside the housing. Proximity limits are attack-cost assumptions, not controls. Price them as difficulty, and put the actual defense in cryptography that does not care where the attacker stands.

questionsV2.question: A tester on an access port now captures only broadcasts and their own sessions, where the old hub captured everything. Which explanation is MOST accurate?

options.A: The switch encrypts frames traveling between its ports, so other stations' traffic is still present in the capture but cryptographically unreadable.
options.B: The switch forwards unicast frames only to the learned destination port, so other conversations no longer reach the tester's port.
options.C: The switch's VLAN configuration has isolated every access port into its own separate per-port broadcast domain.
options.D: The switch performs routing between its ports, so frames cross from one port to another only when a gateway forwards them.

questionsV2.explanation: A switch learns which MAC address lives on which port from source addresses, then forwards each unicast frame only toward its destination; traffic between two other stations therefore has no reason to appear at the tester's port, while broadcasts still flood to all ports of the VLAN, which matches the capture contents exactly, so B. It also frames the honest caveat for the report: this is a forwarding behavior, not a security guarantee, and techniques like MAC flooding or ARP spoofing exist precisely to defeat it. (A) invents a service switches do not provide: frames between ports are unmodified, and an 'unreadable' theory is contradicted by a capture where other traffic is simply absent, not garbled. (C) is refuted by the tester's own evidence: broadcasts were captured, so the port shares a broadcast domain with their senders; one-port-per-VLAN would have silenced those too. (D) moves the device up a layer. A Layer 2 switch forwards frames by MAC with no gateway involved; inter-VLAN routing exists but is not why unicasts go quiet on an access port. Report the mechanism itself, learned per-port forwarding, because knowing why the sniffer went quiet is exactly knowing which attacks make it loud again.

questionsV2.question: Which explanation BEST fits the ward segment receiving no addresses, and points to the standard fix?

options.A: The DHCP scope is exhausted, so the server has no addresses left to offer the branch clients; extend the pool.
options.B: The WAN provider is filtering the lease traffic somewhere in transit; request an exception for those flows.
options.C: The branch clients' requests carry addressing the server cannot recognize; renumber the branch to match the server's scopes.
options.D: DHCP discovery is broadcast, and routers do not forward broadcasts; configure a relay agent on the branch router.

questionsV2.explanation: The evidence isolates the variable: same clients, same server, success on the local LAN, failure across a routed boundary, healthy link. What changes across that boundary is broadcast reach: a client's DHCPDISCOVER is broadcast because the client has no address yet, and routers terminate broadcasts at the segment edge, so the plea for an address dies on the branch wire. The standard cure is a relay agent (IP helper) on the branch router, which converts the broadcast to a unicast aimed at the headquarters server; D explains the failure and names the fix, which is why relays exist in every centralized-DHCP design. (A) cannot survive the control case. An exhausted scope would refuse the same laptops at headquarters too, and exhaustion is a fault that appears under load, not precisely at a new segment's turn-up. (B) contradicts the clean bidirectional link test and, more basically, the traffic pattern: without a relay, no lease traffic enters the WAN to be filtered. (C) reverses DHCP's premise: clients request precisely because they have no addressing, and scope selection is driven by the relay's tagged source information. Protocols that begin from nothing must broadcast, and broadcasts stop at routers, so centralized services for such protocols work only through per-segment relays.

questionsV2.question: A web server compromised through a plugin probed for a week without reaching the database. Which design property MOST directly accounts for the containment?

options.A: The inner screen permitted the web server only one database port inward, so every other probe from it was dropped.
options.B: Address translation at the perimeter hid the internal numbering plan, leaving the attacker unable to identify any internal targets worth probing.
options.C: The portal host's hardening baseline had already removed the scanning and enumeration tooling an intruder would need to probe internal ranges.
options.D: The outer firewall's alerting brought the SOC in early, and its containment actions cut the probing short.

questionsV2.explanation: The screened subnet earned its keep on the inward side: the architecture's premise is that exposed hosts will eventually fall, so the inner screen restricts what a fallen host may initiate (here, one database port to one destination), and a week of probing becomes a week of drops at a policy boundary the attacker cannot alter from the web server. That least-privilege egress from the DMZ is the property doing the containing; A. (B) overrates obscurity: translation hides numbering from the outside, but the attacker was inside the DMZ, learning real reachable addresses from the server's own configuration and its permitted database path. Concealment, unlike filtering, ends at first compromise. (C) is worthwhile friction that cannot carry the outcome: attackers bring or fetch tooling, and hardening the host does not constrain where its packets may go; the firewall does. (D) is contradicted by the timeline: a week of unimpeded probing is the opposite of early detection, and the stem credits design, not response. Measure a DMZ by its inner rules; the design succeeds when a compromised exposed host discovers that almost nothing inward will answer it.

questionsV2.question: Tens of thousands of half-open sessions from spoofed addresses fill the connection backlog. Which security property is MOST directly affected?

options.A: Confidentiality, because the spoofed half-open sessions can read responses cached for other customers.
options.B: Integrity, because sessions abandoned in mid-handshake leave affected customer transactions only partially committed.
options.C: Authenticity, because the source addresses presented on each of the incoming connections are deliberately forged.
options.D: Availability, because legitimate customers can no longer establish sessions with the service.

questionsV2.explanation: Impact classification follows the harm actually realized: the backlog exhaustion means real customers cannot connect, which is a loss of availability, the defining outcome of a SYN flood, so D belongs in the report. (A) has no mechanism behind it: a half-open session is unacknowledged handshake state, not an authenticated channel; the attacker receives nothing through it, and no data is disclosed. (B) confuses connection state with application state: a handshake that never completes never reaches the application, so no transaction exists to be left half-done; integrity would be the finding if an attacker were altering data in flight. (C) is the most tempting wrong answer because the addresses genuinely are forged, but spoofing is the attack's technique, not its impact: authenticity would matter if the forged identity were being trusted for access decisions, whereas here it merely hides the attacker. Report attacks by the property they degrade for users, not by the trick used to mount them; SYN floods spend spoofing to buy denial of service.

questionsV2.question: To justify replacing the scanners urgently, which statement of the obsolete standard's risk is MOST accurate?

options.A: WEP's short initialization vectors force keystream reuse, letting an attacker who captures traffic recover the key within minutes and join the network.
options.B: WEP's weakness is chiefly short passphrases, so configuring the longest supported key makes it acceptable for scanner traffic.
options.C: WEP's flaw is primarily its one-way authentication, so adding MAC-address filtering restores adequate protection for the warehouse fleet.
options.D: WEP is breakable only with prolonged physical access to an access point, so the risk stays confined to the warehouse floor and its equipment.

questionsV2.explanation: The budget case must survive technical challenge, and A is the statement that does: WEP's 24-bit initialization vector space is so small that busy traffic repeats IVs quickly, RC4 keystream reuse plus related-key weaknesses then yield the shared key to passive capture in minutes with public tooling, and the recovered key is the network key, so the attacker joins the same LAN the settlement traffic crosses. Mechanism, feasibility and consequence, each correct. (B) misdiagnoses: the attacks recover whatever key is configured (104-bit keys fall the same way), so 'use a longer key' is the fix for guessable secrets, a different disease. (C) pairs a real observation with a useless remedy: authentication is not the broken part that matters, and MAC filters fall to address spoofing in seconds; a reviewer refutes this in one sentence, taking the budget with it. (D) inverts the exposure: the attack is passive radio capture from anywhere in range, parking lot included. Legacy-crypto findings are argued from the mechanism of the break (small IV space, keystream reuse, passive recovery), because an accurate one-paragraph mechanism is what makes 'replace it now' unanswerable.

questionsV2.question: Which switch capability MOST directly defeats a host announcing itself as the gateway?

options.A: Dynamic ARP inspection, validating ARP replies against trusted address bindings before forwarding them.
options.B: Port security, limiting each access port to a single learned hardware address at a time.
options.C: Storm control, rate-limiting the volume of broadcast and multicast traffic accepted on access ports.
options.D: 802.1X authentication, requiring devices to authenticate successfully before their switch port forwards any traffic.

questionsV2.explanation: The technique is ARP spoofing: unsolicited or false ARP messages claim the gateway's IP maps to the attacker's MAC. Dynamic ARP inspection attacks it at the root: the switch checks every ARP reply against known-good IP-to-MAC bindings (typically from DHCP snooping) and drops the forgeries, so the poisoning never reaches victim caches, regardless of who sent it; that is A, and note it works even against an authorized, already-admitted device. (B) sounds apt but misses: the attacking laptop uses one MAC of its own, so a one-address limit is satisfied while the poisoning proceeds; port security answers the rogue-hub and MAC-flooding problems. (C) governs traffic volume, and gratuitous ARP is a trickle, nowhere near storm thresholds. (D) is the strongest-sounding distractor: it would have kept this unauthorized laptop off entirely, but it authenticates admission, not behavior. A compromised authenticated host could run the identical attack, so it does not defeat the technique itself. Admission control and protocol validation are different layers of defense; ARP spoofing is stopped by validating ARP, not by authenticating ports.

questionsV2.question: Fragmented packets whose offsets overlap so they can never reassemble have crashed a legacy controller twice. Which attack does the evidence MOST specifically indicate?

options.A: Ping of death: fragments that reassemble into a datagram beyond the maximum legal size.
options.B: Smurf: amplified echo replies converging on the controller from a broadcast network.
options.C: Teardrop: deliberately overlapping fragment offsets that crash a vulnerable reassembly implementation.
options.D: SYN flood: connection requests that exhaust the controller's half-open session table.

questionsV2.explanation: The IPS has already isolated the discriminating feature: offsets that overlap. Teardrop-class attacks craft fragment sequences whose offset arithmetic is self-contradictory, and reassembly code that fails to handle the overlap corrupts memory and crashes. Malformed input plus a crashing legacy stack is this evidence exactly, so C. (A) is the sibling fragmentation attack and the intended confusion: ping of death's lever is total reassembled size exceeding 65,535 bytes, not overlap. An analyst who names the wrong lever will chase the wrong patch, since the two bugs live in different checks of the reassembly path. (B) fails on both traffic type and mechanism: a smurf is a flood of well-formed echo replies that saturates capacity; it involves no fragmentation trickery and kills by volume, not by crash. (D) is TCP state exhaustion: a rising tide of SYNs and half-open sessions, degrading service progressively, nothing like a malformed-fragment signature followed by outright crashes. Fragmentation attacks are told apart by their lever, oversize versus overlap, and naming the lever correctly is what turns an alert into the right remediation for the vulnerable stack.

questionsV2.question: Which approach MOST directly addresses the exhaustion mechanism behind the flood?

options.A: Block the flood's source addresses at the perimeter firewall as the SOC identifies them.
options.B: Raise the servers' connection-table limits so that more half-open sessions can be held at once.
options.C: Shorten the servers' keep-alive timers so established HTTP sessions are released sooner.
options.D: Enable SYN cookies, so the servers commit no connection state until a client's final handshake acknowledgment arrives.

questionsV2.explanation: The flood's lever is asymmetry: each spoofed SYN costs the attacker one packet but costs the server a table entry held open for a timeout. SYN cookies remove the lever: the server answers with a SYN-ACK whose sequence number cryptographically encodes the pending connection and stores nothing; only when a real client returns the final ACK does state get created. Spoofed SYNs, whose ACKs will come from nowhere, now cost the server nothing, while legitimate handshakes complete normally, exactly 'keep serving customers during the flood'. D dismantles the exhaustion mechanism itself. (A) chases addresses that are forged and rotating: each block lags the flood by design, legitimate users behind reused addresses become collateral, and the firewall rule base becomes its own exhaustion problem. (B) enlarges the bucket under an open tap; the flood fills any finite table, minutes later; sizing answers organic growth, not adversarial load. (C) tunes the wrong lifecycle phase: keep-alive governs established sessions after the handshake, and the flood never gets that far — its damage is entirely pre-establishment. Durable DoS mitigations attack the attacker's asymmetry: make the unverified party carry the cost of state, and a flood of fakes loses its purchase.

questionsV2.question: Which limitation of the partner's proposed distance-vector protocol is MOST relevant to rejecting it?

options.A: RIP carries its routing updates in cleartext, so route advertisements can be captured and read off the wire by listeners.
options.B: RIP treats 16 hops as unreachable and converges slowly, so both the 18-hop path and the recovery target fail.
options.C: RIP requires a backbone-area hierarchy to scale, which a merged campus network cannot easily support.
options.D: RIP floods complete topology maps on every change, consuming bandwidth on the WAN links between the merged sites.

questionsV2.explanation: Relevance means the limitation that breaks the stated requirements, and RIP breaks both at once: its metric counts to 15, with 16 meaning unreachable, so an 18-hop destination is administratively nonexistent; and its periodic-update, distance-vector convergence takes minutes (with hold-downs), not the seconds required. B is the direct, two-count rejection. (A) is a real hygiene concern (RIPv2 supports authentication, and updates are observable), but confidentiality of advertisements is not among the requirements the proposal must meet, so it cannot carry the rejection. (C) belongs to the wrong protocol: the backbone-area design (area 0) is OSPF's architecture; RIP has no areas at all, and citing this hands the partner an easy rebuttal. (D) also describes the other family: flooding link-state advertisements to build topology maps is OSPF/IS-IS behavior, whereas RIP sends distance vectors, not maps. Reject a protocol on the requirements it measurably fails, for RIP its diameter (15 hops) and convergence time, and keep the failings of one protocol family from being pinned on the other.

questionsV2.question: The inventory shows nothing that still needs the deprecated cipher. What should the engineer do, and why?

options.A: Keep mixed mode, because each client negotiates the strongest cipher it supports, so capable devices already use CCMP.
options.B: Require CCMP only: TKIP is a deprecated RC4-based fallback with known attacks, and permitting it lets devices negotiate downward.
options.C: Retire wireless encryption at the access points and rely on TLS from each application instead, simplifying the radio estate.
options.D: Require CCMP and also suppress SSID broadcast, since network visibility matters more than the cipher choice.

questionsV2.explanation: Every cipher a network will accept is attack surface: TKIP was a transitional wrapper around RC4, deprecated with practical attacks against it, and offering it means the network's floor, not its ceiling, defines the exposure, including for downgrade tricks against the negotiation. With the inventory showing no TKIP-dependent devices, the compatibility rationale is empty, so the fallback is pure liability; the AirLink incident already taught what negotiable fallbacks cost. B removes it. (A) is the seductive half-truth: capable clients do negotiate CCMP for themselves, but the network's security is judged by what it will accept, and mixed mode also drags group (broadcast) traffic down to the weakest common cipher for all clients. (C) misapplies a sound principle: application-layer encryption is defense in depth, not a license to open the radio layer, which alone protects the LAN from unauthenticated joining and local attacks TLS never sees. (D) spends effort on concealment that probing clients defeat, bundled with the correct move to look reasonable. When nothing needs the legacy option, its only remaining function is to weaken you. Disable fallbacks affirmatively; do not trust negotiation to avoid them.

questionsV2.question: A branch rule set permits all inbound traffic above port 1023 so replies can return. Which firewall capability MOST directly admits only genuine return traffic?

options.A: An application-layer proxy gateway terminating each session and re-originating it toward the destination on the client's behalf.
options.B: Restricting the inbound high-port rules to source addresses inside the ISP's own network space.
options.C: Stateful inspection, tracking outbound connections and admitting only packets that match an existing session.
options.D: Network address translation, hiding branch addressing behind a single public address at the perimeter.

questionsV2.explanation: The gap is memory: a static packet filter judges each packet in isolation, so 'replies must get back in' degenerates into 'leave the high ports open'. A stateful firewall records each outbound connection in a state table and admits inbound packets only when they correspond to a tracked session, which is word-for-word the reviewer's requirement; C closes the hole without breaking return traffic. (A) would also achieve it, and more besides: a proxy fully mediates the protocol. But it is the heavier instrument, with per-application support and termination overhead, bought for content inspection; as the direct fix for connection-tracking it exceeds the question. It wins when payload-level policy is required. (B) narrows who can exploit the standing hole yet the hole remains: any host in that ISP space can reach branch high ports unsolicited, and source addresses can be spoofed besides. (D) does incidentally drop unsolicited inbound flows for lack of a translation entry, but it is an addressing mechanism whose 'filtering' is a side effect with no policy control. The next question a reviewer asks is what happens when a mapping exists.

questionsV2.question: Which IPsec configuration BEST meets the trailer's requirements for hidden internal addresses and gateway-terminated cryptography?

options.A: Transport mode using AH, authenticating each packet's origin while leaving its payload readable in transit.
options.B: Tunnel mode using ESP, encrypting each original packet whole inside a new outer header between the gateways.
options.C: Transport mode using ESP, encrypting the payload while the original addresses stay visible for routing.
options.D: Tunnel mode using AH alone, protecting header integrity without concealing the packet contents.

questionsV2.explanation: Two requirements decide this: hiding internal addressing, and gateway-terminated crypto. Tunnel mode encapsulates the entire original IP packet, internal source and destination included, inside a new packet addressed gateway-to-gateway, and ESP encrypts that inner packet, so the carrier sees only the gateways talking; B satisfies both conditions, which is why tunnel-mode ESP is the standard site-to-site construction. (A) fails on both axes: transport mode leaves the original header exposed for routing, and AH provides authentication and integrity with no confidentiality at all; it suits host-to-host traffic that must be genuine but may be public. (C) does encrypt the data, but transport mode by definition preserves the original header, so the internal addresses ride the carrier network in the clear, violating the compliance term; it is the right choice when the communicating hosts themselves are the crypto endpoints. (D) wraps the packet but never encrypts it. AH-only tunnels prove origin, not secrecy. Tunnel mode hides the original packet, transport mode hides only its payload; pick by whether topology itself is sensitive.

questionsV2.question: A live all-hands video will go to 2,000 desktops by multicast. Which protocol delivers the stream only where there are viewers?

options.A: IGMP, letting hosts join and leave multicast groups so the network forwards the stream only to segments with subscribers.
options.B: ICMP, reporting delivery errors and diagnostic information about the stream's path back to its source.
options.C: SNMP, letting the operations team watch link utilization on each distribution switch in real time while the broadcast is running.
options.D: BGP, advertising the multicast group's addresses outward to each of the campus routers ahead of the event.

questionsV2.explanation: Multicast saves the core only if the network knows where the viewers are: IGMP is the membership protocol in which hosts announce joining or leaving a group, and routers (with switches snooping the exchanges) use that state to replicate the stream solely onto segments holding subscribers: one copy in the core, fan-out at the edges, silence on portless segments. A is the missing piece that makes 'only where there are viewers' true. (B) trades on the one-letter similarity: ICMP carries error and diagnostic messages (unreachables, time-exceeded) and manages no group membership; it is the answer to how routers report delivery problems. (C) is how the team would watch the rollout succeed, not how the rollout works; it is management-plane telemetry with no role in forwarding decisions. (D) routes between autonomous systems on the internet's scale; an interior campus stream neither needs nor uses exterior route advertisement, and BGP carries no membership semantics. Efficient one-to-many delivery is two problems, replication (multicast forwarding) and audience discovery (IGMP membership), and the design fails without the second.

questionsV2.question: Which routing protocol BEST fits a 60-site network needing fast reconvergence and regional aggregation, and why?

options.A: RIP, because a simple hop-count metric stays easy to reason about across all 60 sites.
options.B: Static routes pushed to every site by configuration management, avoiding dynamic routing protocols and their failure modes entirely.
options.C: BGP, because a protocol that scales to the entire global internet will comfortably handle routing for a 60-site network.
options.D: OSPF, because routers recompute from a full topology map for fast reconvergence, and its areas match regional aggregation.

questionsV2.explanation: Both requirements select link-state: OSPF routers share a synchronized topology map and recompute paths locally the moment a failure is flooded, delivering the seconds-scale reconvergence asked for, and its area hierarchy exists precisely to summarize regions into a backbone, and the addressing plan maps onto it directly; D is right for reasons that match the requirements point for point. (A) fails the speed requirement: distance-vector convergence with hold-down timers is measured in minutes, and hop count ignores link capacity; simplicity was nobody's stated requirement. (B) removes reconvergence altogether: static routes do not react to failures, so 'within seconds' becomes 'when an operator intervenes'. That is right only for stub sites with a single path. (C) is capable but mis-reasoned and mis-fit: BGP is a path-vector policy protocol for routing between autonomous systems, tuned for stability over speed; 'scales to the internet' is the classic bigger-is-better fallacy, and interior fast convergence is the one thing it is not designed for. Interior networks needing fast failover want link-state protocols, and a design whose areas mirror the address hierarchy is choosing the protocol for what it was built to do.

questionsV2.question: Users will authenticate with directory passwords that must stay protected over the air. Which method BEST fits?

options.A: EAP-TLS, mutually authenticating the client and the server with X.509 certificates issued to each side.
options.B: EAP-MD5, hashing the password exchange so the credential itself is not transmitted over the air.
options.C: LEAP, using a lightweight proprietary vendor challenge-response protocol designed specifically for early wireless deployments.
options.D: PEAP, opening a server-authenticated TLS tunnel and passing the password exchange inside it.

questionsV2.explanation: The constraints are explicit (password authentication, no client PKI, credentials protected over the air), and PEAP is the method shaped to them: the client first validates the server's certificate and builds a TLS tunnel (one server-side certificate is the entire PKI bill), then runs the password exchange inside that encrypted, server-authenticated channel, so credentials neither travel exposed nor get offered to an impostor AP; D satisfies every stated condition. (A) is the stronger method and the wrong fit: mutual certificate authentication presupposes issuing and lifecycle-managing a certificate per client, exactly the PKI the stem rules out; it is the right answer the day that budget exists. (B) fails the transit requirement it pretends to meet: an unprotected challenge-response hash invites offline guessing, the method authenticates no server, and it yields no keying material for the wireless session. (C) is a broken legacy proprietary method whose challenge-response fell to practical cracking tools years ago, and choosing it re-imports the problem. When passwords must cross wireless, wrap them in a server-authenticated tunnel. Read constraints as hard requirements: the technically strongest method is wrong when it needs infrastructure the design cannot have.

questionsV2.question: The bank must block uploads to personal cloud storage and strip risky methods while allowing ordinary browsing. Which control is BEST suited to decisions at that level of detail?

options.A: A stateful inspection firewall filtering each connection by source address, destination address and destination port.
options.B: An access control list applied directly to the router at each branch office's internet uplink.
options.C: A circuit-level gateway that relays outbound TCP sessions to the internet after validating each connection handshake.
options.D: An application-layer proxy gateway that terminates sessions and applies policy to methods and content.

questionsV2.explanation: The policy is written in the vocabulary of the application protocol (this HTTP method but not that one, this action on a site while permitting the site itself), so enforcement requires a device that reads that vocabulary. An application-layer proxy terminates the client's session, sees full requests and payloads, and can strip a method or block an upload while passing the page view: only D operates where the policy's distinctions exist. (A) is an excellent connection gatekeeper, but its decision space is addresses, ports and connection state; an upload and a page view to the same site are identical at that resolution, so it can only allow or forbid the site wholesale. (B) is the same limitation with less: stateless address-and-port matching at the uplink, right for coarse boundary hygiene and blind to content. (C) sits one layer higher than a packet filter yet still below the need: a circuit-level gateway vets and relays sessions without interpreting the data inside them, so it too cannot tell method from method.

questionsV2.question: Which configuration is MOST appropriate for the two application servers?

options.A: Transport mode using ESP, encrypting the payload end to end while the original IP headers route the packets.
options.B: Tunnel mode using ESP terminated on the data center's perimeter firewalls rather than on the two servers themselves.
options.C: Tunnel mode using ESP running directly between the two servers, wrapping every packet inside a second, outer IP header.
options.D: Transport mode using AH, signing each packet so any modification in transit is detected on receipt.

questionsV2.explanation: When the communicating hosts are the security endpoints and the path between them is routable as-is, transport mode is the natural fit: ESP encrypts the payload, the original headers keep doing the routing, and no second IP header is added. That meets the confidentiality requirement at minimum overhead, so A. (B) moves the crypto boundary to devices the requirement excluded: firewall-terminated tunnels leave the server-to-firewall legs unprotected inside the very network the files traverse, and the requirement was host-terminated protection. (C) works and protects the data, but it fails the stated tiebreaker: encapsulating host-to-host traffic adds a redundant outer header carrying the same addresses; tunnel mode earns its overhead when gateways speak for hidden networks, which is the previous question's scenario, not this one. (D) chooses the wrong service: AH detects tampering but transmits the settlement data readable, so confidentiality, the actual requirement, is unmet. Mode follows the endpoints (hosts: transport; gateways: tunnel), and protocol follows the property needed (secrecy: ESP; origin integrity alone: AH).

questionsV2.question: Which design BEST implements the single hardened entry point for enclave administration?

options.A: Firewall rules permitting SSH and RDP from each administrator's registered workstation to the enclave hosts.
options.B: A bastion (jump) host in a controlled segment, the only source permitted to reach enclave management interfaces.
options.C: Individual VPN profiles on administrator laptops, each terminating inside the enclave's server network.
options.D: A dedicated management VLAN trunked from the administrators' desk switches into the enclave switches.

questionsV2.explanation: The architecture asked for is a choke point: one hardened system that every management session must traverse, where MFA is enforced once and session logging is complete. That is the definition of a bastion or jump host, made effective by firewall policy that admits management traffic from it alone; B implements the requirement rather than approximating it. (A) creates as many entry points as there are administrators: each workstation becomes an attack path into the enclave, MFA and logging must be replicated everywhere, and one compromised desktop reaches the servers directly. It is the pattern the requirement exists to eliminate. (C) also multiplies entry points, just tunneled: per-laptop VPNs terminate inside the enclave, so a stolen laptop carries the enclave with it, and sessions bypass any central recording. It suits remote access to a general network, not privileged access to an enclave. (D) extends Layer 2 adjacency across the boundary: a trunked VLAN is connectivity, not control, and offers no authentication or session capture at all. Privileged access wants concentration, one heavily instrumented door, because every additional path into a sensitive zone is a full copy of the risk.

questionsV2.question: After a circuit failed, two routers re-advertised the dead network to each other for minutes, the metric climbing. Which underlying behavior BEST explains the episode?

options.A: Each router floods a complete topology map after every change, so a failure generates duplicated route advertisements.
options.B: The two routers' update timers fell out of synchronization, so each advertised stale route information on a different periodic refresh cycle.
options.C: Routers learn only their neighbors' summarized distances, so two of them can keep re-advertising a failed path to each other.
options.D: The failed circuit kept flapping between up and down states, and every transition triggered a fresh advertisement.

questionsV2.explanation: The stair-step metric is the fingerprint: in distance-vector routing no router sees the topology, each believing whatever distances its neighbors summarize, so when the network died, each router took the other's stale advertisement as evidence of an alternate path, re-advertised it back one hop worse, and the pair inflated the metric in lockstep until the protocol's 'infinity' ceiling declared the route unreachable. That mutual rumour loop is count-to-infinity, and it is why split horizon, poison reverse and a small maximum metric exist; C names the mechanism that generates exactly this trace. (A) describes the other protocol family: link-state routers flood topology advertisements and would each compute the loss locally in seconds, never bidding a metric upward. (B) blames scheduling for a structural problem: timer alignment changes when stale routes are spoken, not why each router believes the other's. (D) predicts a different trace: flapping yields alternating up/down advertisements tracking the circuit, not a monotonic climb to a fixed maximum on a link that stayed dead. Routing-by-rumour fails by believing your own echo; read a steadily inflating metric as count-to-infinity, the signature pathology of distance-vector convergence.

questionsV2.question: Which point in the resolution chain was MOST likely compromised?

options.A: The bank's authoritative name servers, altered to serve the attacker's address for the portal's name.
options.B: The registrar account, with the domain's delegation quietly repointed at attacker-controlled name servers.
options.C: The recursive resolvers' caches, poisoned to return the attacker's address for the portal hostname.
options.D: The customers' local hosts files, each overwritten by malware to pin the portal to the attacker's address.

questionsV2.explanation: Work the chain against the evidence: answers are wrong at the clients, yet the zone's source of truth is clean and the delegation still points at it, so the corruption sits between authority and client, which is the recursive resolver layer, where forged answers can be cached and then served to every user of that resolver; C fits all three facts at once and explains many customers being hit through a shared point. (A) is directly contradicted: the stem verifies the authoritative records unchanged; it would be the finding in a zone-tampering incident. (B) is likewise excluded by the intact delegation, and a registrar hijack typically redirects the whole domain, visible in WHOIS and NS records; it answers a scenario where delegation data changed. (D) could produce identical symptoms on one machine, but requires separate malware on every affected customer, a far larger assumption than one poisoned shared cache, and mass reports across ISPs point upstream. DNS trouble localizes by comparing answers at each tier (client, resolver, authority), and cache poisoning lives in the middle tier that everyone shares.

questionsV2.question: A single crafted packet whose fragments reassemble beyond the maximum legal size crashes a legacy controller. Which attack class does this MOST precisely demonstrate?

options.A: Teardrop: the fragments' offsets deliberately overlap, and the reassembly logic corrupts adjacent memory when it tries to combine them.
options.B: Smurf: amplified echo traffic from many distant sources exhausts the controller's inbound network bandwidth.
options.C: SYN flood: half-open connection state accumulates until the controller's session table is exhausted.
options.D: Ping of death: the reassembled datagram exceeds the maximum legal IP size, overflowing the buffer that receives it.
