questionsV2.explanation: The two facts that classify it are 'single packet' and 'reassembles beyond 65,535 bytes': IP's length field cannot describe a larger datagram, so old stacks allocated buffers assuming that ceiling, and fragments summing past it overflow the buffer on reassembly: a crash from one malformed packet, which is the ping of death; D names both the class and the mechanism the test demonstrated. (A) is the near cousin and the trap: teardrop is also a fragmentation-reassembly exploit, but its lever is overlapping offsets confusing the reassembly logic, not total size exceeding the legal maximum. The stem specifies size, not overlap. (B) and (C) are volume attacks and fail the arithmetic of the evidence: a smurf needs many amplified senders saturating bandwidth, and a SYN flood needs a stream of TCP connection attempts building state; neither can be demonstrated by one ICMP packet, and both degrade service rather than crash a stack. One-packet kills point to malformed-input bugs. Classify fragmentation exploits by their lever, oversize (ping of death) versus overlap (teardrop), and remember such flaws live on in unpatched embedded stacks.

questionsV2.question: The manager wants every device authenticated against corporate identity before its traffic is admitted. Which control BEST meets that?

options.A: 802.1X port-based access control, with a RADIUS server validating each device's credentials or certificate.
options.B: Static MAC-address filtering, maintained by hand by the network team for every access port in the building.
options.C: Assignment of all the lobby wall jacks to a segregated guest VLAN restricted to internet access only.
options.D: DHCP reservations for known machines, so unrecognized devices receive no usable address.

questionsV2.explanation: The requirement has two parts, authentication against corporate identity and enforcement before any traffic passes, and 802.1X is the mechanism built for exactly that pairing: the switch port stays closed to everything except the authentication exchange until the RADIUS server accepts the device's credentials or certificate, so admission is an identity decision, not a wiring decision; hence A. (B) is identity by hardware address, which is no identity at all: MACs are observed on the wire and spoofed in seconds, and a hand-maintained list across a headquarters decays immediately; it approximates the goal only on tiny, static networks. (C) is worthwhile containment and pairs well with 802.1X as the destination for failed authentications, but by itself it authenticates nobody; it answers 'how do we serve visitors safely', not 'how do we admit only authenticated devices'. (D) merely declines to hand out configuration: a visitor who statically assigns an address bypasses it entirely, since the port itself forwards freely. Enforcement must sit at the point of connection and be keyed to identity. Anything that filters after admission, or keys on spoofable attributes, is a courtesy rather than a control.

questionsV2.question: Audits keep finding branch firewall and routing policies drifting from the corporate standard. Which capability MOST directly addresses that?

options.A: It replaces the branches' broadband and LTE circuits with uniformly provisioned MPLS.
options.B: It raises each branch's usable bandwidth by bonding whatever links the site has available.
options.C: It applies centrally defined policy to every branch edge device, independent of each site's underlying transport.
options.D: It encrypts traffic between branches using keys that each site's edge device manages for itself.

questionsV2.explanation: The finding is configuration drift, 200 hand-tended devices diverging from standard, and the SD-WAN property that answers it is the separation of control plane from transport: policy is authored once in the orchestrator and pushed to every edge, so the architecture itself enforces the standard, with no reliance on 200 acts of local discipline, and an audit compares sites against one source of truth; that is C, and 'independent of transport' is what lets one policy span MPLS, broadband and LTE alike. (A) reverses SD-WAN's economics: the technology exists to use cheap heterogeneous links safely, not to standardize on the expensive one, and uniform circuits would not stop local config drift anyway. (B) is a genuine SD-WAN benefit aimed at a different complaint; more bandwidth fixes congestion findings, not policy findings. (D) undercuts itself in the second clause: SD-WAN does encrypt its overlay, but per-site self-managed keying is the decentralization the finding indicts; the value lies in central orchestration of the crypto too. Recurring drift across many sites is a management-plane problem; buy centralization of control, not more capacity or faster links.

questionsV2.question: Which control MOST directly provides that assurance to resolvers?

options.A: DNS over HTTPS between customers' machines and their resolvers, encrypting every query and response in transit.
options.B: Shorter TTL values on the bank's records, so poisoned cache entries expire and are replaced more quickly.
options.C: Restricting zone transfers so that only the bank's own secondary name servers can copy the zone.
options.D: DNSSEC on the bank's zone, publishing signed records that resolvers validate for origin and integrity.

questionsV2.explanation: The requirement is data authenticity, proof that an answer is what the zone owner published, and that is DNSSEC's exact function: records are cryptographically signed in a chain anchored at the root, so a validating resolver detects any forged or altered answer no matter which cache or path supplied it; D matches the requirement verbatim. (A) protects a different property on a different segment: DoH encrypts the client-resolver channel against eavesdropping and tampering en route, but the resolver's answer is trusted as received: a poisoned resolver serves its forgery over beautifully encrypted transport; DoH answers a query-privacy question. (B) shrinks the damage window without adding any verification; poison simply expires sooner and can be re-inserted; a mitigation, not an assurance. (C) guards bulk zone disclosure and copy integrity between the bank's own servers, a hygiene control unrelated to what resolvers can verify. Encryption of the channel and signing of the data are different guarantees, and only signatures survive whatever path the data took.

questionsV2.question: A branch design justifies no inbound filtering because the site is behind address translation. Which evaluation of that is MOST accurate?

options.A: NAT is equivalent to a stateful firewall, since both maintain per-connection state tables that gate what may enter the network.
options.B: NAT obscures internal addressing and incidentally drops unsolicited inbound traffic, but enforcing security policy still requires a firewall.
options.C: NAT reduces security overall, because rewriting packet headers strips the very fields that inspection devices depend on.
options.D: NAT gives translated sessions confidentiality, since outside observers see only the rewritten public addresses on the wire.

questionsV2.explanation: NAT was built to stretch IPv4 addresses: it rewrites headers and keeps translation state so replies find their way back. Two side effects look like security: internal numbering is not visible outside, and unsolicited inbound packets die for lack of a mapping. But side effects have no policy: no rule language, no logging designed for security decisions, and the protection evaporates wherever mappings exist (port forwards, hairpins, protocol helpers) or wherever traffic is solicited, which is how phishing-delivered malware connects out and NAT obligingly sustains the session. B credits the incidental benefit and names the missing thing: enforced, auditable policy, which is a firewall's job. (A) is the equivalence the design note depends on, and it fails at the definition: both keep state, but only one consults policy; a translation table answers 'how do I rewrite this', not 'should this pass'. (C) manufactures a downside from a real nuisance. NAT complicates some inspection and end-to-end protocols, but 'reduces security overall' does not follow. (D) confuses hiding an address with protecting a payload: translated traffic is as readable in transit as any other cleartext. Classify controls by what they were designed to decide. NAT decides address rewriting; only a control whose purpose is admission policy should be cited as your inbound defense.

questionsV2.question: As an interim measure using only the existing access switches, which control MOST directly curbs the mini-switches?

options.A: Reassign the affected wall jacks into an isolated guest VLAN with internet-only access.
options.B: Configure port security, limiting each access port to a small fixed number of learned hardware addresses.
options.C: Deploy 802.1X authentication on every access port, with each connecting device's credentials checked against the corporate directory service.
options.D: Enable DHCP snooping, blocking lease offers that originate from any port not designated as a server port.

questionsV2.explanation: The observable signature of a desk mini-switch is several source MAC addresses appearing on one access port, and port security acts on exactly that signal: cap the learned addresses at one or two, violate into shutdown or restrict, and the fan-out stops working the moment a second device speaks, configured entirely on the switches already in place, which honors both stated constraints; B is the direct interim fit. (A) changes what the extra devices can reach, while leaving them free to connect: the mini-switch keeps working inside the guest VLAN, so the practice is accommodated, not curbed. It is the right move for jacks meant for visitors. (C) is the better end-state and the wrong answer today: 802.1X needs the RADIUS infrastructure the stem rules out; it answers the follow-up question of what the branch should build toward. (D) watches a different protocol: snooping polices rogue DHCP servers and builds binding tables; personal laptops taking leases through a mini-switch never trip it. Pick controls whose trigger condition matches the behavior you want to stop; multiple MACs on one port is the fingerprint here, and port security is the control that reads it.

questionsV2.question: Which measure BEST keeps the promotional site available through the spike and the attack traffic?

options.A: Double the origin's web servers behind the existing load balancer ahead of the launch window.
options.B: Add a second internet circuit at the origin data center, roughly doubling the total ingress bandwidth available for the launch.
options.C: Set aggressive browser-caching headers, so returning visitors render the promotional pages from their own local caches.
options.D: Front the site with a content delivery network, serving cached content from edge locations near the traffic's sources.

questionsV2.explanation: Fifty-fold plus a flood is a scale problem that a single origin cannot meet at the origin: a CDN answers it by moving the serving edge outward: promotional content is cached across many distributed points, each visitor is served nearby, and both the legitimate spike and volumetric attack traffic are spread across the provider's aggregate capacity instead of converging on one building. The origin keeps its architecture and sees a trickle of cache fills; D meets the availability goal within the no-re-platforming constraint, and static promotional content is the ideal cacheable workload. (A) buys 2x against 50x, and compute was never the choke point a volumetric flood aims at; the pipe is. (B) widens that pipe finitely while leaving every packet converging on one location; volumetric attacks are sized in multiples of any circuit pair. (C) helps only visitors who have already been served once, and launch traffic is first visits by definition, and attackers' tools ignore cache headers entirely. Availability at internet scale comes from distributing where demand is absorbed; capacity added at a single point is spent the moment the internet aims at it.

questionsV2.question: Which wireless configuration MOST directly removes the offline guessing exposure?

options.A: WPA2-Personal with a forty-character random passphrase that is rotated every week.
options.B: WPA3-Personal, whose SAE exchange gives a captured handshake no material for offline password guessing.
options.C: Hiding the staff SSID from broadcast and filtering client hardware addresses at each access point.
options.D: WPA2 with TKIP disabled, so every access point requires AES-CCMP for the data frames.

questionsV2.explanation: The exposure is structural to WPA2-PSK: its four-way handshake lets anyone who captures it test passphrase guesses offline, off the air, at hardware speed. SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) redesigns the exchange so each guess requires a live interaction with the network; a capture yields nothing to grind on. That removes the offline attack as a class outright, which is B, and 'MOST directly removes' is the discriminator. (A) is respectable hardening and a truly random forty-character secret resists dictionaries well, but the captured handshake remains attackable offline; the exposure is shrunk, not removed, and weekly rotation of a shared secret across a fleet invites operational leakage. It is the right answer where WPA3 hardware is unavailable. (C) is visibility theater: SSIDs appear in probe and association frames anyway, and MAC filters fall to trivial spoofing; neither touches the handshake. (D) hardens the data cipher, but the dictionary attack targets the key derivation, not TKIP-vs-CCMP. When an attack is inherent to a protocol's design, the fix is the successor protocol that redesigned the exchange; configuration tuning around it only adjusts the attacker's effort.

questionsV2.question: Which protocol change MOST directly prevents the replayed authorization being accepted a second time?

options.A: Upgrading to a stronger cipher, so captured authorization messages take far longer to decrypt.
options.B: Rotating the encryption keys used by each ATM on a daily schedule instead of monthly.
options.C: Hashing each message body, so any modification made to it in transit is detected on receipt.
options.D: Adding timestamps and sequence numbers that the processing center validates, so a repeated message is recognized and refused.

questionsV2.explanation: The demonstration is a replay attack, and its defining lesson is that the attacker needed to read nothing: a captured ciphertext, re-sent intact, is decrypted and honoured by the legitimate recipient like the original. The missing property is freshness: the receiver cannot tell a first presentation from a repeat. It is supplied by validated timestamps, sequence numbers or nonces, which make the duplicate detectably stale; D adds exactly the property whose absence the testers proved. (A) strengthens a lock the attacker never picks: replay works on unread ciphertext, so cipher strength is orthogonal; it is the right investment when the finding is cryptanalysis, not repetition. (B) narrows the replay window to the key's lifetime, and an hour-old message sails through a daily rotation; a mitigation of degree where the question demands one of kind. (C) protects integrity, but the replayed message is unmodified, so a hash over it verifies perfectly and endorses the fraud; integrity checks answer tampering findings. Confidentiality, integrity and freshness are separate guarantees; a protocol can encrypt and authenticate flawlessly and still pay twice, until something in each message proves it is new.

questionsV2.question: Packets shuttled between two misconfigured routers until a header field reached zero and an error returned. Which mechanism limited the damage?

options.A: The TCP retransmission timer, which bounds how long any unacknowledged segment stays in flight before the sending host finally gives up.
options.B: The fragmentation offset field, which forces malformed or oversized packets to be discarded at each hop along the forwarding path they traverse.
options.C: The IP time-to-live field, decremented at each router so that packets caught in forwarding loops are eventually discarded.
options.D: The Ethernet frame check sequence, which discards any frame whose contents were corrupted somewhere in transit between two directly adjacent devices.

questionsV2.explanation: The capture narrates the mechanism: a field decreasing at each router, a discard when it runs out, and 'time exceeded' notifications. That is the IP TTL (hop limit in IPv6), a per-packet self-destruct decremented by every forwarding hop precisely so that a routing loop degrades into discarded packets and error messages instead of a link-saturating storm of immortal traffic. The mutual default routes made the loop; TTL made it survivable, and the same expiry mechanism is what traceroute exploits deliberately. C identifies both mechanism and purpose. (A) lives in the endpoints, not the path: retransmission timers govern when a sender tries again and cannot expire a packet already circling between routers; arguably they add traffic while the loop persists. (B) is a reassembly bookkeeping field; nothing about fragmentation offsets counts hops or expires looping datagrams. (D) checks integrity per link: the shuttling packets were perfectly intact, and corruption detection has no opinion about forwarding sanity. Networks assume routing will sometimes be wrong, so packets carry a hop budget. Recognize TTL expiry and 'time exceeded' backscatter as the visible signature of a loop being safely bled off.

questionsV2.question: Engineering proposes split tunneling to relieve saturated concentrators. What is the MOST accurate statement of the trade-off?

options.A: The tunnel's cryptography is weakened, because the concentrator must maintain two separate policies for every connected client.
options.B: There is no meaningful change, because traffic to the corporate ranges remains encrypted exactly as it was before the split tunnel was introduced.
options.C: Exposure is doubled, because corporate traffic now traverses both the tunnel and the public internet on every request.
options.D: Corporate traffic stays protected, but the endpoint's internet traffic bypasses corporate inspection while the device holds a path into the internal network.

questionsV2.explanation: A trade-off statement has to name what is gained and what is genuinely given up. Split tunneling leaves the corporate flow encrypted and relieves the concentrators (the gain) while sending the endpoint's general internet traffic outside the corporate security stack (web filtering, DLP, monitoring), on a device that simultaneously holds an authenticated route into the LAN: a browser compromise now sits one hop from the internal network with the defenses unsighted. D captures exactly that, which is what a CISO must weigh. (A) invents a cryptographic cost: policy routing decides which packets enter the tunnel and leaves the cipher untouched. (B) is the engineer's half-truth: the encryption claim is correct, but 'no meaningful change' ignores the inspection bypass, which is the entire trade-off. (C) reverses the mechanism: corporate traffic still travels only the tunnel; nothing is sent twice. Evaluate tunneling changes by where the traffic stops being watched, not just where it stays encrypted. Protection and visibility are separate properties.

questionsV2.question: Which statement of the push-button setup risk is MOST accurate?

options.A: It weakens the encryption in use, forcing access points to fall back from AES to TKIP for all clients.
options.B: It broadcasts the network passphrase in cleartext during every new client association handshake, so anyone capturing the exchange can read it directly.
options.C: Its PIN can be brute-forced in hours because each half is validated separately, after which the passphrase is recoverable.
options.D: It lets joining clients bypass captive-portal authentication on nearby guest wireless networks that gate access through a web page.

questionsV2.explanation: Findings survive challenge only when the mechanism is stated correctly: WPS's external-PIN design confirms the two halves of its eight-digit PIN independently, collapsing the search space to a few thousand tries per half, so an online brute force completes in hours and the protocol then hands over the network passphrase. C is the defensible statement and the reason 'disable WPS' is standard remediation. (A) invents a cipher interaction: WPS automates enrollment and has no effect on the AES/TKIP suite the AP negotiates; a reviewer who knows this discards the finding, the credibility failure the stem warns about. (B) also misstates the mechanism: the passphrase is delivered inside the WPS protocol exchange after PIN authentication, not broadcast in cleartext at each association; close enough to sound right, wrong enough to be challenged. (D) connects WPS to captive portals, which are unrelated web-layer gating on open networks.

questionsV2.question: Which response to the network team's argument about individual accounts is MOST accurate?

options.A: The team is right: per-administrator accountability addresses the principal risk, which is untraceable shared access to devices.
options.B: The team is right if management traffic is confined to a dedicated VLAN, since that separation is functionally equivalent to encryption.
options.C: The team is wrong: Telnet carries those individual credentials and every session in cleartext, so interception yields working administrator access; replace it with SSH.
options.D: The team is wrong about switches but right about routers, which sit behind the perimeter and face less interception risk.

questionsV2.explanation: The argument defends the wrong property: TACACS+ gives attribution (who logged in, what they typed), but Telnet transmits the login and the session as cleartext on the wire, so anyone positioned to capture branch traffic collects the very credentials the accounting system so carefully individualizes, plus every configuration detail that scrolls by. Accountability and confidentiality are independent, and the fix is the encrypted equivalent, SSH, which preserves the TACACS+ model intact; C. (A) names a real risk Telnet-with-TACACS+ does solve, then stops one property short: attribution of sessions an attacker can read and hijack is cold comfort. (B) is the segmentation-equals-encryption fallacy this domain keeps refuting: a management VLAN narrows who is positioned to listen, and whoever gets there, by one compromised host or one misconfigured trunk, reads everything; separation bounds exposure, encryption removes it. (D) invents a perimeter distinction with no basis: both device classes carry credentials in the clear, interception risk is about path, not device type, and cleartext administrative access is unacceptable anywhere. Evaluate a protocol against each property separately. Telnet plus perfect AAA still fails confidentiality, and 'we know who logged in' does not answer 'who else was reading'.

questionsV2.question: An external scan shows a remote-shell port open on forty hosts, permitted inbound from any source. Which risk assessment is MOST accurate?

options.A: The exposure is minor, because the service listening on that port encrypts every session between client and server.
options.B: Forty hosts offer remote administrative shells to the whole internet; that access belongs behind one hardened, MFA-protected entry point.
options.C: A false positive in effect: an open port carries no real risk until a vulnerability is published for the service.
options.D: The principal risk is information disclosure through service banners, which changing the daemon's banner text will resolve.

questionsV2.explanation: Port 22 is SSH, remote administrative shell access, so the finding reads: forty separately maintained doors to command-line control, reachable by every address on the internet, each accepting credential-guessing at line rate and each exposed to the next pre-auth vulnerability in its daemon. The assessment that captures both the severity and the fix is B: collapse the surface to a single bastion with MFA, logging, and firewall rules admitting enclave SSH from it alone. Forty exposures become one instrumented chokepoint. (A) mistakes the session's property for the exposure's: encryption protects traffic from observers, and does nothing about who may connect, guess, or exploit; the risk here is reachability, not readability. (C) inverts the discipline: brute force works against weak credentials with no CVE required, and 'wait for the advisory' concedes the race to whoever scans first. Attack surface is managed before vulnerabilities are announced. (D) trims the leaf and leaves the tree: banners ease reconnaissance slightly, and rewording them changes no attacker's ability to connect. Assess an open port by the capability behind it and the audience in front of it. Administrative capability plus a global audience is a critical finding whatever the protocol's cryptography.

questionsV2.question: Which control MOST directly protects the telephony signaling traffic?

options.A: Transporting SIP over TLS, so call setup and teardown exchanges are encrypted between the endpoints and call servers.
options.B: Enabling SRTP, so the media streams carrying the audio between endpoints are encrypted and authenticated.
options.C: Moving the handsets onto a dedicated voice VLAN, separated from the workstation segments of the LAN.
options.D: Enforcing 802.1X on handset ports, so only authorized telephones can join the branch network.

questionsV2.explanation: What leaked is signaling, the SIP conversation that sets calls up and tears them down, and the direct control is to encrypt that channel itself: SIP over TLS wraps the setup exchange, hiding numbers, extensions and, critically, the session keys that the endpoints negotiate for the media; A protects precisely the traffic that was captured. (B) guards the other half of a call: SRTP encrypts the audio stream, but the capture here was of signaling, which SRTP does not touch. Unprotected signaling can expose the very keys SRTP depends on, which is why the two controls are deployed together; B answers the next question, about recorded audio. (C) reduces who can easily reach the packets by separating segments, but a VLAN is a containment measure, and this capture happened on the LAN; traffic within the voice VLAN remains cleartext to anyone who gets there. (D) governs which devices may join, not what their traffic reveals: an authorized-but-compromised host still reads cleartext signaling. Telephony has two channels with two protections, TLS for the signaling and SRTP for the media, and encrypting either one leaves the other exposed.

questionsV2.question: Which attack sequence BEST explains the drops, reconnections and warnings together?

options.A: A deauthentication flood pushed clients off the legitimate network so they would re-associate to an evil twin carrying the same SSID.
options.B: A WPS PIN attack recovered the staff passphrase overnight, after which the attacker quietly joined the staff network as one more ordinary client.
options.C: Wideband jamming across the festival Wi-Fi channels overwhelmed the access points and temporarily forced the staff handhelds onto their cellular fallback connectivity.
options.D: DHCP pool exhaustion on the staff network denied new leases until the access points were power-cycled by staff.

questionsV2.explanation: A good explanation covers every observation: forged deauthentication frames account for the sudden drop; auto-rejoin plus a stronger same-SSID signal accounts for clients landing on the impostor; and traffic now traversing an attacker's network accounts for the TLS certificate warnings. A strings all three into the classic deauth-then-evil-twin sequence, corroborated by the survey. (B) explains at most a quiet attacker presence on the real network: a joined client causes no mass disconnects, no reconnection anomalies, and no certificate errors; it answers a scenario about passphrase compromise, and WPS is an AP-side feature besides. (C) fails on the reconnect: jammed handhelds falling back to cellular would not re-associate to Wi-Fi, and jamming cannot explain a second network advertising the staff SSID. (D) is an availability fault with the wrong footprint: no drop of already-associated clients, no rogue SSID, no TLS warnings. Certificate warnings after an unexplained Wi-Fi bounce are the signature of traffic re-homed through an impostor.

questionsV2.question: Which statement BEST captures the primary risk the unlabeled access point creates?

options.A: The open network lets passers-by consume the corporate internet connection's bandwidth without any usage accounting.
options.B: The device's radio may interfere with the sanctioned access points operating on nearby channels in the same band.
options.C: It creates an unauthenticated radio bridge into the wired LAN that bypasses the perimeter and network access controls.
options.D: Its consumer firmware will fall behind on security patches, since no one in the organization owns its ongoing maintenance.

questionsV2.explanation: Rank the harms and one dwarfs the rest: an open AP bridged to the corporate wired network extends that network, unauthenticated, into radio range. Anyone in the parking lot obtains what amounts to an inside jack, entering behind the firewall, behind admission control, invisible to perimeter monitoring. That nullification of the boundary architecture is the primary risk, and it is why rogue access points are treated as incidents rather than tidiness problems; C. (A) is real and trivial by comparison, a bandwidth and acceptable-use nuisance that would top the list only for an AP isolated from corporate assets. (B) is an airtime-management concern for the wireless team; interference degrades performance and confers no access. (D) is a genuine secondary finding (unowned devices do rot), but patch latency matters on this device mostly because of the exposure C already describes; unmanaged lifecycle is the chronic issue, the open bridge is the acute one. Severity ranking asks what the finding gives an attacker. A rogue AP gives interior network access from outside the walls, which outranks every operational side effect it also causes.

questionsV2.question: Ransomware at a subsidiary is traced to a remote desktop port opened for a vendor and forgotten. Which pairing of lesson and remediation is MOST appropriate?

options.A: The password policy failed; require substantially longer and more complex vendor-account passwords, rotated regularly, while keeping the existing access path unchanged.
options.B: Vendor management failed; terminate the vendor's contract and permanently disable the account that was brute-forced.
options.C: External visibility failed; raise the frequency of the bank's perimeter vulnerability scanning so that temporary firewall openings are discovered and closed sooner.
options.D: Remote desktop was internet-reachable; move it behind an MFA-protected gateway and give every firewall exception an owner and expiry.

questionsV2.explanation: Port 3389 is RDP, interactive desktop control, and the causal chain has two links a report must break: the service was exposed to the whole internet, and the exposure was created ad hoc with no expiry, so it outlived its purpose silently. D fixes both: remote desktop reachable only through an authenticated, MFA-protected gateway ends internet-facing password guessing as an access route, and exceptions carrying owners and expiry dates end the 'temporary and forgotten' pattern that created the target. Lesson is matched to root cause, remediation to lesson. (A) hardens the credential while preserving the exposure: longer, regularly rotated passwords slow guessing against a service that should not be guessable from the internet at all; symptom, not cause. (B) punishes a party the analysis does not blame (the vendor needed access; the bank chose the mechanism), and the pattern survives for the next vendor. (C) buys faster discovery of mistakes the process will keep making: detection of standing exposures is worthwhile, and it is the compensating control, not the fix. Incident lessons should name the decision that created the exposure. Administrative interfaces belong behind authenticated gateways, and every 'temporary' rule needs a mechanism that ends it.

questionsV2.question: Which control MOST directly prevents an eavesdropper recovering conversation content from captured streams?

options.A: SIP over TLS, encrypting the call-setup channel between the handsets and the call servers.
options.B: SRTP, encrypting and authenticating the media streams that actually carry the audio.
options.C: Disabling port mirroring on branch switches except during approved troubleshooting windows.
options.D: Transcoding calls with a proprietary audio codec so captured streams resist casual decoding.

questionsV2.explanation: The recovered artefact is audio, and audio travels in the media stream (RTP), separate from signaling; the control that makes a captured stream unplayable is SRTP, which encrypts and integrity-protects the media packets themselves, so a mirrored copy yields ciphertext wherever it was collected. B addresses the exact loss demonstrated. (A) is the complement, not the fix: TLS on SIP hides call metadata and protects key negotiation, but the audio packets it sets up still travel unencrypted if SRTP is off; it is the right answer to the previous finding, about readable signaling. (C) attacks one collection method rather than the exposure: mirroring is merely how this red team listened; taps, compromised switches, or any on-path position hear the same cleartext, and the control evaporates the moment an attacker can configure a switch. (D) is obscurity with a shelf life: codecs are identified from RTP headers and decoders are public or reversible; 'harder to decode' is not a confidentiality property. Protect the data, not the vantage point: if content is cleartext on the wire, somewhere to stand and listen will always exist.

questionsV2.question: Which characterization of the label-switched service is MOST accurate?

options.A: MPLS encrypts each labeled packet between the provider's edge routers using carrier-managed keys.
options.B: MPLS separates customers' traffic using labels but applies no encryption, so confidentiality rests on trust in the provider.
options.C: MPLS wraps traffic in IPsec automatically whenever a label-switched path crosses the provider's shared core.
options.D: MPLS varies each packet's path through the core unpredictably, which makes interception impractical in the first place.

questionsV2.explanation: MPLS is a forwarding technology: labels steer each customer's packets down its own label-switched paths and keep tenants' traffic logically separated across a shared core, but the payload rides exactly as submitted, cleartext in and cleartext through. 'Private' therefore means separated, and confidentiality reduces to trusting the provider's staff, equipment and interconnects; B gives the architect the accurate characterization, and the standard consequence follows: run IPsec or TLS over the MPLS service for data that matters. (A) asserts a cryptographic service that plain MPLS has no mechanism to perform; label operations are header manipulation, and no carrier keys touch the payload. (C) imagines a default that does not exist; IPsec over MPLS is precisely the customer-side overlay the accurate characterization leads to, never an automatic property of the carrier's LSPs. (D) inverts MPLS's behavior to manufacture comfort: traffic engineering makes paths deterministic along established LSPs, and in any case an observer at one traversed point reads everything regardless of route variety. Like the private APN before it, a carrier's 'private network' is a separation claim. Test it by asking who could read the payload, and encrypt at a layer you control when the answer includes anyone but you.

questionsV2.question: Echo replies arrive from hundreds of hosts the group never contacted, each having received requests appearing to come from it. Which technique BEST explains this traffic pattern?

options.A: A SYN flood launched against the bank's internet gateway with the university's address space forged as the source of every packet.
options.B: A teardrop attack sending overlapping packet fragments through many separate hosts inside the university network.
options.C: A smurf attack, in which echo requests forged with the bank's address reached a broadcast address and every host replied.
options.D: A ping sweep of the bank's public address range conducted from a set of compromised university hosts.

questionsV2.explanation: Every detail is the smurf signature: the victim receives echo replies it never solicited (so its address was forged on someone else's requests), the repliers are ordinary legitimate hosts (so they were used as amplifiers), and they all sit in one network (so one broadcast-addressed request reached them all at once). C reconstructs the mechanism that generates precisely this evidence, one spoofed request multiplied into hundreds of replies. (A) has the spoofing backwards and the protocol wrong: a SYN flood would show TCP SYNs arriving at the bank, and forging the university's addresses would send the backscatter to the university, not replies to the bank. (B) is a malformed-fragment crash attack against a single target's reassembly code; nothing about it recruits hundreds of repliers or involves echo traffic. (D) would produce echo requests arriving at the bank and replies flowing back out; the observed direction is inverted, which is exactly how an analyst distinguishes being scanned from being reflected at. Read amplification attacks from the victim's inbox: unsolicited replies from many honest hosts in one network mean your address was borrowed and a broadcast did the multiplying.

questionsV2.question: Which remote-access approach BEST fits auditors who cannot install software and work from networks allowing only web ports?

options.A: An IPsec VPN, with a preconfigured client software profile distributed to each visiting auditor before the engagement begins.
options.B: PPTP, selected because every major desktop operating system already supports it natively with no additional client software required.
options.C: A clientless TLS (SSL) VPN portal, published on TCP port 443 and reached through a standard browser.
options.D: L2TP over IPsec, relying on the operating system's built-in virtual private network client support.

questionsV2.explanation: Both constraints point the same way: no installable software means the access method must live in what the laptops already have, a browser, and restrictive egress means it must ride the one port those networks reliably pass, 443. A clientless TLS VPN portal satisfies both, brokering the three web applications through an authenticated gateway without touching the endpoint; C is the fit, and web apps are exactly the workload such portals serve. (A) fails the first constraint outright, since a client profile is precisely the software installation the auditors' firms forbid, and IPsec's protocols are commonly dropped by strict egress filtering; it is the right answer for managed corporate laptops needing full network access. (B) clears the install hurdle and fails the security one: PPTP's authentication and cipher (MSCHAPv2, MPPE/RC4) are broken, and it is deprecated; native support does not rehabilitate it. (D) still needs per-laptop VPN configuration and the same firewall-unfriendly IPsec transport underneath. Remote-access selection is constraint-driven: who controls the endpoint and what the intervening networks pass decide the technology before security preferences do.

questionsV2.question: Which measure gives handhelds the MOST reliable way to tell the legitimate network from an impostor?

options.A: Rename the staff SSID to an obscure value and suppress it from the access points' beacon broadcasts.
options.B: Brief staff to join manually and only when the displayed signal strength is high and steady.
options.C: Lock the handhelds to 5 GHz channels, which inexpensive rogue equipment less commonly serves.
options.D: Deploy WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X), with client profiles that validate the authentication server's certificate before connecting.

questionsV2.explanation: An SSID is a self-declared name that any radio can claim, so telling twin from truth requires the network to prove an identity that cannot be copied. Under 802.1X the handheld's supplicant validates the authentication server's certificate before it will complete the join: an evil twin can echo the SSID but cannot present the certificate's private key, so a properly pinned client simply refuses it. That is cryptographic distinction, enforced by configuration rather than vigilance; D. (A) is concealment, and thin: clients probe for hidden SSIDs, advertising the name in every probe, and the twin answers with whatever name it hears; renaming resets the attacker's knowledge for a day. (B) delegates authentication to a bar graph, when the incident's premise is an attacker who transmits stronger; signal strength favors the twin by design. (C) raises the equipment bill trivially (dual-band hardware is commodity), and a band is a venue, not an identity. Names and signal properties are claimable; only a key-backed identity check lets a client refuse a perfect imitation, so make the network authenticate itself to the device.

questionsV2.question: Which explanation of the red team's result is MOST accurate?

options.A: The red team tunneled the data out inside TLS on the permitted port, indistinguishable at the firewall from ordinary encrypted web traffic.
options.B: The rule set must also have been permitting a second port, since one allowed port cannot carry both browsing and the exfiltration.
options.C: The red team split the dataset into small transfers spaced across many days, staying beneath volume-based alerting thresholds.
options.D: The red team routed the data out through the firewall's own management interface, which egress policy does not evaluate.

questionsV2.explanation: A port-only egress policy asks one question, 'is this TCP to 443?', and an attacker's TLS tunnel answers it identically to a browser: the red team wrapped its exfiltration in encrypted traffic to a server it controlled, and at the firewall's level of inspection there is nothing to distinguish stolen gigabytes from a long video call; no rule was broken, which is why no alert fired. A explains the result and exposes the assumption: port filtering was treated as data-loss control, a job that needs TLS-inspecting proxies, egress destination reputation, or DLP with visibility into the tunnel. (B) misunderstands multiplexing: one permitted port carries unlimited concurrent sessions to unlimited destinations, and that generosity is exactly what the tunnel exploits. (C) proposes a real evasion technique that the stem's facts exclude: a single afternoon session is the opposite of low-and-slow, and no volume thresholds existed to duck. (D) invents a bypass with the wrong direction of risk: management interfaces are an attack surface for reaching the firewall, not a side channel exempting traffic through it. An allowed encrypted port is a tunnel anyone may use. Egress control by port number decides where traffic may go, and says nothing about what leaves inside it.

questionsV2.question: Which statement BEST justifies the architect's objection to the wireless design document?

options.A: EAP is a proprietary protocol controlled by a single wireless vendor, and it has since been superseded by newer open standard alternatives.
options.B: EAP mandates RC4 for its inner encryption, which current corporate cryptographic policy no longer permits anywhere in the bank.
options.C: EAP is only an authentication framework; its security depends on the method carried inside it, which may be strong or weak.
options.D: EAP applies only to wired 802.1X deployments and therefore offers no real protection on wireless networks.

questionsV2.explanation: 'Secured by EAP' specifies nothing yet: EAP is a carrier framework, an envelope in which some concrete method performs the actual authentication, and the methods span mutual certificate authentication with strong key derivation (EAP-TLS) down to legacy exchanges with no server authentication or usable keying (EAP-MD5). Until the method is named, the design's security properties are indeterminate, which is precisely a reviewable defect; C is the architect's justification. (A) confuses the framework with LEAP, a vendor's lightweight method that genuinely was proprietary and broken. EAP itself is an open IETF standard, and an objection argued this way gets corrected, not actioned. (B) invents a mandate: EAP specifies no cipher at all, and that indifference is the very reason the method choice carries all the weight, making this backwards in an instructive way. (D) is simply false: carrying EAP over the air (802.1X on WLANs, historically 'EAP over LAN' extended to wireless) is the flagship enterprise Wi-Fi architecture. A framework named in a design is a decision deferred. Review the concrete method, because 'uses EAP' constrains security exactly as much as 'uses encryption' does.

questionsV2.question: Which explanation BEST connects the clock drift to the authentication failures?

options.A: Kerberos rejects authenticators whose timestamps fall outside the permitted clock skew, a freshness check that keeps captured tickets from being replayed.
options.B: Kerberos derives its session keys from the current clock value, so drifted machines compute mismatched keys.
options.C: Ticket lifetimes are measured by the client alone, so a drifted client discards its own still-valid tickets before they have truly expired.
options.D: The domain controllers sign tickets with time-based one-time codes that drifted servers can no longer generate.

questionsV2.explanation: Kerberos builds replay resistance out of time: each request carries an encrypted authenticator whose timestamp the verifier checks against its own clock, and anything outside the allowed skew (five minutes by convention) is refused as possibly re-sent. Twenty minutes of drift puts every honest authenticator outside that window, so authentication fails wholesale until the clocks agree. A ties the symptom to the mechanism and names the security purpose the check serves. (B) misplaces time in the cryptography: session keys come from the KDC's key distribution, encrypted under principal and service keys; the clock gates validity decisions, it is not key material. (C) has the arbiter wrong: lifetimes are stamped into the ticket by the KDC and enforced at validation; clients do not adjudicate their own tickets, and early self-discard would not produce server-side rejections. (D) imports TOTP, a different authentication family, into a protocol that uses plain timestamps within encrypted structures, not generated one-time codes. When authentication breaks in step with clock drift, you are watching an anti-replay freshness check do its job, which is why time synchronization is a security dependency, not an operational nicety.

domains.title: Identity & Access Management (IAM)
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 5 is identification, authentication, authorization and accountability, applied to people, devices and services. It covers access control models, the identity lifecycle, federation, and privileged access.

Case Study: The "Omni-Key" Insider Threat

### Context

QuickCash Inc. operates 300 ATMs. To save time, the regional manager created one administrative account, "SuperAdmin", password "Welcome123!", and shared it among the five field technicians. The account had unrestricted rights on the ATM management console, including PIN resets and account limits. The physical master keys for the ATM safes lived in an unlocked desk drawer in the regional office, in an envelope labelled "ATM Keys".

### What went wrong

A technician who knew he was about to be dismissed logged in as SuperAdmin from home. There was no MFA. He created ten customer accounts with high withdrawal limits, took the master keys from the drawer, drove to five ATMs, put each into service mode with the shared key, and withdrew $200,000 in cash using the accounts he had made.

The logs showed SuperAdmin logging in and SuperAdmin creating accounts. Five people could have been SuperAdmin. QuickCash could not prove which one until the cash was gone.

The white paper's access-management controls read like a list of what QuickCash lacked: MFA for technicians, administrators and any remote access; role-based access limiting each user to the minimum their job needs; default and shared passwords replaced. Its physical controls add key management and unique locks, and it notes that attackers installing malware may pose as technicians precisely because a technician's access is rarely questioned.

### What a practitioner does differently

One identity per person, always. Privileged access goes through a PAM system: the technician checks out a time-limited credential for a named task, the session is recorded, and the credential expires. MFA on every remote and privileged path. Roles split by job: a field technician gets service-mode rights on assigned machines, not console administration; account creation and limit changes belong to a separate role, and setting a limit above a threshold needs a second approver. That is separation of duties, and it would have stopped the fake accounts on the first day.

The leaver process starts when the decision to dismiss is made, before the employee is told. Access ends with the decision, not with the exit interview.

Physical keys are credentials. They live in a key cabinet with a log, under dual control, and a machine entering service mode outside a scheduled ticket raises an alert. The white paper's monitoring section lists exactly the transaction signals that would have fired here: rapid maximum withdrawals and unusual frequency from a single card.

### Outcome

The technician was identified from the ATM's camera, not from the logs. QuickCash retired the shared account, issued individual credentials with MFA, moved the keys into a controlled cabinet, and rewrote its termination procedure so revocation precedes notification.

### What the exam tests

Scenarios like this test IAAA and non-repudiation (shared accounts destroy accountability), least privilege and separation of duties, the account lifecycle and why deprovisioning is time-critical, the access control models and where RBAC fits, the factor types behind MFA, and the idea that physical access is part of identity management, not a separate concern.

### Related reading

The company in this scenario is a composite. The controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on access management, on physical security controls (key management), and on monitoring.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 1 (physical) and Domain 4 (process and governance) controls.

questions.question: Forensic investigators reviewing the QuickCash breach can see that 'SuperAdmin' logged in from a residential IP address and created the fake customer accounts, yet no individual can be charged. Which IAAA failure is the PRIMARY cause of this inability to attribute the actions?

options.A: Authentication - the account was protected by a single weak password
options.B: Identification - five people operated the console under one user identity
options.C: Authorization - the account held far more rights than technicians needed
options.D: Accountability - the console failed to log administrative sessions

questions.explanation: Attribution collapsed because the log could name only an identity, and that identity was shared: with five people behind one account, even perfect logging cannot say who acted. (A) is a real weakness - 'Welcome123!' with no MFA made compromise easy - but even a strong, MFA-protected shared account would still leave five suspects; it explains ease of entry, not loss of attribution. (C) is also true of this environment, but excessive rights widened what the insider could do; that goes to impact and does nothing to name him. (D) misreads the evidence: sessions were logged - the record said 'SuperAdmin logged in' - so accountability failed downstream of shared identification; the logging itself worked. Accountability can only ever be as granular as identification; unique identities are the foundation the other IAAA elements stand on.

questions.question: QuickCash Inc.'s five field technicians share a single 'SuperAdmin' account on the ATM management console. After a technician used it from home to create fake customer accounts and withdraw $200,000, the logs showed only that 'SuperAdmin' logged in, and no individual could be tied to the transactions. The security manager has budget for one change this quarter. Which change should the security manager recommend FIRST?

options.A: Enforce a 16-character password on the shared account and rotate it monthly
options.B: Issue each technician a uniquely named account and disable the shared account
options.C: Require multi-factor authentication for all remote logins to the console
options.D: Reduce the technicians' rights from SuperAdmin to a scoped field-service role

questions.explanation: Identification precedes authentication, authorization and accountability: until each person has a distinct identity, none of the other controls can produce an attributable log entry - MFA on a shared account still writes 'SuperAdmin logged in', and a scoped role shared by five people is still shared. The word FIRST decides it: A, C and D are all correct controls, and all three become fully effective only once B exists; that dependency, not managerial preference, makes B first. (A) strengthens the secret without changing whom the secret identifies - the right answer once accounts are individual and the finding is credential guessability. (C) is a genuinely serious gap, but five technicians sharing one account would share the MFA enrolment, so attribution stays broken - the right answer once unique identities exist and the concern is remote credential theft. (D) limits blast radius rather than restoring attribution - the right answer to how you would limit the damage one compromised account can do.

questions.question: The QuickCash technician reached the ATM console from his home computer using only the shared password. Which additional control would have been MOST effective at stopping this remote use of a credential the attacker already knew?

options.A: A stricter complexity policy applied to every administrative password
options.B: Quarterly security-awareness training on credential handling for technicians
options.C: A second authentication factor, such as a hardware token, for remote sessions
options.D: An intrusion detection sensor alerting the SOC whenever administrative logins originate from residential networks

questions.explanation: Because the attacker legitimately knew the password, the only listed control that stops the session at the point of entry is one demanding evidence he did not have: possession of an enrolled token. Hardening the secret itself (A) still leaves a single factor already known to all five technicians; that would fix a finding of guessability by outsiders. (B) targets negligence, but no amount of training restrains an insider acting deliberately - it belongs where the failure is accidental disclosure. (D) is detective, firing while or after the abuse occurs, and would be the right choice if the question asked how to detect anomalous administrative logins. Against a credential the attacker already holds, prevention must come from a second, different factor.

questions.question: An organization has rolled out app-generated time-based one-time codes as a second factor on its webmail after a wave of account takeovers in which employees typed their passwords into lookalike login sites. Which attack technique is MOST likely to still succeed against the upgraded login?

options.A: Credential stuffing that replays username and password pairs harvested from breaches of unrelated services
options.B: Offline cracking of stolen password hashes using precomputed tables
options.C: A scripted brute-force loop guessing all possible six-digit codes against the login endpoint
options.D: A proxy page that captures and instantly relays both the password and current code

questions.explanation: A TOTP code is bound to a clock, not to the site the user types it into, so an adversary-in-the-middle page can capture the password and the current code and replay both to the real service inside the validity window - the newly deployed control does not break that flow. (A) now fails because a stolen password alone no longer completes login; stuffing would be the residual threat had MFA been skipped. (B) yields passwords and then hits the same second-factor wall; it would be the concern if the question were about theft of an unsalted credential database. (C) is defeated by the 30-second code lifetime combined with ordinary attempt throttling; it would matter only on an endpoint with no rate limiting at all. OTP-based MFA raises the bar yet stays phishable in real time; closing the gap takes an origin-bound, phishing-resistant method such as FIDO2/WebAuthn.

questions.question: An auditor is reviewing QuickCash's proposed console login upgrade, which the standard requires to be genuine multi-factor authentication. Which combination should the auditor accept as meeting that requirement?

options.A: A smart card inserted at the console together with a memorized PIN
options.B: A primary password backed by answers to personal challenge questions
options.C: A fingerprint scan confirmed by an iris scan at the same panel
options.D: A console password plus a second passphrase held by the same technician

questions.explanation: Multi-factor means evidence from two different categories - something you know, have, or are - because credentials of the same category tend to fall to the same attack. A card plus a PIN pairs possession with knowledge: a shoulder-surfed PIN is useless without the card, a stolen card useless without the PIN. (B) stacks knowledge on knowledge; challenge answers are memorized facts, often researchable from social media, and one phishing call can harvest both. (C) stacks inherence on inherence - two strong biometrics, but one category, so it remains single-factor; the second biometric buys accuracy, nothing more. (D) is two knowledge secrets in one head; a single keylogger session captures both. Count the factor categories, not the number of prompts.

questions.question: QuickCash is deploying a second authentication factor for field technicians who service ATMs in rural areas where mobile coverage is unreliable, and company policy bars personal phones from work use. Which factor is MOST appropriate for this workforce?

options.A: One-time codes delivered to each technician by SMS text message
options.B: Push-notification approvals sent to a corporate smartphone application
options.C: A dedicated hardware token displaying time-based one-time codes
options.D: One-time codes emailed to each technician's corporate mailbox

questions.explanation: A hardware TOTP token computes codes locally from a synchronized clock and stored seed, so it needs no signal, no phone and no mailbox - the only option compatible with both stated constraints. Codes over SMS (A) depend on cellular coverage at exactly the sites where it is unreliable, and NIST SP 800-63B additionally classes SMS delivery as a restricted, weaker out-of-band channel; that option suits consumer populations in covered areas. (B) needs a data connection plus a smartphone, colliding with both constraints; it is a good choice for office staff with managed devices. (D) requires network reachability at the ATM site, and if the mailbox is protected by the same password under attack, both factors collapse into one channel. Offline sites need possession factors that compute their codes locally instead of receiving them.

questions.question: Following a rash of account takeovers, an analyst finds the helpdesk resets any password for a caller who can state the employee's birthday and manager's name - details attackers routinely harvest from social media. Which change to the reset process would MOST reduce this exposure?

options.A: Add several further personal questions about employment history to the verification script
options.B: Require reset callers to also state their employee ID number and department
options.C: Rotate the personal verification questions on a monthly schedule across the whole team
options.D: Confirm each request via a push prompt to the employee's enrolled device

questions.explanation: The flaw is structural: every check in the current script is knowledge that lives outside the company's control, so an attacker who researches the target passes it. Routing approval through a device already enrolled to the employee moves verification onto a possession factor the caller cannot fake from research. (A) adds more of the same failed category - employment history is exactly the kind of fact professional networking profiles publish, so it is researchable too - and would help only against unprepared opportunists. (B) fails the same way: employee IDs leak through email signatures and directory exports, so they remain harvestable knowledge. (C) changes which facts are asked without changing that facts are the medium - rotation is the right idea for shared secrets like passwords, misapplied here to identity proofing.

questions.question: Technicians complain that the fingerprint reader guarding the ATM service panel rejects them repeatedly in cold weather, so an administrator lowers the match-confidence threshold until the complaints stop. What is the MOST significant security consequence of this adjustment?

options.A: The false acceptance rate rises, so impostors will match more easily
options.B: The crossover error rate improves, making the sensor more accurate
options.C: The failure-to-enroll rate increases for users with worn fingerprints
options.D: The false rejection rate rises further, locking even more legitimate users out

questions.explanation: False accepts and false rejects sit at opposite ends of one tuning curve: relaxing the threshold to admit poorly captured legitimate prints necessarily also admits poorer impostor prints, trading Type I errors for Type II errors - and a false accept at an unattended cash machine is the expensive direction. (B) misunderstands CER, which is a fixed property of the device measured where FAR equals FRR; moving the operating threshold does not change the sensor's underlying accuracy. (C) confuses verification with registration - failure to enroll happens at enrolment time and is unaffected by the matching threshold. (D) inverts the direction of the change: rejections were the pre-change complaint, and lowering the threshold reduces false rejections; it cannot drive them up.

questions.question: A security team must set biometric matching thresholds for two doors: the unattended vault anteroom, and the staffed main entrance where a guard also checks badges. How should the team bias the two thresholds?

options.A: Apply one uniform threshold at both doors so error rates remain consistent
options.B: Bias the vault door toward acceptance to avoid delaying cash-handling operations
options.C: Bias the vault door toward false rejections and the guarded entrance toward false acceptances
options.D: Bias both doors toward acceptance because badge checks already provide a compensating control everywhere

questions.explanation: The surrounding controls decide which error type is tolerable at each point. At an unattended vault door a false acceptance is unrecoverable, so the threshold should be strict even though staff get rejected more often; at the guarded entrance an occasional false acceptance is caught by the guard, so a looser threshold that cuts queue-building rejections is the better trade. Option (A) treats tuning as a consistency exercise, ignoring that the cost of each error differs by location - uniformity is the right answer only where the doors protect equivalent assets. (B) optimizes convenience precisely where an admitted impostor does the greatest damage. (D) is half right, and 'everywhere' is where it fails: badge checks do compensate at the staffed entrance, but no compensating human control exists at the unattended vault anteroom.

questions.question: An analyst comparing three fingerprint products finds each vendor quotes impressive numbers measured at different threshold settings - one boasts the fewest false accepts, another the fewest rejects. Which figure gives the analyst the fairest single basis for comparing the systems?

options.A: The lowest false acceptance rate that each vendor quotes in its datasheet
options.B: The false rejection rate each vendor measured during its own pilot
options.C: The failure-to-enroll rate observed across the user population
options.D: The crossover error rate, where false accepts and false rejects are equal

questions.explanation: Since FAR and FRR both move with the threshold, any vendor can make either number look excellent by choosing where to measure; the crossover point removes that freedom by fixing the comparison at the setting where the two error rates meet, so a lower CER genuinely means a more accurate sensor. (A) and (B) are each one end of a tunable trade - quoting either alone is exactly the marketing trick the analyst has run into, though each becomes relevant again when tuning the chosen product for its site's risk bias. (C) measures how many users can register at all, which matters for usability and population coverage but says nothing about matching accuracy once enrolled.

questions.question: The post-incident review notes that QuickCash's field technicians only ever performed cash replenishment and diagnostics, yet every technician held full 'SuperAdmin' rights on the console, including PIN reset and account creation. Which principle did this rights assignment MOST directly violate?

options.A: Least privilege, because the accounts carried powers the job did not require
options.B: Separation of duties, because one team both requested and approved its access
options.C: Dual control, because sensitive operations could proceed without a second person
options.D: Need to know, because technicians could browse customer transaction records

questions.explanation: The mismatch the stem describes is between duties and powers: the job needed service functions, the account granted everything, and that surplus of capability is precisely what least privilege forbids. (B) names a real weakness of QuickCash's governance, but the stem describes excessive rights, not a missing split between requesting and approving - separation of duties would be the most direct answer if one person could both initiate and authorize a payment. (C) is about requiring two people for a single sensitive act - a compensating control layered on top, while the stem asks which principle the rights assignment breaks. (D) is the data-access sibling of least privilege and is arguably also violated, but the stem's examples - PIN reset, account creation - are capabilities, not data views, so it is the less direct fit. When powers exceed duties, cite least privilege; reserve need to know for surplus access to information.

questions.question: After the breach, QuickCash must overhaul how ATM safe master keys are managed; today they sit in an unlocked drawer that any office visitor could reach. Which replacement practice would BEST bring physical key handling into line with IAM principles?

options.A: Issue keys individually from an audited cabinet with per-person sign-out records
options.B: Install a camera covering the key storage area so removals can be reviewed
options.C: Move the keys into a locked cabinet whose combination all technicians share
options.D: Remove the identifying label so a visitor cannot tell what the keys open

questions.explanation: Physical keys are credentials, and the case study's core lesson - one identity per person, with attributable use - applies to them exactly as it does to logins. An audited cabinet with individual sign-out restores identification and accountability for every key movement. (B) is purely detective: footage may show who took a key after cash has gone, and cameras are a sound complement once issuance is controlled. (C) upgrades the container but recreates the SuperAdmin defect in physical form - a shared combination is a shared credential, so no removal can be attributed. (D) is security through obscurity; a labeled drawer made the attack easier, but an unlabeled unlocked drawer is still an uncontrolled credential store.

questions.question: A defense contractor is implementing a document system that must enforce government classification markings, with the operating system imposing every access decision so that no file owner can override or reclassify on their own authority. Which access control model fits this requirement?

options.A: Role-based access control driven by job assignments
options.B: Discretionary access control administered by resource owners
options.C: Mandatory access control enforced through security labels
options.D: Attribute-based access control evaluating contextual rules

questions.explanation: Two phrases in the stem are decisive: classification markings, and decisions imposed by the system beyond any owner's authority - the defining pair of properties of mandatory access control, where subjects hold clearances, objects hold labels, and policy is centrally enforced. (A) grants by job function and would let an administrator or role owner adjust assignments, which the requirement excludes; it fits an enterprise organizing access around positions. (B) is the direct opposite of the requirement, since discretion by the owner is exactly what must be removed. (D) could emulate labels among its attributes, but its purpose is dynamic, condition-based decisions rather than a rigid lattice of clearances - the right answer when access must vary with time, location or device.

questions.question: An auditor discovers that spreadsheets holding cardholder data on a Windows file share were readable company-wide because the files' creators had granted 'Everyone' read access on their own initiative. Which characteristic of the environment's access control model made this possible?

options.A: Rule-based control applies one uniform policy to every subject
options.B: Discretionary control leaves grant decisions with each resource owner
options.C: Mandatory control ties every access decision to clearance levels
options.D: Role-based control links permissions to defined job functions

questions.explanation: Windows NTFS permissions follow the discretionary model: whoever owns a file may share it at will, so a well-meaning creator can quietly grant the world access to regulated data, and that owner discretion is the exact mechanism the auditor observed. Option (A) describes system-wide rules such as firewall-style conditions; had one uniform policy governed the share, individual creators could not have loosened it, and the finding would look different. (C) would have made the oversharing impossible, since labels and clearances remove the owner's choice; it explains a different environment, not this one. (D) would bound access by job function, and the finding shows access following individual grant decisions, not roles. DAC's convenience is its risk: owner-controlled sharing scales into uncontrolled sprawl unless monitored or replaced for sensitive data.

questions.question: A retail company with heavy seasonal turnover wants store associates' access created and removed automatically from HR job codes, so every cashier receives an identical, pre-approved permission bundle on day one. Which access control model BEST supports this goal?

options.A: Discretionary access control, letting each store manager grant what is needed
options.B: Mandatory access control, labeling every resource by sensitivity level
options.C: Attribute-based access control, evaluating dynamic conditions at request time
options.D: Role-based access control, mapping permission bundles to defined job functions

questions.explanation: The requirement is standardized bundles keyed to a job code with join-move-leave automation, which is role-based access control's home ground: HR assigns the role, the role carries the pre-approved permissions, and revocation is one membership change. (A) would have hundreds of managers hand-crafting grants, producing inconsistency and orphaned rights at every departure - workable only at very small scale. (B) solves a different problem, protecting classified material through clearance labels, and adds administrative weight with no benefit for uniform retail duties. (C) can express role-like logic through attributes, but its strength is contextual variation per request; for identical static bundles it is added complexity; reach for it when access must depend on time, device or location.

questions.question: QuickCash wants console sessions permitted only when a technician connects from the corporate network, during a scheduled maintenance window, from a managed laptop that passes a patch-level check. Which access control model natively evaluates all of these conditions together?

options.A: Attribute-based access control combining subject, environment and device attributes
options.B: Role-based access control assigning rights by technician job function
options.C: Mandatory access control comparing clearance labels against resource labels
options.D: Discretionary access control letting the console's owner assign permissions

questions.explanation: Network location, time window and device posture are environmental and device attributes, and a policy that must weigh them per request - permit if role is technician AND network is corporate AND time is in window AND laptop is compliant - is the definition of attribute-based access control. (B) answers who may act by job but has no vocabulary for when, from where, or from what device; it would be the pick if the requirement stopped at job function. (C) decides by comparing sensitivity labels to clearances and cannot see clocks or patch levels; its home is classified environments. (D) hands the decision to a resource owner, which changes who decides while adding no vocabulary for conditions.

questions.question: A company has finished consolidating forty applications behind a single sign-on portal. The architecture review board asks what should change about protection of the portal credential itself, now that one login unlocks everything. Which recommendation is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Rotate the retired downstream application passwords on a shorter schedule
options.B: Keep separate standalone passwords for the three most sensitive applications
options.C: Require phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication at the portal login
options.D: Extend the portal session lifetime so users authenticate less often

questions.explanation: Single sign-on deliberately concentrates authentication risk: convenience rises, and the portal credential becomes the key to the kingdom, so the proportionate response is to harden that one credential to a level none of the forty passwords ever needed - strong MFA resistant to real-time phishing. (A) polishes credentials that SSO has made largely irrelevant to the attack path; rotation there would matter if legacy direct logins remained exposed. (B) quietly abandons SSO for the crown jewels, an admission of defeat that also multiplies user friction - defensible only where a system genuinely cannot integrate. (D) moves in the wrong direction, lengthening the window a hijacked session stays valid.

questions.question: An organization wants employees to open a partner-hosted benefits portal from their browsers using their existing corporate directory logins, with the partner receiving no corporate passwords at any point. Which standard is designed for exactly this browser-based federation?

options.A: Kerberos, issuing service tickets from the corporate key distribution center
options.B: SAML 2.0, sending signed authentication assertions from the corporate identity provider
options.C: OAuth 2.0, issuing access tokens that delegate resource rights to the partner
options.D: TACACS+, centralizing authentication for devices at the network perimeter

questions.explanation: Cross-organization web single sign-on is the scenario SAML was built for: the employee authenticates once to the corporate identity provider, the browser carries a signed XML assertion to the partner's service provider, and the partner trusts the assertion instead of ever holding a password. Kerberos (A) excels inside a single realm or trusted domain, but its ticket exchange does not extend across the public internet to an external partner's website. (C) answers a different question - what a client application may access on a user's behalf - and an access token by itself does not assert who the user is. (D) authenticates administrators to routers and switches, an infrastructure AAA role far from browser federation.

questions.question: A development team is building a scheduling app that must read users' calendars hosted by a third-party provider. Product management insists users grant the app limited calendar access without ever revealing their provider passwords. Which framework should the team implement?

options.A: OAuth 2.0, so each user authorizes a scoped access token for the app
options.B: OpenID Connect, so the app receives a signed ID token identifying each authenticated user
options.C: SAML 2.0, so the provider asserts each user's authentication to the app
options.D: Kerberos delegation, so the app forwards each user's service tickets

questions.explanation: The requirement is delegated authorization - let this app read my calendar, nothing more, no password shared - and that is OAuth 2.0's exact purpose: the user consents at the provider, and the app receives an access token limited to the calendar scope. (B) tells the app who the user is, and identity alone confers no right to read resource data; OIDC would be the pick if the app merely needed login. (C) likewise asserts authentication between organizations and carries no resource-scoped delegation for an API. (D) is an intra-domain mechanism for services acting on behalf of users inside one Kerberos realm, not a consumer-web pattern across providers. OAuth answers what may this app touch; OIDC and SAML answer who is this user.

questions.question: A penetration test of a consumer web app finds it treats possession of a bare OAuth 2.0 access token as proof of identity: any valid token presented to the API logs that bearer in as the user. Which change BEST corrects this design flaw?

options.A: Wrap every token exchange in mutually authenticated TLS so tokens cannot be intercepted
options.B: Shorten the access token lifetime so a stolen token expires quickly
