questions.question: An audit after the outage finds that once a maintenance laptop connects to Global ATM Corp's internal network, it can reach every ATM without further checks, because internal traffic is considered trusted. The security team is adopting a zero trust approach. Which change BEST reflects that model?

options.A: Strengthen the perimeter firewall so unmanaged laptops cannot reach the internal network.
options.B: Authenticate and authorize every connection to each ATM, regardless of originating network.
options.C: Require VPN tunnels for remote staff while continuing to trust traffic from on-site devices.
options.D: Grant maintenance laptops standing access after a one-time posture check at enrollment.

questions.explanation: Zero trust removes network location from the trust decision entirely: every request must prove who is asking and whether they are entitled, whether it comes from the data center next door or a coffee shop. B applies exactly that. A is wrong because hardening the perimeter is the model zero trust replaces - once anything gets inside, the flat trust problem the audit found remains untouched. C is wrong for the same reason at a smaller scale: it authenticates the remote path while still equating on-site presence with trustworthiness. D is wrong because a one-time check that confers standing access is the opposite of continuous verification; a laptop compromised the day after enrollment keeps its access. The test for any zero-trust proposal: does location or past verification still buy access? If yes, it is perimeter thinking renamed.

questions.question: A fraud investigation at Global ATM Corp finds that a technician's valid account was used at 3 a.m. from an unusual workstation to query thousands of customer records. Signature-based tools raised no alert, because no malware and no known attack pattern was involved. Which capability would MOST improve detection of this kind of misuse?

options.A: Behavior analytics that baseline each account's normal activity and flag deviations from it.
options.B: An intrusion detection sensor kept current with the newest published attack signatures from the vendor.
options.C: A data loss prevention gateway inspecting outbound email and web uploads for sensitive attachments.
options.D: Quarterly recertification of each technician's access rights by their own reporting line manager.

questions.explanation: When credentials are valid and no exploit is involved, the only remaining signal is that the behavior itself is abnormal - a 3 a.m. login from an unfamiliar workstation running bulk queries deviates sharply from the account's baseline, which is precisely what user and entity behavior analytics is built to score. B is wrong because the stem has already ruled its mechanism out: there is no attack pattern for a signature to match when a legitimate account does illegitimate things. C is wrong because DLP watches data leaving the network; the misuse here was internal querying, which completes before any exfiltration channel is involved. D is wrong because recertification confirms whether access is still appropriate on paper, quarterly - it cannot notice how the access is being used at 3 a.m. Misuse of valid access is caught by behavior, not signatures.

questions.question: Police request the hard drive from an ATM involved in a skimming case, and Global ATM Corp's security manager expects the drive to become evidence in a criminal trial. Which handling practice is MOST important for the drive to survive an admissibility challenge?

options.A: Analyzing the drive promptly so the findings reach investigators while still current.
options.B: Keeping the drive locked in the security manager's desk until police collect it.
options.C: Obtaining written approval from senior management before releasing the drive.
options.D: Documenting every transfer of the drive, with hash values proving its contents unchanged.

questions.explanation: What a court needs is proof that the artifact presented at trial is the same, unaltered artifact taken from the ATM - and only an unbroken chain of custody, with cryptographic hashes verifying integrity at each hand-off, provides that proof. This is the core evidence-handling requirement of NIST SP 800-86. A is wrong because analytical speed has no bearing on authenticity; hasty analysis performed on the original rather than a working copy can itself damage admissibility. B is wrong because locked storage without a documented record still leaves the gap the defense will attack - no one can show who had access to that desk or when. C is wrong because management approval addresses corporate authority to release the drive, not the integrity of what is released. Custody documentation is what converts a hard drive into evidence.

questions.question: An administrator runs a full backup of the log server every Sunday night and a differential backup every other night. The server's disk fails on Thursday morning. Which restore approach returns the server to its most recent recoverable state with the fewest restore operations?

options.A: Sunday's full backup followed by Monday's, Tuesday's, and Wednesday's differentials in order.
options.B: Wednesday night's differential alone, since it holds the newest copy of the data.
options.C: Sunday's full backup followed by Wednesday night's differential.
options.D: Wednesday's differential first, then Sunday's full backup to fill in the older files.

questions.explanation: Each differential captures everything changed since the last full backup, so Wednesday's job already contains Monday's and Tuesday's changes - the full plus the single latest differential is the complete two-step restore. A is wrong only on the efficiency the stem asks about: applying every differential in sequence does reach the same end state, but the earlier tapes are redundant, since each is a subset of Wednesday's. That is the trade against incremental schemes, where every tape in the chain genuinely matters. B is wrong because a differential holds only changes; without the Sunday full underneath it, the unchanged majority of the system is simply absent. D is wrong because restore order matters - laying the full down after the differential overwrites Wednesday's newer files with Sunday's older versions. Know what each backup type contains, and the restore sequence follows.

questions.question: Nightly backups of Global ATM Corp's file server now overrun their window near the end of each week, because every night's job re-copies all changes made since Sunday's full backup. The administrator must shorten the nightly jobs and accepts that restores may take longer. Which scheme BEST fits these priorities?

options.A: Sunday full backups, with nightly incrementals capturing changes since the previous night's job.
options.B: Full backups every night, with compression and deduplication to reduce the volume written.
options.C: Sunday full backups, with nightly copy backups that leave the archive bit untouched.
options.D: Full backups twice a week, with differential backups on each of the remaining nights.

questions.explanation: The growth the administrator is fighting is inherent to differentials - each night re-copies everything since the full - and incrementals remove it by copying only one day's changes, giving the shortest possible nightly job. The cost is exactly the one the stem accepts: a restore must apply the full plus every incremental in the chain. B is wrong because a nightly full is the longest job of all; deduplication trims the data written but the job still reads and processes the entire data set inside the window. A copy backup ignores the archive bit and backs up everything each night regardless of what changed; the volume problem C claims to solve survives untouched. D is wrong because it shrinks the differentials without changing their compounding nature, and it adds a second full-length job to the working week. Choose the backup type by which side of the backup-versus-restore trade the business wants to pay.

questions.question: To reduce data-loss exposure, an administrator adds a midday incremental backup to a scheme that already runs a Sunday full backup and differential backups each night. Afterward, the nightly differentials are found to be missing files that changed during the mornings. What is the MOST likely cause?

options.A: The differential jobs are running short of window time now that a midday job shares the library.
options.B: The midday incremental resets the archive bit, so the differential skips files changed before noon.
options.C: The Sunday full backup is corrupt, which breaks the baseline for the week's dependent backups.
options.D: Differentials capture only the changes made since the previous night's differential ran.

questions.explanation: Differential jobs select files by their archive bit, which is meant to be cleared only by a full or incremental backup - so when a midday incremental clears the bits on the morning's files, the nightly differential no longer sees them as changed. The morning files are safe on the incremental tape, but the differentials silently stop being complete, which is why mixing incrementals into a differential scheme is a classic design error. A is wrong because a scheduling shortage would truncate jobs unpredictably or raise errors, not cleanly omit exactly the pre-noon files every day. C is wrong because a corrupt full breaks restores, not the differential's file selection, and it predates the change that triggered the symptom. D is wrong because it describes incremental behavior; a differential always looks back to the last full, which is precisely why the cleared bits matter.

questions.question: An investigation finds that a contractor emailed a spreadsheet of customer card numbers to a personal address, and the message passed through the corporate mail gateway without any content inspection. The security team's priority is preventing sensitive data from leaving the network this way again. Which control BEST addresses the requirement?

options.A: Encrypting the customer database at rest, with keys held by the security team.
options.B: Annual data-handling training, with signed acknowledgment from all staff and contractors.
options.C: Blocking access to personal webmail sites from the corporate network.
options.D: A data loss prevention gateway that inspects outbound messages and quarantines sensitive content.

questions.explanation: The leak travelled through a channel the company controls - the mail gateway - carrying content the company can recognize, and a DLP gateway is the control that inspects exactly that channel for exactly that content and stops it before it leaves. A is wrong because encryption at rest protects stored data from theft; the contractor accessed the data legitimately and decrypted output is what gets attached to email. B is wrong because awareness reduces accidental mishandling but is not a preventive barrier - it cannot stop the careless or deliberate send the stem describes. C is wrong because the message did not travel through webmail; it went out via the corporate gateway itself, so closing the webmail channel leaves the demonstrated path wide open. Match the control to the channel the data actually left through.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp is served notice of a lawsuit over the outage, and counsel advises that email and system logs from the incident period will be demanded during discovery. The log platform purges records after 90 days by default. What should the security team do FIRST?

options.A: Export all material named in the notice and deliver it to opposing counsel right away.
options.B: Continue the retention schedule, since routine purging is a documented business practice.
options.C: Place a litigation hold that suspends purging for records the case may require.
options.D: Copy last month's logs to tape and let the purge schedule continue for everything else.

questions.explanation: The duty to preserve attaches as soon as litigation is reasonably anticipated, and the litigation hold is the mechanism that discharges it - it suspends every routine destruction process that could touch potentially relevant records, before anything else happens. A is wrong because production comes later in e-discovery and is scoped and negotiated through counsel; handing material to the opposing side immediately is premature and bypasses privilege review. B is wrong because a destruction schedule stops being defensible the moment litigation is anticipated - continuing the purge invites spoliation sanctions precisely because it is automatic. D is wrong on scope: it preserves one month's slice while the purge keeps destroying other records the case may require, and it creates no documented, auditable hold. Preserve broadly first; collection and production follow under counsel's direction.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp is outsourcing overnight monitoring of the ATM fleet to a managed service provider. The operations director wants the provider's response to outages to be enforceable, with defined consequences if targets are missed. Which mechanism BEST provides this?

options.A: A memorandum of understanding recording both parties' intent to cooperate on availability and to respond promptly to outages.
options.B: A service level agreement in the contract, with measurable response times and remedies for missing them.
options.C: An operational level agreement between the provider's internal support tiers.
options.D: The provider's published uptime statistics and reference customers from recent years.

questions.explanation: Enforceability comes from contract terms that are measurable and carry remedies - a service level agreement turns 'respond quickly' into numeric targets with financial consequences the customer can invoke. A is wrong because a memorandum of understanding - even one promising prompt outage response - documents intent, not obligation; it typically has no binding force and no remedy when the provider falls short. C is wrong because an operational level agreement is the provider's internal plumbing between its own teams - it supports their SLA, but Global ATM Corp is not a party to it and cannot enforce it. D is wrong because history and references are due-diligence inputs for selecting a provider; they describe the past and bind no one about the future. When the requirement is enforcement, the answer lives in the contract, and the SLA is the part of the contract built for it.

questions.question: A fraud investigator at Global ATM Corp is assigned to a case involving twelve customer accounts. A review finds that his role lets him read the records of every customer in the bank, and that his database account also carries administrative rights he has never used. Which assessment of the two findings is MOST accurate?

options.A: Reading unrelated customer records breaches need-to-know, while the standing admin rights breach least privilege.
options.B: Both findings are a single defect, because the two principles amount to the same control in practice.
options.C: Least privilege governs which records he may read, and need-to-know limits his system permissions.
options.D: Neither finding is a defect, since investigators require broad reach to follow leads across accounts.

questions.explanation: The two principles constrain different things: need-to-know restricts access to information to what the current task requires - twelve accounts, not every customer - while least privilege restricts system rights and permissions to the minimum the role requires, which unused administrative rights plainly exceed. A maps each finding to the principle it violates. B is wrong because the principles are related but distinct; collapsing them hides the fact that fixing one finding leaves the other open. C is wrong because it swaps the definitions - records are information (need-to-know), permissions are rights (least privilege) - and applying the wrong principle produces the wrong remediation owner. Breadth is granted per investigation on demonstrated need, not as standing access; D overstates the investigator's entitlement, and convenience does not create need. When a question mixes data access with system rights, sort each finding into its own principle first.

questions.question: Only one engineer at Global ATM Corp understands the settlement reconciliation jobs, and internal audit also warns that this engineer could conceal an ongoing fraud indefinitely because nobody else ever touches the process. Which single control BEST addresses both findings?

options.A: Mandatory vacations, with the engineer handing the process to a colleague for two weeks yearly.
options.B: Dual control, with a second person approving each settlement run before it executes.
options.C: Job rotation, cycling other engineers through the settlement role on a regular schedule.
options.D: Enhanced logging of the engineer's activity, with weekly review by the security team.

questions.explanation: The audit describes two exposures with one root: exclusivity. Rotating other engineers through the role attacks both at once - fresh eyes on the process surface irregularities a lone operator could bury, and each rotation builds another person who can run settlements, dissolving the key-person dependency. A is wrong only on coverage: mandatory vacation forces a hand-over that can expose concealment, but two weeks a year leaves the dependency intact for the other fifty. It is the right answer where the sole concern is detecting fraud. B is wrong because an approver checks outcomes without learning to operate the process, so the bank still cannot run settlements without this engineer. D is wrong because the reviewers lack the expertise to judge what they are reading - the stem says nobody else understands the jobs - and logging does nothing for continuity. One control, two findings: pick the one that covers both.

questions.question: The outage review notes that the lead engineer who wrote the patch-deployment change request also approved it in the tracking system and then executed the deployment. Which control principle, applied to the change process, would BEST prevent a recurrence of this failure?

options.A: Least privilege, restricting the engineer's deployment rights to the test collection only.
options.B: Job rotation, assigning a different engineer to handle each month's deployments.
options.C: Defense in depth, layering compensating technical controls around the deployment tooling.
options.D: Separation of duties, so no one person can request, approve, and execute a change.

questions.explanation: The failure was structural: one person held every role in the change, so no independent judgment ever examined the deployment plan before it ran. Separation of duties breaks exactly that - requester, approver, and executor become different people, and the reckless full-fleet push has to convince someone with no stake in the request. A is wrong because someone must ultimately hold production deployment rights; scoping this engineer to test merely relocates the concentration to whoever deploys to production. It answers a different question - how to limit routine standing access. B is wrong because a rotating engineer can still self-request, self-approve, and self-execute; rotation changes who holds the conflict, not whether it exists. C is wrong because defense in depth is an architecture strategy, not a remedy for a missing independent check; layered tooling around an unreviewed decision still deploys the unreviewed decision. Match the principle to the defect: concentrated roles call for separation.

questions.question: An audit finds that four operations staff at Global ATM Corp share one domain administrator password, use it for routine work such as email and browsing, and have left it unchanged for two years. Which approach BEST addresses all three findings?

options.A: A privileged access vault issuing the credential per task to identified users and rotating it after each use.
options.B: A policy requiring the shared password to change every 90 days and whenever a staff member departs.
options.C: Multi-factor authentication enforced on the shared domain administrator account, with a second factor required before every privileged logon.
options.D: Separate personal accounts for each operator, reserved for administrative tasks only.

questions.explanation: Three findings need covering: shared use with no attribution, privileged credentials used for routine work, and a stale secret. A vault covers all three in one mechanism - each check-out ties use to a named person, check-out happens only for a stated administrative task, and automatic rotation after use retires the two-year-old password permanently. D is the strong runner-up: personal admin accounts restore attribution and, used only for administration, separate routine work - but nothing in it rotates or protects the credentials themselves, so the stale-secret finding survives. It is the right answer where no PAM tooling is available. B is wrong because rotating a password that four people still share fixes staleness while leaving the two bigger findings - anonymity and everyday privileged use - untouched. MFA on a shared account strengthens the login without identifying which of the four performed it; C closes none of the attribution problem. Count the findings each option closes; only one closes all three.

questions.question: Forensics on a compromised ATM finds seven years of customer transaction logs stored locally, although operations needs only 90 days of them and no regulation requires local retention. The old data multiplied the breach exposure. Which practice would MOST have limited this exposure?

options.A: Encrypting the local transaction logs, with the decryption keys stored on the ATM.
options.B: A data lifecycle policy purging local logs once their 90-day operational need ends.
options.C: Compressing logs older than 90 days into archives to reduce local disk usage.
options.D: Classifying the transaction logs as sensitive so handling requirements attach to them.

questions.explanation: Data that has been destroyed on schedule cannot be stolen later - lifecycle management exists precisely so that information is disposed of when its business need ends, and here it would have cut the exposed data from seven years to 90 days. A is wrong because encryption whose keys sit on the same compromised device yields the attacker both lock and key; even done properly, it protects the data while leaving seven unnecessary years of it in harm's way. C is wrong because compression changes the format, not the presence - every record remains on the machine for the taking. D is wrong because classification is the input to a lifecycle decision, not the decision itself; a sensitivity label on data that should not exist merely documents the exposure. The cheapest data to defend is the data you no longer hold; minimize before you fortify.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp is returning 200 leased ATMs to the lessor. Each machine contains a self-encrypting drive holding cardholder data, and the lease requires the equipment to come back in working order. Following NIST SP 800-88, which sanitization approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Degauss each drive to magnetically scramble the recorded data before the machines ship.
options.B: Shred the drives and fit replacement blanks into every machine before returning them.
options.C: Perform a cryptographic erase, destroying each drive's media encryption keys and verifying the result.
options.D: Run a quick format on each drive so the file system no longer references the stored data.

questions.explanation: For self-encrypting drives, SP 800-88 recognizes cryptographic erase as a purge technique: destroying the media encryption keys renders the ciphertext permanently unreadable in seconds, and the drive keeps working - which satisfies both the data risk and the lease at once. A is wrong twice over: degaussing leaves flash-based media readable because the data is not stored magnetically, and on drives it does affect, it generally destroys the mechanism, violating the working-order term. B is wrong on proportion rather than principle - shredding does sanitize, but it destroys 200 functional drives and buys replacements to solve a problem cryptographic erase solves for nothing. It is the right answer for media that will never leave in working condition. D is wrong because a quick format clears pointers, not content; trivial recovery tools read formatted data back. Choose the 800-88 method that matches both the media type and what happens to the media next.

questions.question: A fleet audit at Global ATM Corp finds machines running inconsistent settings: some have hardening applied, others have services re-enabled by field technicians, and no record exists of what any machine is supposed to look like. Which process would BEST bring the fleet back under control?

options.A: Monthly vulnerability scans of the fleet, with findings routed to the operations work queue.
options.B: Change control approval requirements for any future technician modification to an ATM.
options.C: Patch management, with security updates deployed automatically across the fleet.
options.D: Configuration management, with an approved baseline and automated detection of drift from it.

questions.explanation: The audit's core finding is the absence of a defined desired state - without one, nobody can even say which machines are wrong. Configuration management supplies that missing piece: an approved, documented baseline for the fleet, plus continuous comparison that surfaces any machine drifting from it, whoever caused the drift. A is wrong because a vulnerability scanner reports known weaknesses, not conformance; a re-enabled service that carries no CVE passes the scan while still violating the intended build. Change control governs future modifications and only the honest ones, which is B's limitation: it cannot describe the current mess or catch undocumented field changes, and without a baseline there is no reference for approving anything. C is wrong because patch level is one attribute of configuration; a fully patched machine with the wrong services running is still out of control. First define correct, then detect departure from it - that is configuration management.

questions.question: Two hours into the fleet outage, the operations bridge is split: one group wants machines kept offline until the driver conflict is fully understood so the failure cannot repeat, while the other wants service restored using a tested workaround, with analysis to follow. Under incident management, which position should the incident manager support?

options.A: Restore service with the tested workaround now, and hand root-cause analysis to problem management.
options.B: Keep the fleet offline until root cause is confirmed, since a recurrence would double the damage.
options.C: Restore service only after the vendor certifies a corrected patch for the dispenser driver.
options.D: Restore half the fleet now, keeping the other half offline for the investigation team.

questions.explanation: Incident management has one objective: return service to normal as fast as safely possible, and a tested workaround achieves it. The discipline deliberately splits duties so that restoration is not held hostage to understanding - root cause belongs to problem management, working after the customers are back online. B is wrong because it applies problem management's goal at incident management's moment; every hour of deliberate downtime is certain harm, weighed against a recurrence the workaround already guards. That caution is the right answer when a restoration path is untested and could worsen the damage. C is wrong because it chains recovery to a third party's timetable when an internal path exists - the vendor fix matters for redeployment later, not for restoring service now. D is wrong on scope: preserving a handful of machines for analysis is legitimate, but idling two thousand confuses evidence preservation with a sampling need. Restore first; understand in parallel.

questions.question: Service has been fully restored after the outage and the incident record is ready to close. Management is pressing to redeploy the security patch quickly, because the vulnerability it fixes remains open across the fleet. As problem management takes over, what should the team do NEXT?

options.A: Redeploy the patch fleet-wide in the next maintenance window, since the fix is already built.
options.B: Perform root-cause analysis of the driver conflict and the process gaps before any redeployment.
options.C: Expand network capacity so a future rollback command can reach machines that are rebooting.
options.D: Close the problem record, since service levels have returned to their normal targets.

questions.explanation: Problem management exists to stop recurrence, and its instrument is root-cause analysis: until the team understands why the patch and the dispenser driver conflicted, and why the process approved a full-fleet push without a viable backout, any redeployment is a rerun of the same bet. The open vulnerability argues for urgency in the analysis, not for skipping it. A is wrong because it repeats the original decision unchanged - the patch that crashed 4,000 machines is 'already built' in exactly the state that crashed them. Saturated bandwidth was a symptom that worsened the incident, not its cause; C plans for the next failure instead of preventing it. D is wrong because restored service closes the incident, not the problem - the defect that produced the outage is still unexplained and unfixed. Incidents end at restoration; problems end at prevention.

questions.question: A payment processor's card-authorization service carries a 30-minute RTO and a near-zero RPO in the business impact analysis, and each hour offline costs roughly two million dollars in fees and penalties. The DR planner must recommend a recovery strategy for this service. Which option is MOST appropriate despite its cost?

options.A: A warm site with servers installed, restored from the previous night's backups at activation.
options.B: A cold site with power, cooling, and connectivity, with equipment shipped in after declaration.
options.C: A reciprocal agreement with a partner processor to share capacity during a disaster.
options.D: A hot site running synchronized systems, ready to take over processing within minutes.

questions.explanation: The BIA numbers dictate the strategy: only a facility that is already running, with data already synchronized, can resume processing inside 30 minutes with near-zero data loss, and the downtime cost of two million dollars an hour is what justifies paying for it. A is wrong on both objectives - bringing a warm site up takes hours to days, and last night's backups forfeit up to a day of authorizations against a near-zero RPO. It is the right answer for systems with day-scale objectives and real budget limits. B is wrong because procuring and building equipment after declaration is a weeks-scale recovery, the opposite end of the spectrum from this requirement. C is wrong because reciprocal capacity is the least dependable option here - the partner's spare capacity, software versions, and compliance posture are outside the processor's control, and card processing is exactly the workload such agreements handle worst. Recovery strategy is not chosen by preference; the RTO and RPO choose it.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp's archived-records system is consulted a few times a month, and the BIA assigns it a two-week RTO and a 24-hour RPO. The continuity budget is tight, and daily backups already go off site. Which recovery strategy is MOST appropriate for this system?

options.A: A hot site keeping a synchronized replica of the records system continuously available.
options.B: A warm site with standby servers that can be restored within a day or two.
options.C: A cold site providing space, power, and connectivity, with hardware procured at declaration.
options.D: A mobile recovery trailer contracted for delivery to the site within 48 hours.

questions.explanation: With two weeks of tolerated downtime and daily off-site backups already covering the 24-hour RPO, the cheapest strategy that can rebuild the system inside a fortnight wins - and a cold site's procure-and-build timeline fits comfortably inside that window at a fraction of any alternative's cost. A is wrong because continuous synchronization buys minutes of recovery for a system the business can live without for fourteen days; that premium belongs on the processing systems, not the archive. B is wrong for the same reason at smaller scale - standby servers recovering in a day answer a requirement nobody set, and the stem says the budget is tight. D is wrong because contracted 48-hour delivery is a speed guarantee this system does not need, priced accordingly, and mobile facilities suit organizations that must recover at or near their own premises. Overshooting an RTO is not safety; it is budget taken from systems that need it more.

questions.question: For its settlement-processing system, a regional bank sets a 48-hour RTO and an 8-hour RPO. The continuity budget was cut this year, and the board has rejected the standing cost of running duplicate live infrastructure. Which recovery strategy BEST balances these constraints?

options.A: A warm site with hardware installed, activated by restoring recent backups and redirecting links.
options.B: A hot site mirroring settlement transactions to a second facility in near real time.
options.C: A cold site whose equipment is ordered from suppliers once a disaster is declared.
options.D: Cloud-hosted replica systems kept running continuously alongside the primary site.

questions.explanation: A warm site is the strategy built for exactly this middle ground: hardware waits installed but idle, so activation is a restore-and-redirect exercise that fits a 48-hour RTO, and backups taken every few hours satisfy an 8-hour RPO - all without the standing cost of live duplicates the board refused. B has the capability but fails the mandate: near-real-time mirroring is precisely the duplicate live infrastructure that was rejected, solving a 48-hour problem with a 48-second answer. C is wrong because procurement lead times make cold-site recovery a matter of weeks; against a 48-hour RTO it fails the requirement outright. D is wrong because moving the duplicate to a cloud provider changes the invoice, not the concept - continuously running replicas are still standing live infrastructure, and metered cloud pricing does not make an always-on footprint free. Read the constraints as a system: the RTO rules out cold, the board's decision rules out hot in any wrapper.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp has just finished writing its first disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch. Nothing in the plan has yet been validated, and management will accept no disruption to production while confidence remains low. Which test type should the team conduct FIRST?

options.A: A parallel test, running recovery systems alongside production and comparing their output.
options.B: A tabletop exercise, walking the recovery team through a disaster scenario against the plan.
options.C: A full interruption test, failing production over to the recovery site and back again.
options.D: An unannounced live drill measuring how staff perform under realistic pressure.

questions.explanation: Testing maturity is a ladder, and an unvalidated plan starts on the bottom rung: a tabletop exercise puts the team around a scenario, exposes missing steps, wrong assumptions, and unclear roles, and costs production nothing - exactly what a first validation is for. A is wrong because a parallel test commits real recovery infrastructure and staff time to executing procedures nobody has yet sanity-checked; it is the right test after paper exercises have wrung out the plan's logic. C is wrong because deliberately failing over production is the highest-risk test in the catalogue, directly violating management's constraint, and running it against an unvalidated plan is how DR tests become disasters. D is wrong because surprise measures readiness, not correctness - springing an unrehearsed plan on unbriefed staff tests people with a document that has never been proofread. Validate the plan before you validate the performance.

questions.question: A field technician reports that a USB stick found plugged into an ATM's maintenance port contains an unknown executable. The SOC wants to learn what the program actually does, and the analysis must neither endanger other systems nor reveal the investigation to the attacker. Which approach BEST meets these requirements?

options.A: Scan the executable with several locally installed anti-malware engines and record their verdicts.
options.B: Upload the file to a public multi-engine analysis portal and review the community results.
options.C: Detonate the executable in an isolated internal sandbox instrumented to record its behavior.
options.D: Run the executable on a spare workstation on the office network under monitoring tools.

questions.explanation: Learning what a program does means letting it run somewhere its actions are captured and cannot escape - an instrumented, isolated sandbox delivers the behavioral record while containing the blast and keeping the sample in-house. A is wrong because local scanning is static and signature-bound: a custom ATM implant will likely return clean verdicts, and no scan reveals runtime behavior like C2 addresses or dispense commands. The second requirement eliminates B: public portals share uploaded samples, and attackers routinely watch for their own binaries appearing there; the upload itself announces that the implant was found. It is a fine first move for commodity malware with no secrecy concern. D is wrong because a spare workstation on the office network satisfies neither requirement: the malware can spread or beacon out from a live segment, and the machine lacks the instrumentation to capture what happened. Contain the execution, record everything, tell no one outside.

questions.question: The SOC wants visibility into attacks against the ATM transaction network. The network team, still wary after the outage, refuses any inline device that could delay or drop legitimate transactions if it fails or misfires. Which monitoring deployment BEST satisfies both teams?

options.A: An inline intrusion prevention appliance operating in blocking mode at the network core.
options.B: A tightened firewall rule set that logs and drops unusual transaction traffic.
options.C: Daily analyst review of NetFlow summaries exported from the core switches.
options.D: A passive intrusion detection sensor on a network tap, alerting the SOC in real time.

questions.explanation: A sensor fed from a tap sees a copy of the traffic while sitting entirely outside the transaction path - if it crashes, misfires, or floods with false positives, not one customer withdrawal is delayed, yet the SOC still gets real-time alerts. That is the whole trade the two teams need. An inline blocking appliance is precisely what the network team refused, making A the wrong choice here: it can drop legitimate transactions on a bad signature and becomes an availability risk in the very path the outage taught them to protect. It is the right choice when active blocking is worth that risk. B is wrong for the same inline reason in different clothing - a drop rule acting on 'unusual' traffic makes the firewall an unsupervised gatekeeper of production transactions. C is wrong because flow summaries reviewed daily provide coarse, delayed visibility; an active attack would be a day old before an analyst saw its outline. Passive visibility first; blocking only where the availability cost is accepted.

questions.question: A critical vulnerability in the ATM transaction switch is being actively exploited across the industry, and the vendor's corrected patch is three weeks away. The exploit's network signature is well documented. After the patching disaster, the CCB insists that any patch must first complete full staging tests. What is the team's BEST course of action?

options.A: Deploy an inline intrusion prevention signature blocking the exploit traffic until the patch clears testing.
options.B: Rely on the passive IDS to alert the SOC whenever exploitation of the switch is attempted.
options.C: Push the vendor patch straight to production, accepting the process risk given the active threat.
options.D: Isolate the transaction switch from the network until the tested patch can be installed.

questions.explanation: With a documented exploit signature, an IPS rule acts as a virtual patch: it blocks the attack traffic in transit, buying the three weeks the vendor and the staging tests need, without touching the fragile switch itself. This is the textbook compensating control for a patch gap. B is wrong because an alert is not a barrier - against active industry-wide exploitation, the SOC would be logging successful compromises as they happen; detection is the right posture only when no preventive option exists. C is wrong because it re-runs the case study: an untested patch pushed to production under time pressure is the exact decision that caused the 18-hour outage, and the CCB has just prohibited it. D is wrong because isolating the transaction switch is a self-inflicted denial of service - three weeks without transaction processing does the attacker's job for them. When patching must wait, block the exploit path in the meantime.

questions.question: During the fraud investigation, analysts needed four days to assemble a timeline: each ATM keeps logs locally with inconsistent clocks and retention periods, and nothing can search across machines or connect events on the ATMs with events on the transaction switch. Which improvement BEST addresses these gaps?

options.A: Extending the local log retention period on every ATM in the fleet to one year.
options.B: A SIEM platform aggregating the logs centrally, with synchronized time and cross-source correlation.
options.C: A SOAR platform automating the response playbooks the SOC executes most often.
options.D: Quarterly audits verifying that each machine is recording the required event types.

questions.explanation: Every pain point in the stem - scattered storage, unsearchable data, clock skew, no way to link ATM events to switch events - is the problem SIEM was invented for: collect centrally, normalize timestamps, and correlate across sources, turning a four-day manual assembly into a query. A is wrong because longer retention preserves more of the same disconnected logs; the investigation was slow because of fragmentation, not because data had expired. C is wrong as a matter of sequence: SOAR automates responses driven by correlated alerts, so without the SIEM's data layer underneath there is nothing meaningful to orchestrate. It is the right investment once alert volume, not visibility, is the bottleneck. D is wrong because auditing what each machine records improves completeness at the edges while leaving the logs exactly as scattered and uncorrelatable as before. Fix visibility first; volume and automation come after.

questions.question: Malware on several ATMs is transmitting stolen card data to an attacker's server over outbound HTTPS. The firewall rules were written years ago: inbound connections are tightly restricted, but the ATMs may open connections to any Internet destination. Which firewall change would BEST contain this exfiltration channel?

options.A: Tighten the inbound rules further, so attackers cannot open new connections from outside.
options.B: Enable deep packet inspection of inbound traffic against known malware signatures.
options.C: Apply egress filtering permitting outbound connections only to the approved processing endpoints.
options.D: Rate-limit outbound traffic from the ATM segment to slow any bulk transfer.

questions.explanation: An ATM has one of the most predictable traffic profiles in computing - it talks to the processing centre and little else - so a default-deny egress policy naming only those endpoints severs the malware's channel outright, no matter how the traffic is encrypted or disguised. A is wrong because the traffic is outbound-initiated; the inbound rules the stem calls tight were never the path, and tightening them further hardens a door the attacker is not using. B is wrong twice: it also inspects the wrong direction, and the exfiltration rides HTTPS, which signature inspection cannot read without a decryption architecture nobody mentioned. C is unaffected by encryption because it acts on destination, not content. D is wrong because throttling is a delay, not a denial - card records are small, and a trickle exfiltrates them almost as well as a flood. Where a system's legitimate destinations are enumerable, enumerate them and deny the rest.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp's Internet-facing transaction gateway is being flooded with packets whose source addresses belong to the bank's own internal ranges, yet the packets are arriving from the Internet. The border design review asks which missing control MOST directly addresses this traffic. Which is it?

options.A: Egress filtering on the border router, restricting which internal traffic may leave for the Internet.
options.B: A web application firewall inspecting the requests reaching the gateway's application layer.
options.C: Geo-blocking of source countries that generate no legitimate customer traffic.
options.D: Ingress filtering at the border, dropping inbound packets that claim internal source addresses.

questions.explanation: A packet arriving from the Internet bearing an internal source address is impossible as legitimate traffic - it can only be spoofed - so an ingress rule at the border that drops such packets removes this entire flood by definition, with zero false-positive risk. A filters the wrong direction: egress rules govern what leaves the network, and this attack is inbound. Egress anti-spoofing is the right answer to the mirror-image question - stopping your own network from sourcing spoofed attacks on others. B is wrong because a WAF reasons about HTTP requests at the application layer, while spoofed-source floods are a network-layer problem best dropped before any application processing spends resources on them. C is wrong because geography keys off the same source addresses the attacker is forging; spoofed internal addresses have no country to block. When traffic is impossible on its face, filter on the impossibility.

questions.question: After a rash of counterfeit-card fraud, Global ATM Corp suspects that a batch of its customers' card numbers has been stolen and offered for sale. The fraud team wants the earliest possible company-specific warning whenever the bank's cards surface on criminal marketplaces. Which capability BEST provides this?

options.A: A dark web monitoring service watching criminal markets for the bank's card ranges and branding.
options.B: A subscription feed of malware hashes and hostile IP addresses seen across the financial sector.
options.C: Fraud scoring in the authorization stream that flags anomalous use of individual cards.
options.D: A data loss prevention program inspecting outbound corporate traffic for card numbers.

questions.explanation: The signal the team wants lives where stolen cards are sold, so the capability that watches those marketplaces for this bank's specific card ranges is the one that raises the alarm while the data is being offered - before large-scale fraudulent use begins. B is wrong because a generic indicator feed describes attacker infrastructure and tooling across the sector; it says nothing about whether this bank's cards are in the current dump. C is right in kind but wrong on timing: authorization scoring catches the cards as criminals use them, an inherently later stage - it is the right answer to how losses get limited once cards are in play. D is wrong because DLP polices the corporate egress path, and skimmed or breached card data has already left through channels DLP never saw. Intelligence about your own stolen data comes from watching where it is traded, not from tools pointed inward.

questions.question: Peer banks have been breached by an intrusion group whose tooling is known to evade signature-based detection, with dwell times of several months. Global ATM Corp's SIEM shows no related alerts. The CISO wants assurance that the group is not already operating inside the network. Which activity BEST provides that assurance?

options.A: Commission a perimeter penetration test to identify exploitable entry paths into the estate.
options.B: Run hypothesis-driven hunts through existing telemetry for the group's known techniques.
options.C: Load the newest vendor detection signatures into the IDS and the SIEM.
options.D: Run an authenticated vulnerability scan across the entire server estate for missing patches.

questions.explanation: Silence from the SIEM is only meaningful if the SIEM could see this adversary, and the stem says it cannot - so a human must form the hypothesis 'assume they are in' and search the raw telemetry for the group's characteristic behaviors: their lateral-movement patterns, persistence mechanisms, and command channels. That is threat hunting, and finding nothing after genuinely looking is what assurance means here. A is wrong because a penetration test discovers ways an attacker could get in, not whether one already did; it answers a prevention question. C is wrong because the group is defined by evading signatures - refreshing the signature set optimizes the exact detection class the adversary is built to defeat. A vulnerability scan inventories weaknesses, and D misses the key point: an intruder who entered months ago may have used a hole long since patched. Alerts answer 'what did the tools see'; hunting answers 'what did the tools miss'.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp's SOC receives hundreds of phishing-report alerts each week. For every one, analysts manually extract the indicators, check them against threat intelligence, search mailboxes for related messages, and quarantine the hits - identical steps each time, consuming most of each shift. Alert quality is good; the volume is the problem. Which improvement BEST addresses it?

options.A: Expand the SOC team so the triage workload spreads across more analysts.
options.B: Tune the SIEM to suppress phishing alerts that score below a severity threshold.
options.C: Outsource the alert triage queue to a managed security service provider.
options.D: Implement SOAR playbooks automating the extraction, lookup, search, and quarantine steps.

questions.explanation: Work that is high-volume, well-understood, and identical every time is the defining use case for security orchestration: a playbook executes the extraction, intelligence lookup, mailbox search, and quarantine in seconds per alert, and analysts touch only the cases that need judgment. A is wrong because hiring scales cost linearly with a volume that will keep growing, and it spends scarce analysts on work that requires none of their skill - the right answer only when the workload genuinely demands human judgment. B is wrong because the stem says alert quality is good: suppression works by ignoring alerts, which converts a workload problem into missed phishing incidents. C is wrong because outsourcing relocates the manual toil without removing it, adds a coordination seam during incidents, and bills for exactly the repetitive steps automation would erase. Automate the repeatable; reserve people for decisions.

questions.question: An incident responder reaches a compromised, still-running ATM believed to hold the attacker's injected code in memory. Management wants the machine analyzed with as little evidence lost as possible. Following the order of volatility in NIST SP 800-86, which action should the responder take FIRST?

options.A: Power the machine down cleanly and create a forensic image of its hard drive.
options.B: Collect the ATM's transaction records from the central switch before they age out.
options.C: Capture the system's memory and other volatile state while the machine is still running.
options.D: Photograph the machine in place and interview branch staff about recent maintenance visits.

questions.explanation: The order of volatility dictates collecting the most perishable evidence first, and everything the stem cares about - the injected code, live network connections, running processes - exists only in memory and vanishes the moment power drops or the system reboots. Memory acquisition therefore leads. A is wrong because it is the classic volatility error: a clean shutdown preserves the disk perfectly while destroying the very RAM-resident evidence the case turns on; imaging the drive is correct as the following step. B is wrong because records on the central switch are among the most durable evidence available - stored remotely, subject to retention schedules measured in months - so deferring them costs nothing. D is wrong because photographs and interviews document context that is not decaying on a timescale of minutes; valuable, but nothing about a staff interview is volatile. Rank every collection task by how fast the evidence evaporates, then work down the list.

questions.question: Prosecutors reviewing Global ATM Corp's skimming case are weighing four items of evidence for trial. Which item is MOST likely to survive an admissibility challenge?

options.A: An analyst's recollection of a forum rumor naming the suspect as an ATM fraudster.
options.B: A hash-verified image of the ATM's drive, collected under a documented chain of custody.
options.C: A junior technician's personal opinion that the malware appeared to be foreign-made.
options.D: A screenshot of the attacker's marketplace listing, sent in by an anonymous tipster.

questions.explanation: Admissible evidence must be relevant to the case, material to its issues, and competent - lawfully obtained and reliable - and the drive image is the only item that can prove its own reliability: the hash values demonstrate the contents are unchanged, and the custody record accounts for every hand it passed through. The rumor A cites is hearsay layered on hearsay: the analyst cannot testify to facts heard third-hand, and no declarant is available to examine. C is wrong because opinion testimony carries weight only from a qualified expert, and a junior technician's impression about malware origin has no established expertise behind it. D is wrong because authenticity cannot be established: an anonymous source means no one can testify to when, where, or how the screenshot was made, or whether it was fabricated. Evidence wins by provenance, and provenance is built at collection time, not at trial.

questions.question: A flood disables Global ATM Corp's head office. The disaster recovery plan performs well: every IT system is restored at the recovery site within its RTO. Even so, the business stalls for days - the call centre has no workspace, the cash-in-transit contracts contain no fallback instructions, and no one holds authority to relocate staff. What does this outcome MOST clearly reveal?

options.A: The organization lacks a business continuity plan covering people, premises, and processes beyond IT.
options.B: The disaster recovery plan's recovery time objectives were set incorrectly for these systems.
options.C: The recovery site was under-provisioned for the workloads it was required to absorb.
options.D: The business impact analysis omitted the head office's IT systems when ranking critical functions.

questions.explanation: Everything that failed here sits outside IT: workspace for staff, supplier arrangements, and decision authority are continuity-of-business concerns, and the discipline that plans for them is business continuity management - the broader layer within which disaster recovery is only the IT component. Working systems with nowhere to sit and no one empowered to act is the signature of a DRP without a BCP. B is wrong because the RTOs were demonstrably achieved; sharpening targets that were met would change nothing about the days of stall. C is wrong for the same reason - the recovery site did its job, restoring every workload within objective; capacity was not the constraint. D is wrong on two counts: the IT systems plainly were covered, since they were restored on time, and a BIA gap in system ranking would have produced slow or missing systems, not homeless staff and silent suppliers. Restored servers are not a restored business.

questions.question: Following a ransomware detonation, Global ATM Corp's crisis team activates its continuity documentation. The recovery engineers ask specifically for the document containing the server rebuild sequences, the order in which systems must be restored, and the technical steps for failing over to the recovery site. Which document should the team hand them?

options.A: The business continuity plan maintained by the corporate resilience office.
options.B: The business impact analysis produced during last year's planning cycle.
options.C: The disaster recovery plan covering the affected systems.
options.D: The crisis communications plan held by corporate affairs.

questions.explanation: Rebuild sequences, restoration order, and failover procedures are the operational core of a disaster recovery plan - the tactical, IT-focused document written precisely so engineers in this moment have step-by-step instructions rather than intentions. A is wrong because the business continuity plan operates a level above: it keeps business functions running through workarounds, alternate facilities, and staffing decisions, and delegates the technical system-restoration detail to the DRP. Handing engineers the BCP gives them strategy when they asked for procedure. B is wrong because the BIA is an analysis input, not an action document - it established which systems matter and how quickly they must return, information already baked into the DRP's priorities. D is wrong because the communications plan scripts messages to customers, regulators, and press; essential during a ransomware event, but not a word of it rebuilds a server. Match the document to the altitude of the question being asked.

questions.question: Global ATM Corp's BIA concludes that the settlement function can survive a maximum of 24 hours of downtime before the bank faces regulatory penalties and unrecoverable losses. The IT recovery proposal for the supporting systems specifies a 36-hour RTO, because faster options exceed this year's budget. How should the BCP coordinator respond?

options.A: Accept the proposal, since budget constraints legitimately override planning targets for a year.
options.B: Raise the documented MTD to 48 hours, since the recovery capability actually available should define the tolerance.
options.C: Accept it if the RPO remains within limits, since data loss outweighs downtime.
options.D: Reject the proposal, because the RTO must fit inside the MTD for the recovery to be viable.

questions.explanation: The maximum tolerable downtime is a statement of business fact - the point at which the organization suffers unrecoverable harm - and every recovery objective is derived beneath it. An RTO of 36 hours against a 24-hour MTD is a plan to recover the systems after the business they support has already been irreparably damaged, so the proposal fails on its face and the gap goes to management as a funding-or-risk decision. Budget pressure does not shrink the harm; A's silent acceptance is risk acceptance without the authority or visibility that decision requires. B is wrong because it reverses the derivation - the MTD comes from impact analysis of penalties and losses, and editing the number does not edit the regulator. C is wrong because the RPO governs data loss, an independent axis; flawless data recovered twelve hours too late still breaches the tolerance. Recovery targets cascade downward from business survival, never upward from this year's budget.

questions.question: The post-mortem examines why the automated rollback failed: the uninstall command never reached the ATMs because 4,000 crashing machines rebooting in a loop saturated the management network. Leadership accepts that despite better staging, some future change will eventually go wrong at scale. Which additional safeguard would BEST ensure a rollback can succeed under those conditions?

options.A: Requiring the CCB to record a named rollback owner for every change it approves.
options.B: A dedicated out-of-band management channel with reserved capacity for recovery commands.
options.C: Compressing rollback packages so they consume less bandwidth on the shared network.
options.D: Scheduling an automatic fleet-wide reboot to clear the check-in storm before rollback.

questions.explanation: The rollback failed for one reason: the recovery path shared the network that the failure itself destroyed. A management channel that is physically or logically separate, with capacity reserved for command traffic, keeps working precisely when the production network is drowning - which is the condition leadership has told the team to plan for. A is wrong because accountability is a governance improvement that changes nothing about deliverability; a named owner issuing commands into a saturated network fails identically. C is wrong because the bottleneck was the storm of 4,000 machines endlessly rebooting and checking in, not the rollback package size; shaving kilobytes off one command does not clear a saturated link. D is wrong because it prescribes more of the disease as the cure - a simultaneous fleet-wide reboot is a re-creation of the very storm that blocked the first rollback. Recovery mechanisms must not depend on the infrastructure whose failure they exist to fix.

stimuli.title: Global ATM: the Toledo prompt
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp operates 5,000 ATMs. Its service desk logs a report from a branch: an ATM in Toledo displayed a command prompt for a few seconds during a maintenance visit. The fleet runs a standard Windows build with anti-malware and a monthly patch cycle. Each machine writes its own event log locally and keeps thirty days of it. There is no rule about which programs may run. The maintenance vendor's technician says he ran a diagnostic tool he downloaded that morning. By the time an analyst calls back, the machine has been rebooted twice.

profile.environment: Standard Windows build · local event logs, 30 days · outsourced maintenance
profile.state: One reported command prompt, machine already rebooted twice

stimuli.title: Global ATM: two exercises
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp has a written disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch behind its 5,000 ATMs, and has run one tabletop against it. The plan names a recovery team of eleven people across three time zones, lists a call tree, and assumes the switch can be brought up at the Columbus site within four hours. Nobody has yet performed any of the steps. The board has approved two exercises this year and will not accept an outage of production. The operations director has asked what the two exercises should be and what evidence each will produce.

profile.regime: State banking examination · card brand availability requirements
profile.environment: Transaction switch · alternate site at Columbus · eleven-person recovery team, three time zones
profile.state: Plan written, one tabletop run, no procedure yet performed

stimuli.title: A patch that took the fleet down
stimuli.text: A security patch put every one of Global ATM Corp's 5,000 machines into a reboot loop, and customers could not withdraw cash for eighteen hours. No card data was exposed and no transaction record was altered. The test lab cannot replicate every dispenser hardware variant in the field, and the vendor certifies patches only against a reference build. Business impact analysis sets a four-hour recovery time objective and a twenty-four-hour maximum tolerable downtime for the fleet. An engineer has found a registry fix that would stop the loop, but the change board does not meet for three days.

profile.environment: Test lab cannot replicate every dispenser variant · vendor certifies against a reference build

stimuli.title: Who may change what, and who checks
stimuli.text: Global ATM Corp's change board is reviewing four backout plans submitted with a proposed dispenser firmware change, and only one of them is a plan at all. An outage review has separately noted that the lead engineer who wrote a deployment change request also approved it in the tracking system and then executed the deployment. A fleet audit found machines running inconsistent settings: some hardened, others with services re-enabled by field technicians, and no record of what any machine is supposed to look like. Operations also want to compare the reliability of two dispenser models over the coming year.

profile.organization: Global ATM Corp · change and configuration management
profile.environment: Firmware changes submitted with backout plans · machines running inconsistent settings
profile.state: Change process being rebuilt after an outage

stimuli.title: Objectives, and whether they were met
stimuli.text: Trentham Payments restored its transaction switch to working order three hours into a recovery test, after which data validation and reconciliation took another three hours before the business could resume processing. The recovery objective is four hours and the maximum tolerable downtime is eight. The business has separately determined the switch database can lose at most fifteen minutes of committed transactions in a disaster, and the architect must pick a data-protection design that meets that without overspending. A monitoring server was down for a day when its single disk failed.

profile.environment: Four-hour recovery objective, eight-hour maximum tolerable downtime · reconciliation after restore

stimuli.title: Copies, mirrors and what each protects
stimuli.text: An administrator at Trentham Payments proposes mirrored disks after a monitoring server was lost to a single disk failure, and asks whether nightly backups can then be retired. The same review found that an operator had accidentally deleted a week of alert history months earlier. An engineer is separately configuring local storage for a log-collection server with four drive bays, needing to tolerate any single drive failing while keeping as much usable capacity as possible. An archived-records system consulted a few times a month carries a two-week recovery objective on a tight budget, and leased machines are being returned.

profile.environment: Four drive bays in the log collector · nightly backups and a proposed mirror · archived records rarely consulted

stimuli.title: Full, differential, incremental
stimuli.text: An administrator at Ashcombe Mutual runs a full backup of the log server every Sunday night and a differential every other night, and the server's disk has failed on a Thursday morning. The nightly jobs have separately begun overrunning their window near the end of each week, because every night re-copies all changes since Sunday; the administrator must shorten them and accepts that restores may take longer. When a midday incremental was added to the existing scheme, the nightly differentials were afterwards found to be missing files changed during the mornings.

profile.environment: Sunday full backups · nightly differentials overrunning · a midday incremental added

stimuli.title: Rehearsing a plan nobody has run
stimuli.text: Ashcombe Mutual has just finished writing its first disaster recovery plan for the transaction switch. Nothing in it has been validated and management will accept no disruption to production while confidence remains low. A flood exercise at another firm is being studied as a warning: every system was restored within its objective, yet the business stalled for days because the call center had no workspace, cash-in-transit contracts held no fallback instructions and nobody held authority to relocate staff. The mutual's own analysis concludes settlement can survive at most twenty-four hours of downtime.

profile.regime: State insurance regulation · board risk appetite
profile.environment: First disaster recovery plan written · nothing validated · flood exposure at head office

stimuli.title: An objective that does not fit inside the tolerance
stimuli.text: Ashcombe Mutual's analysis concludes that its settlement function can survive a maximum of twenty-four hours of downtime before regulatory penalties and unrecoverable losses begin. The information technology recovery proposal for the supporting systems specifies a thirty-six-hour recovery objective, because faster options exceed this year's budget, and the continuity coordinator must respond. The mutual is separately outsourcing overnight monitoring of its machine estate and wants the provider's response to outages to be enforceable with defined consequences. An earlier midday incremental broke the nightly differentials.

profile.environment: 24-hour maximum tolerable downtime · 36-hour recovery proposal · service level agreement being drafted

stimuli.title: A command prompt on a machine in Toledo
stimuli.text: A branch has reported to Halloway Cash Systems that one of its machines displayed a command prompt for a few seconds during a maintenance visit. The fleet runs a standard build with anti-malware and a monthly patch cycle, each machine writes its own event log locally and keeps thirty days of it, and there is no rule about which programs may run. The maintenance technician says he ran a diagnostic tool he downloaded that morning. By the time an analyst called back the machine had been rebooted twice. A USB stick with an unknown executable was found in another machine's port.

profile.environment: Standard build with anti-malware · thirty days of local event log · no rule on which programs may run
profile.state: Machine rebooted twice before an analyst called back

stimuli.title: Evidence that will survive a challenge
stimuli.text: Prosecutors reviewing Halloway Cash Systems' skimming case are weighing four items of evidence for trial and must pick the one most likely to survive challenge. An incident responder has separately reached a compromised machine that is still running and believed to hold the attacker's injected code in memory, and management wants it analyzed with as little evidence lost as possible. The security operations center wants visibility into attacks against the transaction network, but the network team refuses any inline device that could delay or drop legitimate transactions. Egress rules were written years ago.

profile.environment: Skimming case heading to trial · memory-resident code on a running machine
profile.state: Prosecutors weighing four items of evidence

stimuli.title: Blocking what has no patch yet
stimuli.text: A critical vulnerability in Halloway Cash Systems' transaction switch is being actively exploited across the industry, the exploit's network signature is well documented, and the vendor's corrected patch is three weeks away. After an earlier patching disaster the change board insists any patch must first complete full staging tests. The internet-facing gateway is separately being flooded with packets whose source addresses belong to the company's own internal ranges, arriving from outside. Peer firms have been breached by a group whose tooling evades signature detection, with dwell times of months.

profile.environment: Exploit signature published, vendor patch three weeks away · spoofed internal addresses at the border
profile.state: Change board insisting on full staging tests

stimuli.title: Too many alerts, too few people
stimuli.text: Cranfield Bank's security operations center receives hundreds of phishing-report alerts each week, and for every one analysts manually extract the indicators, check them against threat intelligence, search mailboxes for related messages and quarantine the hits: identical steps every time, consuming most of each shift. Alert quality is good; the volume is the problem. A fraud investigation separately needed four days to assemble a timeline because each machine keeps logs locally with inconsistent clocks and nothing can search across them. An audit found maintenance laptops trusted unconditionally once on the internal network.

profile.environment: Hundreds of phishing reports weekly · machine logs local with inconsistent clocks · maintenance laptops trusted once inside
profile.state: Analysts consumed by identical manual steps

stimuli.title: Least privilege, and the people problem
stimuli.text: A fraud investigator at Cranfield Bank assigned to a case involving twelve customer accounts turns out to be able to read the records of every customer in the bank, and his database account also carries administrative rights he has never used. Internal audit separately warns that only one engineer understands the settlement reconciliation jobs and could conceal an ongoing fraud indefinitely because nobody else touches the process. A further audit finds four operations staff sharing one domain administrator password, using it for routine work such as email and browsing, unchanged for two years.

profile.environment: Investigator able to read every customer record · one engineer owns settlement reconciliation · four staff sharing a domain administrator password

questionsV2.question: Management asks which change would have stopped the technician's downloaded tool from running at all. Which control BEST meets that description?

options.A: Anti-malware configured to submit unknown executables to the vendor for analysis.
options.B: A policy forbidding technicians from downloading software to fleet machines.
options.C: Blocking the fleet's outbound web access to sites known to host hacking tools.
options.D: A deny-by-default policy admitting software the organization has explicitly authorized to execute.

questionsV2.explanation: Every option except D starts from a list of things known to be bad, and a diagnostic tool downloaded that morning is on nobody's list. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-7(5) Least Functionality | Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception is the precise control: identify the software authorized to execute, employ a deny-all permit-by-exception policy to allow it, and review and update the list on a defined frequency. Its sibling CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception is the weaker direction, and the catalog says so by structure. Note the vocabulary: Rev 5 uses allow-list and deny-list where older material says whitelisting and blacklisting. A is detective when preventive is asked, and it acts on an executable that is unknown by definition. B is the right control for a different problem, a rule aimed at a person rather than a condition enforced on the machine. C is wrong scope, applying deny-by-exception to the network, where the list can never be complete and the tool arrived on a technician's own laptop anyway. Enumerate the good, not the bad.
questionsV2.recallLine: What would have stopped an unapproved downloaded tool from executing on a fleet machine?

optionsShort.A: Submit unknown executables to the vendor

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: How does the fleet get coverage for a variant the anti-malware vendor has not yet seen?

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What belongs in the maintenance contract about technician conduct on the bank's machines?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What reduces casual access to tooling sites from machines that have no need to browse?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7(5) Authorized Software - Allow-by-Exception
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-7(4) Unauthorized Software - Deny-by-Exception; CM-10 Software Usage Restrictions

questionsV2.question: The analyst finds that the Toledo machine's local log now begins after the second reboot. Which change would MOST improve the company's ability to investigate the next report?

options.A: Extending local log retention on every machine from thirty days to one year.
options.B: Forwarding events to a separate repository as they are written, with synchronized time.
options.C: Requiring technicians to file a written report after every maintenance visit.
options.D: Configuring anti-malware to write its detections into the machine's Windows event log.

questionsV2.explanation: A record that lives only on the machine it describes is a record the machine can lose, and here two reboots were enough. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AU-9(2) Protection of Audit Information | Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components requires audit records to be stored on a system or component physically different from the one being audited, which is the whole answer to this failure. AU-4 Audit Log Storage Capacity, AU-11 Audit Record Retention, and AU-8 Time Stamps with SC-45 System Time Synchronization make the collected records usable across 5,000 machines, and AU-6(3) Correlate Audit Record Repositories is what turns them into a timeline. NIST SP 800-92 is the dedicated log-management guide; the requirement above does not depend on it. A is symptom not cause, treating the age of a record while leaving it in the only place it can be destroyed. C is the right control for a different problem, an administrative account of a visit rather than machine evidence. D is wrong scope, enriching one source on the same host that loses everything. Get the record off the box.
questionsV2.recallLine: Local logs vanished when a machine rebooted. What most improves the next investigation?

optionsShort.A: Extend local retention to a year
optionsShort.B: Forward events to a separate repository
optionsShort.D: Anti-malware writes to the event log

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: How long must records be kept once they are held somewhere they cannot be destroyed?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: How does the company establish what a vendor technician says he did on site?

D.label: wrong scope
D.wouldAnswer: How does the company make sure detections appear alongside system events on the host?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-9(2) Store on Separate Physical Systems or Components
NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AU-4; AU-8 Time Stamps; AU-11 Audit Record Retention; AU-6(3) Correlate Audit Record Repositories; SC-45 System Time Synchronization

questionsV2.question: Analysts confirm unauthorized code on four machines and cannot yet say how it arrived. Management wants the fleet protected today. Which action BEST fits mitigation at this point?

options.A: Reimaging the four machines from the standard build and returning them to service.
options.B: Opening a change request to add allow-listing across the fleet at the next window.
options.C: Isolating the four machines from the management network while the fleet stays monitored.
options.D: Notifying the card brands and the state regulator that a compromise has been confirmed.

questionsV2.explanation: Mitigation is the act of stopping the incident from getting larger while the question of how it started is still open, and isolation is the only option here that does that without destroying the answer. NIST SP 800-61 Rev 3 places this in the Respond Function, where RS.MI-01 covers incidents being contained and RS.MI-02 covers eradication.
