D is wrong because auditing what each machine records improves completeness at the edges while leaving the logs exactly as scattered and uncorrelatable as before. Fix visibility first; volume and automation come after.

questionsV2.question: The team is adopting zero trust. Which change BEST reflects that model for the maintenance laptops?

options.A: Strengthen the perimeter firewall so unmanaged laptops cannot reach the internal network.
options.B: Authenticate and authorize every connection to each ATM, regardless of originating network.
options.C: Require VPN tunnels for remote staff while continuing to trust traffic from on-site devices.
options.D: Grant maintenance laptops standing access after a one-time posture check at enrollment.

questionsV2.explanation: Zero trust removes network location from the trust decision entirely: every request must prove who is asking and whether they are entitled, whether it comes from the data center next door or a coffee shop. B applies exactly that. A is wrong because hardening the perimeter is the model zero trust replaces - once anything gets inside, the flat trust problem the audit found remains untouched. C is wrong for the same reason at a smaller scale: it authenticates the remote path while still equating on-site presence with trustworthiness. D is wrong because a one-time check that confers standing access is the opposite of continuous verification; a laptop compromised the day after enrollment keeps its access. The test for any zero-trust proposal: does location or past verification still buy access? If yes, it is perimeter thinking renamed.

questionsV2.question: Intelligence describes cash-out malware installed through compromised laptops, and the machines run a fixed application set. Which control is MOST effective?

options.A: Signature-based anti-malware on every ATM with definition updates applied daily.
options.B: An endpoint detection agent reporting process activity to the SOC for investigation.
options.C: Monthly authenticated vulnerability scans across the entire ATM fleet.
options.D: Application allow-listing that permits only the approved vendor binaries to run.

questionsV2.explanation: A fixed-function device is the ideal case for a default-deny execution policy: when the legitimate software set never changes, anything outside the approved list is by definition unauthorized, so allow-listing stops even malware no vendor has ever cataloged. A is wrong because signature-based detection recognizes only known samples, and targeted cash-out malware is typically custom-built precisely to evade signatures. B is wrong because an EDR agent is detective - it reports execution to the SOC after the code has already run, which fails the stem's requirement to prevent execution. C is wrong because vulnerability scanning addresses a different problem: it finds weaknesses that might admit an attacker, but does nothing to stop a binary introduced through a legitimate maintenance channel. On fixed-function fleets, define what may run and deny the rest.

questionsV2.question: Two hours into an outage the bridge is split between full understanding and a tested workaround. Which position should the incident manager support?

options.A: Restore service with the tested workaround now, and hand root-cause analysis to problem management.
options.B: Keep the fleet offline until root cause is confirmed, since a recurrence would double the damage.
options.C: Restore service only after the vendor certifies a corrected patch for the dispenser driver.
options.D: Restore half the fleet now, keeping the other half offline for the investigation team.

questionsV2.explanation: Incident management has one objective: return service to normal as fast as safely possible, and a tested workaround achieves it. The discipline deliberately splits duties so that restoration is not held hostage to understanding - root cause belongs to problem management, working after the customers are back online. B is wrong because it applies problem management's goal at incident management's moment; every hour of deliberate downtime is certain harm, weighed against a recurrence the workaround already guards. That caution is the right answer when a restoration path is untested and could worsen the damage. C is wrong because it chains recovery to a third party's timetable when an internal path exists - the vendor fix matters for redeployment later, not for restoring service now. D is wrong on scope: preserving a handful of machines for analysis is legitimate, but idling two thousand confuses evidence preservation with a sampling need. Restore first; understand in parallel.

questionsV2.question: Which assessment of the investigator's two findings is MOST accurate?

options.A: Reading unrelated customer records breaches need-to-know, while the standing admin rights breach least privilege.
options.B: Both findings are a single defect, because the two principles amount to the same control in practice.
options.C: Least privilege governs which records he may read, and need-to-know limits his system permissions.
options.D: Neither finding is a defect, since investigators require broad reach to follow leads across accounts.

questionsV2.explanation: The two principles constrain different things: need-to-know restricts access to information to what the current task requires - twelve accounts, not every customer - while least privilege restricts system rights and permissions to the minimum the role requires, which unused administrative rights plainly exceed. A maps each finding to the principle it violates. B is wrong because the principles are related but distinct; collapsing them hides the fact that fixing one finding leaves the other open. C is wrong because it swaps the definitions - records are information (need-to-know), permissions are rights (least privilege) - and applying the wrong principle produces the wrong remediation owner. Breadth is granted per investigation on demonstrated need, not as standing access; D overstates the investigator's entitlement, and convenience does not create need. When a question mixes data access with system rights, sort each finding into its own principle first.

questionsV2.question: Which single control BEST addresses both the key-person dependency and the fraud exposure?

options.A: Mandatory vacations, with the engineer handing the process to a colleague for two weeks yearly.
options.B: Dual control, with a second person approving each settlement run before it executes.
options.C: Job rotation, cycling other engineers through the settlement role on a regular schedule.
options.D: Enhanced logging of the engineer's activity, with weekly review by the security team.

questionsV2.explanation: The audit describes two exposures with one root: exclusivity. Rotating other engineers through the role attacks both at once - fresh eyes on the process surface irregularities a lone operator could bury, and each rotation builds another person who can run settlements, dissolving the key-person dependency. A is wrong only on coverage: mandatory vacation forces a hand-over that can expose concealment, but two weeks a year leaves the dependency intact for the other fifty. It is the right answer where the sole concern is detecting fraud. B is wrong because an approver checks outcomes without learning to operate the process, so the bank still cannot run settlements without this engineer. D is wrong because the reviewers lack the expertise to judge what they are reading - the stem says nobody else understands the jobs - and logging does nothing for continuity. One control, two findings: pick the one that covers both.

questionsV2.question: Which approach BEST addresses all three findings on the shared administrator password?

options.A: A privileged access vault issuing the credential per task to identified users and rotating it after each use.
options.B: A policy requiring the shared password to change every 90 days and whenever a staff member departs.
options.C: Multi-factor authentication enforced on the shared domain administrator account, with a second factor required before every privileged logon.
options.D: Separate personal accounts for each operator, reserved for administrative tasks only.

questionsV2.explanation: Three findings need covering: shared use with no attribution, privileged credentials used for routine work, and a stale secret. A vault covers all three in one mechanism - each check-out ties use to a named person, check-out happens only for a stated administrative task, and automatic rotation after use retires the two-year-old password permanently. D is the strong runner-up: personal admin accounts restore attribution and, used only for administration, separate routine work - but nothing in it rotates or protects the credentials themselves, so the stale-secret finding survives. It is the right answer where no PAM tooling is available. B is wrong because rotating a password that four people still share fixes staleness while leaving the two bigger findings - anonymity and everyday privileged use - untouched. MFA on a shared account strengthens the login without identifying which of the four performed it; C closes none of the attribution problem. Count the findings each option closes; only one closes all three.

questionsV2.question: Service is restored and the record is ready to close, but the vulnerability remains open across the fleet. What should the team do NEXT?

options.A: Redeploy the patch fleet-wide in the next maintenance window, since the fix is already built.
options.B: Perform root-cause analysis of the driver conflict and the process gaps before any redeployment.
options.C: Expand network capacity so a future rollback command can reach machines that are rebooting.
options.D: Close the problem record, since service levels have returned to their normal targets.

questionsV2.explanation: Problem management exists to stop recurrence, and its instrument is root-cause analysis: until the team understands why the patch and the dispenser driver conflicted, and why the process approved a full-fleet push without a viable backout, any redeployment is a rerun of the same bet. The open vulnerability argues for urgency in the analysis, not for skipping it. A is wrong because it repeats the original decision unchanged - the patch that crashed 4,000 machines is 'already built' in exactly the state that crashed them. Saturated bandwidth was a symptom that worsened the incident, not its cause; C plans for the next failure instead of preventing it. D is wrong because restored service closes the incident, not the problem - the defect that produced the outage is still unexplained and unfixed. Incidents end at restoration; problems end at prevention.

domains.title: Software Development Security
domains.caseStudy:
Domain 8 covers security in the software lifecycle: development methodologies, secure coding, code repositories and build pipelines, application testing, and the risks in software you buy or integrate rather than write.

Case Study: The "GitHub" API Key Leak

### Context

Global Bank built a "Cardless Cash" feature: the mobile app authenticates to a backend API and the ATM dispenses without a card. The right design used OAuth and short-lived tokens. During a hackathon, to save time, the developers hardcoded a master API key into the source. One developer pushed the code to a public GitHub repository to keep working from home.

### What went wrong

Bots that scan GitHub for strings like API_KEY found it within seconds. With the key, attackers authenticated to the backend as an administrator, skipping user authentication entirely. The API did not check whether the caller owned the records it asked for, so any account was readable; one endpoint was vulnerable to injection; and the same access could initiate transfers.

Cardless transactions are, in the white paper's terms, one of the strongest answers to skimming, shimming and card trapping, because there is no card at the fascia to attack. What that trade does is move the trust from the card reader to the mobile app and the API behind it. The paper's section on software vulnerabilities lists the failure modes that then matter: application flaws, insecure configuration, default credentials. It also observes that attack tooling is a commodity now, sold on darknet forums with manuals; scraping bots are the same economics applied to leaked secrets.

### What a practitioner does differently

Secrets never live in code. They live in a vault, are issued to services as short-lived tokens through OAuth 2.0 client credentials, and rotate on a schedule and instantly on suspicion. Secret scanning runs as a pre-commit hook and as a pre-receive hook on the server, so a key cannot reach a repository, public or private.

Authorization is checked per object: every API call verifies the caller owns the record. Queries are parameterized. Both are OWASP Top 10 items (broken access control, injection), and both are found by static analysis and code review before a hackathon branch is anywhere near production. Which is the larger point: hackathon code is a prototype. It enters the normal lifecycle, with threat modelling at design and testing before release, or it does not ship.

Repository policy closes the door the developer walked through: no public repositories for bank code, branch protection, and mandatory review before merge. Monitoring on the API catches an administrator identity doing what no administrator does at 2 AM.

### Outcome

The key was rotated as soon as the leak was found and the public repository taken down. The bank's postmortem added secret scanning to every pipeline, per-object authorization to the API, and a rule that prototype code re-enters the lifecycle at the requirements stage.

### What the exam tests

Expect questions on where security sits in each SDLC phase, on secure coding and the OWASP Top 10 categories this scenario touches (broken access control, injection, identification and authentication failures, cryptographic failures), on secrets management and repository security, on the difference between authentication and authorization, and on why a prototype needs the same gates as production code before it is deployed.

### Related reading

The bank in this scenario is a composite. The trade-off and the controls are documented in:

- [Technical Risks and Attack Vectors Targeting ATMs](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-technical-risks-white-paper.pdf), the sections on contactless and cardless transactions, on software, OS and firmware vulnerabilities, and on secure development practices for ATM applications.
- [ATM Security Capability Maturity Worksheet](https://portfolio.atmavailability.com/atm-capability-maturity-worksheet.pdf), Domain 2, logical and cybersecurity controls.

questions.question: During a hackathon, Global Bank's mobile developers hardcoded the backend Master_API_Key into source code, and the code was later pushed to a public repository. The bank now wants to keep credentials from ever residing in application code again. Which approach best achieves this goal?

options.A: Store credentials in a configuration file that is excluded from version control by .gitignore
options.B: Encrypt the hardcoded key within the source so it is unreadable in the repository
options.C: Restrict every company repository to private visibility so outsiders can no longer browse code
options.D: Retrieve credentials at runtime from a managed secrets vault with access control and rotation

questions.explanation: Code is for logic; secrets belong in a dedicated store. A vault (D) means the credential never enters the codebase at all: the application fetches it at runtime, access is authenticated and audited, and the key can be rotated centrally after any suspected exposure. A is wrong because it merely relocates the secret: a .gitignore entry is advisory, the file still sits unprotected on disks and in backups, and one wrong command commits it anyway; it is the right answer to keeping local developer settings out of a repo, not to protecting production secrets. B is wrong because the application must ship the decryption key too, so the secret remains recoverable from the artifact. That is obfuscation, not protection. C is wrong because it reduces external exposure while leaving the credential in code, visible to every employee, clone, and backup; private repositories leak regularly.

questions.question: A defense contractor is building flight-control software under a contract that fixes all requirements up front, mandates formal documentation with approval gates at every stage, and prohibits scope changes without a contract modification. Which development model is most appropriate for this project?

options.A: Waterfall, because its sequential phases and stage-gate approvals match fixed, documented requirements
options.B: Scrum, because short sprints let the team reprioritize the requirements as work proceeds
options.C: Rapid Application Development, because time-boxed prototyping delivers a working system fastest
options.D: Prototyping, because iterating on partial versions helps stakeholders discover what they need

questions.explanation: The environment described, with stable contractual requirements, formal documentation, and mandatory approval gates, is exactly what Waterfall's sequential, sign-off-driven structure was designed for, and its classic weakness (going back to an earlier phase is expensive) is neutralized when change is contractually prohibited anyway. B is wrong for this project because Scrum's core advantage is absorbing evolving requirements, which the contract forbids; it would be the right choice where needs shift between iterations. C is wrong because RAD deliberately trades documentation and rigor for speed, the opposite of what the mandate demands; it fits when time-to-market dominates. D is wrong because prototyping exists to help stakeholders who cannot yet articulate requirements; here the requirements are already fixed and signed. Choose the lifecycle from the stability of requirements and the rigor demanded, not from fashion.

questions.question: A startup is launching a product in a market where customer needs are poorly understood and expected to shift every few weeks. Leadership wants working software delivered early and refined continuously from real user feedback. Which development approach best fits these conditions?

options.A: Waterfall, since completing the full design before coding avoids expensive rework later
options.B: Cleanroom, since formally verified increments give the highest confidence in each release
options.C: Agile, since short iterations and continuous customer feedback absorb changing requirements
options.D: The V-model, since pairing every build phase with a matching test phase catches defects early

questions.explanation: Rapidly shifting requirements plus a demand for early, continuously refined releases are the exact conditions iterative Agile methods were created for: each short cycle delivers working software and folds user feedback into the next. A is wrong because Waterfall assumes requirements can be fixed before design begins — here they cannot, so the finished design would describe the wrong product; it is the right answer when requirements are stable and change is prohibited. B is wrong because Cleanroom's formal specification and verification are slow and assume a precise spec exists; it suits safety-critical software, not a moving target. D is wrong because the V-model is still a sequential, plan-driven shape; its paired test phases verify a fixed specification and cannot absorb change.

questions.question: An online retailer deploys code to production twenty times a day through an automated pipeline. Security reviews are performed manually by a separate team in the week before each quarterly compliance audit, and findings routinely reach developers months after the code shipped. What is the most effective way to close this gap?

options.A: Slow the release cadence so the security team can manually review every change before deployment
options.B: Integrate automated security testing into the pipeline so every build is checked before release
options.C: Increase the frequency of the compliance audits from quarterly to monthly reporting cycles
options.D: Have developers self-certify each release against a secure-coding checklist at deployment time

questions.explanation: The mismatch here is speed: delivery is automated and continuous while security is manual and periodic. DevSecOps closes it by making security run at the pipeline's own speed: automated static analysis plus dependency and secret scanning on every build, so findings reach the developer in minutes, while the change is still fresh. A is wrong because it sacrifices the delivery capability the business built and still scales linearly with reviewer headcount; reserving manual review for the highest-risk changes is sensible, but as the only control it fails. C is wrong because audits are detective and after the fact regardless of frequency; monthly audits still find problems months of deployments too late. D is wrong because self-certification adds no independent verification; checklists guide developers but do not test the code.

questions.question: A security analyst reviewing web logs finds that a request submitting the login value admin' OR '1'='1 caused the application to return every row of the customer table. The application is fully patched and its server configuration follows the vendor hardening guide. Which type of flaw most likely explains this behavior?

options.A: An injection flaw, because untrusted input was interpreted as part of a database command
options.B: A broken access control flaw, because the user viewed rows belonging to other customers
options.C: A security misconfiguration, because the database account held more privileges than needed
options.D: A cross-site scripting flaw, because attacker-supplied text was reflected in the response

questions.explanation: The tell is the quote and OR '1'='1: the input escaped its role as data and changed the logic of the SQL statement, turning a login check into a query that matches every row. That mechanism, input interpreted as code, defines injection (A). B is wrong because broken access control describes an application that correctly parses a legitimate request but fails to check authorization for it; here the request was malformed on purpose and subverted the query itself. B would be right if a well-formed request for another customer's ID had simply been honored. C is wrong because the stem states the configuration follows the hardening guide; over-privileged accounts amplify the damage of injection but do not create the flaw. D is wrong because XSS executes script in other users' browsers; the victim is the client, not the database. Classify a flaw by its mechanism, not by what data it exposed.

questions.question: A development team must remediate a confirmed SQL injection flaw in a banking application's search feature, and wants the fix that addresses the root cause rather than one that filters attack traffic. Which control should the team implement first?

options.A: Deploy a web application firewall with rules that detect and drop known injection patterns
options.B: Sanitize request input by stripping quotes, comments, and SQL keywords before processing
options.C: Rewrite the data-access code to use parameterized queries that bind input as data values
options.D: Encrypt the customer database so records extracted through the flaw stay unreadable

questions.explanation: Injection exists because input and query text are concatenated into one string the database must reinterpret. Parameterized queries (C) remove that root cause: the statement's structure is compiled first and input is bound strictly as data, so no input value can change what the query does. A is wrong as a primary fix because a WAF is a compensating control, pattern-based and bypassable through encoding tricks, and it leaves the vulnerable code in place. It serves well as an interim shield while the code fix is developed, or for a product you cannot modify. B is wrong because blacklist-style stripping chases an open-ended set of bypasses and can break legitimate input (O'Brien); validation is worthwhile defense in depth, not the cure. D is wrong because the application must decrypt data to serve queries, so data stolen through the application arrives in plaintext; encryption at rest answers stolen-media risk, a different problem.

questions.question: Customers of a web forum report that simply viewing a certain product review causes their browsers to send their session cookies to an unknown domain. Investigators find script tags stored in the review text, which the page renders verbatim for every visitor. Which remediation most directly addresses this vulnerability?

options.A: Add anti-forgery tokens to every state-changing form so requests from other sites are rejected
options.B: Move all pages to HTTPS so session cookies are protected from network eavesdropping
options.C: Use parameterized queries so review text cannot alter the structure of database commands
options.D: Encode user-supplied content on output so browsers render it as text rather than script

questions.explanation: This is stored cross-site scripting: attacker-supplied markup was saved and later delivered into victims' pages, where the browser executed it. The defect is at the rendering step, so the direct fix is contextual output encoding (D): the stored text is displayed as inert characters, never parsed as script; a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add depth. A is wrong because anti-forgery tokens counter CSRF, where an attacker forges requests using the victim's session; here the attacker injected script, a different mechanism. B is wrong because TLS protects cookies in transit; these cookies are being read and exfiltrated by script running inside the page itself, over any transport. C is wrong because parameterized queries stop SQL injection; the review was stored through a legitimate write, and the database behaved correctly throughout.

questions.question: A bank customer, while logged in to online banking in one tab, opens an email link in another. A transfer the customer never initiated is immediately sent, and server logs show the request arrived from the customer's own browser carrying a valid session cookie. Which control would most effectively prevent this class of attack?

options.A: Require multi-factor authentication when the customer first signs in to the banking site
options.B: Embed unpredictable per-session tokens in forms and reject requests that lack a valid one
options.C: Encode all user-supplied content the application displays to keep scripts from executing
options.D: Lock accounts after repeated failed logins to defeat automated password guessing

questions.explanation: What happened is cross-site request forgery: the attacker's page made the victim's browser submit a request, and the browser helpfully attached the session cookie, so the server saw an authenticated transfer. An anti-CSRF token (B) defeats it because the forging site cannot read the unpredictable token to include it, so the forged request fails validation; SameSite cookie attributes reinforce the same boundary. A protects the wrong moment: MFA strengthens the login event, and this attack rides a session that is already authenticated. MFA at sign-in is the right answer to stolen credentials, and step-up MFA per transfer would be a separate, additional control. C is wrong because output encoding counters XSS; no script was injected into the bank's pages here. D is wrong because there were no failed logins; the attacker never touched credentials.

questions.question: A crash dump from a C-based payment service shows that an oversized message-length field in a client packet overwrote the function's return address, after which the service executed attacker-supplied instructions. The team must correct the defect in the code itself. Which change best addresses the root cause?

options.A: Validate length fields and use bounds-checked memory operations for every buffer write
options.B: Enable address space layout randomization so injected code lands at unpredictable locations
options.C: Filter inbound packets at the network firewall to drop traffic from untrusted address ranges
options.D: Raise the service's logging level so malformed packets are recorded for later investigation

questions.explanation: A buffer overflow happens when code writes more data into a buffer than was allocated, corrupting adjacent memory, in this case the saved return address. The root cause is the unchecked write, so the fix is in the code: validate untrusted length fields and use bounds-checked operations so an oversized value can no longer spill past the buffer (A); migrating hot paths to a memory-safe language is the same idea taken further. B is wrong as the answer here because ASLR is an exploit mitigation: it makes a successful overflow harder to weaponize but leaves the memory-corruption defect in place; it is the right answer for hardening a platform in depth. C fails because the service must accept client packets to function, and any permitted source can send the malformed field; that is scope, not cause. D is wrong because logging is detective; it records the compromise without preventing it. Mitigations raise attacker cost, but only correct code removes the vulnerability.

questions.question: A newly hired application security lead must choose a starting point for developer training and secure-coding standards at a company that has no existing program and a small budget. How should the lead best use the OWASP Top 10 in this effort?

options.A: Adopt it as the complete set of security requirements the finished application must satisfy
options.B: Treat it as a substitute for penetration testing, since it already lists the likely findings
options.C: Use it as an awareness baseline that focuses training on the most common web risk categories
options.D: Apply it as a hardening checklist for the servers that will host the company's applications

questions.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is an awareness document: a consensus ranking of the most prevalent categories of web application risk. That makes it an ideal seed for a first training curriculum and coding standard: maximum coverage of common failure classes for minimal budget (C). A is wrong because OWASP itself warns the Top 10 is a starting point, not a complete requirements set; when the lead needs verification-grade requirements, the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) is the right artifact. B is wrong because a list of risk categories cannot examine an actual implementation; testing finds the specific instances a list can only name. D is wrong because the Top 10 addresses application-layer risks; server hardening belongs to configuration baselines such as CIS Benchmarks.

questions.question: A document portal serves files through /download?file=report.pdf. An auditor demonstrates that requesting file=..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd returns the server's password file. The developers must correct the flaw in the application itself. Which fix is most effective?

options.A: Reject any filename containing the ../ character sequence before it reaches the file system call
options.B: Canonicalize each requested path and serve it only if it resolves inside the approved directory
options.C: Run the web server behind a reverse proxy that hides internal directory names from clients
options.D: Require users to authenticate before the download endpoint will serve them any file

questions.explanation: This is a path traversal flaw, and the durable fix is to resolve the requested path to its canonical form and then check it against an allow-list boundary (B): whatever encoding or nesting the attacker uses, the final resolved path either falls inside the approved directory or is refused. A is wrong because it is a blacklist: the auditor's own request already used %2F encoding, and variants such as double encoding, ....//, or absolute paths slip past literal matching; filtering one bad pattern treats the symptom while the resolution logic stays broken. C is wrong because hiding directory names is obscurity; the operating system still resolves the traversal sequence regardless of what the client can see. D is wrong because authentication changes who can exploit the flaw, not whether it exists; any logged-in user could still walk out of the web root. Validate the destination the path resolves to, never the characters it contains.

questions.question: A payment form accepts a destination-account field that feeds several downstream systems. The team maintains an ever-growing filter of known malicious strings, yet bypasses keep appearing after each release. Which validation strategy would most durably reduce this input risk?

options.A: Expand the filter with new attack strings as each bypass technique is discovered in the wild
options.B: Move the existing filter into client-side JavaScript so bad input is caught before submission
options.C: Normalize input to lowercase before matching it against the list of known malicious patterns
options.D: Accept only input matching the defined format for account numbers and reject everything else

questions.explanation: Valid account numbers form a small, precisely definable set, while the space of malicious strings is unbounded, so define the former and reject everything else. Allow-list validation (D) is durable because a brand-new attack technique still fails the format check; nobody has to anticipate it. A merely continues the losing race the stem describes: a blacklist is always one bypass behind, by construction. B is wrong because client-side checks improve user experience but provide no security: an attacker posts directly to the server, skipping the JavaScript entirely; validation must be enforced server-side. C is wrong because normalization only tightens the matching of a blacklist that remains reactive at its core; it hardens the wrong model.

questions.question: An administrator investigating a server sees connections in firewall logs that no local tool reports; process listings, file searches, and the installed antivirus all show nothing unusual. The team suspects kernel-level malware is concealing its presence. What is the most reliable way to restore trust in this system?

options.A: Rebuild the system from known-good installation media and restore data from clean backups
options.B: Run a full scan with the installed antivirus using its most aggressive detection settings
options.C: Delete the executables owning the suspicious connections and then reboot the server
options.D: Patch the operating system to the current level so the malware can no longer operate

questions.explanation: A rootkit subverts the operating system itself, so every answer that system gives, from process lists to scan results, is suspect; the firewall seeing traffic the host denies is the classic symptom. Once the kernel is untrusted, the only way to re-establish a trusted computing base is to rebuild from media you trust and restore data verified clean (A). B is wrong because the antivirus runs on, and asks questions of, the compromised OS; the rootkit filters what it is allowed to see; aggressive settings do not fix a lying oracle. B is reasonable when the suspected malware is ordinary user-mode code. C is wrong twice over: the hiding means you cannot reliably find the owning executables, and deleting visible components leaves whatever the kernel implant protects. D is wrong because patching closes entry vectors for the future; it does not evict malware already resident below the tools that would remove it.

questions.question: A company's antivirus quarantines one variant of a malware family, yet new infections keep appearing; each captured sample has a different hash and byte pattern although its behavior on the host is identical every time. Which detection approach is best suited to this threat?

options.A: Distribute the newest signature databases to every endpoint several times per day
options.B: Block executable email attachments at the gateway so samples cannot reach users
options.C: Deploy behavior-based monitoring that flags the malware's actions rather than its code
options.D: Compare file hashes on each host against the list of previously quarantined samples

questions.explanation: Identical behavior with a different hash every generation is the fingerprint of polymorphic malware: it re-encrypts or mutates its code on each infection, so static patterns never stabilize. What it cannot cheaply change is what it does: the files it touches, the persistence it sets, the traffic it sends. That is why behavior-based or heuristic detection (C) catches the family that signatures keep missing. A is wrong because faster signature delivery still loses the race: each new variant is born unsigned; frequency does not fix a model keyed to bytes that keep changing. B is wrong in scope; it narrows one delivery vector while the family may arrive by web, removable media, or lateral movement, and it still detects nothing. D is wrong because hash comparison is the most brittle signature of all: a single changed byte produces a new hash, which is precisely the property the malware exploits. When the code mutates, anchor detection to the behavior that stays constant.

questions.question: A hospital's risk committee is prioritizing defenses after a nearby facility paid attackers to recover encrypted patient records. The committee wants the single control that most reduces the business impact of a successful ransomware attack. Which option should it choose?

options.A: An endpoint protection platform that detects and quarantines known ransomware families
options.B: Offline, regularly tested backups kept isolated from production networks and credentials
options.C: Full-disk encryption on all servers so stolen patient records remain confidential
options.D: A cyber-insurance policy that reimburses ransom payments and recovery expenses

questions.explanation: The discriminator is impact of a successful attack: the committee is asking what limits the damage once prevention has already failed. Ransomware is fundamentally an availability attack, and isolated, tested backups (B) restore availability without paying: offline and credential-separated because modern operators hunt down and encrypt or delete any backup they can reach, and tested because an unrestorable backup is discovered at the worst possible moment. A is wrong for this question because detection reduces the likelihood of success, which the stem has already conceded; it is the right answer to lowering the odds of infection. C is wrong because your own disk encryption does nothing against the attacker layering their encryption on top; it addresses confidentiality of stolen media, a different threat. D is wrong because insurance transfers part of the financial loss while patient care stays down; payment is no guarantee of working decryption and may raise legal issues.

questions.question: During an acrimonious layoff period, a database administrator with commit access inserts code that will delete the payroll tables if his employee ID ever disappears from the HR system. Which safeguard would most likely catch this insertion before it reaches production?

options.A: Antivirus scanning on the database server to detect malicious executable files
options.B: Full-disk encryption of the storage volumes holding the payroll tables
options.C: An annual disaster-recovery exercise proving that payroll can be restored intact from backup tapes
options.D: Mandatory peer review of every code change before it can be merged and deployed

questions.explanation: This is a logic bomb: legitimate-looking code carrying a malicious trigger. Because it is written by an authorized insider and contains no malware signature, the control most likely to catch it is another human reading the change. Mandatory peer review (D) puts a second set of eyes on a deletion routine conditioned on an HR lookup, an obvious red flag, and its mere existence deters the attempt. A fails because the bomb is source code committed through normal channels, not a foreign binary; antivirus is the right answer for commodity malware dropped onto the host. B is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality of data at rest, and the bomb will delete data through fully authorized paths that decrypt transparently. C is wrong for this question because recovery exercises are corrective; they limit the damage after detonation, which makes them the right answer to reducing impact, not to catching the insertion beforehand. Insider code threats are defeated by process controls on the change pipeline, not by malware tooling.

questions.question: Help-desk tickets reveal that several employees installed a free PDF converter from a download site; the tool works exactly as advertised, but network monitoring shows it also opens a remote-control channel to an external host. Which control would most effectively have prevented these installations?

options.A: Application allow-listing that permits only approved software to execute on endpoints
options.B: A security awareness campaign warning staff about software from unofficial sources
options.C: An intrusion detection sensor tuned to alert on remote-access tool network traffic
options.D: Prompt operating system patching to close the vulnerabilities the malware exploited

questions.explanation: A working program that secretly carries a hostile payload is a Trojan horse, and its defining property is that the user willingly runs it, so the strongest defense is one that does not depend on the user's judgment. Application allow-listing (A) blocks the unapproved binary from executing at all, no matter how convincing it looked or who double-clicked it. B is wrong as the most effective choice because awareness is administrative and probabilistic: it lowers the click rate but some installs still happen, as this incident shows; it is the right complement, and the right answer where technical enforcement is infeasible. C is wrong because IDS is detective; it raises an alert after the channel opens rather than preventing the installation the question asks about. D is wrong because no vulnerability was exploited: the user granted execution voluntarily, so patching, the right answer for worm-style exploitation, has nothing here to close.

questions.question: Overnight, malware spreads to hundreds of servers across a flat internal network while no user is logged in anywhere; each infected host scans for neighbors exposing the same vulnerable file-sharing service and infects them directly. Which combination of controls best limits this class of attack in the future?

options.A: Phishing simulations and awareness training so employees stop opening malicious attachments
options.B: Timely patching of exposed network services plus segmentation to contain lateral movement
options.C: Stronger password complexity requirements and lockout thresholds across all accounts
options.D: Full backups of every server retained for ninety days at a separate offsite location

questions.explanation: Self-propagation through a vulnerable network service with zero user involvement is the signature of a worm, and the stem hands you both contributing causes: an unpatched exposed service, and a flat network where every host can reach every other. Patching removes the exploitable flaw; segmentation shrinks the population each infected host can even reach; together (B) they attack propagation at both ends. A guards the human vector, and the defining clue is that no human acted; training is the right answer when malware arrives by phishing or Trojanized downloads. C is wrong because the worm exploited a service flaw, not credentials; hardening passwords is the right answer when spread rides password spraying or credential reuse. D is wrong for this question because backups are corrective; they rebuild servers after the damage and do nothing to limit the spread itself. Read the propagation mechanism first; it tells you which control family is even in play.

questions.question: An analyst studying an outbreak finds malicious code that appends itself to spreadsheet macro files; it lies dormant until an infected file is opened, and it spreads only when users share those files with each other. Nothing propagates unless a person opens a document. How should the analyst classify this malware?

options.A: A worm, since it eventually reached many machines across the company's network
options.B: A logic bomb, since it stays dormant until a specific condition has been met
options.C: A virus, since it attaches to host files and requires user execution to spread
options.D: A rootkit, since it conceals its code inside legitimate document files

questions.explanation: Two properties decide the classification: the code attaches itself to a host file, and it advances only when a human opens that file. Host-dependence plus required user execution defines a virus, in this case a macro virus (C). A is wrong because a worm's defining trait is autonomous spread, exploiting services with no user action; the stem states the opposite, and mere breadth of infection does not make a worm. B is wrong because a logic bomb is code planted in a system awaiting a trigger; it does not replicate by attaching to files; the dormancy here is just the wait for an ordinary open, which is the execution vector, not a chosen trigger condition. D is wrong because a rootkit's concealment means subverting the operating system so that tools cannot see it; riding inside a document is a carrier, not OS-level hiding.

questions.question: A university network team receives abuse complaints that campus machines are flooding an external website. Investigation shows two hundred workstations making identical periodic connections to one overseas domain, from which they fetch commands. Which control would most reduce the ongoing harm from this compromise?

options.A: Requiring password changes for all users whose workstations were observed beaconing
options.B: Encrypting the hard drives of the affected workstations to protect the stored data
options.C: Scheduling monthly vulnerability scans across the campus workstation address space
options.D: Egress filtering and DNS monitoring to block and expose command-and-control traffic

questions.explanation: Two hundred hosts beaconing to one domain for instructions is a botnet, and a bot's value to its herder depends entirely on the command-and-control channel. Cutting that channel at the network edge (D), by blocking the domain, filtering outbound traffic, and watching DNS, both stops the flooding and enumerates the infected hosts for cleanup; it attacks the one thing every bot must do. A misreads the cause: the workstations are compromised by resident malware, not by stolen passwords; new credentials on an infected host are promptly available to the malware anyway. B is wrong because disk encryption protects data confidentiality on lost or stolen media and is irrelevant to a machine actively attacking others while running. C is wrong for the timescale asked about: scanning is preventive hygiene that may reduce future infections, but a monthly detective cycle does nothing about the harm in progress.

questions.question: A vendor discloses that attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in its widely deployed VPN appliance and states that no patch will be available for several weeks. An organization depends on this appliance for all remote access. What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?

options.A: Wait for the vendor patch, since interim changes to the appliance would need rework later
options.B: Apply compensating controls, restricting exposure of the device and increasing monitoring
options.C: Run signature-based antivirus scans against the appliance to remove any implanted malware
options.D: Formally accept the risk, documenting that exploitation is unlikely before the patch ships

questions.explanation: Active exploitation with no patch available is the zero-day window, and the playbook for it is compensating controls (B): shrink the attack surface (restrict which addresses can reach the device, disable the vulnerable feature if the advisory allows, add virtual-patch rules where possible) and watch it closely for indicators of compromise while the fix is pending. A is wrong because it leaves the sole remote-access path exposed for weeks of known, in-the-wild exploitation; a little rework is a trivial price. C is wrong because signature tools recognize known malware, an unknown exploit's payload rarely has one yet, and appliances seldom support host scanners anyway. It is the right reflex for commodity infections, not this one. D is wrong because its own premise is false: exploitation is not unlikely, it is happening now; acceptance is legitimate only when the exposure is genuinely tolerable or mitigation costs more than the risk. When no patch exists, reduce exposure and heighten detection; documenting a risk is not the same as treating it.

questions.question: A team is starting a multi-year system that depends on an unproven biometric technology. Management's chief concern is that unexplored technical risks could sink the project, and it wants each round of work to begin with an explicit risk evaluation before more money is committed. Which lifecycle model best fits this need?

options.A: The spiral model, in which each cycle opens with objectives and a fresh risk analysis
options.B: Extreme Programming, in which paired developers and test-first coding control quality
options.C: The waterfall model, in which risks are addressed once during the initial planning phase
options.D: Rapid Application Development, in which quick prototypes surface problems through user feedback

questions.explanation: Management has literally described the spiral model's engine: repeated cycles that each begin by setting objectives, evaluating risks and alternatives, often retiring the worst risk with a prototype, before committing to the next round of investment (A). It was conceived precisely for large projects burdened with unproven technology. B is wrong because XP's practices manage code quality within iterations; they provide no project-level gate that weighs risk before funding continues. C is wrong because a single up-front risk pass cannot handle risks that only surface mid-build, and with novel technology most of them do; waterfall fits stable, well-understood work. D is wrong because RAD's prototypes optimize for speed and requirements discovery through user reaction; user feedback exposes usability gaps, not systematic engineering risk, and RAD imposes no formal risk-evaluation checkpoint.

questions.question: A software firm loses a government bid because it cannot demonstrate the maturity of its development processes; internally, project success still depends on individual heroics and no two teams work alike. Leadership wants a recognized framework for assessing and improving how the organization builds software. Which framework best meets this goal?

options.A: STRIDE, which categorizes design-level threats to a system under development
options.B: CVSS, which scores the severity of published vulnerabilities on a common scale
options.C: The OWASP Top 10, which ranks the most critical web application risk categories
options.D: CMMI, which appraises process maturity in staged levels and guides improvement

questions.explanation: The firm's problem is the process itself: ad hoc, heroics-dependent, inconsistent across teams, which is the textbook description of the lowest maturity level. CMMI (D) is built for exactly this: it appraises how an organization develops software against defined maturity levels, produces the recognized rating acquirers ask for, and lays out the practice areas to institutionalize next. A is wrong because STRIDE examines one system's design for threat categories; it says nothing about how consistently the organization works. It is the right answer during a product's design phase. B is wrong because CVSS rates individual known vulnerabilities for prioritization; it measures findings, not capability. C is wrong because the Top 10 educates developers about common application risks; awareness of risks is not evidence of repeatable process. Distinguish product-level tools (threats, vulnerabilities, risks) from organization-level frameworks that measure and mature the process itself.

questions.question: Following a disappointing CMMI appraisal, an organization launches a process-improvement program using the IDEAL model. The improvement team is eager to begin rewriting development procedures immediately. According to the model, what must happen first?

options.A: Acting on the weakest findings from the appraisal to demonstrate early momentum
options.B: Diagnosing the current state of practice against the desired future state
options.C: Initiating the effort by securing sponsorship, resources, and an improvement infrastructure
options.D: Learning from a pilot project so that later phases can be adjusted with evidence

questions.explanation: IDEAL sequences an improvement program as Initiating, Diagnosing, Establishing, Acting, Learning, and the ordering is the model's whole point. Before anything else, the Initiating phase (C) sets the business context, wins executive sponsorship, and builds the infrastructure (charter, roles, resources) that will carry the effort; improvement programs launched without that foundation stall as soon as the work gets contentious or expensive. B is wrong only in its timing: diagnosing comes second, and a diagnosis performed with no sponsor or charter produces findings nobody is bound to act on. A is wrong because Acting is the fourth phase; rushing straight to fixes is precisely the trap the eager team in the stem is walking into, changes without diagnosis or plan. D is wrong because Learning is the final phase, harvesting lessons to refine the next pass.

questions.question: A billing team discovers that a customer's mailing address differs across three tables in the same database; an update routine changed one copy but missed the others, and refunds are now being mailed to an outdated address. Which database design practice most directly prevents this class of defect?

options.A: Normalization, so each fact is stored once and referenced rather than duplicated
options.B: Transparent encryption, so address data is protected from any unauthorized reading
options.C: Nightly integrity jobs that compare the three address copies and report mismatches
options.D: Database activity monitoring that logs every change made to customer records

questions.explanation: Three divergent copies of one fact is an update anomaly, and update anomalies are exactly what normalization exists to eliminate: store the address once, reference it by key everywhere else, and there is no second or third copy to miss (A); the defect becomes structurally impossible. C is a detective patch on the symptom: it tolerates the redundancy, lets copies diverge, and then notices, with refunds already misdirected in the meantime; reconciliation jobs are the right answer only for data you cannot restructure, such as feeds from external systems. B is wrong because encryption addresses confidentiality; every one of the three copies can be perfectly encrypted and still inconsistent. D is wrong because an audit log records who changed what, which serves accountability and forensics but does nothing to keep the copies in step.

questions.question: A clinic's reporting system hides individual diagnoses but permits statistical queries. A clerk runs a count of patients with a rare condition across the ward, then the same count excluding one named patient, and subtracts the results to learn that patient's diagnosis. Neither query exceeded the clerk's permissions. Which term best describes this attack?

options.A: SQL injection, because crafted queries extracted data the interface was built to conceal
options.B: Inference, because a protected fact was deduced from individually authorized results
options.C: Privilege escalation, because the clerk obtained information above their access level
options.D: Aggregation, because a large volume of harmless records was fused into a sensitive whole

questions.explanation: The clerk never broke a rule: each query was authorized and well formed. Yet arithmetic across the answers revealed a fact the system withholds. Deducing protected information from legitimately obtainable results is an inference attack (B), and it is countered by controls on the answers, not the access: minimum query-set sizes, noise or perturbation in statistics, and polyinstantiation in multilevel databases. A is wrong because injection means input that subverts the structure of the query itself; these queries ran exactly as designed. C is wrong because no permission boundary was crossed or elevated, which is what makes inference so hard to police; escalation would involve gaining rights the clerk was never granted. D is the closest wrong answer: aggregation is the sibling threat in which many individually non-sensitive records are combined until the collection itself is sensitive. Here the clerk combined two statistics to derive one specific withheld fact: deduction, not accumulation. Aggregation piles data up; inference reasons a secret out, and access control alone stops neither.

questions.question: A logistics contractor is granted access to several databases, each individually rated non-sensitive: truck maintenance schedules, fuel purchases, and driver duty rosters. By correlating them, the contractor reconstructs the timing and routes of classified weapons shipments. Which security concern does this scenario best illustrate?

options.A: Inference, since the contractor deduced one hidden value from a permitted statistical result
options.B: Collusion, since several parties pooled their separate accesses to reach protected data
options.C: Data remanence, since sensitive residue persisted inside systems rated non-sensitive
options.D: Aggregation, since individually non-sensitive data sets combined into sensitive knowledge

questions.explanation: Every source the contractor touched was legitimately non-sensitive; the classified picture emerged only when the sources were correlated. That is aggregation (D): the combination carries a higher sensitivity than any of its parts, which is why access decisions must consider what a subject can assemble in total: need-to-know evaluated across holdings, not per database. A is the closest wrong answer: inference is the sibling concern where someone reasons a specific withheld fact out of permitted answers, as with statistical queries; here nothing was individually withheld or deduced; the sensitivity arose from assembly. B is wrong because collusion requires multiple actors combining their separate privileges; this was one contractor acting within one set of grants. C is wrong because remanence is data physically surviving on media after deletion or reuse; nothing here was residual; the databases were serving their intended content.

questions.question: During a funds transfer, a database server crashed after debiting the source account but before crediting the destination; on restart, the half-completed change remained in the database and the money was missing from both accounts. Which ACID property did the transaction processing fail to uphold?

options.A: Atomicity, because a transaction's operations must apply entirely or leave no effect at all
options.B: Isolation, because concurrent transactions must remain invisible to one another while running
options.C: Durability, because once a transaction commits its effects must survive crashes and remain permanent
options.D: Consistency, because each transaction must move the database between valid states

questions.explanation: The debit and credit form one logical transaction, and the system let half of it persist. The property that forbids exactly that is atomicity (A): all of a transaction's operations commit together, or recovery rolls every one of them back so the transaction never happened; a correct engine would have undone the debit on restart. D is the tempting wrong answer because the books are certainly now inconsistent; but the unbalanced state is the consequence, and consistency between valid states is what atomic all-or-nothing execution exists to preserve. Consistency is the direct culprit when a transaction commits while violating a declared rule or constraint. B does not fit because isolation governs interference between transactions running concurrently, and this failure involved a single transaction and a crash. C is wrong because durability protects work that had committed; the problem here is the mirror image: uncommitted, partial work that survived when it should have vanished. Partial effects persisting after recovery point at atomicity; constraint violations at commit point at consistency.

questions.question: A penetration tester on a coffee-shop network captures traffic from a company web portal that uses HTTPS for its login page but plain HTTP for everything afterward. Using a session cookie copied from another patron's traffic, the tester opens that user's account without ever entering credentials. Which change most directly defeats this attack?

options.A: Enforce a stronger password policy, since the portal's accounts were too easily guessed
options.B: Add a CAPTCHA challenge to the login form to block automated credential attacks
options.C: Serve every page over TLS and mark the session cookie with the Secure attribute
options.D: Shorten the password expiration interval so captured credentials age out quickly

questions.explanation: The attacker performed session hijacking: the login was protected, but the session cookie, which is the credential after login, traveled in cleartext on every subsequent request and was simply copied. Extending TLS to the whole session and setting the cookie's Secure attribute (C) keeps the token off the wire in readable form and instructs the browser never to send it over an unencrypted connection; regenerating session IDs and HttpOnly add depth. A, B, and D all defend the authentication step, and the tester never touched it: no password was guessed (A), no automated login attempts occurred (B), and no credential was captured to age out (D); a hijacked session bypasses all three. A would be right against brute-force guessing, B against credential-stuffing bots, D against stale stolen passwords.

questions.question: An application review finds that the session cookie can be read by any script running in the page and is also transmitted when users follow links over unencrypted connections. Which pair of cookie attributes most directly closes these two exposures?

options.A: Domain and Path, which limit the hosts and URL prefixes to which the cookie is sent
options.B: HttpOnly and Secure, which deny script access and restrict the cookie to encrypted transport
options.C: Max-Age and Expires, which bound how long the browser retains the session cookie
options.D: SameSite and Path, which control whether cross-site navigation includes the cookie

questions.explanation: Map each finding to the attribute built for it: script access to the cookie is removed by HttpOnly, which hides the cookie from the page's JavaScript so even a successful XSS payload cannot read it; cleartext transmission is removed by Secure, which forbids the browser from sending the cookie over anything but an encrypted connection (B). A is wrong because Domain and Path only scope which requests include the cookie; within that scope, scripts can still read it and HTTP links still carry it. D is wrong for the same reason at a different boundary: SameSite governs whether cross-site requests attach the cookie, which is a CSRF defense, and neither finding involves cross-site requests. C is wrong because lifetime limits shrink the window of misuse without closing either exposure: a cookie can be stolen by script or sniffed off the wire in its first minute.

questions.question: A monitoring service alerts a bank that a production API key is visible in a public repository, pushed there three days ago by a developer. The security team confirms the key grants administrative access to the transaction backend. What should the team do first?

options.A: Delete the offending file from the repository and rewrite its commit history to purge the key
options.B: Make the repository private so that no additional external parties can view the key
options.C: Revoke the exposed key immediately and issue a replacement through approved channels
options.D: Interview the developer to establish how the key came to be committed and pushed

questions.explanation: Automated bots scrape public repositories for credential patterns within seconds of a push; after three days, the only safe assumption is that the key has already been copied. Nothing that changes who can see the repository going forward alters that, so the first move is to make the stolen value worthless: revoke it and reissue through a proper channel (C), then hunt for fraudulent use during the exposure window. A treats the visible symptom: history rewriting is worth doing afterward for hygiene, but it cannot recall the copies already harvested, and doing it first leaves an active admin credential in attackers' hands meanwhile. B fails the same way: private visibility stops future viewers, not past ones. D matters for the lessons-learned and for fixing the process, but root-cause interviews come after containment, not before it.

questions.question: After a credential leak, a bank decides that commits containing secrets must be blocked before they can ever enter the central code repository, in a way that individual developers cannot bypass from their own machines. Which mechanism best meets this requirement?

options.A: A server-side pre-receive hook that scans incoming pushes and rejects any containing secrets
options.B: A client-side pre-commit hook on every developer workstation that runs local secret scanning
options.C: A nightly scheduled job that scans the repository contents and alerts on any secrets found
options.D: A mandatory code-review checklist item requiring reviewers to look for embedded credentials

questions.explanation: The requirement has two halves, enforcement before the secret enters the shared repository and enforcement developers cannot switch off, and only a control running on the server itself satisfies both. A pre-receive hook (A) evaluates every push at the moment the server is asked to accept it and refuses the whole push if a secret is detected: nothing to install, nothing to bypass. B is the closest wrong answer: client-side hooks give excellent fast feedback, but they live on machines the developer controls: they can be skipped with a flag, and a fresh clone simply does not have them; they complement the server hook, they cannot replace it. C is wrong on timing: by the nightly run the secret has been in shared history for hours, cloned and mirrored. D is wrong because human review is fallible, and in pull-request workflows the code has already been pushed to the server before anyone reviews it. Guarantees of the form 'never enters the repository' can only be enforced where the repository lives.

questions.question: An architecture team is designing a new payment API and wants a structured way to enumerate potential threats (spoofed callers, tampered messages, repudiated transactions, leaked records) before any code has been written. Which technique fits this stage of the lifecycle best?

options.A: Scoring each of the system's known vulnerabilities with CVSS to rank their severity
options.B: Running a dynamic application security test against the deployed staging environment
options.C: Commissioning an external penetration test of the completed payment service
options.D: Threat modeling with STRIDE to categorize design-level threats to each component

questions.explanation: At design time there is no code, no build, and no findings, only architecture. The one technique that operates on architecture alone is threat modeling, and STRIDE (D) is a natural choice here because the team's worry list maps onto its categories one for one: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, plus denial of service and elevation of privilege they have not thought of yet, which is exactly the value of using a structured taxonomy over brainstorming. A is wrong because CVSS scores vulnerabilities that have been discovered in something that exists; there is nothing to score yet. B is wrong because DAST probes a running application: right technique, later phase, once a staging build exists. C is wrong the same way at still a later stage: penetration testing validates the finished, deployed service.

questions.question: A threat-modeling workshop for a trading platform produces forty distinct threats, far more than the team can address this quarter. The security lead needs a repeatable way to rank them so that remediation effort goes to the worst ones first. Which method is designed for this purpose?

options.A: STRIDE, which sorts each threat into one of six categories of malicious behavior
options.B: DREAD, which scores each threat on factors such as damage potential and exploitability
options.C: CVSS, which computes severity scores for vulnerabilities published against shipped software
options.D: CMMI, which appraises the maturity of an organization's development processes

questions.explanation: Ranking forty hypothetical threats needs a rating scheme, and DREAD (B) is exactly that: each threat is scored on Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability, Affected users, and Discoverability, and the totals give a defensible, repeatable priority order for remediation. A cannot rank anything: STRIDE was the enumeration step the workshop just completed; it tells you what kind each threat is, and nothing about which is worse; category membership carries no severity. C is the plausible near-miss: CVSS also produces severity numbers, but it is built for disclosed vulnerabilities in released software, scoring concrete flaws with known exploit characteristics; design-stage threats have no CVE, no patch state, and often no implementation yet. It is the right answer when the input is a vulnerability-scan report. D is wrong because CMMI evaluates how the organization builds software, an entirely different altitude from ranking one system's threats. STRIDE finds and names threats, DREAD ranks them; CVSS rates real vulnerabilities after release.

questions.question: Weeks after launching a public API, a retailer finds one client has issued millions of requests enumerating sequential customer identifiers, and stolen credential lists are being replayed against the login endpoint at high speed. Which pair of controls most directly counters this abuse?

options.A: Moving the API to an undocumented URL path and randomizing its response formats
options.B: Deploying additional API servers behind a load balancer to absorb the request volume
options.C: Rate limiting per client plus strong authentication with authorization checks on every object
options.D: Requiring API consumers to accept terms of service that prohibit automated scraping

questions.explanation: Both abuse patterns exploit the same two gaps: nothing slows a caller down, and nothing verifies that a caller may access the specific record it names. Per-client rate limiting throttles the millions-of-requests behavior that enumeration and credential replay both depend on, and object-level authorization ensures that even a valid session can only retrieve its own records (C), closing the sequential-ID harvest. A is wrong because hidden paths and shuffled formats are security through obscurity; the current abuser already found the API, and any future one will. B is wrong because adding capacity treats hostile traffic as a scaling problem; it makes the abuse run more smoothly at higher cost to the retailer. D is wrong as a technical counter because a terms-of-service document enforces nothing at request time; it has real value as the legal basis for action against an identified abuser, which makes it a complement, not a control.

questions.question: Stakeholders for a new claims-processing interface cannot articulate what they need; two requirements workshops have produced contradictory documents. The delivery lead wants an approach that lets users react to something concrete before the team commits to full development. Which approach best serves this goal?

options.A: Completing a comprehensive requirements specification and having every stakeholder sign it
options.B: Adopting cleanroom methods so that defects are formally prevented from the earliest phase
options.C: Proceeding directly to full construction so users can react to the finished system itself
options.D: Building a limited working model of the interface for stakeholders to evaluate and refine

questions.explanation: When stakeholders cannot say what they want, showing beats asking: a prototype (D) gives them something concrete to react to, converts vague or contradictory wishes into specific corrections, and costs little enough to throw away and iterate, which is the entire reason prototyping exists as a development approach. A doubles down on the technique that has already failed twice; signatures on an ambiguous document create commitment, not clarity, and the conflicts will resurface as change requests during build. B is wrong because cleanroom's formal rigor prevents implementation defects; it verifies the software against its specification, and here the specification itself is the problem: a formally verified wrong product is still wrong. C is wrong because it takes the largest possible bet on the least information; feedback arrives only after the full cost is sunk, when rework is most expensive. Prototype when requirements are the risk; formalize when correctness against known requirements is the risk.

questions.question: To hit a marketing deadline, a team adopts rapid application development: time-boxed cycles, heavy prototyping, and minimal up-front design. The CISO is asked to name the greatest security risk this delivery style introduces. Which answer is most accurate?

options.A: Schedule pressure squeezes security requirements and testing out of each compressed cycle
options.B: The extensive documentation the method demands will delay security review sign-offs
options.C: Requirements frozen at project start will block security fixes once the cycles begin
options.D: The absence of user involvement means real-world abuse goes unconsidered until launch

questions.explanation: RAD's defining trade is rigor for speed. When a time-box tightens, whatever is not demanded by the demo gets cut, and security work such as threat modeling and security test cases is the classic casualty; worse, prototypes that were never meant for production get promoted into it under deadline pressure with their shortcuts intact (A). This is the very pattern behind Global Bank's hackathon key. B is wrong because it describes the opposite methodology: RAD is documentation-light by design; heavy documentation gates belong to waterfall-style processes. C is wrong for the same reason: RAD embraces changing requirements across iterations; frozen baselines are a plan-driven trait. D is wrong because RAD is built around continuous user involvement; the subtle truth, worth keeping, is that users exercise intended behavior while abusers exercise unintended behavior. But the option's premise, absent involvement, is simply false. Fast lifecycles do not forbid security work, they starve it. The countermeasure is making security part of each cycle's definition of done.

questions.question: A medical-device maker must build infusion-pump firmware for which regulators demand evidence that defects are prevented during development rather than found and patched afterward, and that failure rates be certified statistically. Which software engineering approach best aligns with these demands?

options.A: Extreme Programming, relying on test-driven development and continuous pair review
options.B: Cleanroom engineering, using formal specification, verification, and statistical quality control
options.C: Rapid application development, iterating prototypes quickly until users accept the behavior
options.D: Scrum, delivering the firmware in sprints with a defect backlog groomed by the product owner

questions.explanation: The regulator's two demands are the two pillars of cleanroom software engineering (B): defects are prevented before test through formal specification and mathematically based verification of the code, and quality is then demonstrated through statistical usage testing that supports certified reliability claims, precisely the evidence sought. A is the strongest wrong answer: TDD and pair programming are powerful, but they find defects moments after they are written; that is still detect-and-fix, not formal prevention, and XP offers no statistical certification of failure rates. It is the right choice for quality-focused commercial teams without a certification burden. C is wrong because RAD optimizes speed and user acceptance; its tolerance for rough prototypes is the opposite of certifiable rigor. D is wrong because Scrum is a management wrapper that explicitly routes defects into a backlog for later resolution; it prescribes no engineering rigor at all.

questions.question: An organization adopting Scrum asks its security architect how security work should fit a process that ships a product increment at the end of every two-week sprint. Which arrangement best integrates security with this cadence?

options.A: Hold all security requirements for a hardening phase scheduled after the final sprint
options.B: Have the security team test a copy of the product on its own quarterly timetable
options.C: Put security items in the product backlog and security checks in the definition of done
options.D: Dedicate one sprint per quarter entirely to security fixes while feature work pauses

questions.explanation: In Scrum, work exists only if it is in the product backlog, and quality bars exist only in the definition of done, so that is where security must live (C): threat-driven requirements and abuse cases enter the backlog to be prioritized alongside features, and the definition of done makes passing security checks a condition of calling any increment complete. Every sprint then ships software that has met the bar. A is wrong because it recreates the bolt-on waterfall pattern inside an iterative process, and every increment before that final phase ships unexamined. B is wrong because out-of-band quarterly testing lags up to six releases behind; findings arrive divorced from the sprint that caused them. D is the seductive anti-pattern: a periodic security sprint batches risk, lets unvetted features ship for months between passes, and frames security as a tax that pauses real work. It is defensible only as an occasional remediation push on top of, never instead of, per-sprint integration.

questions.question: A product group plagued by defects reaching production is adopting Extreme Programming. The quality manager asks which XP practices will most directly catch defects at the moment the code is being written. Which pairing should the manager highlight?
