options.A: The planning game and small releases, which shorten the feedback loop with customers
options.B: Collective code ownership and coding standards, which keep the code base uniform
options.C: On-site customer and system metaphor, which keep development aligned with business intent
options.D: Pair programming and test-driven development, which review and test code as it is typed

questions.explanation: The discriminator is at the moment the code is being written, and two XP practices operate at exactly that instant (D): in test-driven development the failing test exists before the code, so the first run verifies the new logic immediately; in pair programming a second developer is reviewing each line as it appears, catching slips that the author is blind to. Together they are XP's tightest defect-feedback loop. A operates at the wrong range: the planning game and small releases work at release granularity; they surface wrong priorities and integration surprises in days or weeks, not keystrokes. B is wrong because shared ownership and standards improve maintainability and consistency, which prevents some future defects but examines nothing as it is created. C is wrong because the on-site customer and metaphor align the product with business intent: they catch building the wrong thing, not building the thing wrong.

questions.question: A regulator requires a bank to demonstrate that no change to its payment module is written and merged by a single unreviewed developer, and expects the review to occur as early in development as possible. Which practice most directly satisfies this requirement?

options.A: Pair programming, in which a second developer reviews each line as it is being written
options.B: Static analysis in the pipeline, which examines every commit for known insecure patterns
options.C: Raising unit-test coverage thresholds so that untested changes cannot be merged
options.D: Annual secure-coding training so that each developer can review their own work reliably before merging

questions.explanation: The requirement names two things: a second person on every change, and review at the earliest possible point. Pair programming (A) delivers both at once: the navigator is a continuous human reviewer sitting beside the author, so no line is ever written unobserved, and the review happens at the moment of creation rather than at a later gate. It is two-person integrity applied to code. B is wrong because a static analyzer, however valuable, is not a reviewer: it matches known insecure patterns and misses flawed business logic; a bogus transfer-approval rule sails through; it is the right automated complement, not the human control the regulator described. C is wrong because coverage measures how much code the author's own tests execute; it neither adds a second person nor evaluates intent. D is wrong because training improves the individual, and self-review is precisely what the requirement rules out. When a control demands independent human review, only another human, pairing or a required reviewer, satisfies it; automation assists, it does not substitute.

questions.question: A bank wants its pipeline to catch hardcoded credentials and injection-prone code in its own source before each merge, without waiting for a build to be deployed anywhere. Which testing technology is the most appropriate choice?

options.A: Dynamic application security testing, which probes a running application from the outside
options.B: Static application security testing, which examines source code without executing it
options.C: Software composition analysis, which flags known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies
options.D: Interactive application security testing, which instruments the app while tests exercise it

questions.explanation: Two constraints in the stem decide this: the flaws live in first-party source (hardcoded secrets, injection-prone patterns), and the check must run before merge, when nothing is deployed. Only static analysis (B) works under both: it reads the code itself, so a credential string or an unsanitized query concatenation is visible directly, and it needs no running instance. A is wrong because DAST attacks an application from outside while it runs; it cannot see a hardcoded key that never appears in a response, and there is no running app at merge time. It is the right tool against the deployed build in staging. D fails for the same reason one layer in: IAST observes an instrumented application during test execution, so it also requires a runtime. C is wrong on target rather than timing: SCA inventories the third-party libraries you import and matches them against known-vulnerability data; it does not analyze the code your own developers wrote. SAST reads your source, DAST probes your running app, IAST watches from inside it, SCA audits what you imported. Pick by where the flaw lives and what exists when you test.

questions.question: A penetration test of a production banking app uncovers a URL, absent from all design documents, that grants administrative access with no credentials; version control shows a developer added it during testing to save time and never removed it. What is the most accurate name for this finding?

options.A: A logic bomb left in the code awaiting a trigger condition chosen by the developer
options.B: A Trojan horse embedded in the application and disguised as a legitimate feature
options.C: A maintenance hook, an undocumented backdoor that bypasses normal authentication
options.D: A race condition that intermittently allows requests to skip the authentication check

questions.explanation: An undocumented access path that developers created for their own convenience and that sidesteps authentication is the definition of a maintenance hook, a backdoor (C). Intent barely matters: left in production, it grants the same unauthenticated administrative access to whoever finds it, which is why removal must be verified before release. A is wrong because a logic bomb carries a malicious payload waiting on a trigger, such as a date or an HR record change; this URL does nothing on its own and harbors no destructive action. B is wrong because a Trojan horse is malicious software a victim is deceived into installing because it appears desirable; this is the bank's own application, not a disguised foreign program. D is wrong because a race condition is a timing defect, authentication skipped only when operations interleave badly, appearing intermittently; this bypass is deterministic and works on every request. Deliberate shortcut paths are backdoors, and the fix is process: code review and pre-release checks that hunt for them.

questions.question: A mobile team plans to protect the API key shipped inside its Android app by running the code through an obfuscator, arguing that renamed classes and scrambled control flow will keep the key safe. Which assessment of this plan is most accurate?

options.A: Adequate, because obfuscated binaries cannot be decompiled back into readable source
options.B: Adequate, provided the key is also encrypted inside the binary before obfuscation
options.C: Insufficient, because obfuscation degrades performance too severely for production apps
options.D: Insufficient, because obfuscation only delays analysis; the secret should move server-side

questions.explanation: Anything the app can use at runtime, an attacker holding the binary can eventually recover by decompiling, hooking the app, or dumping memory at the moment the key is used. Obfuscation raises the effort and is worth applying as one layer, but it converts none of that into confidentiality; a secret shipped to every customer's device is disclosed by design, so the durable fix is architectural: keep the key server-side and issue short-lived, per-user tokens to the client (D). A is wrong on its facts: decompilers process obfuscated code readily; the output is uglier, not unreadable. B is wrong because it recurses: the app must carry the decryption key to use the encrypted one, and that key is recoverable the same way. C reaches the right verdict for a wrong reason; modern obfuscation overhead is modest, and rejecting a control on false grounds discredits the review.

questions.question: A web application lets users submit a URL to generate a link preview. An attacker submits http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and the application returns the cloud account's temporary credentials, fetched by the application server itself. Which vulnerability class does this demonstrate?

options.A: Server-side request forgery, since the server was induced to request an internal resource
options.B: Cross-site request forgery, since a forged request was executed without a victim's intent
options.C: XML external entity injection, since a parser was made to retrieve a protected document
options.D: An open redirect, since the application forwarded a browser to an attacker-chosen address

questions.explanation: The decisive detail is who made the request: the application server itself fetched the metadata address on the attacker's behalf. Abusing a server's own network position to reach resources the attacker cannot touch directly, such as internal services or the cloud metadata endpoint that only the instance may query, is server-side request forgery (A); the fix is an allow-list of fetchable destinations with internal and link-local ranges denied. B is the classic confusion: in CSRF the forged request is sent by a victim's browser, riding that user's session; here there is no victim user and the server is the one doing the fetching. C is wrong because XXE requires an XML parser resolving external entities; a URL form field involves no XML; XXE is better thought of as one specific vector that can produce SSRF-like fetches. D is wrong because an open redirect bounces the client's browser to another site; this server retrieved the content itself and handed it back. SSRF forges requests from the server, CSRF forges them from the user; identify the party being tricked.

questions.question: A Java service accepts serialized objects from partner systems over the Internet and rebuilds them in memory; researchers show that a crafted object chain in this stream executes arbitrary commands during reconstruction. Which remediation most effectively addresses the root cause?

options.A: Encrypt the serialized stream in transit so intermediaries are unable to modify the objects
options.B: Add a web application firewall rule that inspects payloads for known gadget-chain signatures
options.C: Replace native object deserialization with a data-only format validated against a strict schema
options.D: Shorten connection timeouts so any single compromised session has a limited useful lifetime

questions.explanation: Insecure deserialization is dangerous because rebuilding a native object graph lets the sender choose which classes get instantiated, and chains of innocent classes can be assembled into code execution. The root-cause fix removes that power from the sender: exchange plain data in a format such as JSON, validate it against a strict schema, and construct objects yourself (C); where native deserialization is unavoidable, a tight class allow-list is the fallback. A protects the wrong layer: encryption authenticates the channel, not the content's safety. The malicious payload comes from a partner system, or from a partner that has itself been compromised, and travels happily through the encrypted pipe. B is wrong because signature matching known gadget chains is a reactive race with researchers who keep finding new ones; it earns its keep only as an interim virtual patch. D is wrong because the exploit fires during reconstruction of a single message; session lifetime never enters into it. Never let untrusted bytes decide what code runs; deserialize data, not objects.

questions.question: An invoice-upload feature parses customer XML. A tester uploads a file whose DOCTYPE declaration defines an external entity pointing at /etc/passwd, and the parsed output returns that file's contents. Which change best fixes this flaw at its source?

options.A: Validate that uploaded invoices are well-formed XML before passing them to the parser
options.B: Configure the XML parser to disable document type definitions and external entity resolution
options.C: Run the upload service in a container so its file reads are confined to the container image
options.D: Scan uploaded files with antivirus to reject those containing known malicious markup

questions.explanation: XML external entity injection is unusual among injection flaws: the vulnerability is a feature, not a bug. The parser is doing exactly what DTD processing specifies, resolving an entity that happens to point at a local file, so the source-level fix is configuration: turn off DTDs and external entity resolution in the parser (B), and the attack ceases to be expressible. A is wrong because the tester's exploit file is perfectly well-formed XML; well-formedness checks syntax, and this attack is syntactically impeccable. C is wrong because containment shrinks the blast radius without fixing the flaw: everything inside the container, including its own credentials and configuration secrets, remains readable, and SSRF-style entity fetches still reach the network. It is reasonable defense in depth. D is wrong because antivirus recognizes known malware, and a three-line DOCTYPE crafted for this one application matches nothing in a signature set. When a parser's features are the attack surface, hardening its configuration is the fix, a lesson that generalizes to any dangerous default.

questions.question: A logged-in customer of a banking site changes the number in the URL /statements?account=1001 to 1002 and receives another customer's statement. The request was well formed, contained no attack syntax, and the server processed it exactly as designed. Which weakness best explains this behavior?

options.A: An injection flaw, because the customer's input altered how the server-side query executed
options.B: A security misconfiguration, because a hardening option that conceals identifiers was disabled
options.C: A cryptographic failure, because financial records reached a party unauthorized to read them
options.D: Broken access control, because the application never checked object-level authorization

questions.explanation: Everything about this request was legitimate except the outcome: the user was authenticated, the syntax was clean, and the server did what its code says, which is precisely the point. The code never asks whether the requester owns account 1002 before serving it, a missing object-level authorization check known as an insecure direct object reference, the canonical broken access control flaw (D) and the same defect that let Global Bank's leaked key read any customer's records. A does not apply: injection means input that changes the structure or logic of a command; here the query ran exactly as designed with a different, valid parameter; nothing was subverted. B is wrong because misconfiguration lives in settings, defaults, and deployment options; this flaw lives in application logic, and no configuration toggle supplies a missing ownership check. C is wrong because cryptographic failures concern absent or weak protection of data; the TLS on this site could be flawless and the flaw would remain untouched.

questions.question: A scan of a newly deployed application server finds the vendor's sample applications still installed, an admin console reachable with the documented default password, directory listing enabled, and stack traces returned to clients on error. Under which OWASP risk category do these findings best fit?

options.A: Security misconfiguration, since insecure default settings and features were left in place
options.B: Broken access control, since unauthorized parties could reach administrative functions
options.C: Vulnerable and outdated components, since the server carried unneeded sample software
options.D: Identification and authentication failures, since a default password guarded the console

questions.explanation: Look for the common cause: sample apps present, default credentials unchanged, directory listing on, verbose errors leaking internals: four symptoms of one omission, an unhardened out-of-the-box deployment. That is security misconfiguration (A), and its remedy is a repeatable hardening baseline applied to every build, not four one-off fixes. B is wrong because broken access control describes missing or faulty authorization logic in the application; here the checks exist and were simply undermined by a published password. That is a settings problem, not a logic problem. C is wrong because the components category targets software that is outdated or known-vulnerable; the samples' sin is being present and unneeded, a deployment choice, whatever their patch level. D is the defensible near-miss: the default password in isolation could file under authentication failures, and on a question about that single finding it would be the answer. But it cannot account for directory listings, stack traces, or sample apps, and the question asks where the findings as a set belong.

questions.question: Forensic investigators determine that attackers were active inside a retailer's network for five months. In that time no alerts fired; the web servers kept only seven days of logs, application logins were never recorded, and log review was a manual task performed quarterly. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

options.A: Deploying stronger encryption for stored data so future intrusions yield nothing readable
options.B: Centralized log collection with longer retention and automated alerting on suspicious activity
options.C: Commissioning an annual external penetration test to uncover exploitable weaknesses
options.D: Adopting a stricter rotation schedule for all privileged administrator account passwords

questions.explanation: Five months of undetected activity is a visibility failure, and the stem lists its three ingredients: logs that expire in a week, security-relevant events never captured, and review too infrequent and manual to notice anything. The remedy attacks all three (B): collect logs centrally where intruders cannot quietly erase them, retain them well beyond realistic dwell times so investigations have evidence, and let automation watch continuously so detection happens in hours, not quarters. A is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality against stolen media and eavesdroppers; attackers operating through compromised applications and accounts read data exactly as legitimate users do, and encryption restores no visibility. C is a point-in-time probe for ways in; this organization's demonstrated failure is not knowing when someone is already inside. D is wrong because nothing ties the intrusion to stale passwords, and rotation would not have surfaced the five-month presence. Fix the control family the incident actually indicts. Long dwell times indict detection, so build logging and monitoring before buying more prevention.

questions.question: In a post-incident review of the Global Bank key leak, the team maps events to STRIDE. One member asks how to categorize the moment the Master_API_Key became readable by anyone browsing the public repository, before any attacker had used it. Which STRIDE category best fits that specific event?

options.A: Spoofing, because the key would later let outsiders authenticate as an administrator
options.B: Tampering, because the repository's contents were changed by the developer's push
options.C: Information disclosure, because a secret became visible to parties never meant to see it
options.D: Elevation of privilege, because possession of the key conferred administrative rights

questions.explanation: Precision about which event is being classified decides this question. The event named in the stem is the exposure itself, a confidential value becoming readable by unauthorized parties, and confidentiality violations are STRIDE's information disclosure category (C), regardless of whether anyone had exploited the exposure yet. A and D fail on phase, not on substance: when attackers later authenticated to the API as an administrator using the stolen key, that was spoofing, and the administrative capability they gained maps to elevation of privilege — each is the right answer to a question about the attack that followed, not about the leak. B fails on definition: tampering is unauthorized modification of data or code, and the developer's push was an authorized, well-intentioned change that happened to be unsafe; nothing was maliciously altered. A real incident spans several STRIDE categories in sequence; classify each event on the timeline separately instead of forcing one label onto the whole story.

questions.question: A bank's platform team runs two hundred microservices that call each other directly. Security requires mutual TLS and per-call authorization between every pair of services, but modifying two hundred codebases has been ruled out as infeasible. Which approach best delivers these controls?

options.A: An API gateway at the network edge that authenticates external clients before they enter
options.B: A perimeter firewall policy limiting which outside networks can reach the service cluster
options.C: A shared library implementing TLS and authorization, to be integrated into each service
options.D: A service mesh whose sidecar proxies supply mutual TLS and policy without code changes

questions.explanation: The requirement is service-to-service (east-west) security at a scale where touching application code is off the table, and that is the problem service meshes were built for (D): a sidecar proxy deployed beside each service intercepts its traffic, so mutual TLS, service identity, and per-call authorization policy are supplied by infrastructure, uniformly and without modifying any of the two hundred codebases. A is wrong on direction: a gateway guards north-south traffic where external clients enter; once inside, service-to-service calls never traverse it. It is the right answer for authenticating outside consumers. B is wrong on granularity as well as direction: a perimeter policy knows networks and ports, not service identities, and offers nothing between two services inside the cluster. C meets the functional need but fails the stated constraint: it requires integrating and re-releasing every service, and forever ties security upgrades to two hundred deployment schedules.

questions.question: A review of a company's container platform finds application containers running as root, built from unscanned images pulled from public registries, on shared hosts. Which change most reduces the risk of container compromise and escape?

options.A: Installing traditional antivirus agents inside every running application container
options.B: Scanning images for known vulnerabilities and running containers as non-root users
options.C: Moving all images into a private registry while continuing to build them unchanged
options.D: Restarting every container on a nightly schedule so intrusions do not persist

questions.explanation: The review names the two dominant risks and B answers both: scanning images before deployment catches the known-vulnerable packages that public-registry images routinely carry, the most likely route to compromise, and dropping root strips a compromised container of the privileges that make kernel exploits and host escape practical on a shared node. A is wrong because an in-container antivirus agent is a host-era control transplanted badly: it bloats the image, sees only one container's namespace, and does nothing about the vulnerable packages or the root privilege; container defense lives in image hygiene and runtime policy. C is wrong because provenance without inspection just relocates the risk: the same unscanned, vulnerable images are served from a private address. It is worthwhile against registry tampering, as a complement to scanning. D is wrong because recycling containers evicts an intruder only until the same unpatched flaw readmits them; persistence is not the vulnerability, and treating restarts as cleansing mistakes the symptom for the cause.

questions.question: A development team is migrating a document-processing workload from self-managed virtual machines to a serverless functions platform. The operations lead asks which security responsibilities the team retains after the migration. What is the most accurate answer?

options.A: Securing the function code, its dependencies, its secrets, and its least-privilege IAM roles
options.B: Patching the operating system kernels of the servers on which the functions execute
options.C: Hardening the hypervisor layer that isolates the provider's tenants from one another
options.D: Managing host firewalls and antivirus on the machines running the function runtime

questions.explanation: Serverless shifts the shared-responsibility line sharply toward the provider, but never past the customer's own workload. What remains is everything the team writes or configures (A): the function code and its input handling, the third-party dependencies bundled with it (composition analysis still applies), the secrets it uses, and above all the IAM role it executes under, since over-permissioned functions are the signature serverless failure. B and D are wrong for the same reason: in a functions platform the customer cannot even reach the operating system, hosts, or runtime; the provider owns their patching and protection; both answers describe responsibilities the team held on its old self-managed VMs and would still hold under IaaS. C is wrong one layer deeper still: hypervisor isolation between tenants is the provider's responsibility in every cloud service model, and no customer ever hardens it.

questions.question: When a critical flaw is announced in a popular open-source logging library, a bank needs to know within hours which of its four hundred applications embed a vulnerable version, including transitive dependencies pulled in automatically during builds. Which tooling most directly answers this question?

options.A: Static analysis of each application's own source code for insecure logging patterns
options.B: Dynamic scanning of the running applications to probe for exploitable behaviors
options.C: A questionnaire asking each development team to list the libraries their apps use
options.D: Software composition analysis that inventories every dependency against vulnerability data

questions.explanation: The question being asked, which applications contain component X at a vulnerable version, is an inventory question, and software composition analysis (D) is the tooling built to answer it: it resolves each application's full dependency tree, transitive imports included, records exact versions, and matches them against vulnerability advisories, turning a fleet-wide audit into a query. A is wrong on target: static analysis examines code your own developers wrote for flaw patterns; it does not catalogue which third-party library versions the build pulled in. The flaw here is in someone else's code. B is wrong on speed and coverage: dynamically probing four hundred applications takes far longer than hours, and a vulnerable library that the scanner's inputs never trigger produces no signal while still being present. C is wrong because developers reliably know their direct imports and reliably do not know the transitive ones, which is exactly where such libraries hide, and any answers gathered are stale by the next build.

questions.question: Customers of a network-management vendor are breached through a signed, official product update that contained hidden malicious code; investigators find the vendor's build server had been compromised months earlier, and every customer who applied the legitimate update received the implant. Which term best describes this attack?

options.A: A watering-hole attack, since victims were compromised at a resource they habitually trust
options.B: Spear phishing, since the malicious payload reached a specifically chosen set of targets
options.C: A supply chain attack, since the vendor's build pipeline was subverted to reach its customers
options.D: An insider threat, since the compromise originated within the vendor's own build systems

questions.explanation: The attackers never touched the victims directly: they compromised a supplier's build pipeline so that the trusted product itself became the delivery vehicle, arriving with a valid signature through the official update channel, which is the definition of a supply chain attack (C) and the SolarWinds pattern precisely. The signature is what makes it devastating: the victims' verification checks passed, because the code was signed after the implant was inserted. A is the closest wrong answer: a watering hole also exploits a trusted habit, but it poisons a website the targets visit and exploits their browsers there; here the poison traveled inside a purchased product's update, not a webpage. B is wrong because spear phishing works by deceiving chosen individuals into opening a lure; no human at any customer was deceived; administrators applied a legitimate update correctly. D is wrong because an insider threat is an authorized person misusing their own access; the build server was breached by external attackers, and location inside the vendor does not make them insiders. When upstream trust is the vector, defenses shift to vendor assurance, build integrity, and monitoring what updates actually do.

questions.question: After a supply chain compromise, regulators ask a software vendor to state precisely which open-source and commercial components, at which versions, ship inside each of its products. The vendor cannot answer without weeks of archaeology. Which artifact, produced with each release, would have provided the answer immediately?

options.A: A software bill of materials enumerating every component and version in each release
options.B: A penetration test report demonstrating the release resisted realistic attack attempts
options.C: A hardware asset inventory recording every server involved in building the product
options.D: A change log summarizing the features and fixes the release delivered to customers

questions.explanation: The regulators are asking for a parts list, and that is literally what a software bill of materials is (A): a machine-readable inventory, generated at build time, of every component a release contains, direct and transitive, open-source and commercial, with versions and origins. With an SBOM per release, the question 'which products contain component X?' becomes a lookup; without one, it becomes the weeks of archaeology the vendor is now doing. B is wrong because a penetration test report attests to behavior under attack at a point in time; it contains no component inventory and cannot say what is inside the product. C inventories the wrong things: the build servers are infrastructure, and listing them says nothing about what went into the shipped artifact. D is wrong because change logs describe features and fixes for human readers; they rarely mention dependencies at all, let alone exhaustively with versions.

questions.question: A payments provider must ship a rewritten authentication service to production. The change passed every test, but leadership fears an unforeseen defect could lock out the entire customer base at once. Which deployment strategy best limits the blast radius of such a defect?

options.A: Blue-green deployment, cutting all traffic over to the new version while the old stands ready
options.B: A canary release, sending a small share of live traffic to the new version under monitoring
options.C: A big-bang upgrade during a weekend maintenance window with extended staff on call
options.D: Two additional weeks of soak testing in staging before releasing to every customer at once

questions.explanation: Leadership's fear is a defect that tests did not catch, so the strategy must assume the defect ships and minimize who meets it. A canary release (B) does exactly that: a small fraction of real production traffic exercises the new version while metrics are watched, so a lockout bug strands one percent of customers for minutes rather than all of them, and rollback is a routing change. A is the strong near-miss: blue-green also offers instant rollback, but its cutover sends one hundred percent of users to the new version, so the entire customer base is exposed during the window before the defect is noticed; it is the right answer when the priority is a fast, clean switch and versions cannot serve traffic side by side. C is wrong because timing does not shrink exposure; every customer still hits the new code at once, just on a Sunday. D is wrong because the feared defect is precisely the kind staging did not produce; more of the same environment yields more of the same blind spot; only production traffic reveals production behavior. When residual risk is unknown unknowns, expose it to the smallest real audience first.

questions.question: A product manager reports that the redesigned login page is shown to half of all users while the rest see the old page, and argues that because real users are exercising the new page in production, it has effectively been security tested. How should the security team respond to this claim?

options.A: Agree, because production traffic exercises more code paths than scripted security scans
options.B: Agree, provided the experiment runs long enough to reach statistical significance
options.C: Disagree, because A/B testing compares feature performance, not resistance to attack
options.D: Disagree, because only half of the users saw the new page, so coverage was incomplete

questions.explanation: An A/B test is a controlled experiment on user behavior: two variants, live traffic split between them, business metrics compared: completion rates, conversions. Its participants are benign users doing intended things, so it generates no evidence about malicious inputs, session handling under attack, or authentication bypass attempts; security assurance requires deliberately adversarial testing, DAST or penetration testing, before the redesign reaches anyone (C). A measures the wrong dimension, breadth of benign traffic: normal users walk happy paths no matter how many of them there are, while attacks are crafted inputs that ordinary usage never produces. B is wrong because statistical significance strengthens the UX conclusion only; a rigorous experiment measuring the wrong property yields a very confident answer to a different question. D is the trap for careful readers: it rejects the claim for a wrong reason, since routing every user to the new page would still test nothing adversarial; endorsing that reasoning would imply full exposure equals security testing.

questions.question: To meet a hackathon deadline, Global Bank's developers hardcoded an API key and skipped input validation, filing tickets to redo both properly later. A year on, the tickets remain open, and the estimate to retrofit the fixes has tripled as new features were built on top. Which concept should the security manager use to frame this situation for executives?

options.A: Risk transference, since responsibility now rests with whoever approved the deadline
options.B: Residual risk, since some exposure legitimately remains after controls are applied
options.C: Sunk cost, since money already spent on the shortcuts ought not drive decisions
options.D: Technical debt, since deferred engineering shortcuts compound in cost and risk over time

questions.explanation: The pattern in the stem is the definition of technical debt (D): a deliberate shortcut taken for speed, a promise to fix it later, and a remediation bill that grows as new work is layered on top. The metaphor is what makes it board-ready: the shortcut borrowed time, the tripling estimate is the interest, and this debt's principal is security exposure: a live administrative credential and unvalidated input sitting in production, which is why security debt demands tracking and scheduled repayment like any liability. A is wrong because transference means shifting risk to another party, an insurer or contractor, through a formal arrangement; an executive having approved a deadline shifts nothing; the bank still holds every consequence. B is wrong because residual risk is what remains after controls are implemented and is often acceptable; these controls were never implemented, so the exposure is untreated, not residual. C is wrong because sunk cost is a decision-making principle about ignoring unrecoverable past spending; the manager's problem is the future, costs still growing, not attachment to money already gone. Name deferred security work as debt with compounding interest; executives fund debt repayment far more readily than vague hygiene.

stimuli.title: Global Bank: the pipeline rebuild
stimuli.text: Global Bank is rebuilding the build pipeline for Cardless Cash, its cardless ATM withdrawal service, after a master key committed to source reached a public repository. The new design keeps the same three teams and the same weekly release. Secrets move to a managed vault. Builds run on shared runners any team can queue work on, and the repository is private, but every developer can push to the main branch. Nobody can currently say which build produced the artefact running in production. The bank's examiner has asked for evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's own rules, not merely that the rules exist somewhere.

profile.organization: Global Bank · Cardless Cash mobile app and API
profile.environment: Private repository · shared build runners · weekly release · managed secret vault
profile.state: Pipeline rebuild after a hardcoded key reached a public repository

stimuli.title: A key in a public repository
stimuli.text: A monitoring service tells Global Bank that a production API key for its Cardless Cash service, the mobile app that lets customers withdraw at an ATM without a card, is sitting in a public repository. A developer pushed it there three days ago while working from home during a hackathon, and scanning bots reach new repositories within seconds. The key grants administrative access to the transaction backend. It is also compiled into the Android and iOS clients already in the app stores. The bank bought a managed secret vault last year and never wired it into anything, and nothing in its process would stop a credential being committed.

profile.organization: Global Bank · Cardless Cash mobile app and API
profile.environment: Hackathon build · public repository · clients already in the app stores
profile.state: Key public for three days, still valid

stimuli.title: Walking a payment API endpoint by endpoint
stimuli.text: Coastal Savings processes card transactions for its own customers and for eight hundred merchants. An administrator credential has been found reaching its backend from outside the company, and the security team is now walking the customer API endpoint by endpoint. Statements are served from a path carrying the account number in the query string. The login endpoint builds its database query by concatenating the values submitted to it. Nothing in the API records which caller owns which record. Forensic work has been slow: the servers keep seven days of logs, application logins were never recorded at all, and log review is a manual quarterly task.

profile.environment: REST API · mobile and web clients · seven-day log retention
profile.state: Administrator credential found reaching the backend from outside

stimuli.title: A penetration test of the customer portal
stimuli.text: Global Bank commissioned a penetration test of its customer web portal, the browser front end customers use for statements and transfers. The testers were given one customer login and nothing else. Every finding sits in a part of the portal that renders or fetches content on a user's behalf: a review board that stores and redisplays what customers type, the funds-transfer form, a document download endpoint that takes a filename, and a link-preview feature that fetches whatever URL a user supplies. The portal runs inside the bank's cloud account, on instances that can reach the cloud provider's own metadata service.

profile.environment: Browser front end for statements and transfers · runs in the bank's cloud account

stimuli.title: The oldest code in the estate
stimuli.text: Northbridge Clearing settles interbank payments and takes files and messages from card processors and correspondent banks all day. Its partner integration service is the oldest code it runs: a C daemon that parses binary payment messages, a Java component that accepts serialized objects from partner systems over the internet and rebuilds them in memory, and an XML invoice upload used by three suppliers. A destination-account field feeds several downstream systems, and the team maintains an ever-growing filter of known malicious strings against it. None of the service has ever been fuzzed, and a settlement transfer crashed the daemon last week.

profile.environment: C payment daemon · Java object stream · XML invoice upload
profile.state: Never fuzzed; the daemon crashed last week

stimuli.title: How a portal holds a session
stimuli.text: Kestrel Mutual, a general insurer, has commissioned a review of how its policyholder portal handles a session once someone has signed in. The login page is served over HTTPS and every page after it over plain HTTP. The session cookie can be read by any script running in the page, and is transmitted whenever a user follows a link over an unencrypted connection. Version control shows a URL one developer added during testing to save time and never removed. The application server underneath was deployed straight from the vendor's installer and has never been hardened.

profile.environment: HTTPS login, HTTP thereafter · application server from the vendor's installer

stimuli.title: Global Bank: four programs, four models
stimuli.text: Global Bank's program office is starting four builds in one quarter and must pick a delivery model for each. A regulatory reporting system is fixed by contract: every requirement is agreed up front, formal documentation with approval gates at every stage is mandated, and scope cannot change without a contract modification. A new consumer feature enters a market whose customer needs are poorly understood and expected to shift every few weeks. A multi-year biometric authentication program depends on technology nobody has proved. And a claims-processing interface has produced two contradictory requirements documents from stakeholders who cannot say what they need.

profile.regime: Banking examination · fixed-price supplier contract on one program
profile.environment: Four builds starting in the same quarter
profile.state: Delivery model not yet chosen for any of them

stimuli.title: Two squads, two cadences
stimuli.text: Global Bank's payments squad has moved to two-week sprints and ships a product increment at the end of each one. Defects keep reaching production anyway. The regulator has told the bank that no change to the payment module may be written and merged by a single unreviewed developer, and expects that review to happen as early in development as possible. Marketing has separately put another squad on a hard launch date using time-boxed cycles, heavy prototyping and minimal up-front design, and the CISO has been asked what that approach costs in security terms.

profile.organization: Global Bank · payments and marketing squads
profile.regime: Banking examination · regulator directive on the payment module
profile.environment: Two-week sprints, an increment each sprint · a second squad on a hard launch date

stimuli.title: A firm that cannot show how it builds
stimuli.text: Ardent Systems writes software for payment terminals. It lost a government bid because it could not demonstrate the maturity of its development processes: internally, project success still depends on individual heroics and no two teams work alike. An improvement program has been funded and the team wants to start rewriting development procedures immediately. Its terminal firmware is separately certified, and the certifier demands evidence that defects are prevented during development rather than found and patched afterwards, with failure rates certified statistically. Two shortcuts taken to hit a deadline a year ago, a hardcoded credential and skipped input validation, still have open tickets and a tripled estimate.

profile.environment: No two teams work alike · terminal firmware certified separately
profile.state: Improvement program funded after a lost bid

stimuli.title: Twenty deploys a day
stimuli.text: Vantage Retail deploys to production twenty times a day through an automated pipeline. Security review is manual, performed by a separate team in the week before each quarterly compliance audit, so findings routinely reach developers months after the code shipped. A rewritten authentication service has passed every test and is ready to ship, but leadership fears an unforeseen defect could lock out the entire customer base at once. The company is in an acrimonious layoff period and a database administrator due to leave still holds commit access. The product manager has begun showing a redesigned login page to half of all users.

profile.environment: Automated pipeline, twenty production deploys a day · manual security review before each audit
profile.state: Rewritten authentication service ready to ship

stimuli.title: A flaw in a library everybody uses
stimuli.text: A critical flaw is announced in a widely used open-source logging library, and exploitation is already being reported. Global Bank runs four hundred applications and cannot say within hours which of them embed a vulnerable version, including the dependencies pulled in automatically during builds. In the same week a network-management vendor discloses that its customers were breached through a signed, official product update: investigators found the vendor's build server had been compromised months before. And the bank's own VPN appliance carries an actively exploited flaw for which the manufacturer says no patch will exist for several weeks.

profile.environment: Open-source logging library in unknown numbers of builds · vendor-supplied VPN appliance

stimuli.title: Two hundred services, no shared plumbing
stimuli.text: Trellis Pay is moving its payments backend off self-managed virtual machines. Two hundred microservices call each other directly, and security now requires mutual TLS and per-call authorization between every pair; modifying two hundred codebases has been ruled out as infeasible. A review of the container platform finds application containers running as root, built from unscanned images pulled from public registries, on shared hosts. A document-processing workload is moving to a serverless functions platform. The architects want the new payment API's threats enumerated before code is written, and the API it replaces is already taking millions of requests enumerating sequential customer identifiers, with stolen credential lists replayed against its login.

profile.environment: Two hundred microservices · container platform on shared hosts · serverless functions

stimuli.title: A first application security lead
stimuli.text: Global Bank has hired its first application security lead into a company with no existing program, a small training budget and no secure-coding standard, and the lead must choose a starting point for developer training. A threat-modeling workshop for the trading platform has just produced forty distinct threats, far more than the team can address this quarter, and the lead needs a repeatable way to decide which ones get remediation effort first. A separate review is examining an episode in which a master API key became readable by anyone browsing a public repository, and is classifying each event in it.

profile.organization: Global Bank · new application security function
profile.environment: No existing program · small training budget · trading platform under review

stimuli.title: Three incidents on the store estate
stimuli.text: Vantage Retail's in-store machines run a fixed, unchanging set of approved applications and staff cannot administer them. The security team is reviewing three incidents from the quarter. On one server, firewall logs show connections that no local tool reports: process listings, file searches and the installed antivirus all show nothing unusual. Antivirus quarantines one variant of a malware family, yet new infections keep appearing, each sample carrying a different hash and byte pattern while behaving identically on the host. And help-desk tickets reveal that several employees installed a free PDF converter which works as advertised and also opens a remote-control channel.

profile.environment: Fixed set of approved applications · staff cannot administer their machines

stimuli.title: An overnight spread, and two peer reports
stimuli.text: Overnight, malware spread to hundreds of Halden Logistics servers across a flat internal network while no user was logged in anywhere: each infected host scanned for neighbors exposing the same vulnerable file-sharing service and infected them directly. Through the sector information-sharing group it belongs to, the company received two reports the same week. A university network team traced abuse complaints to two hundred campus workstations making identical periodic connections to one overseas domain from which they fetch commands. A hospital paid attackers to recover encrypted patient records. An analyst is separately classifying code that appends itself to spreadsheet macro files.

profile.environment: Hundreds of servers on one flat segment · two peer reports received the same week

stimuli.title: Global Bank: the reporting warehouse
stimuli.text: Global Bank's reporting warehouse serves branch operations, fraud analytics and its cash-in-transit contractor from one database. A customer's mailing address differs across three tables: an update routine changed one copy and missed the others, and refunds are being posted to an outdated address. The fraud reporting view hides individual case records but permits statistical queries. The contractor holds access to three datasets each rated non-sensitive on its own: vehicle maintenance schedules, fuel purchases and crew duty rosters. Nobody has reviewed what those three together would tell a reader, because each was approved on its own rating.

profile.environment: One database serving branch operations, fraud analytics and a logistics contractor

questionsV2.question: The examiner wants evidence that the pipeline enforces the bank's rules rather than merely documenting them. Which approach BEST produces that evidence?

options.A: A quarterly audit sampling merged changes against the written development standard.
options.B: A checklist each team lead signs before a release is promoted into production.
options.C: Policy expressed as machine-checked pipeline rules that fail the build and record the result.
options.D: A dashboard showing how many findings each team closed in the most recent release.

questionsV2.explanation: An examiner asking for enforcement is asking for something that cannot have been skipped, and a rule that runs is the only artefact on this list with that property. It also produces its own evidence as a by-product, which is the second half of what was asked. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement is the nearest control in the catalog, and it is new in Revision 5; CM-6 Configuration Settings governs the settings the rules assert. NIST SP 800-218 PO.3.3 requires the toolchain to be configured to generate artifacts that support the security checks. Worth being precise: the phrase software-defined security appears in no NIST document, so SC-50 is a functional match rather than a name match, and it should be presented that way. A is detective when preventive is asked, sampling a quarter after the fact. B is symptom not cause, capturing a person's assertion rather than an enforced condition. D is the right control for a different problem, measuring remediation throughput. Evidence is what the machine produced, not what the team promised.
questionsV2.recallLine: An examiner wants proof the pipeline enforces the rules rather than documenting them. What produces it?

A.label: detective when preventive is asked
A.wouldAnswer: How does the bank confirm periodically that enforced rules still match the written standard?

B.label: symptom not cause
B.wouldAnswer: How is accountability for a release assigned to a named person?

D.label: right control, wrong problem
D.wouldAnswer: How does the bank track whether teams are working through their open findings?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | SC-50 Software-Enforced Separation and Policy Enforcement (new in Rev 5); CM-6 Configuration Settings
NIST SP 800-218 | PO.3.3 toolchain generates supporting artifacts

questionsV2.question: Any team can queue work on the shared build runners. Which risk does that arrangement MOST directly create for the Cardless Cash release?

options.A: One team's build step can read another team's secrets or artefacts.
options.B: Builds will queue behind each other and the weekly release will slip.
options.C: Teams will adopt different build tools and the artefacts will diverge.
options.D: The runners will fall behind on operating-system patches between releases.

questionsV2.explanation: A build runner is a machine that holds every credential its jobs need and every artefact they produce, and a shared runner holds all of them at once. A job is arbitrary code by definition, so the team that queues it inherits whatever the runner can reach, and the vault the bank has just bought does not help once a job can ask the vault on someone else's behalf. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-6 Least Privilege, SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality, and SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources are the controls that name this class of exposure; note that SC-2's Revision 4 title was Application Partitioning. NIST SP 800-218 PO.5 requires environments involved in software development to be separated and protected. B is the right control for a different problem, a capacity concern rather than a security one. C is wrong scope, a consistency issue between teams rather than a boundary failure inside one runner. D is a correct action but not the first one, a real maintenance gap that shared queueing did not cause. Ask what the runner can reach.
questionsV2.recallLine: Any team can queue jobs on shared build runners. Which risk does that most directly create?

optionsShort.A: Cross-team access to secrets and artefacts

B.label: right control, wrong problem
B.wouldAnswer: What should the platform team plan for if release throughput is the concern?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What does a shared toolchain standard fix across three independent teams?

D.label: correct but not first
D.wouldAnswer: What maintenance obligation applies to build infrastructure regardless of who queues on it?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-6 Least Privilege; SC-2 Separation of System and User Functionality (renamed from Rev 4 Application Partitioning); SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources
NIST SP 800-218 | PO.5 secure development environments

questionsV2.question: Every developer can push directly to the main branch of the private repository. Which control BEST addresses the exposure that creates?

options.A: Scanning the repository's history for secrets committed before the vault existed.
options.B: Requiring commits to be signed so each change can be attributed to a developer.
options.C: Restricting repository read access to the three teams that work on it.
options.D: Requiring an independent review and a passing check before a change enters main.

questionsV2.explanation: The last incident began with one developer's decision reaching production with nobody in between, and a repository where anyone can push to main reproduces exactly that condition inside a private repository instead of a public one. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 CM-3 Configuration Change Control requires proposed changes to be reviewed and approved or disapproved with explicit consideration of security and privacy impact analyses, and AC-5 Separation of Duties is why the reviewer is somebody else. NIST SP 800-218 adds the software-specific half: PS.1 protects all forms of code from unauthorized access and tampering, and PW.7 covers reviewing or analyzing human-readable code before release. A is wrong phase, cleaning up history without governing what enters main next. B is detective when preventive is asked, producing attribution after the change has landed. C is wrong scope, narrowing who can read rather than who can change. A gate on the branch is the control; everything else describes the branch.
questionsV2.recallLine: Every developer can push straight to main. Which control best addresses that exposure?

optionsShort.C: Restrict who can read the repository
optionsShort.D: Independent review and check before main

A.label: wrong phase
A.wouldAnswer: What should the bank do about credentials committed before the vault was introduced?

B.label: detective when preventive is asked
B.wouldAnswer: How does the bank establish afterwards which developer authored a given change?

C.label: wrong scope
C.wouldAnswer: What limits disclosure of source to people outside the three teams?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | CM-3 Configuration Change Control; AC-5 Separation of Duties
NIST SP 800-218 | PS.1 protect code from unauthorized access and tampering; PW.7 review human-readable code

questionsV2.question: The rebuilt API will issue short-lived tokens instead of a master key. Which additional check MOST directly addresses the failure that let attackers read any account?

options.A: Rate limiting each token so a caller cannot enumerate accounts quickly.
options.B: Verifying on every request that the token's subject owns the record requested.
options.C: Rotating the token signing key on a schedule the managed vault enforces.
options.D: Logging every API call with its token subject and the record it touched.

questionsV2.explanation: Short-lived tokens fix who is calling. The original failure was that the API never asked whether the caller was entitled to the object it named, so any authenticated caller could read any account, and a token with a fifteen-minute lifetime does that just as thoroughly as a master key did. NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-3 Access Enforcement requires the system to enforce approved authorizations for logical access to information, and AC-6 Least Privilege sizes what those authorizations should be. OWASP Top 10:2025 places object-level authorization failures under A01 Broken Access Control, which in the 2025 edition also absorbs server-side request forgery. A is symptom not cause, slowing the enumeration while still returning records the caller should not see. C is the right control for a different problem, protecting the token's integrity rather than the decision made after it is validated. D is detective when preventive is asked. Authentication says who; authorization has to say what, and every request needs both.
questionsV2.recallLine: Short-lived tokens replace a master key. What still has to be checked on every request?

optionsShort.B: Check the subject owns the record
optionsShort.D: Log every call and record touched

A.label: symptom not cause
A.wouldAnswer: What limits the damage a caller can do per minute once authorization is already correct?

C.label: right control, wrong problem
C.wouldAnswer: What limits the value of a signing key that has been exposed?

D.label: detective when preventive is asked
D.wouldAnswer: How does the bank reconstruct which records an abusive caller reached?

sources: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 | AC-3 Access Enforcement; AC-6 Least Privilege
OWASP Top 10:2025 | A01 Broken Access Control

questionsV2.question: The key is still live and the repository is still public. What should the team do FIRST?

options.A: Delete the offending file from the repository and rewrite its commit history to purge the key
options.B: Make the repository private so that no additional external parties can view the key
options.C: Revoke the exposed key immediately and issue a replacement through approved channels
options.D: Interview the developer to establish how the key came to be committed and pushed

questionsV2.explanation: Automated bots scrape public repositories for credential patterns within seconds of a push; after three days, the only safe assumption is that the key has already been copied. Nothing that changes who can see the repository going forward alters that, so the first move is to make the stolen value worthless: revoke it and reissue through a proper channel (C), then hunt for fraudulent use during the exposure window. A treats the visible symptom: history rewriting is worth doing afterward for hygiene, but it cannot recall the copies already harvested, and doing it first leaves an active admin credential in attackers' hands meanwhile. B fails the same way: private visibility stops future viewers, not past ones. D matters for the lessons-learned and for fixing the process, but root-cause interviews come after containment, not before it.

questionsV2.question: Commits containing secrets must be blocked before they reach the central repository, in a way an individual developer cannot bypass from their own machine. Which mechanism BEST meets this?

options.A: A server-side pre-receive hook that scans incoming pushes and rejects any containing secrets
options.B: A client-side pre-commit hook on every developer workstation that runs local secret scanning
options.C: A nightly scheduled job that scans the repository contents and alerts on any secrets found
options.D: A mandatory code-review checklist item requiring reviewers to look for embedded credentials

questionsV2.explanation: The requirement has two halves, enforcement before the secret enters the shared repository and enforcement developers cannot switch off, and only a control running on the server itself satisfies both. A pre-receive hook (A) evaluates every push at the moment the server is asked to accept it and refuses the whole push if a secret is detected: nothing to install, nothing to bypass. B is the closest wrong answer: client-side hooks give excellent fast feedback, but they live on machines the developer controls: they can be skipped with a flag, and a fresh clone simply does not have them; they complement the server hook, they cannot replace it. C is wrong on timing: by the nightly run the secret has been in shared history for hours, cloned and mirrored. D is wrong because human review is fallible, and in pull-request workflows the code has already been pushed to the server before anyone reviews it. Guarantees of the form 'never enters the repository' can only be enforced where the repository lives.

questionsV2.question: The bank now wants credentials never to reside in application code again. Which approach BEST achieves this goal?

options.A: Store credentials in a configuration file that is excluded from version control by .gitignore
options.B: Encrypt the hardcoded key within the source so it is unreadable in the repository
options.C: Restrict every company repository to private visibility so outsiders can no longer browse code
options.D: Retrieve credentials at runtime from a managed secrets vault with access control and rotation

questionsV2.explanation: Code is for logic; secrets belong in a dedicated store. A vault (D) means the credential never enters the codebase at all: the application fetches it at runtime, access is authenticated and audited, and the key can be rotated centrally after any suspected exposure. A is wrong because it merely relocates the secret: a .gitignore entry is advisory, the file still sits unprotected on disks and in backups, and one wrong command commits it anyway; it is the right answer to keeping local developer settings out of a repo, not to protecting production secrets. B is wrong because the application must ship the decryption key too, so the secret remains recoverable from the artifact. That is obfuscation, not protection. C is wrong because it reduces external exposure while leaving the credential in code, visible to every employee, clone, and backup; private repositories leak regularly.

questionsV2.question: The bank also wants each merge checked for hardcoded credentials and injection-prone code in its own source, without waiting for a build to be deployed anywhere. Which testing technology fits BEST?

options.A: Dynamic application security testing, which probes a running application from the outside
options.B: Static application security testing, which examines source code without executing it
options.C: Software composition analysis, which flags known vulnerabilities in third-party dependencies
options.D: Interactive application security testing, which instruments the app while tests exercise it

questionsV2.explanation: Two constraints in the stem decide this: the flaws live in first-party source (hardcoded secrets, injection-prone patterns), and the check must run before merge, when nothing is deployed. Only static analysis (B) works under both: it reads the code itself, so a credential string or an unsanitized query concatenation is visible directly, and it needs no running instance. A is wrong because DAST attacks an application from outside while it runs; it cannot see a hardcoded key that never appears in a response, and there is no running app at merge time. It is the right tool against the deployed build in staging. D fails for the same reason one layer in: IAST observes an instrumented application during test execution, so it also requires a runtime. C is wrong on target rather than timing: SCA inventories the third-party libraries you import and matches them against known-vulnerability data; it does not analyze the code your own developers wrote. SAST reads your source, DAST probes your running app, IAST watches from inside it, SCA audits what you imported. Pick by where the flaw lives and what exists when you test.

questionsV2.question: The mobile team proposes to protect the key still shipped inside the Android app by running the code through an obfuscator. Which assessment of that plan is MOST accurate?

options.A: Adequate, because obfuscated binaries cannot be decompiled back into readable source
options.B: Adequate, provided the key is also encrypted inside the binary before obfuscation
options.C: Insufficient, because obfuscation degrades performance too severely for production apps
options.D: Insufficient, because obfuscation only delays analysis; the secret should move server-side

questionsV2.explanation: Anything the app can use at runtime, an attacker holding the binary can eventually recover by decompiling, hooking the app, or dumping memory at the moment the key is used. Obfuscation raises the effort and is worth applying as one layer, but it converts none of that into confidentiality; a secret shipped to every customer's device is disclosed by design, so the durable fix is architectural: keep the key server-side and issue short-lived, per-user tokens to the client (D). A is wrong on its facts: decompilers process obfuscated code readily; the output is uglier, not unreadable. B is wrong because it recurses: the app must carry the decryption key to use the encrypted one, and that key is recoverable the same way. C reaches the right verdict for a wrong reason; modern obfuscation overhead is modest, and rejecting a control on false grounds discredits the review.

questionsV2.question: A logged-in customer changes the number in /statements?account=1001 to 1002 and receives another customer's statement. The request was well formed and was processed exactly as designed. Which weakness explains this?

options.A: An injection flaw, because the customer's input altered how the server-side query executed
options.B: A security misconfiguration, because a hardening option that conceals identifiers was disabled
options.C: A cryptographic failure, because financial records reached a party unauthorized to read them
options.D: Broken access control, because the application never checked object-level authorization

questionsV2.explanation: Everything about this request was legitimate except the outcome: the user was authenticated, the syntax was clean, and the server did what its code says, which is precisely the point. The code never asks whether the requester owns account 1002 before serving it, a missing object-level authorization check known as an insecure direct object reference, the canonical broken access control flaw (D) and the same defect that let Global Bank's leaked key read any customer's records. A does not apply: injection means input that changes the structure or logic of a command; here the query ran exactly as designed with a different, valid parameter; nothing was subverted. B is wrong because misconfiguration lives in settings, defaults, and deployment options; this flaw lives in application logic, and no configuration toggle supplies a missing ownership check. C is wrong because cryptographic failures concern absent or weak protection of data; the TLS on this site could be flawless and the flaw would remain untouched.

questionsV2.question: A request submitting the login value admin' OR '1'='1 returns every row of the customer table, on a fully patched and hardened server. Which type of flaw MOST likely explains this?

options.A: An injection flaw, because untrusted input was interpreted as part of a database command
options.B: A broken access control flaw, because the user viewed rows belonging to other customers
options.C: A security misconfiguration, because the database account held more privileges than needed
options.D: A cross-site scripting flaw, because attacker-supplied text was reflected in the response

questionsV2.explanation: The tell is the quote and OR '1'='1: the input escaped its role as data and changed the logic of the SQL statement, turning a login check into a query that matches every row. That mechanism, input interpreted as code, defines injection (A). B is wrong because broken access control describes an application that correctly parses a legitimate request but fails to check authorization for it; here the request was malformed on purpose and subverted the query itself. B would be right if a well-formed request for another customer's ID had simply been honored. C is wrong because the stem states the configuration follows the hardening guide; over-privileged accounts amplify the damage of injection but do not create the flaw. D is wrong because XSS executes script in other users' browsers; the victim is the client, not the database. Classify a flaw by its mechanism, not by what data it exposed.

questionsV2.question: The team must remediate that flaw at its root rather than filter attack traffic. Which control should it implement FIRST?

options.A: Deploy a web application firewall with rules that detect and drop known injection patterns
options.B: Sanitize request input by stripping quotes, comments, and SQL keywords before processing
options.C: Rewrite the data-access code to use parameterized queries that bind input as data values
options.D: Encrypt the customer database so records extracted through the flaw stay unreadable

questionsV2.explanation: Injection exists because input and query text are concatenated into one string the database must reinterpret. Parameterized queries (C) remove that root cause: the statement's structure is compiled first and input is bound strictly as data, so no input value can change what the query does. A is wrong as a primary fix because a WAF is a compensating control, pattern-based and bypassable through encoding tricks, and it leaves the vulnerable code in place. It serves well as an interim shield while the code fix is developed, or for a product you cannot modify. B is wrong because blacklist-style stripping chases an open-ended set of bypasses and can break legitimate input (O'Brien); validation is worthwhile defense in depth, not the cure. D is wrong because the application must decrypt data to serve queries, so data stolen through the application arrives in plaintext; encryption at rest answers stolen-media risk, a different problem.

questionsV2.question: Investigators establish the attackers were active for five months and no alert ever fired. Which improvement should the security program prioritize?

options.A: Deploying stronger encryption for stored data so future intrusions yield nothing readable
options.B: Centralized log collection with longer retention and automated alerting on suspicious activity
options.C: Commissioning an annual external penetration test to uncover exploitable weaknesses
options.D: Adopting a stricter rotation schedule for all privileged administrator account passwords

questionsV2.explanation: Five months of undetected activity is a visibility failure, and the stem lists its three ingredients: logs that expire in a week, security-relevant events never captured, and review too infrequent and manual to notice anything. The remedy attacks all three (B): collect logs centrally where intruders cannot quietly erase them, retain them well beyond realistic dwell times so investigations have evidence, and let automation watch continuously so detection happens in hours, not quarters. A is wrong because encryption protects confidentiality against stolen media and eavesdroppers; attackers operating through compromised applications and accounts read data exactly as legitimate users do, and encryption restores no visibility. C is a point-in-time probe for ways in; this organization's demonstrated failure is not knowing when someone is already inside. D is wrong because nothing ties the intrusion to stale passwords, and rotation would not have surfaced the five-month presence. Fix the control family the incident actually indicts. Long dwell times indict detection, so build logging and monitoring before buying more prevention.

questionsV2.question: Simply viewing a certain product review causes browsers to send their session cookies to an unknown domain; script tags stored in the review text are rendered verbatim to every visitor. Which remediation MOST directly addresses this?

options.A: Add anti-forgery tokens to every state-changing form so requests from other sites are rejected
options.B: Move all pages to HTTPS so session cookies are protected from network eavesdropping
options.C: Use parameterized queries so review text cannot alter the structure of database commands
options.D: Encode user-supplied content on output so browsers render it as text rather than script

questionsV2.explanation: This is stored cross-site scripting: attacker-supplied markup was saved and later delivered into victims' pages, where the browser executed it. The defect is at the rendering step, so the direct fix is contextual output encoding (D): the stored text is displayed as inert characters, never parsed as script; a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies add depth. A is wrong because anti-forgery tokens counter CSRF, where an attacker forges requests using the victim's session; here the attacker injected script, a different mechanism. B is wrong because TLS protects cookies in transit; these cookies are being read and exfiltrated by script running inside the page itself, over any transport. C is wrong because parameterized queries stop SQL injection; the review was stored through a legitimate write, and the database behaved correctly throughout.

questionsV2.question: A customer signed in to the portal opens an email link in another tab, and a transfer they never initiated is sent from their own browser with a valid session cookie. Which control BEST prevents this?

options.A: Require multi-factor authentication when the customer first signs in to the banking site
options.B: Embed unpredictable per-session tokens in forms and reject requests that lack a valid one
options.C: Encode all user-supplied content the application displays to keep scripts from executing
options.D: Lock accounts after repeated failed logins to defeat automated password guessing

questionsV2.explanation: What happened is cross-site request forgery: the attacker's page made the victim's browser submit a request, and the browser helpfully attached the session cookie, so the server saw an authenticated transfer. An anti-CSRF token (B) defeats it because the forging site cannot read the unpredictable token to include it, so the forged request fails validation; SameSite cookie attributes reinforce the same boundary. A protects the wrong moment: MFA strengthens the login event, and this attack rides a session that is already authenticated. MFA at sign-in is the right answer to stolen credentials, and step-up MFA per transfer would be a separate, additional control. C is wrong because output encoding counters XSS; no script was injected into the bank's pages here. D is wrong because there were no failed logins; the attacker never touched credentials.

questionsV2.question: The download endpoint serves /download?file=report.pdf, and requesting file=..%2F..%2F..%2Fetc%2Fpasswd returns the server's password file. Which fix is MOST effective?

options.A: Reject any filename containing the ../ character sequence before it reaches the file system call
options.B: Canonicalize each requested path and serve it only if it resolves inside the approved directory
options.C: Run the web server behind a reverse proxy that hides internal directory names from clients
options.D: Require users to authenticate before the download endpoint will serve them any file

questionsV2.explanation: This is a path traversal flaw, and the durable fix is to resolve the requested path to its canonical form and then check it against an allow-list boundary (B): whatever encoding or nesting the attacker uses, the final resolved path either falls inside the approved directory or is refused. A is wrong because it is a blacklist: the auditor's own request already used %2F encoding, and variants such as double encoding, ....//, or absolute paths slip past literal matching; filtering one bad pattern treats the symptom while the resolution logic stays broken. C is wrong because hiding directory names is obscurity; the operating system still resolves the traversal sequence regardless of what the client can see. D is wrong because authentication changes who can exploit the flaw, not whether it exists; any logged-in user could still walk out of the web root. Validate the destination the path resolves to, never the characters it contains.

questionsV2.question: The link-preview feature is given http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ and returns the cloud account's temporary credentials, fetched by the application server itself. Which vulnerability class is this?

options.A: Server-side request forgery, since the server was induced to request an internal resource
options.B: Cross-site request forgery, since a forged request was executed without a victim's intent
options.C: XML external entity injection, since a parser was made to retrieve a protected document
options.D: An open redirect, since the application forwarded a browser to an attacker-chosen address
